Definition 1.1.6: A class of subsets of Ω is a λ-system or a λ-class if (i) $\Omega \in { \mathcal { L } } , ( { \mathrm { i i } } ) \ A , B \in { \mathcal { L } } , A \subset B \Rightarrow B \setminus A \in { \mathcal { L } }$ , and (iii) $A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { L } } , A _ { n } \subset A _ { n + 1 }$ for all $\begin{array} { r } { n \geq 1 \Rightarrow \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } \in \mathcal { L } . } \end{array}$ 

Example 1.1.9: Every σ-algebra $\mathcal { F }$ is a λ-system. But an algebra need not be a λ-system. 

It is easily checked that if $\mathcal { L } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathcal { L } _ { 2 }$ are λ-systems, then $\mathcal { L } _ { 1 } \cap \mathcal { L } _ { 2 }$ is also a λ-system. Recall that $\sigma \langle B \rangle$ , the σ-algebra generated by $B ,$ is the intersection of all σ-algebras containing  and is also the smallest σ-algebra containing . Similarly, for any $B \subset { \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ , the λ-system generated by , denoted by $\lambda \langle B \rangle$ , is defined as the intersection of all λ-systems containing . It is the smallest λ-system containing . 

Theorem 1.1.2: (The π-λ theorem). If is a π-system, then $\lambda \langle { \mathcal C } \rangle = \sigma \langle { \mathcal C } \rangle$ 

Proof: For any ${ \mathcal { C } } , \sigma \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle$ is a λ-system and $\sigma \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ contains . Thus, $\lambda \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle \subset$ $\sigma \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ for any . Hence, it sufices to show that if  is a π-system, then $\lambda \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle$ is a σ-algebra . Since $\lambda \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle$ is a λ-system, it is closed under complementation and monotone increasing unions. By Proposition 1.1.1, it is enough to show that it is closed under intersection. Let $\lambda _ { 1 } ( { \mathcal { C } } ) \equiv \{ A : A \in \lambda \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle , A \cap B \in$ $\lambda \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle$ for all $B \in { \mathcal { C } } \}$ . Then, $\lambda _ { 1 } ( \mathcal { C } )$ is a λ-system and  being a π-system, $\lambda _ { 1 } ( { \mathcal { C } } ) \supset { \mathcal { C } }$ . Therefore, $\lambda _ { 1 } ( \mathcal { C } ) \supset \lambda \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ . But $\lambda _ { 1 } ( { \mathcal { C } } ) \subset \lambda \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle$ . So $\lambda _ { 1 } ( \mathcal { C } ) = \lambda \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ 

Next, let $\lambda _ { 2 } ( \mathcal { C } ) \equiv \{ A : A \in \lambda \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle , A \cap B \in \lambda \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ for all $B \in \lambda \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle \}$ . Then $\lambda _ { 2 } ( \mathcal { C } )$ is a λ-system and by the previous step $\mathcal { C } \subset \lambda _ { 2 } ( \mathcal { C } ) \subset \lambda \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ . Hence, it follows that $\lambda _ { 2 } ( \mathcal { C } ) = \lambda \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle , \mathrm { i . e . , } \lambda \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ is closed under intersection. This completes the proof of the theorem. ✷ 

Corollary 1.1.3: If  is a π-system and $\mathcal { L }$ is a λ-system containing $\mathcal { C }$ , then ${ \mathcal { L } } \supset \sigma \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle$ 

Remark 1.1.1: There are several equivalent definitions of λ-systems; see, for example, Billingsley (1995). A closely related concept is that of a monotone class; see, for example, Chung (1974). 

## 1.2 Measures

A set function is an extended real valued function defined on a class of subsets of a set Ω. Measures are nonnegative set functions that, intuitively speaking, measure the content of a subset of Ω. As explained in Section 2 of the introductory chapter, a measure has to satisfy certain natural requirements, such as the measure of the union of a countable collection of disjoint sets is the sum of the measures of the individual sets. Formally, one has the following definition. 

Definition 1.2.1: Let Ω be a nonempty set and $\mathcal { F }$ be an algebra on $\Omega .$ Then, a set function $\mu$ on $\mathcal { F }$ is called a measure if 

(a) $\mu ( A ) \in [ 0 , \infty ]$ for all $A \in { \mathcal { F } }$ ; 

(b) $\mu ( \varnothing ) = 0 ;$ 

(c) for any disjoint collection of sets $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \dotsc , \in { \mathcal { F } }$ with $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { F } }$ 

$$
\mu \left(\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(A _ {n}\right).
$$

As discussed in Section 2 of the introductory chapter, these conditions on µ are equivalent to finite additivity and monotone continuity from below. 

Proposition 1.2.1: Let Ω be a nonempty set and $\mathcal { F }$ be an algebra of subsets of Ω and $\mu$ be a set function on $\mathcal { F }$ with values in $[ 0 , \infty ]$ and with $\mu ( \varnothing ) = 0$ . Then, µ is a measure if µ satisfies 

(iii) : (finite additivity) for all $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } \in { \mathcal { F } }$ with $A _ { 1 } \cap A _ { 2 } = \emptyset , \mu ( A _ { 1 } \cup A _ { 2 } ) =$ $\mu ( A _ { 1 } ) + \mu ( A _ { 2 } )$ , and 

(iii) : (monotone continuity from below or, $m . c . f . b .$ , in short) for any collection $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ of sets in $\mathcal { F }$ such that $A _ { n } \subset A _ { n + 1 }$ for all $n \geq 1$ 

and $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { ; }$ 

$$
\mu \left(\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu (A _ {n}).
$$

Proof: Let $\mu$ be a measure on ${ \mathcal F } .$ . Since $\mu$ satisfies (iii), taking $A _ { 3 } , A _ { 4 } , \dotsc$ to be yields $( \mathrm { i i i } ) _ { a } ^ { \prime }$ . This implies that for A and B in ${ \mathcal { F } } , A \subset B \Rightarrow$ $\mu ( B ) = \mu ( A ) + \mu ( B \setminus A ) \geq \mu ( A ) , { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ ., µ is monotone. To establish $( \mathrm { i i i } ) _ { b } ^ { \prime } ,$ note that if $\mu ( A _ { n } ) = \infty$ for some $n = n _ { 0 }$ , then $\mu ( A _ { n } ) = \infty$ for all $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ and $\textstyle \mu ( \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n } ) = \infty$ and (iii) holds in this case. Hence, suppose that $\mu ( A _ { n } ) < \bar { \infty }$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Setting $B _ { n } = A _ { n } \backslash A _ { n - 1 }$ for $n \geq 1$ (with $A _ { 0 } = \varnothing )$ , by $( \operatorname { i i i } ) _ { a } ^ { \prime } , \mu ( B _ { n } ) = \mu ( A _ { n } ) - \mu ( A _ { n - 1 } )$ . Since $\{ B _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a disjoint collection of sets in $\mathcal { F }$ with $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } B _ { n } = \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n }$ , by (iii) 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu \Big (\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n} \Big) & = & \mu \Big (\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} B _ {n} \Big) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (B _ {n}) = \lim _ {N \to \infty} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {N} [ \mu (A _ {n}) - \mu (A _ {n - 1}) ] \\ & = & \lim _ {N \to \infty} \mu (A _ {N}), \end{array}
$$

and so $( \mathrm { i i i } ) _ { b } ^ { \prime }$ holds also in this case. 

Conversely, let $\mu$ satisfy $\mu ( \varnothing ) = 0$ and $( \mathrm { i i i } ) _ { a } ^ { \prime }$ and $( \mathrm { i i i } ) _ { b } ^ { \prime }$ . Let $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a disjoint collection of sets in $\mathcal { F }$ with $\textstyle \bigcup _ { i > 1 } A _ { i } \in { \mathcal { F } }$ . Let $\textstyle C _ { n } = \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } A _ { j }$ for $n \geq 1$ . Since $\mathcal { F }$ is an algebra, $C _ { n } \in \mathcal { F }$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Also, $C _ { n } \stackrel { \smile } { \subset } C _ { n + 1 }$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Hence, $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } C _ { n } = \bigcup _ { j \geq 1 } A _ { j }$ . By $( \mathrm { i i i } ) _ { b } ^ { \prime } ,$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu \Big (\bigcup_ {j \geq 1} A _ {j} \Big) & = & \mu \Big (\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} C _ {n} \Big) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu (C _ {n}) \\ & = & \lim _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \mu (A _ {j}) \quad (\text {by (iii)} _ {a} ^ {\prime}) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (A _ {j}). \end{array}
$$

Thus, (iii) holds. 

Remark 1.2.1: The definition of a measure given in Definition 1.2.1 is valid when $\mathcal { F }$ is a σ-algebra. However, very often one may start with a measure on an algebra and then extend it to a measure on the σ-algebra $\sigma \langle \mathcal { A } \rangle$ . This is why the definition of a measure on an algebra is given here. In the same vein, one may begin with a definition of a measure on a class of subsets of Ω that form only a semialgebra (cf. Definition 1.3.1). As described in the introductory chapter, such preliminary collections of sets are “nice” sets for which the measure may be defined easily, and the extension to a $\sigma -$ algebra containing these sets may be necessary if one is interested in more general sets. This topic is discussed in greater detail in the next section. 

Definition 1.2.2: A measure $\mu$ is called finite or infinite according as $\mu ( \Omega ) < \infty \mathrm { o r } \mu ( \Omega ) = \infty$ . A finite measure with $\mu ( \Omega ) = 1$ is called a probability measure. A measure $\mu$ on a σ-algebra $\mathcal { F }$ is called $\sigma { - } f i n i t e$ if there exist a countable collection of sets $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \dotsc , \in { \mathcal { F } }$ , not necessarily disjoint, such that 

$$
\text {(a)} \bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n} = \Omega \quad \text {and} \quad (\mathrm{b}) \mu (A _ {n}) <   \infty \quad \text {for all} \quad n \geq 1.
$$

Here are some examples of measures. 

Example 1.2.1: (The counting measure). Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty set and $\mathcal { F } _ { 3 } = \mathcal { P } ( \Omega )$ be the set of all subsets of $\Omega$ (cf. Example 1.1.2). Define 

$$
\mu (A) = | A |, \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {3},
$$

where $| A |$ denotes the number of elements in A. It is easy to check that $\mu$ satisfies the requirements $\mathrm { ( a ) - ( c ) }$ of a measure. This measure $\mu$ is called the counting measure on Ω. Note that $\mu$ is finite if Ω is finite and it is σ-finite if Ω is countably infinite. 

Example 1.2.2: (Discrete probability measures). Let $\omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } , \ldots , \in \Omega$ and $p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } , . . . \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ be such that $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } p _ { i } = 1$ . Define for any $A \subset \Omega$ 

$$
P (A) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} p _ {i} I _ {A} (\omega_ {i}),
$$

where $I _ { A } ( \cdot )$ denotes the indicator function of a set $A .$ defined by $I _ { A } ( \omega ) = 0$ or 1 according as $\omega \not \in A$ or $\omega \in A$ . For any disjoint collection of sets $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \dotsc \in { \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P \bigg (\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {i} \bigg) & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} p _ {j} I _ {\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {i}} (\omega_ {j}) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} p _ {j} \bigg (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} I _ {A _ {i}} (\omega_ {j}) \bigg) \\ & = & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \bigg (\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} p _ {j} I _ {A _ {i}} (\omega_ {j}) \bigg) \\ & = & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} P (A _ {i}), \end{array}
$$

where interchanging the order of summation is permissible since the summands are nonnegative. This shows that P is a probability measure on ${ \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ 

Example 1.2.3: (Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures on R). As mentioned in the previous chapter (cf. Section 2), a large class of measures on the Borel σ-algebra (R) of subsets of R, known as the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures, arise from nondecreasing right continuous functions $F : \mathbb { R }  \mathbb { R }$ . For each such $F ,$ , the corresponding measure $\mu _ { F }$ satisfies $\mu _ { F } ( ( a , b ] ) = F ( b ) - F ( a )$ for all $- \infty < a < b < \infty$ . The construction of these $\mu _ { F } \mathrm { { ' s } }$ via the extension theorem will be discussed in the next section. Also, note that if $A _ { n } \ =$ $( - n , n ) , n = 1 , 2 , \ldots$ , then $\textstyle \mathbb { R } = \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n }$ and $\mu _ { F } ( A _ { n } ) < \infty$ for each $n \geq 1$ (such measures are called Radon measures) and thus, $\mu _ { F }$ is necessarily σ-finite. 

Proposition 1.2.2: Let µ be a measure on an algebra ${ \mathcal F } ,$ and let $A , B , A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { k } \in { \mathcal { F } } , 1 \leq k < \infty$ . Then, 

(i) (Monotonicity) $\mu ( A ) \leq \mu ( B ) \ i f A \subset B ;$ 

(ii) (Finite subadditivity) $\mu ( A _ { 1 } \cup . . . \cup A _ { k } ) \leq \mu ( A _ { 1 } ) + . . . + \mu ( A _ { k } )$ ; 

(iii) (Inclusion-exclusion formula) $I f \mu ( A _ { i } ) < \infty$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \mu (A _ {1} \cup \ldots \cup A _ {k}) & = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \mu (A _ {i}) - \sum_ {1 \leq i <   j <   k} \mu (A _ {i} \cap A _ {j}) \\ & + \ldots + (- 1) ^ {k - 1} \mu (A _ {1} \cap \ldots \cap A _ {k}). \end{array}
$$

Proof: $\mu ( B ) = \mu ( A \cup ( A ^ { c } \cap B ) ) = \mu ( A ) + \mu ( B \setminus A ) \geq \mu ( A )$ , by (a) and (c) of Definition 1.2.1. This proves (i). 

To prove (ii), note that if either $\mu ( A )$ or $\mu ( B )$ is finite, then $\mu ( A \cap B ) < \infty$ by (i). Hence, using the countable additivity property (c), we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu (A \cup B) & = & \mu (A) + \mu (B \setminus A) \\ & = & \mu (A) + [ \mu (B \setminus A) + \mu (A \cap B) ] - \mu (A \cap B) \\ & = & \mu (A) + \mu (B) - \mu (A \cap B). \end{array}\tag{2.1}
$$

Hence, (ii) follows from (2.1) and by induction. 

To prove (iii), note that the case $k = 2$ follows from (2.1). Next, suppose that (iii) holds for all sets $A _ { 1 } , \dotsc , A _ { k } \in { \mathcal { F } }$ with $\mu ( A _ { i } ) < \infty$ for all $i =$ $1 , \ldots , k$ for some $k = n , n \in \mathbb { N }$ . To show that it holds for $k = n + 1$ , note that by (2.1), 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & \mu \bigg (\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n + 1} A _ {i} \bigg) \\ = & \mu \bigg (\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n} A _ {i} \bigg) + \mu (A _ {n + 1}) - \mu \bigg (\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (A _ {i} \cap A _ {n + 1}) \bigg) \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l l} = & \bigg \{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mu (A _ {i}) - \sum_ {1 <   i <   j \leq n} \mu (A _ {i} \cap A _ {j}) + \dots + (- 1) ^ {n - 1} \mu (A _ {1} \cap \ldots \cap A _ {n}) \bigg \} \\ & + \mu (A _ {n + 1}) - \Bigg [ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mu (A _ {i} \cap A _ {n + 1}) - \sum_ {1 \leq i <   j \leq n} \mu (A _ {i} \cap A _ {j} \cap A _ {n + 1}) \\ & \qquad + \dots + (- 1) ^ {n - 1} \mu (A _ {1} \cap \ldots \cap A _ {n + 1}) \Bigg ] \\ = & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n + 1} \mu (A _ {i}) - \sum_ {1 \leq i <   j \leq n + 1} \mu (A _ {i} \cap A _ {j}) + \dots + (- 1) ^ {n} \mu \bigg (\bigcap_ {j = 1} ^ {n + 1} A _ {j} \bigg). \end{array}
$$

By induction, this completes the proof of Proposition 1.2.2. 

In Proposition 1.2.1, it was shown that a set function $\mu$ on an algebra $\mathcal { F }$ is a measure if it is finitely additive and monotone continuous from below. A natural question is: if $\mu$ is a measure on $\mathcal { F }$ and $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a collection of decreasing sets in $\mathcal { F }$ with $A \equiv \bigcap _ { n > 1 } A _ { n }$ also in $\mathcal { F }$ , does the relation $\mu ( A ) = \mathrm { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \mu ( A _ { n } )$ hold, i.e., does monotone continuity from above hold? The answer is positive under the assumption $\mu ( A _ { n _ { 0 } } ) < \infty$ for some $n _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { N }$ . It turns out that, in general, this assumption cannot be dropped (Problem 1.18). 

Proposition 1.2.3: Let µ be a measure on an algebra $\mathcal { F }$ 

(i) (Monotone continuity from above) Let $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of sets in $\mathcal { F }$ such that $A _ { n + 1 } \subset A _ { n }$ for all $n \geq 1$ and $\begin{array} { r } { A \equiv \bigcap _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { F } } } \end{array}$ . Also, let $\mu ( A _ { n _ { 0 } } ) < \infty$ for some $n _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { N }$ . Then, 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu (A _ {n}) = \mu (A).
$$

(ii) (Countable subadditivity) $I f \left\{ A _ { n } \right\} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sequence of sets in $\mathcal { F }$ such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { F } }$ , then 

$$
\mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (A _ {n}).
$$

Proof: To prove part (i), without loss of generality $\left( \mathrm { w . l . o . g . } \right)$ , assume that $n _ { 0 } = 1 , \mathrm { i . e . , } \mu ( A _ { 1 } ) < \infty$ . Let $C _ { n } = A _ { 1 } \setminus A _ { n }$ for $n \geq 1$ , and $C _ { \infty } = A _ { 1 } \backslash A$ Then $C _ { n }$ and $C _ { \infty }$ belong to $\mathcal { F }$ and $C _ { n } \uparrow C _ { \infty }$ . By Proposition $1 . 2 . 1 \ ( \mathrm { i i i } ) _ { b } ^ { \prime }$ $( \mathrm { i . e . }$ , by the m.c.f.b. property), $\mu ( C _ { n } ) \uparrow \mu ( C _ { \infty } )$ and by $( \mathrm { i i i } ) _ { a } ^ { \prime }$ , (i.e., finite additivity), $\mu ( C _ { n } ) = \mu ( A _ { 1 } ) - \mu ( A _ { n } )$ for all $1 \leq n < \infty$ , due to the fact $\mu ( A _ { 1 } ) < \infty$ . This proves (i). 

To prove part (ii), let $\textstyle D _ { n } = \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } A _ { i } , n \geq 1$ . Then, $D _ { n } \uparrow D \equiv \bigcup _ { i \geq 1 } A _ { i }$ Hence, by m.c.f.b. and finite subadditivity, 

$$
\mu (D) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu (D _ {n}) \leq \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mu (A _ {i}) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (A _ {n}).
$$

Theorem 1.2.4: (Uniqueness of measures). Let $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ be two finite measures on a measurable space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ . Let $\mathcal { C } \subset \mathcal { F }$ be a π-system such that ${ \mathcal F } = \sigma \langle { \mathcal C } \rangle$ . If $\mu _ { 1 } ( C ) = \mu _ { 2 } ( C )$ for all $C \in { \mathcal { C } }$ and $\mu _ { 1 } ( \Omega ) = \mu _ { 2 } ( \Omega )$ , then $\mu _ { 1 } ( A ) = \mu _ { 2 } ( A )$ for all $A \in { \mathcal { F } }$ 

Proof: Let ${ \mathcal { L } } \equiv \{ A : A \in { \mathcal { F } } , \mu _ { 1 } ( A ) = \mu _ { 2 } ( A ) \}$ . It is easy to verify that $\mathcal { L }$ is a λ-system. Since $\mathcal { C } \subset \mathcal { L }$ , by Theorem 1.1.2, $\mathcal { L } = \sigma \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle = \mathcal { F }$ ✷ 

## 1.3 The extension theorems and Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures

As discussed earlier, in many situations, one starts with a given set function $\mu$ defined on a small class of subsets of a set Ω and then wants to extend $\mu$ to a larger class  by some approximation procedure. In this section, a general result in this direction, known as the extension theorem, is established. This is then applied to the construction of Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures on Euclidean spaces. For another application, see Chapter 6. 

## 1.3.1 Caratheodory extension of measures

Definition 1.3.1: Let Ω be a nonempty set and let ${ \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ be the power set of Ω. A class ${ \mathcal { C } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ is called a semialgebra if (i) A, $B \in \mathcal { C } \Rightarrow A \cap B \in \mathcal { C }$ and (ii) for any $A \in { \mathcal { C } }$ , there exist sets $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } , \ldots , B _ { k } \in { \mathcal { C } }$ , for some $1 \leq$ $k < \infty$ , such that $B _ { i } \cap B _ { j } = \varnothing$ for $i \neq j$ , and $\textstyle A ^ { c } = \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } B _ { i }$ 

Example 1.3.1: $\Omega = \mathbb { R } , \ { \mathcal { C } } \equiv \{ ( a , b ] , ( b , \infty ) : - \infty  \leq a , b < \infty \}$ 

Example 1.3.2: $\Omega = \mathbb { R } , \ : \mathcal { C } \equiv \{ I : I$ is an interval . An interval I in R is a set in R such that $a , b \in I , a < b \Rightarrow ( a , b ) \subset I .$ 

Example 1.3.3: $\Omega = \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , \mathcal { C } \equiv \{ I _ { 1 } \times I _ { 2 } \times \mathbf { \Omega } \times I _ { k } : I _ { j }$ is an interval in $\mathbb { R }$ for $1 \leq j \leq k \}$ 

Recall that a collection $\mathcal { A } \subset \mathcal { P } ( \Omega )$ is an algebra if it is closed under finite union and complementation. It is easily verified (Problem 1.19) that the smallest algebra containing a semialgebra $\mathcal { C }$ is ${ \mathcal { A } } ( { \mathcal { C } } ) \equiv \{ A : A =$ $\textstyle \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } B _ { i } , B _ { i } \in { \mathcal { C } }$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , k , k < \infty , \}$ , i.e., the class of finite unions of sets from . 

Definition 1.3.2: A set function µ on a semialgebra , taking values in $\bar { \mathbb { R } } _ { + } \equiv [ 0 , \infty ]$ , is called a measure if $( \mathrm { i } ) \ \mu ( \emptyset ) = 0$ and (ii) for any sequence of sets $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset { \mathcal { C } }$ with $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { C } }$ , and $A _ { i } \cap A _ { j } = \varnothing$ for $i \neq j$ 2 $\begin{array} { r } { \mu ( \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } ) = \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu ( A _ { n } ) } \end{array}$ 

Proposition 1.3.1: Let µ be a measure on a semialgebra . Let $\mathcal { A } \equiv \mathcal { A } ( \mathcal { C } )$ be the smallest algebra generated by . For each $A \in { \mathcal { A } }$ , set 

$$
\bar {\mu} (A) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \mu (B _ {i}),
$$

if the set A has the representation $\textstyle A = \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } B _ { i }$ for some $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { k } \in$ $\mathcal { C } , k < \infty$ with $B _ { i } \cap B _ { j } = \varnothing$ for $i \neq j$ . Then, 

(i) µ¯ is independent of the representation of A as $\textstyle A = \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } B _ { i }$ ; 

(ii) µ¯ is finitely additive on , i.e., A, $B \in \mathcal A , A \cap B = \emptyset \Rightarrow \bar { \mu } ( A \cup B ) =$ $\bar { \mu } ( A ) + \bar { \mu } ( B )$ ; and 

(iii) µ¯ is countably additive on $\mathcal { A } , i . e . , i f A _ { n } \in \mathcal { A }$ for all $n \geq 1 , A _ { i } \cap A _ { j } = \emptyset$ for all $i = j$ , and $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { A } }$ , then 

$$
\bar {\mu} \left(\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \bar {\mu} (A _ {n}).
$$

Proof: Parts (i) and (ii) are easy to verify. Turning to part (iii), let each $\begin{array} { r } { n \geq 1 , A _ { n } = \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { k _ { n } } B _ { n j } , B _ { n j } \in \mathcal C , \{ B _ { n j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { k _ { n } } } \end{array}$ disjoint. Since $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { A } }$ then exist disjoint sets $\{ B _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \subset { \mathcal { C } }$ such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } = \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } B _ { i }$ . Now 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} B _ {i} & = & B _ {i} \cap \Big (\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n} \Big) = \bigcup_ {n \geq 1} (B _ {i} \cap A _ {n}) \\ & = & \bigcup_ {n \geq 1} \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {k _ {n}} (B _ {i} \cap B _ {n j}). \end{array}
$$

Since for all i, $B _ { i } \in \mathcal { C } , B _ { i } \cap B _ { n j } \in \mathcal { C }$ for all $j , n$ and $\mu$ is a measure on 

$$
\mu (B _ {i}) = \sum_ {n \geq 1} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k _ {n}} \mu (B _ {i} \cap B _ {n j}).
$$

Thus, 

$$
\bar {\mu} \left(\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \mu \left(B _ {i}\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \sum_ {n \geq 1} \left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k _ {n}} \mu \left(B _ {i} \cap B _ {n j}\right)\right)
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l l} = & \sum_ {n \geq 1} \bigg (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k _ {n}} \mu (B _ {i} \cap B _ {n j}) \bigg) \\ = & \sum_ {n \geq 1} \bar {\mu} (A _ {n}), \end{array}
$$

since 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} A _ {n} & = & A _ {n} \cap \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {k} B _ {i} \\ & = & \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {k _ {n}} (B _ {i} \cap B _ {n j}). \end{array}
$$

Thus, the set function $\bar { \mu }$ defined above is a measure on ${ \mathcal { A } } .$ . To go beyond $\mathcal { A } = \mathcal { A } ( \mathcal { C } )$ to $\sigma \langle \mathcal { A } \rangle$ , which is also the same as $\sigma \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ (see Problem 1.19 (ii)), the first step involves using the given set function $\mu$ on $\mathcal { C }$ to define a set function $\mu ^ { * }$ on the class of all subsets of $\Omega _ { : }$ , i.e., on ${ \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ , where for any $A \in { \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega ) , \mu ^ { * } ( A )$ is an estimate ‘from above’ of the µ-content of A. 

Definition 1.3.3: Given a measure $\mu$ on a semialgebra $\mathcal { C } _ { : }$ , the outer measure induced by $\mu$ is the set function $\mu ^ { * }$ , defined on ${ \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ , as 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A) \equiv \inf \left\{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (A _ {n}): \{A _ {n} \} _ {n \geq 1} \subset \mathcal {C}, A \subset \bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n} \right\}.\tag{3.1}
$$

Thus, a given set $A$ is covered by countable unions of sets from $\mathcal { C }$ and the sums of the measures on such covers are computed and $\mu ^ { * } ( A )$ is the greatest lower bound one can get in this way. It is not dificult to show that on $\mathcal { C }$ and $\mathcal { A } .$ , this is not an overestimate. That is, $\mu ^ { * } = \mu$ on $\mathcal { C }$ and on $\mathcal { A } , \mu ^ { \ast } = \bar { \mu }$ . Now suppose $\mu ( \Omega ) < \infty$ . Let $A \subset \Omega$ be a set such that the overestimates of the µ-contents of A and $A ^ { c }$ , namely, $\mu ^ { * } ( A )$ and $\mu ^ { * } ( A ^ { c } )$ add up to $\mu ( \Omega )$ , i.e., 

$$
\mu (\Omega) = \mu^ {*} (\Omega) = \mu^ {*} (A) + \mu^ {*} (A ^ {c}).\tag{3.2}
$$

Then, there is no room for error and the estimates $\mu ^ { * } ( A )$ and $\mu ^ { * } ( A ^ { c } )$ are in fact not overestimates at all. In this case, the set A may be considered ‘exactly measurable’ by this approximation procedure. This observation motivates the following definition. 

Definition 1.3.4: A set A is said to be $\mu ^ { * } { - } m e a s u r a b l e$ if 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \mu^ {*} (E \cap A) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A ^ {c}) \text {   for   all   } E \subset \Omega .\tag{3.3}
$$

In other words, an analog of (3.2) should hold in every portion $E$ of $\Omega$ for a set $A$ to be $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable. 

It can be shown (Problem 1.20) that $\mu ^ { * }$ defined in (3.1) satisfies: 

$$
\mu^ {*} (\emptyset) = 0,\tag{3.4}
$$

$$
A \subset B \Rightarrow \mu^ {*} (A) \leq \mu^ {*} (B),\tag{3.5}
$$

and for any $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset \mathcal { P } ( \Omega )$ 2 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} A _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (A _ {n}).\tag{3.6}
$$

Definition 1.3.5: Any set function $\mu ^ { * } : \mathcal { P } ( \Omega )  \bar { \mathbb { R } } _ { + } \equiv [ 0 , \infty ]$ satisfying (3.4)–(3.6) is called an outer measure on Ω. 

The following result (due to C. Caratheodory) yields a measure space on Ω starting from a general outer measure $\mu ^ { * }$ that need not arise from a measure $\mu$ as in (3.1). 

Theorem 1.3.2: Let $\mu ^ { * }$ be an outer measure on Ω, i.e., it satisfies $( 3 . 4 ) \mathrm { - }$ $( 3 . 6 )$ . Let ${ \mathcal { M } } \equiv { \mathcal { M } } _ { \mu ^ { * } } \equiv \{ A : A \ $ is µ∗-measurable, i.e., A satisfies (3.3) . Then 

(i)  is a σ-algebra, 

(ii) $\mu ^ { * }$ restricted to  is a measure, and 

(iii) $\mu ^ { * } ( A ) = 0 \Rightarrow { \mathcal { P } } ( A ) \subset { \mathcal { M } } .$ 

Proof: From (3.3), it follows that $\emptyset \in { \mathcal { M } }$ and that $A \in { \mathcal { M } } \Rightarrow A ^ { c } \in { \mathcal { M } }$ Next, it will be shown that is closed under finite unions. Let $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } \in { \mathcal { M } }$ Then, for any $E \subset \Omega$ 5 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu^ {*} (E) & = & \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1} ^ {c}) \quad (\text {since} A _ {1} \in \mathcal {M}) \\ & = & \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1} \cap A _ {2}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1} \cap A _ {2} ^ {c}) \\ & & + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1} ^ {c} \cap A _ {2}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1} ^ {c} \cap A _ {2} ^ {c}) \quad (\text {since} A _ {2} \in \mathcal {M}). \end{array}
$$

But $\left( A _ { 1 } \cap A _ { 2 } \right) \cup \left( A _ { 1 } \cap A _ { 2 } ^ { c } \right) \cup \left( A _ { 1 } ^ { c } \cap A _ { 2 } \right) = A _ { 1 } \cup A _ { 2 }$ . Since $\mu ^ { * }$ is subadditive, it follows that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E \cap (A _ {1} \cup A _ {2})) \leq \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1} \cap A _ {2}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1} \cap A _ {2} ^ {c}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {1} ^ {c} \cap A _ {2}).
$$

Thus 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) \geq \mu^ {*} (E \cap (A _ {1} \cup A _ {2})) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap (A _ {1} \cup A _ {2}) ^ {c}).
$$

The subadditivity of $\mu ^ { * }$ yields the opposite inequality and so, $A _ { 1 } \cup A _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { M }$ and hence, is an algebra. To show that is a σ-algebra, it sufices to show that  is closed under monotone unions, i.e., $A _ { n } \in \mathcal { M } , A _ { n } \subset A _ { n + 1 }$ for all $\begin{array} { r } { n \geq 1 \Rightarrow A \equiv \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } \in \mathcal { M } } \end{array}$ . Let $B _ { 1 } = A _ { 1 }$ and $B _ { n } = A _ { n } \cap A _ { n - 1 } ^ { c }$ for all $n \geq 2$ . Then, for all $n \geq 1 , \ B _ { n } \ \in \ { \mathcal { M } }$ (since  is an algebra), $\textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } B _ { j } = A _ { n }$ , and $\textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } B _ { j } = A$ . Hence, for any $E \subset \Omega$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu^ {*} (E) & = & \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {n}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {n} ^ {c}) \\ & = & \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {n} \cap B _ {n}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {n} \cap B _ {n} ^ {c}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {n} ^ {c}) \\ & & (\text { since } B _ {n} \in \mathcal {M}) \\ & = & \mu^ {*} (E \cap B _ {n}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {n - 1}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {n} ^ {c}) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \mu^ {*} (E \cap B _ {j}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {n} ^ {c}) \quad (\text { by   iteration }) \\ & \geq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \mu^ {*} (E \cap B _ {j}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A ^ {c}) \quad (\text { by   monotonicity }). \end{array}
$$

Now letting $n  \infty$ , and using the subadditivity of $\mu ^ { * }$ and the fact that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } B _ { j } = A$ , one gets 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu^ {*} (E) & \geq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (E \cap B _ {j}) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A ^ {c}) \\ & \geq & \mu^ {*} (E \cap A) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A ^ {c}). \end{array}
$$

This completes the proof of part (i). 

To prove part (ii), let $\{ B _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset { \mathcal { M } }$ and $B _ { i } \cap B _ { j } = \varnothing$ for $i \neq j$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { A _ { j } = \bigcup _ { i = j } ^ { \infty } B _ { i } , j \in \mathbb { N } } \end{array}$ . Then, by ${ \bf ( i ) } , A _ { j } \in \mathcal { M }$ for all $j \in \mathbb N$ and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} \mu^ {*} (A _ {1}) & = & \mu^ {*} (A _ {1} \cap B _ {1}) + \mu^ {*} (A _ {1} \cap B _ {1} ^ {c}) \quad (\text { since } B _ {1} \in \mathcal {M}) \\ & = & \mu^ {*} (B _ {1}) + \mu^ {*} (A _ {2}) \\ & = & \mu^ {*} (B _ {1}) + \mu^ {*} (B _ {2}) + \mu^ {*} (A _ {3}) \quad (\text { by   iteration }) \\ & = & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mu^ {*} (B _ {i}) + \mu^ {*} (A _ {n + 1}) \quad (\text { by   iteration }) \\ & \geq & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mu^ {*} (B _ {i}) \quad \text { for   all } \quad n \geq 1. \end{array}
$$

Now letting $n  \infty ,$ , one has $\textstyle \mu ^ { * } ( A _ { 1 } ) \geq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu ^ { * } ( B _ { i } )$ . By subadditivity of $\mu ^ { * }$ , the opposite inequality holds and so 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A _ {1}) = \mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} B _ {i}\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (B _ {i}),
$$

proving (ii). 

As for (iii), note that by monotonicity, $\mu ^ { * } ( A ) = 0 , B \subset A \Rightarrow \mu ^ { * } ( B ) = 0$ and hence, for any E, $\mu ^ { * } ( E \cap B ) = 0$ . Since $\mu ^ { * } ( E ) \geq \mu ^ { * } ( E \cap B ^ { c } )$ , this implies $\mu ^ { * } ( E ) \geq \mu ^ { * } ( E \cap B ^ { c } ) + \mu ^ { * } ( E \cap B )$ . The opposite inequality holds by the subadditivity of $\mu ^ { * }$ . So $B \in { \mathcal { M } }$ , and (iii) is proved. ✷ 

Definition 1.3.6: A measure space $( \Omega , \mathscr { F } , \nu )$ is called complete if for any $A \in { \mathcal { F } }$ with $\nu ( A ) = 0 \Rightarrow { \mathcal { P } } ( A ) \subset { \mathcal { F } }$ 

Thus, by part (iii) of the above theorem, $( \Omega , \mathcal { M } _ { \mu ^ { * } } , \mu ^ { * } )$ is a complete measure space. Now the above theorem is applied to a $\mu ^ { * }$ that is generated by a given measure µ on a semialgebra via (3.1). 

Theorem 1.3.3: (Caratheodory’s extension theorem). Let µ be a measure on a semialgebra $\mathcal { C }$ and let $\mu ^ { * }$ be the set function induced by $\mu$ as defined by (3.1). Then, 

(i) $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure, 

(ii) $\mathcal { C } \subset \mathcal { M } _ { \mu ^ { * } }$ , and 

(iii) $\mu ^ { * } = \mu$ on ${ \mathcal { C } } ,$ where $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu } \mathrm { : }$ is as in Theorem 1.3.2. 

Proof: The proof of (i) involves verifying $( 3 . 4 ) \ – ( 3 . 6 )$ , which is left as an exercise (Problem 1.20). To prove (ii), let $A \in { \mathcal { C } } .$ . Let $E \subset \Omega$ and $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset \mathcal C$ be such that $E \subset \textstyle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n }$ . Then, for all $i \in \mathbb { N } , A _ { i } =$ $( A _ { i } \cap { \bar { A } } ) \cup ( A _ { i } \cap B _ { 1 } ) \cup . . . \cup ( A _ { i } \cap B _ { k } )$ where $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { k }$ are disjoint sets in such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } B _ { j } = A ^ { c }$ . Since $\mu$ is finitely additive on ${ \mathcal { C } } _ { : }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu (A _ {i}) & = & \mu (A _ {i} \cap A) + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} \mu (A _ {i} \cap B _ {j}) \\ \Rightarrow & \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (A _ {n}) & = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (A _ {n} \cap A) + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} \mu (A _ {n} \cap B _ {j}) \\ & \geq & \mu^ {*} (E \cap A) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A ^ {c}), \end{array}
$$

since $\{ A _ { n } \cap A \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $\{ A _ { n } \cap B _ { j } : 1 \leq j \leq k , n \geq 1 \}$ are both countable subcollections of $\mathcal { C }$ whose unions cover $E \cap A$ and $E \cap A ^ { c }$ , respectively. From the definition of $\mu ^ { * } ( E )$ , it now follows that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) \geq \mu^ {*} (E \cap A) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap A ^ {c}).
$$

Now the subadditivity of $\mu ^ { * }$ completes the proof of part (ii). 

To prove (iii), let $A \in { \mathcal { C } }$ . Then, by definition, $\mu ^ { * } ( A ) \leq \mu ( A )$ . If $\mu ^ { * } ( A ) =$ $\infty$ , then $\mu ( A ) = \infty = \mu ^ { * } ( A )$ . If $\mu ^ { * } ( A ) < \infty$ , then by the definition of ‘infimum,’ for any $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset { \mathcal { C } }$ such that $A \subset \textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n }$ and 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (A _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (A) + \epsilon .
$$

But $\begin{array} { r } { A = A \cap ( \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n } ) = \bigcup _ { n > 1 } ( A \cap A _ { n } ) } \end{array}$ . Note that the set function $\bar { \mu }$  defined in Proposition 1.3.1 is a measure on $\scriptstyle { \mathcal { A } } ( { \mathcal { C } } )$ and it coincides with $\mu$ on . Since $A , A \cap A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { C } }$ for all $n \geq 1$ , by Proposition 1.2.3 (b) applied to $\bar { \mu } ,$ 

$$
\mu (A) = \bar {\mu} (A) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \bar {\mu} (A \cap A _ {n}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \bar {\mu} (A _ {n}) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (A _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (A) + \epsilon .
$$

Alternately, w.l.o.g., assume that $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ are disjoint. Then $A = A \cap$ $\begin{array} { r } { \dot { \bigcup } _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } = \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } ( A \cap A _ { n } ) } \end{array}$ . Since $A \cap A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { C } }$ for all $n _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , by the countable additivity of $\mu$ on $\begin{array} { r } { \mathscr { C } , \mu ( A ) = \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu ( A \cap A _ { n } ) \leq \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu ( A _ { n } ) = \mu ^ { * } ( A ) + \epsilon . \bigr ) } \end{array}$ Since $\epsilon > 0$  is arbitrary, this yields $\mu ( A ) \leq \mu ^ { * } ( A )$ -✷ 

Thus, given a measure $\mu$ on a semialgebra ${ \mathcal { C } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ , there is a complete measure space $( \Omega , \mathcal { M } _ { \mu ^ { * } } , \mu ^ { * } )$ such that $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu ^ { \ast } } \supset \mathcal { C }$ and $\mu ^ { * }$ restricted to $\mathcal { C }$ equals $\mu$ . For this reason, $\mu ^ { * }$ is called an extension of $\mu .$ . The measure space $( \Omega , \mathcal { M } _ { \mu ^ { * } } , \mu ^ { * } )$ is called the Caratheodory extension of $\mu .$ Since $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu } ^ { \mathrm { ~ ~ } } ;$ is a $\sigma -$ algebra and contains ${ \mathcal { C } } , { \mathcal { M } } _ { \mu ^ { * } }$ must contain $\sigma \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ , the σ-algebra generated by $\mathcal { C } _ { : }$ , and thus, $( \Omega , \sigma \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle , \mu ^ { * } )$ is also a measure space. However, the latter may not be complete (see Section 1.4). 

Now the above method is applied to the construction of Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures on R and $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ 

## 1.3.2 Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures on R

Let $F : \mathbb { R }  \mathbb { R }$ be nondecreasing. For $x \in \mathbb { R }$ , let $F ( x + ) \equiv \operatorname* { l i m } _ { y \downarrow x } F ( y )$ and $F ( x - ) \ \equiv \ \operatorname* { l i m } _ { y \uparrow x } F ( y )$ . Set $F ( \infty ) \ = \ \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \uparrow \infty } F ( x )$ and $F ( - \infty ) \ =$ $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \downarrow - \infty } F ( y )$ . Let 

$$
\mathcal {C} \equiv \left\{(a, b ]: - \infty \leq a \leq b <   \infty \right\} \cup \left\{(a, \infty): - \infty \leq a <   \infty \right\}.\tag{3.7}
$$

Define 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu_ {F} ((a, b ]) & = & F (b +) - F (a +), \\ \mu_ {F} ((a, \infty)) & = & F (\infty) - F (a +). \end{array}\tag{3.8}
$$

Then, it may be verified that 

<sup>(i)</sup> C <sup>is</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>semialgebra;</sup> 

(ii) $\mu _ { F }$ is a measure on . (For (ii), one needs to use the Heine-Borel theorem. See Problems 1.22 and 1.23.) 

Let $( \mathbb { R } , \mathcal { M } _ { \mu _ { F } ^ { * } } , \mu _ { F } ^ { * } )$ be the Caratheodory extension of $\mu _ { F }$ , i.e., the measure space constructed as in the above two theorems. 

Definition 1.3.7: Let $F : \mathbb { R }  \mathbb { R }$ be nondecreasing. The (measure) space $( \mathbb { R } , \mathcal { M } _ { \mu _ { F } ^ { * } } , \mu _ { F } ^ { * } )$ is called a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure space and $\mu _ { F } ^ { * }$ is the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure generated by F. 

Since $\sigma \langle { \mathcal C } \rangle = B ( { \mathbb R } )$ , the class of all Borel sets of R, every Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure $\mu _ { F } ^ { * }$ is also a measure on (R, (R)). Note also that $\mu _ { F } ^ { * }$ is finite on bounded intervals. 

Conversely, given any Radon measure $\mu$ on (R, (R)), i.e., a measure on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ ) that is finite on bounded intervals, set 

$$
F (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \mu ((0, x ]) & \text { if } x > 0 \\ 0 & \text { if } x = 0 \\ - \mu ((x, 0 ]) & \text { if } x \leq 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $\mu _ { F } = \mu$ on $\mathcal { C } .$ By the uniqueness of the extension (discussed later in this section, see also Theorem 1.2.4), it follows that $\mu _ { F } ^ { * }$ coincides with $\mu$ on $B ( \mathbb { R } )$ . Thus, every Radon measure on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ is necessarily a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure. 

Definition 1.3.8: (Lebesgue Measure on R). When $F ( x ) \equiv x , x \in \mathbb { R }$ the measure $\mu _ { F } ^ { * }$ is called the Lebesgue measure and the σ-algebra $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu _ { F } ^ { * } }$ is called the class of Lebesgue measurable sets. 

The Lebesgue measure will be denoted by $m ( \cdot )$ or $\mu _ { L } ( \cdot )$ . Given below are some important results on $m ( \cdot )$ 

(i) It follows from equation (3.1), that $\mu _ { F } ^ { * } ( \{ x \} ) = F ( x + ) - F ( x - )$ and hence = 0 if F is continuous at x. Thus $m ( \{ x \} ) \equiv 0$ on R. 

(ii) By countable additivity of $m ( \cdot ) , m ( A ) = 0$ for any countable set A. 

(iii) (Cantor set). There exists an uncountable set C such that $m ( C ) = 0$ An example is the Cantor set constructed as follows: Start with $I _ { 0 } =$ [0, 1]. Delete the open middle third, i.e., $\left( { \frac { 1 } { 3 } } , { \frac { 2 } { 3 } } \right)$ . Next from the closed intervals $I _ { 1 1 } = [ 0 , { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 3 } } ]$ and $I _ { 1 2 } = [ \frac { 2 } { 3 } , 1 ]$ delete the open middle thirds, i.e., $\left( { \frac { 1 } { 9 } } , { \frac { 2 } { 9 } } \right)$ and $\left( { \frac { 7 } { 9 } } , { \frac { 2 } { 9 } } \right)$ , respectively. Repeat this process of deleting the middle third from each of the remaining closed intervals. Thus at stage n there will be $2 ^ { n - 1 }$ new closed intervals and $2 ^ { n - 1 }$ deleted open intervals, each of length $\frac { 1 } { 3 ^ { n } }$ . Let $U _ { n }$ denote the union of all the deleted open intervals at the nth stage. Then $\{ U _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ are disjoint open sets. Let $\textstyle U \equiv \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } U _ { n }$ . By countable additivity 

$$
m (U) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} m (U _ {n}) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {2 ^ {n - 1}}{3 ^ {n}} = 1.
$$

Let $C \equiv [ 0 , 1 ] - U$ . Since U is open and [0,1] is closed, C is nonempty. It can be shown that $\begin{array} { r } { C \equiv \{ x : x = \sum _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } \frac { a _ { i } } { 3 ^ { i } } , a _ { i } = 0 } \end{array}$ or 2 (Problem 

1.33). Thus C can be mapped in (1–1) manner on to the set of all sequences $\{ \delta _ { i } \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ such that $\delta _ { i } = 0 \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } 2$ . But this set is uncountable. Since $m ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) = 1$ , it follows that $m ( C ) = 0$ . For more properties of the Cantor set, see Rudin (1976) and Chapter 4. 

(iv) $m ( \cdot )$ is invariant under reflection and translation. That is, for any E in $B ( \mathbb { R } )$ ， 

$$
m (- E) = m (E) \quad \text { and } \quad m (E + c) = m (E)
$$

for all c in R where $- E = \{ - x : x \in E \}$ and $E + c = \{ y : y =$ $x + c , x \in E \}$ . This follows from Theorem 1.2.4 and the fact that the claim holds for intervals (cf. Problem 2.48). 

(v) There exists a subset $A \subset \mathbb { R }$ such that $A \notin \mathcal { M } _ { m }$ . That is, there exists a non-Lebesgue measurable set. The proof of this requires the use of the axiom of choice (cf. A.1). For a proof see Royden (1988). 

## 1.3.3 Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$

Let $F : \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }  \mathbb { R }$ satisfy 

$$
F (a _ {2}, b _ {2}) - F (a _ {2}, b _ {1}) - F (a _ {1}, b _ {2}) + F (a _ {1}, b _ {1}) \geq 0,\tag{3.9}
$$

and 

$$
F (a _ {2}, b _ {2}) - F (a _ {1}, b _ {1}) \geq 0,\tag{3.10}
$$

for all $a _ { 1 } \leq a _ { 2 } , b _ { 1 } \leq b _ { 2 }$ . Extend $F$ to ${ \bar { \mathbb { R } } } ^ { 2 }$ by appropriate limiting procedure. Let 

$$
\mathcal {C} _ {2} \equiv \{I _ {1} \times I _ {2}: I _ {1}, I _ {2} \in \mathcal {C} \},\tag{3.11}
$$

where $\mathcal { C }$ is as in (3.7). Next, for ${ \cal I } _ { 1 } \ = \ ( a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } ] , \ { \cal I } _ { 2 } \ = \ ( b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } ] , \mathrm { ~ \ - \ } \infty \ <$ $a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } < \infty$ , set 

$$
\mu_ {F} \left(I _ {1} \times I _ {2}\right) \equiv F \left(a _ {2} +, b _ {2} +\right) - F \left(a _ {2} +, b _ {1} +\right) - \left(F \left(a _ {1} +, b _ {2} +\right) + F \left(a _ {1} +, b _ {1} +\right)\right),\tag{3.12}
$$

where for any $a , b \in \mathbb { R } , F ( a + , b + )$ is defined as 

$$
F (a +, b +) \equiv \lim _ {a ^ {\prime} \downarrow a, b ^ {\prime} \downarrow b} F (a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}).
$$

Note that by (3.10), the limit exists and hence, $F ( a + , b + )$ is well defined. Further, by (3.9), the right side of (3.12) is nonnegative. Next extend the definition of $\mu _ { F }$ to unbounded sets in $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 }$ by the limiting procedure: 

$$
\mu_ {F} (I _ {1} \times I _ {2}) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {F} \big ((I _ {1} \times I _ {2}) \cap J _ {n} \big),\tag{3.13}
$$

where $J _ { n } = ( - n , n ] \times ( - n , n ]$ . Then it may be verified (Problems 1.24, 1.25) that 

(i) $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 }$ is a semialgebra 

(ii) $\mu _ { F }$ is a measure on $\mathcal { C } _ { 2 }$ 

Let $( \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } , \mathcal { M } _ { \mu _ { F } ^ { * } } , \mu _ { F } ^ { * } )$ be the measure space constructed as in the above two theorems. The measure $\mu _ { F } ^ { * }$ is called the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure generated by $F$ and $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu _ { F } ^ { * } }$ a Lebesgue-Stieltjes σ-algebra. Again, in this case, $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu ^ { * } }$ includes the σ-algebra $\sigma \langle { \mathcal C } \rangle \equiv B ( { \mathbb R } ^ { 2 } )$ and so $( \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } , B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } ) , \mu _ { F } ^ { * } )$ is also a measure space. If $F ( a , b ) = a b$ , then $\mu _ { F }$ is called the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ 

A similar construction holds for any $\mathbb { R } ^ { k } , k < \infty$ 

## 1.3.4 More on extension of measures

Next the uniqueness of the extension $\mu ^ { * }$ and approximation of the $\mu ^ { * } -$ measure of a set in $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu } \mathrm { : }$ by that of a set from the algebra $\mathcal { A } \equiv \mathcal { A } ( \mathcal { C } )$ are considered. As in the case of measures defined on an algebra, a measure $\mu$ on a semialgebra ${ \mathcal { C } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ is said to be $\sigma { - } f i n i t e$ if there exists a countable collection $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset { \mathcal { C } }$ such that (i) $\mu ( A _ { n } ) < \infty$ for each $n \geq 1$ and (ii) $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n } = \Omega$ . The following approximation result holds. 

Theorem 1.3.4: Let $A \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mu ^ { \ast } }$ <sub>∗</sub> and $\mu ^ { * } ( A ) < \infty$ . Then, for each $\epsilon > 0$ 2 there exist $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } , \ldots , B _ { k } \in { \mathcal { C } } , k < \infty$ with $B _ { i } \cap B _ { j } = \varnothing$ for $1 \leq i \neq j \leq k$ such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(A \triangle \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {k} B _ {j}\right) <   \epsilon ,
$$

where for any two sets $E _ { 1 }$ and $E _ { 2 } , E _ { 1 } \triangle E _ { 2 }$ is the symmetric diference of $E _ { 1 }$ and $E _ { 2 }$ , defined by $E _ { 1 } \triangle E _ { 2 } \equiv ( E _ { 1 } \cap E _ { 2 } ^ { c } ) \cup ( E _ { 1 } ^ { c } \cap E _ { 2 } )$ 

Proof: By definition of $\mu ^ { * } , \mu ^ { * } ( A ) < \infty$ implies that for every $\epsilon > 0$ , there exist $\{ B _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset \mathcal C$ such that $A \subset \textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } B _ { n }$ and 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (B _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (A) + \epsilon / 2 <   \infty .
$$

Since $B _ { n } \in \mathcal { C } , B _ { n } ^ { c }$ is a finite union of disjoint sets from . W.l.o.g., it can be assumed that $\{ B _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ are disjoint. (Otherwise, one can consider the sequence $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } \cap B _ { 1 } ^ { c } , B _ { 3 } ^ { - } \cap B _ { 2 } ^ { c } \cap B _ { 1 } ^ { c } , . . . . )$ Next, $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu ( B _ { n } ) < \infty$ implies that for every $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists $k \in \mathbb N$ such that $\textstyle \sum _ { n = k + 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu ( B _ { n } ) < { \frac { \epsilon } { 2 } }$ Since both A and $\textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } B _ { j }$ are subsets of $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } B _ { n }$ 2 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(A \triangle \left[ \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {k} B _ {j} \right]\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(A ^ {c} \cap \left[ \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} B _ {j} \right]\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {j = k + 1} ^ {\infty} B _ {j}\right).
$$

But since $\mu ^ { * }$ is a measure on $ ( \Omega , { \mathcal M } _ { \mu ^ { * } } ) , \ \mu ^ { * } ( \bigcup _ { n > 1 } B _ { n } ) \ = \ \mu ^ { * } ( A ) \ +$ $\textstyle \mu ^ { * } ( ( \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } B _ { n } ) \cap A ^ { c } )$ . Further, since $\mu ^ { * } ( A ) < \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & \mu^ {*} \Big (\Big [ \bigcup_ {n \geq 1} B _ {n} \Big ] \cap A ^ {c} \Big) \\ = & \mu^ {*} \Big (\bigcup_ {n \geq 1} B _ {n} \Big) - \mu^ {*} (A)) \\ \leq & \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (B _ {n}) - \mu^ {*} (A), \quad (\text {since} \mu^ {*} \text {is countably subadditive}) \\ = & \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (B _ {n}) - \mu^ {*} (A), \quad (\text {since} \mu^ {*} = \mu \text {on} \mathcal {C}) \\ <   & \frac {\epsilon}{2} \quad (\text {by the choice of} \{B _ {n} \} _ {n \geq 1}). \end{array}
$$

Also, by the definition of $k .$ 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {j = k + 1} ^ {\infty} B _ {j}\right) \leq \sum_ {j = k + 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (B _ {j}) = \sum_ {j = k + 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (B _ {j}) <   \frac {\epsilon}{2}.
$$

Thus, $\mu ^ { * } ( A \triangle \{ \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } B _ { j } \} ) < \epsilon$ . This completes the proof of the theorem. ✷ 

Thus, every $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable set of finite measure is nearly a finite union of disjoint elements from the semialgebra . This was enunciated by J.E. Littlewood as the first of his three principles of approximation (the other two being: every Lebesgue measurable function is nearly continuous (cf. Theorem 2.5.12) and every almost everywhere convergent sequence of functions on a finite measure space is nearly uniformly convergent (Egorov’s theorem) cf. Theorem 2.5.11). 

One may strengthen Theorem 1.3.4 to prove the following result on regularity of Radon measures on $\left( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } ) \right)$ (cf. Problem 1.32). See also Rudin (1987), Chapter 2. 

Corollary 1.3.5: (Regularity of measures). Let µ be a Radon measure on $( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } ) )$ ) for some $k \in \mathbb { N } , i . e . , \mu ( A ) < \infty$ for all bounded sets $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } )$ Let $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } )$ be such that $\mu ( A ) < \infty$ . Then, for each $\epsilon > 0$ , there exist a compact set K and an open set G such that $K \subset A \subset G$ and $\mu ( G \backslash K ) < \epsilon$ 

The following uniqueness result can be established by an application of the above approximation theorem (Theorem 1.3.4) or by applying the $\pi - \lambda$ theorem (Corollary 1.1.3), as in Theorem 1.2.4 (Problem 1.26). 

Theorem 1.3.6: (Uniqueness). Let µ be a $\sigma { - } f i n i t e$ measure on a semialgebra . Let ν be a measure on the measurable space $( \Omega , \sigma \langle { \mathcal { C } } \rangle )$ such that $\nu = \mu$ on . Then $\nu = \mu ^ { * }$ on $\sigma \langle \mathcal { C } \rangle$ 

An application of Theorem 1.3.4 yields an useful approximation result known as Lusin’s theorem (see Theorem 2.1.3 in Section 2.1) for approximating Borel measurable functions by continuous functions. 

## 1.4 Completeness of measures

Recall from Definition 1.3.6 that a measure space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mu )$ is called complete if for any $A \in { \mathcal { F } } , \mu ( A ) = 0 , B \subset A \ \Rightarrow B \in { \mathcal { F } }$ . That is, for any set $A$ in $\mathcal { F }$ whose $\mu$ measure is zero, all subsets of a set A are also in $\mathcal { F }$ For example, the very construction of the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure for a nondecreasing F on R, discussed in Section 1.3, yields a complete measure space $( \mathbb { R } , \mathcal { M } _ { \mu _ { F } ^ { * } } , \mu _ { F } ^ { * } )$ . The Borel σ-algebra (R) is a sub-σ-algebra of $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu _ { F } ^ { * } }$ and $( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) , \bar { \mu } _ { F } ^ { * } )$ need not be complete. For example, if $\mu _ { F }$ is the Lebesgue measure, then the Cantor set C (Section 1.3.2) has measure 0 and hence the Lebesgue σ-algebra contains the power set of $C$ and hence has cardinality larger than that of R. It can be shown that the cardinality of $B ( \mathbb { R } )$ is the same as that of R (see Hewitt and Stromberg (1965)). For another example, if $F$ is a degenerate distribution at 0, i.e., $F ( x ) = 0$ for $x \ < \ 0$ and $F ( x ) = 1$ for $x \ge 0$ , then $\mathcal { M } _ { \mu _ { F } ^ { * } } = \mathcal { P } ( \mathbb { R } )$ , the power set of R (Problem 1.28), and hence $( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) , \mu _ { F } )$ is not complete. The same is true for any discrete distribution function. However, it is always possible to complete an incomplete measure space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mu )$ by adding new sets to $\mathcal { F }$ . This procedure is discussed below. 

Theorem 1.4.1: Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Let $\tilde { \mathcal { F } } \equiv \{ A : B _ { 1 } \subset A \subset$ $B _ { 2 } ~ f o r$ some $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { F }$ satisfying $\mu ( B _ { 2 } \setminus B _ { 1 } ) = 0 \}$ . For any $A \in { \tilde { \mathcal { F } } }$ , set ${ \tilde { \mu } } ( A ) = \mu ( B _ { 1 } ) = \mu ( B _ { 2 } )$ for any pair of sets $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { F }$ with $B _ { 1 } \subset A \subset B _ { 2 }$ and $\mu ( B _ { 2 } \setminus B _ { 1 } ) = 0$ . Then 

(i) $\tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ is a σ-algebra and $\mathcal { F } \subset \tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ 2 

(ii) $\tilde { \mu }$ is well defined, 

(iii) $( \Omega , \tilde { \mathcal { F } } , \tilde { \mu } )$ is a complete measure space and ${ \tilde { \mu } } = \mu$ on $\mathcal { F }$ 

Proof: 

(i) Since $A \in { \tilde { \mathcal { F } } }$ , there exist $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { F } , \ B _ { 1 } \subset A \subset B _ { 2 }$ and $\mu ( B _ { 2 } \backslash B _ { 1 } ) =$ 0. Clearly, $B _ { 2 } ^ { c } \subset A ^ { c } \subset B _ { 1 } ^ { c }$ , and $B _ { 1 } ^ { c } , B _ { 2 } ^ { c } \in \mathcal { F }$ and $\mu ( B _ { 1 } ^ { c } \setminus B _ { 2 } ^ { c } ) = \mu ( B _ { 2 } \setminus$ $B _ { 1 } ) = 0$ and so $A ^ { c } \in \tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ . Next, let $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \subset \tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ and $A = \textstyle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n }$ Then, for each n there exist $B _ { 1 n }$ and $B _ { 2 n }$ in $\mathcal { F }$ such that $B _ { 1 n } \subset \sp { - } A _ { n } \subset$ $B _ { 2 n }$ and $\mu ( B _ { 2 n } \setminus B _ { 1 n } ) = 0$ . Let $\textstyle B _ { 1 } = \bigcup _ { n > 1 } B _ { 1 n }$ and $B _ { 2 } = \textstyle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } B _ { 2 n } .$ Then $B _ { 1 } \subset A \subset B _ { 2 } , B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { F }$ and $\bar { B _ { 2 } } \setminus B _ { 1 } \subset \bigcup _ { n > 1 } ( B _ { 2 n } \top B _ { 1 n } )$ and hence $\begin{array} { r } { \mu ( B _ { 2 } \setminus B _ { 1 } ) \leq \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu ( B _ { 2 n } \setminus B _ { 1 n } ) = 0 } \end{array}$ <sub>.</sub> <sub>Thus,</sub> $A \in { \tilde { \mathcal { F } } }$ and hence $\tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ is a σ-algebra. Clearly, $\mathcal { F } \subset \tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ since for every $A \in { \mathcal { F } }$ , one may take $B _ { 1 } = B _ { 2 } = A$ 

(ii) Let $B _ { 1 } \subset A \subset B _ { 2 } , B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } \subset A \subset B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } , B _ { 1 } , B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , B _ { 2 } , B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } \in { \mathcal { F } }$ and $\mu ( B _ { 2 } { \ } )$ $B _ { 1 } ) = 0 = \mu ( B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } \setminus B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } )$ . Then $B _ { 1 } \cup B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } \subset A \subset B _ { 2 } \cap B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$ and $\left( B _ { 2 } \cap B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } \right) \backslash$ $( B _ { 1 } \cup B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ) = ( B _ { 2 } \cap B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ) \cap ( B _ { 1 } ^ { c } \cap B _ { 1 } ^ { ' c } ) \subset B _ { 2 } \cap B _ { 1 } ^ { c }$ . Thus 

$$
\mu ([ B _ {2} \cap B _ {2} ^ {\prime} ] \setminus [ B _ {1} \cup B _ {1} ^ {\prime} ]) = 0.
$$

Hence, $\begin{array} { r } { \mu ( B _ { 2 } ) = \mu ( B _ { 1 } ) + \mu ( B _ { 2 } \setminus B _ { 1 } ) = \mu ( B _ { 1 } ) \le \mu ( B _ { 1 } \cup B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ) = \mu ( B _ { 2 } \cap B _ { 2 } ) } \end{array}$ $B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ) \leq \mu ( B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$ . By symmetry $\mu ( B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ) \leq \mu ( B _ { 2 } )$ and so $\mu ( B _ { 2 } ) = \mu ( B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$ But $\mu ( B _ { 2 } ) = \mu ( B _ { 1 } )$ and $\mu ( B _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ) = \mu ( B _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } )$ and also all four quantities agree. 

(iii) It remains to show that $\tilde { \mu }$ is countably additive and complete on ${ \tilde { \mathcal { F } } } .$ . Let $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be a disjoint sequence of sets from $\tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ and let $A =$ $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } A _ { n }$ . Let $\{ B _ { 1 n } \} _ { n \ge 1 } , \{ B _ { 2 n } \} _ { n \ge 1 } , B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 }$ be as in the proof of (i). Then, the fact that $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ are disjoint implies $\{ B _ { 1 n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ are also disjoint. And since $\begin{array} { r } { B _ { 1 } = \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } B _ { 1 n } } \end{array}$ and $\mu$ is a measure on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ 2 

$$
\mu (B _ {1}) \equiv \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} (B _ {1 n}).
$$

Also, by definition of $B _ { 1 n } \mathrm { \ ' s } , \mu ( B _ { 1 n } ) = \tilde { \mu } ( A _ { n } )$ for all $n \geq 1$ , and by (i), ${ \tilde { \mu } } ( A ) = \mu ( B _ { 1 } )$ . Thus, 

$$
\tilde {\mu} (A) = \mu (B _ {1}) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} (B _ {1 n}) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \tilde {\mu} (A _ {n}),
$$

establishing the countable additivity of $\tilde { \mu } .$ 

Next, suppose that $A \in { \tilde { \mathcal { F } } }$ and $\tilde { \mu } ( A ) = 0$ . Then there exist $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { F }$ such that $B _ { 1 } \subset A \subset B _ { 2 }$ and $\mu ( B _ { 2 } \backslash B _ { 1 } ) = 0$ . Further, by definition of ${ \tilde { \mu } } , \mu ( B _ { 2 } ) = { \tilde { \mu } } ( A ) = 0$ . If $D \subset A$ , then $\emptyset \subset D \subset B _ { 2 }$ and $\mu ( B _ { 2 } \setminus \varnothing ) = 0$ Therefore, $D \in \tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ and hence $( \Omega , \tilde { \mathcal { F } } , \tilde { \mu } )$ is complete.

## 2.1 Measurable transformations

Oftentimes, one is not interested in the full details of a measure space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mu )$ but only in certain functions defined on Ω. For example, if Ω represents the outcomes of 10 tosses of a fair coin, one may only be interested in knowing the number of heads in the 10 tosses. It turns out that to assign measures (probabilities) to sets (events) involving such functions, one can allow only certain functions (called measurable functions) that satisfy some ‘natural’ restrictions, specified in the following definitions. 

Definition 2.1.1: Let Ω be a nonempty set and let $\mathcal { F }$ be a σ-algebra on Ω. Then the pair $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ is called a measurable space. If $\mu$ is a measure on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ , then the triplet $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mu )$ is called a measure space. If in addition, µ is a probability measure, then $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \mu )$ is called a probability space. 

## Definition 2.1.2:

(a) Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ be a measurable space. Then a function $f : \Omega$ to R is called $\langle \mathcal { F } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable (or ${ \mathcal { F } } .$ measurable) if for each a in R 

$$
f ^ {- 1} \big ((- \infty , a ] \big) \equiv \{\omega : f (\omega) \leq a \} \in \mathcal {F}.\tag{1.1}
$$

(b) Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ be a probability space. Then a function $X : \Omega  \mathbb { R }$ is called a random variable, if the event 

$$
X ^ {- 1} ((- \infty , a ]) \equiv \{\omega : X (\omega) \leq a \} \in \mathcal {F}
$$

for each a in R, i.e., a random variable is a real valued -measurable function on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ 

It will be shown later that condition (1.1) on f is equivalent to the stronger condition that $f ^ { - 1 } ( A ) \in { \mathcal { F } }$ for all Borel sets $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } )$ . Since for any Borel set $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } ) , f ^ { - 1 } ( A )$ is a member of the underlying σ-algebra ${ \mathcal F } _ { : }$ , one can assign a measure to the set $f ^ { - 1 } ( A )$ using a measure $\mu$ on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ Note that for an arbitrary function T from $\Omega  \mathbb { R } , T ^ { - 1 } ( A )$ need not be a member of $\mathcal { F }$ and hence such an assignment may not be possible. Thus, condition (1.1) on real valued mappings is a ‘natural’ requirement while dealing with measure spaces. 

The following definition generalizes (1.1) to maps between two measurable spaces. 

Definition 2.1.3: Let $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } ) , i = 1 , 2$ be measurable spaces. Then, a mapping $T : \Omega _ { 1 } \to \Omega _ { 2 }$ is called measurable with respect to the σ-algebras $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle$ (or $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle$ -measurable) if 

$$
T ^ {- 1} (A) \in \mathcal {F} _ {1} \quad \text { for   all } \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {2}.
$$

Thus, X is a random variable on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ if X is $\langle \mathcal { F } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable. Some examples of measurable transformations are given below. 

Example 2.1.1: Let $\Omega \ = \ \{ a , b , c , d \} , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \ = \ \{ \Omega , \emptyset , \{ a \} , \{ b , c , d \} \}$ and let $\mathcal { F } _ { 3 } =$ the set of all subsets of Ω. Define the mappings $T _ { i } : \Omega \to \Omega , i = 1 , 2$ 2 by 

$$
T _ {1} (\omega) \equiv a \text {   for   } \omega \in \Omega
$$

and 

$$
T _ {2} (\omega) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} a & \text { if } \omega = a, b \\ c & \text { if } \omega = c, d. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then, $T _ { 1 }$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 3 } \rangle$ -measurable since for any $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { 3 } , T _ { 1 } ^ { - 1 } ( A ) = \Omega$ or according as $a \ \in \ A$ or $a \not \in A$ . By similar arguments, it follows that $T _ { 2 }$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 3 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle$ -measurable. However, $T _ { 2 }$ is not $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 3 } \rangle$ -measurable since $T _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( \{ a \} ) = \{ a , b \} \notin { \mathcal { F } } _ { 2 }$ 

As this simple example shows, measurability of a given mapping critically depends on the σ-algebras on its domain and range spaces. In general, if $T$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle$ -measurable, then $T$ is $\langle \tilde { \mathcal { F } } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle$ -measurable for any σ-algebra $\tilde { \mathcal { F } } _ { 1 } \supset \mathcal { F } _ { 1 }$ and $T$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \tilde { \mathcal { F } } _ { 2 } \rangle$ -measurable for any $\tilde { \mathcal { F } } _ { 2 } \subset \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ 

Example 2.1.2: Let $T : \mathbb { R }  \mathbb { R }$ be defined as 

$$
T (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \sin 2 x & \text {if} x > 0 \\ 1 + \cos x & \text {if} x \leq 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

Is T measurable w.r.t. the Borel σ-algebras $\langle B ( \mathbb { R } ) , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle \colon$ If one is to apply the definition directly, one must check that $T ^ { - 1 } ( A ) \in { \cal B } ( \mathbb { R } )$ for all $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } )$ . However, finding $T ^ { - 1 } ( A )$ for all Borel sets A is not an easy task. In many instances like this one, verification of the measurability property of a given mapping by directly using the definition can be dificult. In such situations, one may use some easy-to-verify suficient conditions. Some results of this type are given below. 

Proposition 2.1.1: Let $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } ) , i = 1 , 2 , 3$ be measurable spaces. 

(i) Suppose that ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { 2 } = \sigma { \langle \mathcal { A } \rangle }$ for some class of subsets of $\Omega _ { 2 } , \ J f \ T$ $\Omega _ { 1 }  \Omega _ { 2 }$ is such that $T ^ { - 1 } ( A ) \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { 1 }$ for all $A \in { \mathcal { A } }$ , then T is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle .$ measurable. 

(ii) Suppose that $T _ { 1 } : \Omega _ { 1 } \to \Omega _ { 2 }$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle$ -measurable and $T _ { 2 } : \Omega _ { 2 } $ $\Omega _ { 3 }$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 3 } \rangle$ -measurable. Let $T = T _ { 2 } \circ T _ { 1 } : \Omega _ { 1 }  \Omega _ { 3 }$ denote the composition of T and $T _ { 2 }$ , defined by $T ( \omega _ { 1 } ) = T _ { 2 } ( T _ { 1 } ( \omega _ { 1 } ) ) , \ \omega _ { 1 } \in \Omega _ { 1 }$ Then, T is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 3 } \rangle$ -measurable. 

## Proof:

(i) Define the collection of sets 

$$
\mathcal {F} = \{A \in \mathcal {F} _ {2}: T ^ {- 1} (A) \in \mathcal {F} _ {1} \}.
$$

Then, 

(a) $T ^ { - 1 } ( \Omega _ { 2 } ) = \Omega _ { 1 } \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \Rightarrow \Omega _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { F } .$ 

(b) If $A \in { \mathcal { F } }$ , then $T ^ { - 1 } ( A ) \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { 1 } \Rightarrow ( T ^ { - 1 } ( A ) ) ^ { c } \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { 1 } \Rightarrow T ^ { - 1 } ( A ^ { c } ) =$ $( T ^ { - 1 } ( A ) ) ^ { c } \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { 1 }$ , implying $A ^ { c } \in { \mathcal { F } }$ 

(c) If $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \dotsc , \in { \mathcal { F } }$ , then, $T ^ { - 1 } ( A _ { i } ) \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 }$ for all $i \geq 1$ . Since $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 }$ is a σ-algebra , $\begin{array} { r } { T ^ { - 1 } ( \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n } ) = \bigcup _ { n > 1 } T ^ { - 1 } ( A _ { n } ) \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } } \end{array}$ . Thus, $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { F } }$  . (See also Problem 2.1 on de Morgan’s laws.) 

Hence, by ${ \mathrm { ( a ) } } , { \mathrm { ( b ) } } , { \mathrm { ( c ) } } , { \mathcal { F } }$ is a σ-algebra and by hypothesis ${ \mathcal { A } } \subset { \mathcal { F } }$ Hence, ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { 2 } = \sigma { \langle } A { \rangle } \subset { \mathcal { F } } \subset { \mathcal { F } } _ { 2 }$ . Thus, $\mathcal { F } = \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ and $T$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle -$ measurable. 

(ii) Let $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { 3 }$ . Then, $T _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( A ) \in \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ , since $T _ { 2 }$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 3 } \rangle$ -measurable. Also, by the $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \rangle$ -measurability of $T _ { 1 } , T ^ { - 1 } ( A ) = T _ { 1 } ^ { - 1 } ( T _ { 2 } ^ { - 1 } ( A ) ) \in$ $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 }$ , showing that T is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 3 } \rangle$ -measurable. ✷

Although the converse to the above proposition is not true, a result due to Lusin says that except on a set of small measure, f coincides with a continuous function. This is stronger than the statement that except on set of small measure, f is close to a continuous function. For the statement and proof of Lusin’s theorem, see Theorem 2.5.12.

Since $g = g _ { 1 } \circ f ;$ , g is $\langle \mathcal { F } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable, by Proposition 2.1.1 (ii). The proofs of (iii) and (iv) are similar to that of (ii) and hence, are omitted. ✷

The proof of Corollary 2.1.4 is omitted.
