For $A = A _ { 1 } \times A _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { C } , \mu _ { 2 } ( A _ { 1 \omega _ { 1 } } ) = \mu _ { 2 } \bar { ( A _ { 2 } ^ { - } ) } I _ { A _ { 1 } } ( \omega _ { 1 } )$ and hence $\mathcal { C } \subset \mathcal { L }$ . Since is a π-system, by Corollary 1.1.3, it follows that $\mathcal { L } = \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . Thus, $\mu _ { 2 } ( A _ { 1 \omega _ { 1 } } )$ , considered as a function of $\omega _ { 1 }$ , is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable for all $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ , proving (i). 

Next, consider part (ii). By part $( \mathrm { i } ) , \mu _ { 1 2 }$ is a well-defined set function on $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . It is easy to check that $\mu _ { 1 2 }$ is a measure on $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ (Problem 5.1). Similarly, $\mu _ { 2 1 }$ is a well-defined measure on $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . Since $\mu _ { 1 2 } ( A ) =$ $\mu _ { 2 1 } ( A ) = \mu _ { 1 } ( A _ { 1 } ) \mu _ { 2 } ( A _ { 2 } )$ for all $A = A _ { 1 } \times A _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { C }$ and is a π-system generating $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ , it follows from Theorem 1.2.4 that $\mu _ { 1 2 } ( A ) = \mu _ { 2 1 } ( A )$ for all $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . This proves (ii) for the case where $\mu _ { i } ( \Omega _ { i } ) < \infty , i = 1 , 2$ Next, suppose that $\mu _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { s } } }$ are σ-finite. Then, there exist disjoint sets $\{ B _ { i n } \} _ { n \ge 1 } \subset \mathcal F _ { i }$ , such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } B _ { i n } = \Omega _ { i }$ and $\mu _ { i } ( B _ { i n } ) < \infty$ for all $n \geq 1$ $i = 1 , 2$ . Define the finite measures 

$$
\mu_ {i n} (D) = \mu_ {i} (D \cap B _ {i n}), \quad D \in \mathcal {F} _ {i},
$$

for $n \geq 1 , i = 1 , 2$ . The arguments above with $\mu _ { i }$ replaced by $\mu _ { i n }$ imply that for any $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mu _ { 2 n } ( A _ { 1 \omega _ { 1 } } )$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable for all $n \geq 1$ . Since $\mu _ { 2 }$ is a measure on $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mu _ { 2 } ( A _ { 1 \omega _ { 1 } } ) = \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu _ { 2 n } ( A _ { \omega _ { 1 } } ) } \end{array}$ and hence, considered as a function of $\omega _ { 1 }$ , it is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , B ( \bar { \mathbb { R } } ) \rangle$ -measurable for all $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . Thus, the set function $\mu _ { 1 2 }$ of (1.4) is well defined in the σ-finite case as well. Similarly, $\mu _ { 2 1 }$ of (1.5) is a well-defined set function on $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . Let $\mu _ { 1 2 } ^ { ( m , n ) }$ and $\mu _ { 2 1 } ^ { ( m , n ) }$ , respectively, denote the set functions defined by (1.4) and (1.5) with $\mu _ { 1 }$ replaced by $\mu _ { 1 m }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ replaced by $\mu _ { 2 n } , m \geq 1 , n \geq 1$ . Then, by repeated use of the MCT, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu_ {1 2} (A) & = & \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} \mu_ {2} (A _ {1 \omega_ {1}}) \mu_ {1} (d \omega_ {1}) \\ & = & \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {\infty} \biggl (\int_ {B _ {1 m}} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu_ {2} (A _ {1 \omega_ {1}} \cap B _ {2 n}) \biggr) \mu_ {1} (d \omega_ {1}) \\ & = & \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {B _ {1 m}} \mu_ {2} (A _ {1 \omega_ {1}} \cap B _ {2 n}) \mu_ {1} (d \omega_ {1}) \end{array}
$$

$$
= \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu_ {1 2} ^ {(m, n)} (A), \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {1} \times \mathcal {F} _ {2}\tag{1.6}
$$

and similarly, 

$$
\mu_ {2 1} (A) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu_ {2 1} ^ {(m, n)} (A), \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {1} \times \mathcal {F} _ {2}.\tag{1.7}
$$

Since $\mu _ { 1 2 } ^ { ( m , n ) }$ and $\mu _ { 2 1 } ^ { ( m , n ) }$ are (finite) measures, it is easy to check that $\mu _ { 1 2 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 1 }$ are measures on $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . Also, by the finite case, $\mu _ { 1 2 } ^ { ( m , n ) } ( A _ { 1 } \times A _ { 2 } ) =$ $\mu _ { 2 1 } ^ { ( m , n ) } ( A _ { 1 } \times A _ { 2 } )$ for all $n \geq 1 , m \geq 1$ and hence 

$$
\mu_ {1 2} (A _ {1} \times A _ {2}) = \mu_ {2 1} (A _ {1} \times A _ {2}) \quad \text { for   all } \quad A _ {1} \times A _ {2} \in \mathcal {C}.
$$

Next note that $\{ B _ { 1 m } \times B _ { 2 n } : m \geq 1 , n \geq 1 \}$ is a partition of $\Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 }$ by $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ sets and by (1.6) and (1.7), for all $m \geq 1 , n \geq 1$ 2 

$$
\mu_ {1 2} (B _ {1 m} \times B _ {2 n}) = \mu_ {1} (B _ {1 m}) \mu_ {2} (B _ {2 n}) = \mu_ {2 1} (B _ {1 m} \times B _ {2 n}) <   \infty .
$$

Hence, $\mu _ { 1 2 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 1 }$ are σ-finite on $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . Since $\mu _ { 1 2 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 1 }$ agree on and $\mathcal { C }$ is a π-system generating the product σ-algebra, it follows that $\mu _ { 1 2 } ( A ) = \mu _ { 2 1 } ( A )$ for all $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ and it is the unique measure satisfying $\mu ( A _ { 1 } \times A _ { 2 } ) = \mu _ { 1 } ( A _ { 1 } ) \mu _ { 2 } ( A _ { 2 } )$ for all $A _ { 1 } \times A _ { 2 } \in { \mathcal { C } }$ . This completes the proof of the theorem. ✷ 

Remark 5.1.1: In the above theorem, the σ-finiteness condition on the measures $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ cannot be dropped. For example, let $\Omega _ { 1 } = \Omega _ { 2 } = [ 0 , 1 ]$ 5 $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } = \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } = \mathcal { B } ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) , \mu _ { 1 } =$ the Lebesgue measure and $\mu _ { 2 } =$ the counting measure. Clearly $\mu _ { 2 }$ is not σ-finite since [0, 1] is uncountable. Let A be the diagonal set in the product space $[ 0 , 1 ] \times [ 0 , 1 ]$ , i.e., $A = \left\{ \left( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } \right) \in \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } \right.$ $\omega _ { 1 } = \omega _ { 2 } \}$ . Then $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , A _ { 1 \omega _ { 1 } } = \{ \omega _ { 1 } \}$ and $A _ { 2 \omega _ { 2 } } = \{ \omega _ { 2 } \}$ . Further, $\mu _ { 2 } ( A _ { 1 \omega _ { 1 } } ) = 1$ for all $\omega _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 1 } ( { \cal A } _ { 2 \omega _ { 2 } } ) = 0$ for all $\omega _ { 2 }$ . Thus $\mu _ { 1 2 } ( A ) =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } } \mu _ { 2 } ( A _ { 1 \omega _ { 1 } } ) \mu _ { 1 } ( d \omega _ { 1 } ) = 1 } \end{array}$ , but $\begin{array} { r } { \mu _ { 2 1 } ( A ) = \int _ { \Omega _ { 2 } } \mu _ { 1 } ( A _ { 2 \omega _ { 2 } } ) \mu _ { 2 } ( d \omega _ { 2 } ) = 0 } \end{array}$ , and hence, $\mu _ { 1 2 } ( A ) \neq \mu _ { 2 1 } ( A )$ 

Remark 5.1.2: Although this approach allows one to compute the product measure $\mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 }$ of a set $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ , the measure space $( \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times$ $\mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } )$ may not be complete even if both $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } , \mu _ { i } ) , i = 1 , 2$ are complete (Problem 5.2). However, the approach based on the extension theorem yields a product measure space that is complete. See Remark 5.2.2 for further discussion on the topic. 

## Definition 5.1.3:

(a) The unique measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ defined in Theorem 5.1.2 (iii) is called the product measure and is denoted by $\mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 }$ 

(b) The measure space $( \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } , \mathscr { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathscr { F } _ { 2 } , \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } )$ is called the product measure space. 

Formulas $( 1 . 4 )$ and (1.5) give two diferent ways of evaluating $\mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } ( A )$ for an $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . In the next section, integration of a measurable function $f : \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } \to \mathbb { R }$ w.r.t. the product measure $\mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 }$ is considered and the above approach is extended to justify evaluation of the integral iteratively. 

## 5.2 Fubini-Tonelli theorems

Let $f : \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } \to \mathbb { R }$ be a $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable function. Relations (1.4) and (1.5) suggest that the integral of f w.r.t. $\mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 }$ may be evaluated as iterated integrals, using the formulas 

$$
\int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2} (d (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2})) = \int_ {\Omega_ {2}} \left[ \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {1} (d \omega_ {1}) \right] \mu_ {2} (d \omega_ {2})\tag{2.1}
$$

and 

$$
\int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2} (d (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2})) = \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} \left[ \int_ {\Omega_ {2}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {2} (d \omega_ {2}) \right] \mu_ {1} (d \omega_ {1}).\tag{2.2}
$$

Here, the left sides of both (2.1) and (2.2) are simply the integral of $f$ on the space $\Omega = \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 }$ w.r.t. the measure $\mu = \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 }$ . The expressions on the right sides of (2.1) and (2.2) are, however, iterated integrals, where integrals of sections of f are evaluated first and then the resulting sectional integrals are integrated again to get the final expression. Conditions for the validity of (2.1) and (2.2) are provided by the Fubini-Tonelli theorems stated below. 

Theorem 5.2.1: (Tonelli’s theorem). Let $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } , \mu _ { i } ) , i = 1$ , 2 be σ-finite measure spaces and let $f : \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } \to \mathbb { R } _ { + }$ be a nonnegative $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } .$ measurable function. Then 

$$
g _ {1} (\omega_ {1}) \equiv \int_ {\Omega_ {2}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {2} (d \omega_ {2}): \Omega_ {1} \to \bar {\mathbb {R}} \quad i s \quad \langle \mathcal {F} _ {1}, \mathcal {B} (\bar {\mathbb {R}}) \rangle - m e a s u r a b l e\tag{2.3}
$$

and 

$$
g _ {2} (\omega_ {2}) \equiv \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {1} (d \omega_ {1}): \Omega_ {2} \to \bar {\mathbb {R}} \quad i s \quad \langle \mathcal {F} _ {2}, \mathcal {B} (\bar {\mathbb {R}}) \rangle - m e a s u r a b l e.\tag{2.4}
$$

Further 

$$
\int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f d \mu = \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1} d \mu_ {1} = \int_ {\Omega_ {2}} g _ {2} d \mu_ {2},\tag{2.5}
$$

where $\mu = \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 }$ 

Proof: If $f = I _ { A }$ for some $A$ in $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ , the result follows from Theorem 5.1.2. By the linearity of integrals, the result now holds for all simple nonnegative functions $f .$ . For a general nonnegative function $f ,$ there exist a sequence $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ of nonnegative simple functions such that $f _ { n } ( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } )$ ↑ $f ( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } )$ for all $( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } ) \in \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 }$ . Write $\begin{array} { r } { g _ { 1 n } ( \omega _ { 1 } ) = \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } } f _ { n } ( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } ) \mu _ { 2 } ( d \omega _ { 2 } ) } \end{array}$ Then, g <sub>n</sub> is -measurable for all $n \geq 1 , g _ { 1 n } \mathrm { ' s }$  are nondecreasing, and by the MCT, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} g _ {1} (\omega_ {1}) & \equiv & \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {2} (d \omega_ {2}) \\ & = & \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int f _ {n} (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {2} (d \omega_ {2}) \\ & = & \lim _ {n \to \infty} g _ {1 n} (\omega_ {1}) \end{array}\tag{2.6}
$$

for all $\omega _ { 1 } \in \Omega _ { 1 }$ . Thus, by Proposition 2.1.5, g<sub>1</sub> is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , B ( \bar { \mathbb { R } } ) \rangle$ -measurable. Since (2.5) holds for simple functions, $\textstyle \int f _ { n } d \mu = \int g _ { 1 n } d \mu _ { 1 }$ for all $n \geq 1$  Hence, by repeated applications of the MCT, it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int f d \mu & = & \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int f _ {n} d \mu = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int g _ {1 n} d \mu_ {1} \\ & = & \int (\lim _ {n \to \infty} g _ {1 n}) d \mu_ {1} = \int g _ {1} d \mu_ {1}. \end{array}
$$

The proofs of (2.4) and the second equality in (2.5) are similar. 

Theorem 5.2.2: (Fubini’s theorem). Let $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } , \mu _ { i } ) , ~ i = 1 , 2$ be σ-finite measure spaces and let $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } )$ . Then there exist sets $B _ { i } \in \mathcal { F } _ { i } , i = 1$ , 2 such that 

(i) $\mu _ { i } ( \Omega _ { i } \setminus B _ { i } ) = 0 ~ f o r ~ i = 1 , 2 ,$ 

(ii) for $\omega _ { 1 } \in B _ { 1 } , f ( \omega _ { 1 } , \cdot ) \in L ^ { 1 } ( \Omega _ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mu _ { 2 } ) ,$ 

(iii) the function 

$$
g _ {1} (\omega_ {1}) \equiv \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \int_ {\Omega_ {2}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {2} (d \omega_ {2}) & \text { for } \quad \omega_ {1} \text { in } B _ {1} \\ 0 & \text { for } \quad \omega_ {1} \text { in } B _ {1} ^ {c} \end{array} \right.
$$

is <sub>1</sub>-measurable and 

$$
\int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1} d \mu_ {1} = \int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f d (\mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2}),\tag{2.7}
$$

(iv) for $\omega _ { 2 } \in B _ { 2 } , f ( \cdot , \omega _ { 2 } ) \in L ^ { 1 } ( \Omega _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 1 } )$ 2 

(v) the function 

$$
g _ {2} (\omega_ {2}) \equiv \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) \mu_ {1} (d \omega_ {1}) & \text { for } \quad \omega_ {2} \text { in } B _ {2} \\ 0 & \text { for } \quad \omega_ {2} \text { in } B _ {2} ^ {c} \end{array} \right.
$$

is $\mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ -measurable and 

$$
\int_ {\Omega_ {2}} g _ {2} d \mu_ {2} = \int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f d (\mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2}).\tag{2.8}
$$

Remark 5.2.1: An informal statement of the above theorem is as follows. If f is integrable on the product space, then the sectional integrals $\begin{array} { r l } { \int _ { \Omega _ { 2 } } f ( \omega _ { 1 } , \cdot ) d \mu _ { 2 } } \end{array}$ and $\textstyle \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } } f ( \cdot , \omega _ { 2 } ) d \mu _ { 1 }$ are well defined a.e., and their integrals w.r.t. $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ , respectively, are equal to the integral of f w.r.t. the product measure $\mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 }$ 

## Proof: By Tonelli’s theorem

$$
\int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} | f | d (\mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2}) = \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} \left(\int_ {\Omega_ {2}} | f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}) | \mu_ {2} (d \omega_ {2})\right) \mu_ {1} (d \omega_ {1}).
$$

So $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } } | f | d ( \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } ) < \infty } \end{array}$ implies that $\mu _ { 1 } ( B _ { 1 } ^ { c } ) = 0$ where ${ \cal B } _ { 1 } = \{ \omega _ { 1 } :$ $\textstyle \int | f ( \omega _ { 1 } , \cdot ) | d \mu _ { 2 } < \infty \}$ . Also, by Tonelli’s theorem 

$$
g _ {1 1} (\omega_ {1}) \equiv \int_ {\Omega_ {2}} f ^ {+} (\omega_ {1}, \cdot) d \mu_ {2} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad g _ {1 2} (\omega_ {1}) \equiv \int_ {\Omega_ {2}} f ^ {-} (\omega_ {1}, \cdot) d \mu_ {2}
$$

are both $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 }$ -measurable and 

$$
\int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1 1} d \mu_ {1} = \int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f ^ {+} d (\mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2}), \quad \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1 2} d \mu_ {1} = \int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f ^ {-} d (\mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2}).\tag{2.9}
$$

Since $g _ { 1 }$ defined in (iii) can be written as $g _ { 1 } = ( g _ { 1 1 } - g _ { 1 2 } ) I _ { B _ { 1 } } , g _ { 1 }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 ^ { - } }$ measurable. Also, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} | g _ {1} | d \mu_ {1} & \leq & \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1 1} d \mu_ {1} + \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1 2} d \mu_ {1} \\ & = & \int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f ^ {+} d (\mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2}) + \int_ {\Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2}} f ^ {-} d (\mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2}) \\ & <   & \infty . \end{array}
$$

Further, as $\int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } } | f | d \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } < \infty$ , by (2.9), $g _ { 1 1 }$ and $g _ { 1 2 } \in L ^ { 1 } ( \Omega _ { 1 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 1 } )$ Noting that $\mu _ { 1 } ( B _ { 1 } ^ { c } ) = 0$ , one gets 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1} d \mu_ {1} & = & \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} (g _ {1 1} - g _ {1 2}) I _ {B _ {1}} d \mu_ {1} \\ & = & \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1 1} I _ {B _ {1}} d \mu_ {1} - \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1 2} I _ {B _ {1}} d \mu_ {1} \\ & = & \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1 1} d \mu_ {1} - \int_ {\Omega_ {1}} g _ {1 2} d \mu_ {1} \end{array}
$$

which, by (2.9), equals $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } } f ^ { + } d ( \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } ) - \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } } f ^ { - } d ( \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } ) \ = \quad } \end{array}$ $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } } f d ( \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } ) } \end{array}$  . Thus, <sub>(</sub>ii<sub>)</sub> and <sub>(</sub>iii<sub>)</sub> of the theorem have been estab-lished as well as (i) for $i = 1$ . The proofs of (iv) and (v) and that of (i) for $i = 2$ are similar. ✷ 

An application of the Fubini-Tonelli theorems gives an integration by parts formula. Let $F _ { 1 }$ and $F _ { 2 }$ be two nondecreasing right continuous functions on an interval [a, b]. Let $\mu _ { i }$ be the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure on $B ( [ a , b ] )$ corresponding to $F _ { i } , \ i \ = \ 1 , 2$ . The ‘integration by parts’ formula allows one to write $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { ( a , b ] } F _ { 1 } ( x ) d F _ { 2 } ( x ) \ \equiv \ \int _ { ( a , b ] } F _ { 1 } d \mu _ { 2 } } \end{array}$ in terms of $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { ( a , b ] } F _ { 2 } ( x ) d F _ { 1 } ( x ) \equiv \int _ { ( a , b ] } F _ { 2 } \dot { d } \mu _ { 1 } } \end{array}$ 

Theorem 5.2.3: Let $F _ { 1 } , F _ { 2 }$ be two nondecreasing right continuous functions on $[ a , b ]$ with no common points of discontinuity in $( a , b ]$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {(a, b ]} F _ {1} (x) d F _ {2} (x) = F _ {1} (b) F _ {2} (b) - F _ {1} (a) F _ {2} (a) - \int_ {(a, b ]} F _ {2} (x) d F _ {1} (x).\tag{2.10}
$$

Proof: Note that $\big ( ( a , b ] , \mathcal { B } ( a , b ] , \mu _ { i } \big ) , \ i = 1 , 2$ are finite measure spaces. Consider the product space $\left( ( a , b ] \times ( a , b ] , \mathcal { B } ( ( a , b ] \times ( a , b ] ) , \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } \right)$ . Define the sets 

and 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} A & = & \{(x, y): a <   x \leq y \leq b \} \\ B & = & \{(x, y): a <   y \leq x \leq b \} \\ C & = & \{(x, y): a <   x = y \leq b \}. \end{array}
$$

For notational simplicity, write $A _ { x }$ and $A _ { y }$ for the x-section and the $y -$ section of $A ,$ respectively, and similarly, for the sets B and C. Since $F _ { 1 }$ and $F _ { 2 }$ have no common points of discontinuity, by Theorem 5.1.2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2} (C) & = & \int_ {(a, b ]} \mu_ {2} (C _ {x}) \mu_ {1} (d x) \\ & = & \int_ {(a, b ]} \mu_ {2} (\{x \}) \mu_ {1} (d x) \\ & = & 0. \end{array}\tag{2.11}
$$

(see Problem 5.3). And by Theorem 5.1.2, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2} (A) & = & \int_ {(a, b ]} \mu_ {1} (A _ {y}) \mu_ {2} (d y) \\ & = & \int_ {(a, b ]} \mu_ {1} ((a, y ]) \mu_ {2} (d y) \\ & = & \int_ {(a, b ]} [ F _ {1} (y) - F _ {1} (a) ] d F _ {2} (y) \end{array}\tag{2.12}
$$

and similarly, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2} (B) & = & \int_ {(a, b ]} \mu_ {2} (B _ {x}) \mu_ {1} (d x) \\ & = & \int_ {(a, b ]} [ F _ {2} (x) - F _ {2} (a) ] d F _ {1} (x). \end{array}\tag{2.13}
$$

Next note that $( \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } ) ( ( a , b ] \times ( a , b ] ) = \mu _ { 1 } ( ( a , b ] ) \cdot \mu _ { 2 } ( ( a , b ] ) = [ F _ { 1 } ( b ) -$ $F _ { 1 } ( a ) ] [ F _ { 2 } ( b ) - F _ { 2 } ( a ) ]$ . Hence, by (2.11)–(2.13), 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & [ F _ {1} (b) - F _ {1} (a) ] [ F _ {2} (b) - F _ {2} (a) ] \\ = & (\mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2}) ((a, b ] \times (a, b ]) \\ = & \mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2} (A) + \mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2} (B) - \mu_ {1} \times \mu_ {2} (C) \\ = & \int_ {(a, b ]} [ F _ {1} (y) - F _ {1} (a) ] d F _ {2} (y) + \int_ {(a, b ]} [ F _ {2} (x) - F _ {2} (a) ] d F _ {1} (x), \end{array}
$$

which yields (2.10), thereby completing the proof of Theorem 5.2.3. ✷ 

If $F _ { 1 }$ and $F _ { 2 }$ are absolutely continuous with nonnegative densities $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure on $( a , b ]$ , then (2.10) yields 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {b} F _ {1} (x) f _ {2} (x) d x = F _ {1} (b) F _ {2} (b) - F _ {1} (a) F _ {2} (a) - \int_ {a} ^ {b} F _ {2} (x) f _ {1} (x) d x.\tag{2.14}
$$

If $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ are any two Lebesgue integrable function on $( a , b ]$ that are not necessarily nonnegative, one can decompose $f _ { i }$ as $f _ { i } = f _ { i } ^ { + } - f _ { i } ^ { - }$ and apply (2.14) to $f _ { i } ^ { + } { } ^ { \mathrm { s } }$ and $f _ { i } ^ { - } \ ' _ { \mathrm { s } }$ separately. Then, by linearity, it follows that the relation (2.14) also holds for the given $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ . Thus, the standard ‘integration by parts’ formula is a special case of Theorem 5.2.3. Relations (2.10) and (2.14) can be extended to unbounded intervals under suitable conditions on $F _ { 1 }$ and $F _ { 2 }$ (Problem 5.5). 

Remark 5.2.2: The measure space $\left( \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } , \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } \right)$ constructed using the integrals in (1.4) and (1.5) is not necessarily complete. As mentioned at the beginning of this section, the approach based on the extension theorem (applied to the set function defined in (1.1) on the algebra of finite disjoint unions of measurable rectangles) does yield a complete measure space $( \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } , { \mathcal { M } } , \lambda )$ such that $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 } \subset \mathcal { M }$ and $\lambda ( A ) = ( \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } ) ( A )$ for all A in $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { F } _ { 2 }$ . To compute the integral f dλ of an -measurable function f w.r.t. λ, formula (2.5) in Tonelli’s theorem and formulas (2.7) and (2.8) in Fubini’s theorem continue to be valid with some modifications. In the following, a modified statement of Fubini’s theorem is presented. Similar modification also holds for Tonelli’s theorem (cf. Royden (1988), Chapter 12, Section 4). 

Theorem 5.2.4: Let $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } , \mu _ { i } ) , \ i \ = \ 1 , 2$ be σ-finite measure spaces and let $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } , \mathcal { M } , \mu _ { 1 } \times \mu _ { 2 } )$ . Let $\left( \Omega _ { i } , \bar { \mathcal { F } } _ { i } , \bar { \mu } _ { i } \right)$ be the completion of $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } , \mu _ { i } ) , i = 1 , 2$ . Then there exist sets $B _ { i }$ in $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { \mathcal { F } } _ { i } , i = 1 } \end{array}$ , 2 such that 

(i) $\bar { \mu } _ { i } ( B _ { i } ^ { c } ) = 0 , i = 1 , 2 .$ 

(ii) for $\omega _ { 1 } \in B _ { 1 } , f ( \omega _ { 1 } , \cdot )$ is $\bar { \mathcal { F } } _ { 2 } { \cdot } m e a s u r a b l e .$ 

(iii) $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \Omega _ { 2 } } | f ( \omega _ { 1 } , \cdot ) | d \bar { \mu } _ { 2 } < \infty \ f o r \ a l l \ \omega _ { 1 } \in B _ { 1 } } \end{array}$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (i v) g _ {1} (\omega_ {1}) \equiv \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \int_ {\Omega_ {2}} f (\omega_ {1}, \cdot) d \bar {\mu} _ {2} & \text {for} \quad \omega_ {1} \text {in} B, \\ 0 & \text {for} \quad \omega_ {1} \text {in} B _ {1} ^ {c} \end{array} \right. \\ i s \bar {\mathcal {F}} _ {1} \text {-measurable}, \end{array}
$$

(v) $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } } g _ { 1 } d \bar { \mu } _ { 1 } = \int _ { \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } } f d \lambda . } \end{array}$ 

Further, a similar statement holds for $i = 2$ 

## 5.3 Extensions to products of higher orders

Definition 5.3.1: Let $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } ) , i = 1 , \ldots , k$ be measurable spaces, $2 \leq$ $k < \infty$ . Then 

(a) $\times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \Omega _ { i } = \Omega _ { 1 } \times \ldots \times \Omega _ { k } = \{ ( \omega _ { 1 } , \ldots , \omega _ { i } ) : \omega : \in \Omega _ { i } { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } i = 1 , \ldots , k \}$ is called the product set of $\Omega _ { 1 } , \ldots , \Omega _ { k }$ 

(b) A set of the form $A _ { 1 } \times \ldots \times A _ { k }$ with $A _ { i } \in \mathcal { F } _ { i } , 1 \le i \le k$ is called a measurable rectangle. The product σ-algebra on $\times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \Omega _ { i }$ , denoted by $\times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \mathcal { F } _ { i }$ , is the σ-algebra generated by the collection of all measurable rectangles, i.e., 

$$
\times_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \mathcal {F} _ {i} = \sigma \langle \{A _ {1} \times \dots \times A _ {k}: A _ {i} \in \mathcal {F} _ {i}, 1 \leq i \leq k \} \rangle .
$$

(c) $\left( \times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \Omega _ { i } , \times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \mathcal { F } _ { i } \right)$ is called the product space or the product measurable space. When $\left( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } \right) = \left( \Omega , \mathcal { F } \right)$ for all $1 \leq i \leq k$ , the product space will be denoted by $( \Omega ^ { k } , \mathcal { F } ^ { k } )$ 

To define the product measure, one starts with a natural set function on ${ \mathcal { C } } ,$ , the class of all measurable rectangles, extends it to the algebra $\mathcal { A }$ of finite disjoint unions of measurable rectangles by linearity, and then uses the extension theorem (Theorem 1.3.3) to obtain a measure on the product space. The details of this construction are now described below. 

Define a set function $\mu$ on by 

$$
\mu (A) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \mu (A _ {i})\tag{3.1}
$$

where $A = A _ { 1 } \times A _ { 2 } \times \quad \times A _ { k }$ with $A _ { i } \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { i } , i = 1 , 2 , \dotsc , k$ . Next extend it to the algebra  by linearity. If $B \in { \mathcal { A } }$ is of the form $B = \textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { m } B _ { j }$ where $\{ B _ { j } : 1 , \ldots , m \} \subset { \mathcal { C } }$ are disjoint, then define $\mu ( B )$ by 

$$
\mu (B) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \mu (B _ {j}).\tag{3.2}
$$

If the set $B \in { \mathcal { A } }$ admits two diferent representations as finite unions of measurable rectangles then it is not dificult to verify that the value of $\mu ( B )$ remains unchanged. Next it is shown that $\mu$ is a measure on ${ \mathcal { A } } .$ 

Proposition 5.3.1:. Let µ be as defined by $( 3 . 1 )$ and (3.2) above on the algebra . Then, it is countably additive on $\mathcal { A }$ 

Proof: Let $\{ B _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \subset { \mathcal { A } }$ be disjoint such that $B = \textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } B _ { n }$ also belongs to ${ \mathcal { A } } .$ . It is enough to show that 

$$
\mu (B) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (B _ {n}).\tag{3.3}
$$

Let B and $\{ B _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ admit the representations $B \textstyle = \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { \ell } A _ { i }$ and $B _ { j } =$ $\textstyle \bigcup _ { r = 1 } ^ { \ell _ { j } } A _ { j r }$ where  and $\ell _ { j }$ are (finite) integers, $A _ { i } , A _ { j r } \in \mathcal { C }$ and each of the collections $\{ A _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { \ell }$ and $\left\{ A _ { j r } \right\} _ { r = 1 } ^ { \ell _ { j } } , j \ge 1$ is disjoint. Then each $A _ { i }$ can be written as 

$$
A _ {i} = A _ {i} \cap \left[ \bigcup_ {n \geq 1} B _ {n} \right] = \bigcup_ {n \geq 1} \bigcup_ {r = 1} ^ {\ell_ {n}} (A _ {i} \cap A _ {n r}).
$$

Suppose it is shown that for each $i \geq 1$ 5 

$$
\mu (A _ {i}) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {\ell_ {j}} \mu (A _ {i} \cap A _ {j r}).\tag{3.4}
$$

Then, by (3.2), 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu (B) & = & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} \mu (A _ {i}) \\ & = & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {\ell_ {j}} \mu (A _ {i} \cap A _ {j r}) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {\ell_ {j}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} \mu (A _ {i} \cap A _ {j r}) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {\ell_ {j}} \mu (B \cap A _ {j r}), \end{array}
$$

where the last equality follows from the representation of $B \cap A _ { j r }$ as $\cup _ { i = 1 } ^ { \ell } ( A _ { i } \cap A _ { j r } )$ and the fact that $A _ { i } \cap A _ { j r } \in \mathcal { C }$ for all $i , j , r$ . Since $A _ { j r } \subset B _ { j } \subset B$ , the above yields 

$$
\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {\ell_ {j}} \mu (A _ {j r}) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (B _ {j}) \quad (\text { by   (3.2) })
$$

which establishes (3.3). 

Thus, it remains to show (3.4). This is implied by the following: Let $\textstyle C = \bigcup _ { n > 1 } C _ { n }$ where $\{ C _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ is a collection of disjoint measurable rectangles and $C$ is also a measurable rectangle. Then 

$$
\mu (C) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (C _ {i}).\tag{3.5}
$$

Let $C = A _ { 1 } \times A _ { 2 } \times \quad \times A _ { k }$ and $C _ { i } = A _ { i 1 } \times A _ { i 2 } \times \quad \times A _ { i k } , i = 1 , 2 , \ldots .$ Since $\textstyle C = \bigcup _ { n > 1 } C _ { n }$ and $\{ C _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ are disjoint, this implies $I _ { C } ( \omega _ { 1 } , \dots , \omega _ { k } ) =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } I _ { C _ { i } } ( \omega _ { 1 } , \dot { . } . . , \omega _ { k } ) } \end{array}$ , for all $( \omega _ { 1 } , \ldots , \omega _ { k } ) \in \Omega _ { 1 } \times \ldots \times \Omega _ { k }$ . That is, 

$$
\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {k} I _ {A _ {j}} (\omega_ {j}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {k} I _ {A _ {i j}} (\omega_ {j})\tag{3.6}
$$

for all $( \omega _ { 1 } , \ldots , \omega _ { k } ) \in \Omega _ { 1 } \times \ldots \times \Omega _ { k }$ . Integration of both sides of (3.6) w.r.t. $\mu _ { 1 }$ over $\Omega _ { 1 }$ yields 

$$
\mu_ {1} (A _ {1}) \left(\prod_ {j = 2} ^ {k} I _ {A _ {j}} (\omega_ {j})\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu_ {1} (A _ {i 1}) \prod_ {j = 2} ^ {k} I _ {A _ {i j}} (\omega_ {j}),
$$

and by iteration 

$$
\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {k} \mu_ {j} (A _ {j}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {k} \mu_ {j} (A _ {i j}).
$$

Hence, (3.5) follows. 

By the extension theorem (Theorem 1.3.3), there exists a σ-algebra and a measure $\bar { \mu }$ such that 

(i) $( \times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \Omega _ { i } , { \mathcal { M } } , \bar { \mu } )$ is complete, 

(ii) $\times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } { \mathcal { F } } _ { i } \subset { \mathcal { M } }$ and 

$$
\text {(iii)} \bar {\mu} (A) = \mu (A) \quad \text { for   all } \quad A \in \mathcal {A}.
$$

Thus, the above procedure yields an extension $\bar { \mu }$ of $\mu$ on ${ \mathcal { A } } ,$ and this extension is unique when all the $\mu _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { s } } }$ are σ-finite. Further, under the hypothesis that $\mu _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mu _ { k }$ are σ-finite, the analogs of formulas (1.4) and (1.5) for computing the product measure of a set via the iterated integrals are valid. More generally, the Tonelli-Fubini theorems extend to the k-fold product spaces in an obvious manner. For example, if $\left( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } , \mu _ { i } \right)$ are σ-finite measure spaces for $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ and $f$ is a nonnegative measurable function on $( \times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \Omega _ { i } , \times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \mathcal F _ { i } , \bar { \mu } )$ , then 

$$
\int f d \bar {\mu} = \int_ {\Omega_ {i _ {1}}} \int_ {\Omega_ {i _ {2}}} \dots \int_ {\Omega_ {i _ {k}}} f (\omega_ {1}, \omega_ {2}, \quad \omega_ {k}) \mu_ {i _ {1}} (d \omega_ {i _ {1}}) \ldots \mu_ {i _ {k}} (d \omega_ {i _ {k}})
$$

for any permutation $( i _ { 1 } , i _ { 2 } , \ldots , i _ { k } )$ of $( 1 , 2 , \ldots , k )$ 

Definition 5.3.2: The measure space $( \times _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \Omega _ { i } , { \mathcal { M } } , \bar { \mu } )$ is called the complete product measure space and $\bar { \mu }$ the complete product measure. 

Remark 5.3.1: If $( \Omega _ { i } , \mathcal { F } _ { i } , \mu _ { i } ) \equiv ( \mathbb { R } , \mathcal { L } , m )$ where $\mathcal { L }$ is the Lebesgue $\sigma -$ algebra and m is the Lebesgue measure, then the above extension coincides with the $( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , \mathcal { L } ^ { k } , m ^ { k } )$ , where $\mathcal { L } ^ { k }$ is the Lebesgue σ-algebra in $\mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ and $m ^ { k }$ is the k dimensional Lebesgue measure. 

## 5.4 Convolutions

## 5.4.1 Convolution of measures on (R, (R))

In this section, convolution of measures on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ is discussed. From  -this, one can easily obtain convolution of sequences, convolution of functions in $L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ and convolution of functions with measures. 

Proposition 5.4.1: Let µ and λ be two σ-finite measures on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ For any Borel set A in $B ( \mathbb { R } )$ , let 

$$
(\mu * \lambda) (A) \equiv \int \int I _ {A} (x + y) \mu (d x) \lambda (d y).\tag{4.1}
$$

Then $( \mu * \lambda ) ( \cdot )$ <sup>is</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>measure</sup> <sup>on</sup> <sup>R,</sup> B<sup>(R) .</sup> 

Proof: Let $h ( x , y ) \equiv x + y$ for $( x , y ) \in \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R }$ . Then $h : \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } \to$ R is continuous and hence is $\langle B ( \mathbb { R } ) \times B ( \mathbb { R } ) , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable. Consider the measure $\left( \mu \times \lambda \right) h ^ { - 1 } ( \cdot )$ on R, (R) induced by the map h and the measure $\mu \times \lambda$ on $\langle \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \times B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ . Clearly 

$$
(\mu * \lambda) (\cdot) = (\mu \times \lambda) h ^ {- 1} (\cdot)
$$

and hence the proposition is proved. 

Definition 5.4.1: For any two σ-finite measures $\mu$ and λ on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ ， the measure $( \mu * \lambda ) ( A )$ defined in (4.1) is called the convolution of $\mu$ -and λ. 

The following proposition is easy to verify. 

Proposition 5.4.2: Let $\mu _ { 1 } , ~ \mu _ { 2 } , ~ \mu _ { 3 }$ be σ-finite measures $o n \ \left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ Then 

(i) (Commutativity) $\mu _ { 1 } * \mu _ { 2 } = \mu _ { 2 } * \mu _ { 1 }$ • 

(ii) (Associativity) $\mu _ { 1 } * ( \mu _ { 2 } * \mu _ { 3 } ) = ( \mu _ { 1 } * \mu _ { 2 } ) * \mu _ { 3 } ,$ 

(iii) (Distributive) $\mu _ { 1 } * ( \mu _ { 2 } + \mu _ { 3 } ) = \mu _ { 1 } * \mu _ { 2 } + \mu _ { 1 } * \mu _ { 3 } ,$ 

(iv) (Identity element) $\mu _ { 1 } * \delta _ { \{ 0 \} } = \mu _ { 1 }$ 

where $\delta _ { \{ 0 \} } ( \cdot )$ is the delta measure at 0, i.e., $\theta ,$ 

$$
\delta_ {\{0 \}} (A) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & i f \quad 0 \in A, \\ 0 & i f \quad 0 \not \in A \end{array} \right.
$$

for all $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } )$ 

Remark 5.4.1: (Extension to $\mathbb { R } ^ { k } )$ . Definition 5.4.1 extends to measures on $\left( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } ) \right)$ for any integer $k \geq 1$ as well as to any space that is a com- -mutative group under addition such as the sequence space $\mathbb { R } ^ { \infty }$ , the function spaces ${ \mathit { { C } } } [ 0 , 1 ]$ and ${ \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , \infty )$ . These are relevant in the study of stochastic processes. 

Remark 5.4.2: (Sums of independent random variables). It will be seen in Chapter $7$ that if X and $Y$ are two independent random variables on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ , then $P _ { X }$ * $P _ { Y } = P _ { X + Y }$ where for any random variable $Z$ on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P ) , P _ { Z }$ is the distribution of $Z , { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ , the probability measure on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ induced by $P$ and Z, i.e., $P _ { Z } ( \cdot ) = P Z ^ { - 1 } ( \cdot )$ on $B ( \mathbb { R } )$ 

Remark 5.4.3: (Extension to signed measures). Let $\mu$ and λ be two finite signed measures on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ as defined in Section 4.2. Let $\mu = \mu ^ { + } - \mu ^ { - }$ 2 $\lambda = \lambda ^ { + } - \lambda ^ { - }$  -be the Jordan decomposition of $\mu$ and $\lambda ,$ respectively. Then the product measure $\mu \times \lambda$ can be defined as the signed measure 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu \times \lambda & \equiv & \left[ (\mu^ {+} \times \lambda^ {+}) + (\mu^ {-} \times \lambda^ {-}) \right] - \left[ (\mu^ {+} \times \lambda^ {-}) + (\mu^ {-} + \lambda^ {+}) \right] \\ & \equiv & \gamma_ {1} - \gamma_ {2}, \quad \text { say. } \end{array}\tag{4.2}
$$

This is well defined since the measures $( \mu ^ { + } \times \lambda ^ { + } ) + ( \mu ^ { - } \times \lambda ^ { - } )$ and $( \mu ^ { + } \times$ $\lambda ^ { - } ) + ( \mu ^ { - } \times \lambda ^ { + } )$ are both finite measures. Now the definition of convolution of measures in (4.1) carries over to signed measures using the definition of integration w.r.t. signed measures discussed in Section 4.2. 

Definition 5.4.2: Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be (finite) signed measures on a measurable space $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ . The convolution of $\mu$ and $\nu ,$ denoted by $\mu * \nu$ is the signed  -measure defined by 

$$
(\mu * \nu) (A) = \int \int I _ {A} (x + y) d (\mu \times \nu)
$$

$$
= \int \int I _ {A} (x + y) d \gamma_ {1} - \int \int I _ {A} (x + y) d \gamma_ {2}\tag{4.3}
$$

where $\gamma _ { 1 }$ and $\gamma _ { 2 }$ are as in (4.2). 

## 5.4.2 Convolution of sequences

Definition 5.4.3: Let $\tilde { a } \equiv \{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ and $\tilde { b } \equiv \{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be two sequences of real numbers. Then the convolution of a˜ and $\tilde { b }$ denoted by ${ \tilde { a } } * { \tilde { b } }$ is the sequence 

$$
(\tilde {a} * \tilde {b}) (n) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} a _ {j} b _ {n - j}, n \geq 0.\tag{4.4}
$$

If $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty } \left| a _ { j } \right| < \infty$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty } \left| b _ { j } \right| < \infty$ , then $\tilde { a } * \tilde { b }$ corresponds to the convolution of the signed measures $\tilde { a }$ and $\tilde { b }$ on $\mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ , defined by $\tilde { a } ( i ) = a _ { i } , \tilde { b } ( i ) = b _ { i }$ 2 $i \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ 

## Example 5.4.1:

(a) Let $b _ { n } \equiv 1$ for $n \geq 0$ . Then for any $\begin{array} { r } { \{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 } , ( \tilde { a } * \tilde { b } ) ( n ) = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { n } a _ { j } , } \end{array}$ 

(b) Fix $0 < p < 1 , k _ { 1 } , k _ { 2 }$ positive integers. For $n \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ , let 

$$
a _ {n} \equiv \binom {k _ {1}} {n} p ^ {n} (1 - p) ^ {k _ {1} - n} I _ {[ 0, k _ {1} ]} (n)
$$

$$
b _ {n} \equiv \binom {k _ {2}} {n} p ^ {n} (1 - p) ^ {k _ {2} - n} I _ {[ 0, k _ {2} ]} (n).
$$

Then $\begin{array} { r } { ( \tilde { a } \ast \tilde { b } ) ( n ) = \binom { k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } } { n } p ^ { n } ( 1 - p ) ^ { k _ { 2 } - n } I _ { [ 0 , k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } ] } ( n ) . } \end{array}$ 

(c) Fix $0 < \lambda _ { 1 } , \lambda _ { 2 } < \infty$ . Let 

$$
a _ {n} \equiv e ^ {- \lambda_ {1}} \frac {\lambda_ {1} ^ {n}}{n !}, n = 0, 1, 2, \dots
$$

$$
b _ {n} \equiv e ^ {- \lambda_ {2}} \frac {\lambda_ {2} ^ {n}}{n !}, n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots .
$$

$$
\text { Then } (\tilde {a} * \tilde {b}) (n) = e ^ {- (\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2})} \frac {(\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {2}) ^ {n}}{n !}, n = 0, 1, 2, \dots .
$$

The verification of these claims is left as an exercise (Problem 5.20). 

A useful technique to determine $\tilde { a } * \tilde { b }$ is the use of generating functions. This will be discussed in Section 5.5. 

## 5.4.3 Convolution of functions in $L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$

Let $L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) \equiv L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) , m )$ where $m ( \cdot )$ is the Lebesgue measure. In the following, for $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ , f dm will also be written as $\textstyle \int f ( x ) d x$ 

Proposition 5.4.3: Let $f , g \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . Then for almost all $\textit { x } \left( w . r . t . \ m \right)$ 2 

$$
\int | f (x - u) | | g (u) | d u <   \infty .\tag{4.5}
$$

Proof: Let $k ( x , u ) = f ( x - u ) g ( u )$ . Since $\pi ( x , u ) \equiv x - u$ is a continuous map from $\mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ , it is $\langle B ( \mathbb { R } ) \times B ( \mathbb { R } ) , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable. Also, since $f$ and g are Borel measurable, it follows that $k : \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ is $\langle B ( \mathbb { R } ) \times$ $B ( \mathbb { R } ) , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \rangle$ -measurable. Also note that by the translation invariance of $m _ { ; }$ $\begin{array} { r } { \int | f ( x - u ) | d x = \int | f ( x ) | d x } \end{array}$ for any Borel measurable $f : \mathbb { R }  \mathbb { R }$ . Hence,  by Tonelli’s theorem, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int \int | k (x, u) | d x d u & = & \int \Big (\int | k (x, u) | d x \Big) d u \\ & = & \int | g (u) | \Big (\int | f (x) | d x \Big) d u \\ & = & \| g \| _ {1}   \| f \| _ {1} <   \infty . \end{array}\tag{4.6}
$$

Also by Tonelli’s theorem 

$$
\int \int | k (x, u) | d x d u = \int \Big (\int | k (x, u) | d u \Big) d x.
$$

By (4.6), this yields 

$$
\int | k (x, u) | d u <   \infty \quad \text { a.e. } \quad (m)
$$

which is the same as (4.5). 

Definition 5.4.4: Let $f , g \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb R )$ . Then the convolution of f and $^ { g , }$ denoted by $f * g$ is the function defined a.e. (m) by 

$$
(f * g) (x) \equiv \int f (x - u) g (u) d u.\tag{4.7}
$$

Note that by (4.5) this is well defined. 

Proposition 5.4.4: Let $f , g \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . Then 

(i) $f * g = g * f$ 

(ii) $f \ast g \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ and $\| f \ast g \| _ { 1 } \leq \| f \| _ { 1 } \| g \| _ { 1 }$ 

(iii) $\begin{array} { r } { \int f * g d m = \Big ( \int f d m \Big ) \Big ( \int g d m \Big ) . } \end{array}$ 

Proof: For (i), use the change of variable $u  x - u$ and the translation invariance of m. For (ii) use (4.6). For (iii), use Fubini’s theorem. ✷ 

It is easy to see that if $\mu$ and λ denote the signed measures with Radon-Nikodym derivatives $f$ and g, respectively, w.r.t. m, then $\mu * \lambda$ is the signed measure with Radon-Nikodym derivative $f * g$ w.r.t. m. 

## Example 5.4.2: Here are two examples from probability theory.

(a) (Convolutions of Uniform $[ 0 , 1 ]$ densities). Let $f = g = I _ { [ 0 , 1 ] }$ . Then 

$$
(f * g) (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{c c} x & 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\ 2 - x & 1 \leq x \leq 2. \end{array} \right.
$$

(b) (Convolutions of $N ( 0 , 1 )$ densities). Let $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x ) \equiv g ( x ) \equiv \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi } } e ^ { - \frac { x ^ { 2 } } { 2 } } } \end{array}$ ， $- \infty < x < \infty$ . Then $\begin{array} { r } { ( f * g ) ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi } } \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 } } e ^ { - \frac { x ^ { 2 } } { 4 } } , - \infty < x < \infty } \end{array}$ 

## $5 . 4 . 4$ Convolution of functions and measures

Let $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ and λ be a signed measure. Let $\textstyle \mu ( A ) \equiv \int _ { A } f d m , A \in { \mathcal { B } } ( \mathbb { R } )$ Then it can be shown that $\mu * \lambda$ is dominated by m and its Radon-Nikodym derivative is given by 

$$
f * \lambda (x) \equiv \int f (x - u) \lambda (d u), x \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{4.8}
$$

Note that $f * \lambda$ in (4.8) is well defined for any nonnegative Borel measurable $f$ and any measure λ on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ . 

## 5.5 Generating functions and Laplace transforms

Definition 5.5.1: Let $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be a sequence in R and let $\rho \quad =$ ${ \Big ( } \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } { \big | } a _ { n } { \big | } ^ { 1 / n } { \Big ) } ^ { - 1 }$ . The power series 

$$
A (s) \equiv \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} a _ {n} s ^ {n},\tag{5.1}
$$

defined for all s in $( - \rho , \rho )$ , is called the generating function of $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ 

Note that the power series in (5.1) converges absolutely for $| s | < \rho$ and $\rho$ is called the radius of convergence of $A ( s )$ (cf. Appendix A.2). 

The usefulness of generating functions is given by the following: 

Proposition 5.5.1: Let $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ and $\{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be two sequences in R. Let $\{ c _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be the convolution of $\left\{ a _ { n } \right\}$ and $\left\{ b _ { n } \right\}$ . That is, 

$$
c _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} a _ {j} b _ {n - j}, n \geq 0.
$$

Then 

$$
C (s) = A (s) B (s)\tag{5.2}
$$

for all s in $( - \rho , \rho )$ , where $A ( \cdot ) , \ B ( \cdot )$ , and $C ( \cdot )$ are, respectively, the generating function of the sequences $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 } , \{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ and $\{ c _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ and $\rho = \operatorname* { m i n } ( \rho _ { a } , \rho _ { b } )$ with $\rho _ { a } = \big ( \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } | a _ { n } | ^ { 1 / n } \big ) ^ { - 1 }$ and $\rho _ { b } = \big ( \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } | b _ { n } | ^ { 1 / n } \big ) ^ { - 1 }$ 

Proof: By Tonelli’s theorem applied to the counting measure on the product space $( \mathbb { Z } _ { + } \times \mathbb { Z } _ { + } )$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} | s | ^ {n} \bigg (\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} | a _ {j} |   | b _ {n - j} | \bigg) \\ = & \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} | a _ {j} |   | s | ^ {j} \bigg (\sum_ {n = j} ^ {\infty} | s | ^ {n - j} | b _ {n - j} | \bigg) \\ = & A (| s |) B (| s |) <   \infty \quad \text { if } \quad | s | <   \rho . \end{array}
$$

Now by Fubini’s theorem, (5.2) follows. 

It is easy to verify the claims in Example 5.4.1 by using the above proposition and the uniqueness of the power series coeficients (Problem 5.20). 

Proposition 5.5.2: (Renewal sequences). Let $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 } , \{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 } , \{ p _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be sequences in R such that 

$$
a _ {n} = b _ {n} + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} a _ {n - j} p _ {j}, n \geq 0\tag{5.3}
$$

and $p _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then 

$$
A (s) = \frac {B (s)}{1 - P (s)}
$$

for all s such that $| s | < \rho$ and $P ( s ) \neq 1$ , where $\rho = \mathrm { m i n } ( \rho _ { b } , \rho _ { p } ) , \ \rho _ { b } =$ $\big ( \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } | b _ { n } | ^ { 1 / n } \big ) ^ { - 1 } , \rho _ { p } = \big ( \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } | p _ { n } | ^ { 1 / n } \big ) ^ { - 1 }$ 

For applications of this to renewal theory, see Chapter 8. 

Definition 5.5.2: (Laplace transform). Let $f : [ 0 , \infty ) \to \mathbb { R }$ be Borel measurable. The function 

$$
(L f) (s) \equiv \int_ {[ 0, \infty)} e ^ {s x} f (x) d x,\tag{5.4}
$$

defined for all s in R such that 

$$
\int_ {[ 0, \infty)} e ^ {s x} | f (x) | d x <   \infty ,\tag{5.5}
$$

is called the Laplace transform of f. 

It is easily seen that if (5.5) holds for some $s = s _ { 0 }$ , then it does for all $s < s _ { 0 }$ . The analog of Proposition 5.5.1 is the following. 

Proposition 5.5.3: Let f, $g \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . Then 

$$
L (f * g) (s) = L f (s) L g (s)\tag{5.6}
$$

for all s such that (5.5) holds for both f and $g$ . 

Definition 5.5.3: (Laplace-Stieltjes transform). Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ such that $\mu \big ( ( - \infty , 0 ) \big ) = 0$ . The function 

$$
\mu^ {*} (s) \equiv L \mu (s) \equiv \int_ {[ 0, \infty)} e ^ {s x} \mu (d x)
$$

is called the Laplace-Stieltjes transform of $\mu .$ . Clearly, $\mu ^ { * } ( s )$ is well defined for all $s$ in R. However, $\mu ^ { * } ( s _ { 0 } ) = \infty$ implies $\mu ^ { * } ( s ) = \infty$ for $s \geq s _ { 0 }$ 

Proposition 5.5.4: Let $\mu$ and λ be measures on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ such that $\mu \big ( ( - \infty , 0 ) \big ) = 0 = \lambda \big ( ( - \infty , 0 ) \big )$ . Then 

$$
L (\mu * \lambda) (s) = L \mu (s) L \lambda (s) f o r a l l s \text { in } \mathbb {R}.
$$

For an inversion formula to obtain a probability measure $\mu$ from $L \mu ( \cdot )$ ， see Feller (1966), Section 13.4. 

## 5.6 Fourier series

In this section, $L ^ { p } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ stands for $L ^ { p } \bigl ( [ 0 , 2 \pi ] , B ( [ 0 , 2 \pi ] ) , m \bigr )$ where $m ( \cdot )$ is Lebesgue measure and $0 < p < \infty$ 

Definition 5.6.1: For $f \in L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] , n \geq 0$ , let 

$$
a _ {n} \equiv \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) \cos n x d x
$$

$$
{b _ {n}} \equiv {\frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) \sin n x d x,}\tag{6.1}
$$

$$
s _ {n} (f, x) \equiv a _ {0} + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \left(a _ {j} \cos j x + b _ {j} \sin j x\right).\tag{6.2}
$$

Then $\{ a _ { n } , b _ { n } , n = 0 , 1 , 2 , . . . \}$ are called the Fourier coeficients of $f$ and the sequence $\{ s _ { n } ( f , x ) : n = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots \}$ is called the partial sum sequence of the Fourier series expansion $o f f$ 

Since $\mathcal { C } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] \subset L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] \subset L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , the Fourier coeficients and the partial sum sequence of the Fourier series are well defined for $f$ in ${ \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ and f in $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . J. Fourier introduced these series in the early 19th century to approximate certain functions exhibiting a periodic behavior that arose in the study of physics and mechanics and in particular in the theory of heat conduction (see K¨orner (1989) and Bhatia (2003)). 

A natural question is: In what sense does $s _ { n } ( f , x )$ approximate $f ( x ) \ell$ It turns out that one can prove the strongest results for f in ${ \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , less stronger results for $f$ in $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , and finally, for f in $L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ 

In the early 19th century it was believed that for any f in ${ \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ $s _ { n } ( f , x )$ converged to $f ( x )$ for all x in $[ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . But in 1876, D. Raymond constructed a continuous function f for which $\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \operatorname* { l i m } } } _ { n \to \infty } | s _ { n } ( f ; x _ { 0 } ) | = \infty } \end{array}$ for some $x _ { 0 }$ . However, Fejer showed in 1903 that for f in $\mathcal { C } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] , s _ { n } ( f , \cdot )$ does converge to $f$ uniformly in the Cesaro sense. 

Theorem 5.6.1: $( F e j e r )$ . Let $f \in \mathcal { C } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ and $s _ { n } ( f , \cdot ) , n \geq 0$ be as in Definition 3.4.1. Let 

$$
\mathcal {D} _ {n} (f, \cdot) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} s _ {j} (f, \cdot), n \geq 1.\tag{6.3}
$$

Then 

$$
\mathcal {D} _ {n} (f, \cdot) \to f (\cdot) \quad u n i f o r m l y o n \quad [ 0, 2 \pi ] \quad a s \quad n \to \infty .\tag{6.4}
$$

For the proof of this result, the following result of some independent interest is needed. 

Lemma 5.6.2: (Fejer). Let for m $\geq 1$ 

$$
K _ {m} (x) \equiv 1 + \frac {2}{m} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m - 1} (m - j) \cos j x, x \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{6.5}
$$

Then 

(i) 

$$
K _ {m} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{c c c} \frac {1}{m} \bigg (\frac {\sin \frac {m x}{2}}{\sin \frac {x}{2}} \bigg) ^ {2} & \text {if} & x \neq 0 \\ m & \text {if} & x = 0. \end{array} \right.\tag{6.6}
$$

(ii) For $\delta > 0$ 

$$
\sup \{K _ {m} (x): \delta \leq | x | \leq 2 \pi - \delta \} \rightarrow 0 \quad a s \quad m \rightarrow \infty .\tag{6.7}
$$

(iii) 

$$
\frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} K _ {m} (x) d x = 1.\tag{6.8}
$$

Proof: Clearly, (iii) follows from (6.5) on integration. Also, (ii) follows from (i) since for $\delta \leq x \leq 2 \pi - \delta$ 2 

$$
K _ {m} (x) \leq \frac {1}{m} \frac {1}{(\sin {\frac {\delta}{2}}) ^ {2}} \rightarrow 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad m \rightarrow \infty .
$$

To establish (i) note that using Euler’s formula (cf. Section A.3, Appendix) $e ^ { \iota x } = \cos x + \iota$ sin x, $K _ { m } ( x )$ can be written as 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} K _ {m} (x) & = & \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {j = - (m - 1)} ^ {(m - 1)} (m - | j |) e ^ {\iota j x} \\ & = & \frac {1}{m} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {2 (m - 1)} (m - | j - (m - 1) |) e ^ {\iota (j - (m - 1)) x} \\ & = & \frac {1}{m} \bigg (\sum_ {k = 0} ^ {m - 1} e ^ {\iota (k - \frac {m - 1}{2}) x} \bigg) ^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

For $x \neq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} {K _ {m} (x)} & = & {\frac {1}{m} \Big (e ^ {- \frac {\iota (m - 1) x}{2}} \frac {1 - e ^ {\iota m x}}{1 - e ^ {\iota x}} \Big) ^ {2},} \\ & = & {\frac {1}{m} \Big (\frac {e ^ {- \frac {\iota m x}{2}} - e ^ {\frac {\iota m x}{2}}}{e ^ {- \frac {\iota x}{2}} - e ^ {\frac {\iota x}{2}}} \Big) ^ {2},} \\ & = & {\frac {1}{m} \Big (\frac {\sin \frac {m x}{2}}{\sin \frac {x}{2}} \Big) ^ {2}.} \end{array}
$$

For $x = 0 .$ , (6.5) yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} K _ {m} (0) & = & 1 + \frac {2}{m} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m - 1} (m - j) \\ & = & 1 + \frac {2}{m} \frac {(m - 1) m}{2} = m. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 5.6.1: Let $f \in { \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . Let $\{ a _ { n } , b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 } , \ s _ { n } ( f , \cdot )$ 2 $\mathcal { D } _ { m } ( f , \cdot )$ be as in (6.1), (6.2), and (6.3). Then from the definition of $a _ { n } , b _ { n } , n \geq 0$ , it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mathcal {D} _ {m} (f, \cdot) & = & \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} K _ {m} (x - u) f (u) d u \\ & = & \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x - u) K _ {m} (u) d u \end{array}\tag{6.9}
$$

where $K _ { m } ( \cdot )$ is defined in (6.5) and $f ( \cdot )$ is extended to all of R periodically with period 2π. Since $f \in { \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , given $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
x, y \in [ 0, 2 \pi ], | x - y | <   \delta \Rightarrow | f (x) - f (y) | <   \epsilon .
$$

Also from (6.7), for this $\delta > 0$ , there exist an $m _ { 0 }$ such that m $\geq m _ { 0 } \Rightarrow$ sup $\left\{ K _ { m } ( x ) : \delta \leq x \leq 2 \pi - \delta \right\} < \epsilon$ . Now (6.9) yields, for $x \in [ 0 , 2 \pi ] , m \geq m _ { 0 }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} | \mathcal {D} _ {m} (f, x) - f (x) | & \leq & \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} | f (x - u) - f (x) | K _ {m} (u) d u \\ & = & \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {(\delta \leq u \leq 2 \pi - \delta) ^ {c}} | f (x - u) - f (x) | K _ {m} (u) d u \\ & & + \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {(\delta \leq u \leq 2 \pi - \delta)} | f (x - u) - f (x) | K _ {m} (u) d u \\ & \leq & \frac {1}{2 \pi} (\epsilon + 2 \| f \| \epsilon 2 \pi) \end{array}
$$

where $\| f \| = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ | f ( x ) | : x \in [ 0 , 2 \pi ] \}$ . Thus, $m \geq m _ { 0 } \Rightarrow \operatorname* { s u p } \{ | \mathcal { D } _ { m } ( f , x ) -$ $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x ) \vert : x \in [ 0 , 2 \pi ] \} \leq \epsilon { \frac { ( 1 + 4 \pi \| f \| ) } { 2 \pi } } } \end{array}$ . Since $\epsilon > 0$ is arbitrary, the proof of Theorem $5 . 6 . 1$ is complete. ✷ 

An immediate consequence of Theorem 5.6.1 is the completeness of the trigonometric functions. 

Theorem 5.6.3: The collection $\mathcal { T } _ { 0 } \equiv \{ \cos n x : n = 0 , 1 , 2 , . . . \} \cup \{ \sin n x :$ $n = 1 , 2 , \ldots \}$ is a complete orthogonal system for $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ 

Proof: By Theorem 5.6.1 for each $f \in { \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ and $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists a finite linear combination $\mathcal { D } _ { m } ( f , \cdot )$ of $\left\{ \cos n x : n = 0 , 1 , 2 , . . . \right\}$ and sin nx : $n = 1 , 2 , \ldots \}$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} | f - \mathcal {D} _ {m} (f, \cdot) | ^ {2} d x \\ \leq 2 \pi (\sup \{| f (x) - \mathcal {D} _ {m} (f, x) |: x \in [ 0, 2 \pi ] \}) ^ {2} <   \epsilon^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

Also, from Theorem 2.3.14 it is known that given any $g \in L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , and any $\epsilon > 0$ , there is a $f \in { \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { 2 \pi } | f - g | ^ { 2 } d x < \epsilon ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . Thus, for any $g \in L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] , \epsilon > 0$ , there is a $f \in { \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ and an m $\geq 1$ such that 

$$
\left\| g - \mathcal {D} _ {m} (f, \cdot) \right\| _ {2} <   2 \epsilon .
$$

That is, the set $\tau$ of all finite linear combinations of the functions in the class $\mathcal { T } _ { 0 }$ is dense in $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . Further, it is easy to verify that $h _ { 1 } , h _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { T } _ { 0 }$ 2 $h _ { 1 } \neq h _ { 2 }$ implies 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} h _ {1} (x) h _ {2} (x) d x = 0,
$$

i.e., $\mathcal { T } _ { 0 }$ is an orthogonal family. Since $\mathcal { T } _ { 0 }$ is orthogonal and $\tau$ is dense in $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , $\mathcal { T } _ { 0 }$ is complete. ✷ 

Definition 5.6.2: A function in $\tau$ is called a trigonometric polynomial. Thus, the above theorem says that trigonometric polynomials are dense in $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . Completeness of $\tau$ in $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , \bar { 2 } \pi ]$ and the results of Section 3.3 lead to 

Theorem 5.6.4: Let $f \in L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . Let $\{ ( a _ { n } , b _ { n } ) , n \ = \ 0 , 1 , 2 , . . . \}$ and $\{ s _ { n } ( f , \cdot ) \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be the associated Fourier coeficient sequences and partial sum sequence of the Fourier series for f as in Definition 5.6.1. Then 

(i) $s _ { n } ( f , \cdot ) \to f \ i n \ L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] ,$ 

(ii) $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } ( \breve { a } _ { n } ^ { 2 } + \breve { b } _ { n } ^ { 2 } ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } \int _ { 0 } ^ { 2 \pi } | f | ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ dx where for $n \ge 0 , \breve { a } _ { n } = a _ { n } / c _ { n }$ , with $\begin{array} { r } { c _ { n } ^ { 2 } \ = \ \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } \int _ { 0 } ^ { 2 \pi } ( \cos n x ) ^ { 2 } d x \ = \ \frac 1 2 } \end{array}$ , and for $\begin{array} { r } { n \ge 1 , ~ \breve { b } _ { n } = \frac { b _ { n } } { d _ { n } } } \end{array}$ with $d _ { n } ^ { 2 } =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } \int _ { 0 } ^ { 2 \pi } ( \sin n x ) ^ { 2 } d x = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ 

(iii) Further, if f, $\begin{array} { r l r } { g } & { { } \in } & { L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] } \end{array}$ , then $\begin{array} { l l l } { { { \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } } \int _ { 0 } ^ { 2 \pi } f g d x } } & { { = } } & { { a _ { 0 } \alpha _ { 0 } \ + } } \end{array}$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \left( { \frac { a _ { n } \alpha _ { n } } { c _ { n } ^ { 2 } } } + { \frac { b _ { n } \beta _ { n } } { d _ { n } ^ { 2 } } } \right) } \end{array}$ , where $\{ ( a _ { n } , b _ { n } ) \quad : \quad n = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots \}$ and $\{ ( \alpha _ { n } , \dot { \beta _ { n } } ) : n = 0 , 1 , \dot { 2 } , . . . \}$ are, respectively, the Fourier coeficients of f and g. 

Clearly (ii) above is a restatement of Bessel’s equality. Assertion (iii) is known as the Parseval identity. As for convergence pointwise or almost everywhere, A. N. Kolmogorov showed in 1926 (see K¨orner (1989)) that there exists an $f \in L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ such that ${ \overline { { \operatorname* { l i m } } } } _ { n \to \infty } | s _ { n } ( f , x ) | = \infty$ everywhere on $[ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . This led to the belief that for $f \notin { \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , the mean square convergence of (i) in Theorem 5.6.4 cannot be improved upon. But L. Carleson showed in 1964 (see K¨orner (1989)) that for f in $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] , s _ { n } ( f , \cdot ) \to f ( \cdot )$ almost everywhere. Finally, turning to $L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , one has the following: 

Theorem 5.6.5: Let $f \in L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . Let $\left\{ \left( a _ { n } , b _ { n } \right) : n \geq 0 \right\}$ be as in (6.1) and satisfy $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } ( | a _ { n } | + | b _ { n } | ) < \infty$ . Let $s _ { n } ( f , \cdot )$ be as in $( 6 . 2 )$ . Then $s _ { n } ( f , \cdot )$ converges uniformly on [0, 2π] and the limit coincides with f almost everywhere. 

Proof: Note that $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } ( | a _ { n } | + | b _ { n } | ) < \infty$ implies that the sequence $\{ s _ { n } ( f , \cdot ) \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a Cauchy sequence in the Banach space ${ \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ with the sup-norm. Thus, there exists a $g$ in ${ \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ such that $s _ { n } ( f , \cdot ) \to g$ uniformly on [0, 2π]. It is easy to check that this implies that g and $f$ have the same Fourier coeficients. Set $h = g - f$ . Then $h \in L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ and the Fourier coeficients of h are all zero. This implies that h is orthogonal to the members of the class  , which in turn yields that h is orthogonal to all 

continuous functions in ${ \mathcal { C } } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , i.e., 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} h (x) k (x) d x = 0
$$

for all $k \in \mathcal { C } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . Since $h \in L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ and for any interval $A \subset [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ 2 there exists a sequence $\{ k _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ of uniformly bounded continuous functions, such that $k _ { n }  I _ { A }$ a.e. (m), by the DCT, 

$$
\int h (x) I _ {A} (x) d x = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int h (x) k _ {n} (x) d x = 0.
$$

This in turn implies that $h = 0 { \mathrm { ~ a . e . , ~ i . e . , ~ } } g = f { \mathrm { ~ a . e . } }$ 

Remark 5.6.1: If $f \in L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , the Fourier coeficients $\{ a _ { n } , b _ { n } \}$ are square summable and hence go to zero as $n \to \infty$ . What if $f \in L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ] ?$ 

If $f \in L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , one can assert the following: 

Theorem 5.6.6: (Riemann-Lebesgue lemma). Let $f \in L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ . Then 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) \cos n x d x = 0 = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) \sin n x d x.
$$

Proof: The lemma holds if $f = I _ { A }$ for any interval $A \subset [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ and since step functions $( { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ , linear combinations of indicator functions of intervals) are dense in $L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ , the lemma is proved. ✷ 

It can be shown that the mapping $f  \{ ( a _ { n } , b _ { n } ) \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ from $L ^ { 1 } [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ to bivariate sequences that go to zero as $n  \infty$ is one-to-one but not onto (Rudin (1987), Chapter 5). 

Remark 5.6.2: (The complex case). Let $T \equiv \{ z : z = e ^ { \imath \theta } , 0 \leq \theta \leq 2 \pi \}$ be the unit circle in the complex plane C. Every function $g : T  \mathbb { C }$ can be identified with a function f on R by $f ( t ) = g ( e ^ { \iota t } )$ . Clearly, $f ( \cdot )$ is periodic on R with period $2 \pi$ . In the rest of this section, for $0 < p < \infty , L ^ { p } ( T )$ will stand for the collection of all Borel measurable functions $f : [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ to C such that $\textstyle \int _ { [ 0 , 2 \pi ] } | f | ^ { p } d m < \infty$ where $m ( \cdot )$ is the Lebesgue measure. A trigonometric polynomial is a function of form 

$$
f (\cdot) \equiv \sum_ {n = - k} ^ {k} \alpha_ {n} e ^ {\imath n x} \equiv a _ {0} + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {k} (a _ {n} \cos n x + b _ {n} \sin n x),
$$

$k < \infty$ , where $\{ \alpha _ { n } \} , \{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ , and $\{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ are sequences of complex numbers. 

The completeness of the trigonometric polynomials proved in Theorem 5.6.3 implies that the family $\{ e ^ { \iota n x } : n = 0 , \pm 1 , \pm 2 , \ldots \}$ is a complete orthonormal basis for $L ^ { 2 } ( T )$ , which is a complex Hilbert space. 

Thus Theorem 5.6.4 carries over to this case. 

## Theorem 5.6.7:

(i) Let $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( T )$ . Then, 

$$
\sum_ {n = - k} ^ {k} \alpha_ {n} e ^ {\iota n x} \rightarrow f i n L ^ {2} (T)
$$

where 

$$
\alpha_ {n} \equiv \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) e ^ {- \imath n s} d x, n \in \mathbb {Z}.
$$

Further, 

$$
\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} | \alpha_ {n} | ^ {2} = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} | f | ^ {2} d m.
$$

(ii) For any sequence $\{ \alpha _ { n } \} _ { n \in \mathbb { Z } }$ of complex numbers such that $\scriptstyle \sum _ { n = - \infty } ^ { \infty } | \alpha _ { n } | ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , the sequence $\begin{array} { r } { \left\{ f _ { k } ( x ) \equiv \sum _ { n = - k } ^ { k } \alpha _ { n } e ^ { \iota n x } \right\} _ { k \geq 1 } } \end{array}$ converges in $L ^ { 2 } ( T )$ to a unique f such that 

$$
\alpha_ {n} = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) e ^ {- \imath n x} d x.
$$

(iii) For any f, $g \in L ^ { 2 } ( T )$ 

$$
\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} \alpha_ {n} \bar {\beta} _ {n} = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) \overline {{g (x)}} d x
$$

where 

$$
\alpha_ {n} = \hat {f} (n) = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) e ^ {- \iota n x} d x,
$$

$$
\beta_ {n} = \hat {g} (n) = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} g (x) e ^ {- \iota n x} d x, n \in \mathbb {Z}.
$$

Further, 

$$
\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} | \alpha_ {n} \beta_ {n} | <   \infty .
$$

$L ^ { 2 } ( T )$ is isomorphic to $\ell _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { Z } )$ , the Hilbert space of all square summable sequences of complex numbers on $\mathbb { Z }$ 

Similarly, Theorem 5.6.5 carries over to the complex case. 

Theorem 5.6.8: Let $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( T )$ . Suppose 

$$
\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} | \hat {f} (n) | <   \infty
$$

where 

$$
\hat {f} (n) = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} f (x) e ^ {- \iota n x} d x, n \in \mathbb {Z}.
$$

Then 

$$
s _ {n} (f, x) \equiv \sum_ {j = - n} ^ {n} \hat {f} (j) e ^ {- \iota j x}
$$

converges uniformly on $[ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ and the limit coincides with f a.e. and hence $f$ is continuous a.e. 

## 5.7 Fourier transforms on R

In this section and in Section 5.8, let $L ^ { p } ( \mathbb { R } )$ stand for 

$$
L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R}) \equiv \{f: f: \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {C}, \text {   Borel   measurable,   } \int_ {\mathbb {R}} | f | ^ {p} d m <   \infty \}\tag{7.1}
$$

where $m ( \cdot )$ is Lebesgue measure. Also, for $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , \int _ { \mathbb { R } }$ fdm will often be written as $\textstyle \int f ( x ) d x$ . Let 

$$
\mathcal {C} _ {0} \equiv \{f: f: \mathbb {R} \to \mathbb {C}, \text {   continuous   and   } \lim _ {| x | \to \infty} f (x) = 0 \}.\tag{7.2}
$$

Definition 5.7.1: For $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , t \in \mathbb { R }$ 

$$
\hat {f} (t) \equiv \int f (x) e ^ {- \iota t x} d x\tag{7.3}
$$

is called the Fourier transform of f. 

Proposition 5.7.1: Let $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ and ${ \hat { f } } ( \cdot )$ be as in (7.3). Then 

(i) $\hat { f } ( \cdot ) \in \mathcal { C } _ { 0 }$ 

$$
(i i) \text {   If   } f _ {a} (x) \equiv f (x - a), a \in \mathbb {R}, \text {   then   } \hat {f} _ {a} (t) = e ^ {\iota t a} \hat {f} (t), t \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

Proof: 

(i) For any $t \in \mathbb { R } , t _ { n } \to t \Rightarrow e ^ { \iota t _ { n } x } f ( x ) \to e ^ { \iota t x } f ( x )$ for all $x \in \mathbb { R }$ and since $| e ^ { \iota t _ { n } x } f ( x ) | \leq | f ( x ) |$ for all n and x, by the DCT ${ \hat { f } } ( t _ { n } ) \to { \hat { f } } ( t )$ . To show that ${ \hat { f } } ( t ) \to 0 { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } | t | \to \infty .$ , the same proof as that of Theorem 5.6.6 works. Thus, it holds if $f = I _ { [ a , b ] }$ , for $a , b \in \mathbb { R } , a < b$ and since the step functions are dense in $L ^ { 1 } ( { \dot { \mathbb { R } } } )$ , it holds for all $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ 

(ii) This is a consequence of the translation invariance of $m ( \cdot ) , \operatorname { i . e . , } m ( A +$ $a ) = m ( A )$ for all $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } ) , a \in \mathbb { R }$ ✷ 

The continuity of ${ \hat { f } } ( \cdot )$ can be strengthened to diferentiability if, in addition to $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , x f ( x ) \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . More generally, if $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ and $x ^ { k } f ( x ) \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ for some $k \geq 1$ , then ${ \hat { f } } ( \cdot )$ is diferentiable k-times with all derivatives $\hat { f } ^ { ( r ) } ( t ) \to 0$ as $| t |  \infty$ for $r \leq k$ (Problem 5.22). 

Proposition 5.7.2: Let $f , g \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb R )$ and $f * g$ be their convolution as defined in $( 4 . 7 )$ . Then 

$$
\widehat {f * g} = \hat {f} \hat {g}.\tag{7.4}
$$

Proof: 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \widehat {f * g} (t) & = & \int_ {\mathbb {R}} e ^ {- \iota t x} \Big (\int_ {\mathbb {R}} f (x - u) g (u) d u \Big) d x \\ & = & \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \Big (\int_ {\mathbb {R}} e ^ {- \iota t (x - u)} f (x - u) e ^ {- \iota t u} g (u) d u \Big) d x \\ & = & \int_ {\mathbb {R}} (f _ {t} * g _ {t}) (x) d x \end{array}\tag{7.5}
$$

where $f _ { t } ( x ) = e ^ { - \iota t x } f ( x ) , g _ { t } ( x ) = e ^ { - \iota t x } g ( x )$ . Thus, by Proposition 5.4.4 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \widehat {f * g} (t) & = & \Big (\int_ {\mathbb {R}} f _ {t} (x) d x \Big) \Big (\int_ {\mathbb {R}} g _ {t} (x) d x \Big) \\ & = & \hat {f} (t) \hat {g} (t). \end{array}
$$

The process of recovering f from ${ \hat { f } } ( { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ , that of finding an inversion formula) can be developed along the lines of Fejer’s theorem (Theorem 5.6.1). 

Theorem 5.7.3: (Fejer’s theorem). Let $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } ) , \hat { f } ( \cdot )$ be as in (7.3) and 

$$
{S _ {T} (f, x)} \equiv {\frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {- T} ^ {T} \hat {f} (t) e ^ {\iota t x} d t, T \geq 0,}\tag{7.6}
$$

$$
D _ {R} (f, x) \equiv \frac {1}{R} \int_ {0} ^ {R} S _ {T} (f, x) d T, R \geq 0.\tag{7.7}
$$

(i) $I f f$ is continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ and f is bounded on R, then 

$$
\lim _ {R \to \infty} D _ {R} (f, x _ {0}) = f (x _ {0}).\tag{7.8}
$$

(ii) If f is uniformly continuous and bounded on $\mathbb { R }$ , then 

$$
\lim _ {R \to \infty} D _ {R} (f, \cdot) = f (\cdot) \text {   uniformly   on   } \mathbb {R}.\tag{7.9}
$$

(iii) As $R \to \infty$ 

$$
D _ {R} (f, \cdot) \to f (\cdot) \quad i n \quad L ^ {1} (\mathbb {R}).\tag{7.10}
$$

(iv) If $f \in L ^ { p } ( \mathbb { R } ) , 1 \leq p < \infty$ , then as $R \to \infty$ ， 

$$
D _ {R} (f, \cdot) \to f (\cdot) \quad i n \quad L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R}).\tag{7.11}
$$

Corollary 5.7.4: (Uniqueness theorem). If f and $g \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ and ${ \hat { f } } ( \cdot ) =$ ${ \hat { g } } ( \cdot )$ , then $f = g a . e . \ ( m )$ 

Proof: Let $h = f - g$ . Then $h \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ and $\hat { h } ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ . Thus, $S _ { T } ( h , \cdot ) \equiv 0$ and $D _ { R } ( h , \cdot ) \equiv 0$ where $S _ { T } ( h , \cdot )$ and $D _ { R } ( h , \cdot )$ are as in (7.6) and (7.7). Hence by Theorem 5.7.3 (iii), $h = 0$ a.e. (m), i.e., f = g a.e. (m). ✷ 

Corollary 5.7.5: (Inversion formula). Let $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ and ${ \hat { f } } \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ Then 

$$
f (x) = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \hat {f} (t) e ^ {\iota t x} d x \quad a. e. \quad (m).\tag{7.12}
$$

Proof: Since ${ \hat { f } } \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ , by the DCT, 

$$
S _ {T} (f, x) \rightarrow \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \hat {f} (t) e ^ {\iota t x} d t \quad \mathrm{as} \quad T \rightarrow \infty
$$

for all x in R and hence $D _ { R } ( f , x )$ has the same limit as $R \to \infty$ . Now (7.12) follows from (7.10). ✷ 

The following results, i.e., Lemma 5.7.6 and Lemma 5.7.7, are needed for the proof of Theorem 5.7.3. The first one is an analog of Lemma 5.6.2. 

Lemma 5.7.6: (Fejer). For $R > 0$ , let 

$$
K _ {R} (x) \equiv \frac {1}{2 \pi} \frac {1}{R} \int_ {0} ^ {R} \Big (\int_ {- T} ^ {T} e ^ {\iota t x} d t \Big) d T.\tag{7.13}
$$

Then 

(i) 

$$
K _ {R} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {1}{\pi} \frac {(1 - \cos R x)}{x ^ {2}}, & x \neq 0 \\ \frac {R}{2 \pi} & x = 0, \end{array} \right.\tag{7.14}
$$

and hence $K _ { R } ( \cdot ) \geq 0$ 

(ii) For $\delta > 0$ 

$$
\int_ {| x | \geq \delta} K _ {R} (x) d x \to 0 \quad a s \quad R \to \infty .\tag{7.15}
$$

(iii) 

$$
\int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} K _ {R} (x) d x = 1.\tag{7.16}
$$

Proof: 

(i) $\begin{array} { r } { K _ { R } ( 0 ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi R } \int _ { 0 } ^ { R } ( 2 T ) d T = \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } R . } \end{array}$ . For $x \neq 0$ and $R > 0$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} {K _ {R} (x)} & = & {\frac {1}{2 \pi R} \int_ {0} ^ {R} \frac {2 \sin T x}{x} d T} \\ & = & {\frac {1}{2 \pi R} \frac {2 (1 - \cos R x)}{x ^ {2}}.} \end{array}
$$

(ii) For $\delta > 0$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} 0 \leq \int_ {| x | \geq \delta} K _ {R} (x) d x & \leq & \frac {2}{2 \pi R} \int_ {| x | \geq \delta} \frac {1}{x ^ {2}}   d x \\ & = & \frac {2}{\pi R} \frac {1}{\delta} \to 0 \quad \text { as } \quad R \to \infty . \end{array}
$$

(iii) 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} K _ {R} (x) d x & = & \frac {2}{\pi} \frac {1}{R} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \Big (\frac {1 - \cos R x}{x ^ {2}} \Big) d x \\ & = & \frac {2}{\pi} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \Big (\frac {1 - \cos u}{u ^ {2}} \Big) d u. \end{array}
$$

Now 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1 - \cos u}{u ^ {2}} d u} \\ & {= \lim _ {L \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {L} \Big (\frac {1 - \cos u}{u ^ {2}} \Big) d u \quad \mathrm{(bytheMCT)}} \\ & {= \lim _ {L \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {L} \Big (\int_ {0} ^ {u} \sin x d x \Big) \frac {1}{u ^ {2}} d u} \\ & {= \lim _ {L \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {L} \sin x \Big (\int_ {x} ^ {L} \frac {1}{u ^ {2}} d u \Big) d x \quad \mathrm {(byFubin i^ {\prime} stheorem)}} \\ & {= \lim _ {L \to \infty} \Big (\int_ {0} ^ {L} \frac {\sin x}{x} d x - \frac {1}{L} \int_ {0} ^ {L} \sin x d x \Big)} \\ & {= \lim _ {L \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {L} \frac {\sin x}{x} d x \quad \mathrm{since} \quad \Big | \int_ {0} ^ {L} \sin x d x \Big | \leq 1.} \end{array}
$$

Thus, 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1 - \cos u}{u ^ {2}} d u = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\sin x}{x} d x = \frac {\pi}{2}\tag{7.17}
$$

(cf. Problem 5.9). Hence (iii) follows. 

Lemma 5.7.7: Let $f \in L ^ { p } ( \mathbb { R } ) , 0 < p < \infty$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} | f (x - u) - f (x) | ^ {p} d x \rightarrow 0 \quad a s \quad | u | \rightarrow 0.\tag{7.18}
$$

Proof: The lemma holds if $f \in \mathcal { C } _ { K } , \mathrm { i . e . }$ , if f is continuous on R (with values in C) and vanishes outside a bounded interval. By Theorem 2.3.14, such functions are dense in $L ^ { p } ( \mathbb { R } )$ . So given $f \in L ^ { p } ( \mathbb { R } ) , 0 < p < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ , let $g \in { \mathcal { C } } _ { K }$ be such that 

$$
\int | f - g | ^ {p} d m <   \epsilon .
$$

For any $0 < p < \infty$ , there is a $0 < c _ { p } < \infty$ such that for all $x , y , z \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 2 $| x + y + z | ^ { p } \leq c _ { p } ( | x | ^ { p } + | y | ^ { p } + | z | ^ { p } )$ . Then, 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \int | f (x - u) - f (x) | ^ {p} d x \\ \leq & c _ {p} \int \big (| f (x - u) - g (x - u) | ^ {p} + | g (x - u) - g (x) | ^ {p} \\ & + \int | g (x) - f (x) | ^ {p} \big) d x \\ = & c _ {p} \Big (2 \epsilon + \int | g (x - u) - g (x) | ^ {p} \Big) d u. \end{array}
$$

So 

$$
\varlimsup_ {| u | \rightarrow 0} \int | f (x - u) - f (x) | ^ {p} d x \leq c _ {p}   2 \epsilon .
$$

Since $\epsilon > 0$ is arbitrary, the lemma is proved. 

Proof of Theorem 5.7.3: From (7.7) 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} D _ {R} (f, x) & \equiv & \frac {1}{2 \pi R} \int_ {0} ^ {R} \Big (\int_ {- T} ^ {T} e ^ {\iota t x} \Big (\int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- \iota t y} f (y) d y \Big) d t \Big) d T \\ & = & \frac {1}{2 \pi} \frac {1}{R} \int_ {0} ^ {R} \Big (\int_ {- T} ^ {T} \Big (\int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} e ^ {\iota t u} f (x - u) d u \Big) d t \Big) d T. \end{array}
$$

Now Fubini’s theorem yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} D _ {R} (f, x) & = & \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} f (x - u) \Big (\frac {1}{2 \pi} \frac {1}{R} \int_ {0} ^ {R} \Big (\int_ {- T} ^ {T} e ^ {t t u} d t \Big) d R \Big) d u \\ & = & \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} f (x - u) K _ {R} (u) d u \end{array}\tag{7.19}
$$

where $K _ { R } ( \cdot )$ is as in (7.13). 

Now let f be continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ and bounded on R by $M _ { f }$ . Fix $\epsilon > 0$ and choose $\delta > 0$ such that $| x - x _ { 0 } | < \delta \Rightarrow | f ( x ) - f ( x _ { 0 } ) | < \epsilon$ . From (7.16) and (7.19), 

$$
D _ {R} (f, x _ {0}) - f (x _ {0}) = \int \left(f (x _ {0} - u) - f (x _ {0})\right) K _ {R} (u) d u
$$

implying 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} | D _ {R} (f, x _ {0}) - f (x _ {0}) | & \leq & \int_ {| u | <   \delta} | f (x _ {0} - u) - f (x _ {0}) | K _ {R} (u) d u \\ & & + \int_ {| u | \geq \delta} | f (x _ {0} - u) - f (x _ {0}) | K _ {R} (u) d u \\ & & <   \epsilon + 2 M _ {f} \int_ {| u | \geq \delta} K _ {R} (u) d u. \end{array}
$$

Now from (7.15), it follows that 

$$
\varlimsup_ {R \to \infty} | D _ {R} (f, x _ {0}) - f (x _ {0}) | \leq \epsilon ,
$$

proving (i). 

The proof of (ii) is similar to this and is omitted. 

Clearly (iv) implies (iii). To establish (iv), note that for $1 \leq p < \infty$ , by Jensen’s inequality (which applies since $K _ { R } ( u ) \geq 0$ and $K _ { R } ( u ) d u = 1 )$ for x in R, 

$$
\left| D _ {R} (f, x) - f (x) \right| ^ {p} \leq \int \left| \left(f (x - u) - f (x)\right) \right| ^ {p} K _ {R} (u) d u
$$

and hence 

$$
\int | D _ {R} (f, x) - f (x) | ^ {p} d x \leq \int \Big (\int | f (x - u) - f (x) | ^ {p} d x \Big) K _ {R} (u) d u.
$$

Now (7.18) and the arguments in the proof of (i) yield (iv). 

## 5.8 Plancherel transform
