## 11 Central Limit Theorems

## 11.1 Lindeberg-Feller theorems

The central limit theorem (CLT) is one of the oldest and most useful results in probability theory. Empirical findings in applied sciences, dating back to the 17th century, showed that the averages of laboratory measurements on various physical quantities tended to have a bell-shaped distribution. The CLT provides a theoretical justification for this observation. Roughly speaking, it says that under some mild conditions, the average of a large number of iid random variables is approximately normally distributed. A version of this result for 0–1 valued random variables was proved by DeMoivre and Laplace in the early 18th century. An extension of this result to the averages of iid random variables with a finite second moment was done in the early 20th century. In this section, a more general set up is considered, namely, that of the limit behavior of the row sums of a triangular array of independent random variables. 

Definition 11.1.1: For each $n \geq 1$ , let $\{ X _ { n 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n r _ { n } } \}$ be a collection of random variables defined on a probability space $\left( \Omega _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } , P _ { n } \right)$ such that $X _ { n 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n r _ { n } }$ are independent. Then, $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is called a triangular array of independent random variables. 

Let $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a triangular array of independent random variables. Define the row sums 

$$
S _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} X _ {n j}, n \geq 1.\tag{1.1}
$$

Suppose that $E X _ { n j } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { ~  ~ { ~ < ~ } ~ } \infty$ for all $j , n$ . Write $\begin{array} { r c l } { s _ { n } ^ { 2 } } & { = } & { \operatorname { V a r } ( S _ { n } ) } \end{array} =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } \mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { n j } ) , n \geq \mathbf { \bar { 1 } } } \end{array}$ . The following condition, introduced by Lindeberg, plays an important role in establishing convergence of $\left( \frac { S _ { n } - E S _ { n } } { s _ { n } } \right)$ to a standard normal random variable in distribution. 

Definition 11.1.2: Let $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a triangular array of independent random variables such that 

$$
E X _ {n j} = 0, 0 <   E X _ {n j} ^ {2} \equiv \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} <   \infty \quad \text { for   all } \quad 1 \leq j \leq r _ {n}, n \geq 1.\tag{1.2}
$$

Then, $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is said to satisfy the Lindeberg condition if for every $\epsilon > 0$ 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} s _ {n} ^ {- 2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon s _ {n}) = 0,\tag{1.3}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { s _ { n } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } \sigma _ { n j } ^ { 2 } , n \ge 1 } \end{array}$ 

Example 11.1.1: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables with $E X _ { 1 } = \mu$ and $\operatorname { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Consider the centered and scaled sample mean 

$$
T _ {n} = \frac {\sqrt {n} (\bar {X} _ {n} - \mu)}{\sigma}, n \geq 1,\tag{1.4}
$$

where ${ \bar { X } } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { j }$ . Note that $T _ { n }$ can be written as the row sum of a triangular array of independent random variables: 

$$
T _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} X _ {n j},\tag{1.5}
$$

where $X _ { n j } = ( X _ { j } - \mu ) / \{ \sigma { \sqrt { n } } \} , 1 \leq j \leq n , n \geq 1$ . Clearly, $\left\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq \right.$ $j \leq n \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ satisfies (1.2) with $\begin{array} { r } { \sigma _ { n j } ^ { 2 } = E X _ { n j } ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { n \sigma ^ { 2 } } \mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) = 1 / n } \end{array}$ for all $1 \leq j \leq n$ , and hence, $\begin{array} { r } { s _ { n } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \bar { \sigma } _ { n j } ^ { 2 } = 1 } \end{array}$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Now, for any $\epsilon > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & s _ {n} ^ {- 2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon s _ {n}) \\ = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} E \Big (\frac {X _ {j} - \mu}{\sigma \sqrt {n}} \Big) ^ {2} I \Big (\Big | \frac {X _ {j} - \mu}{\sigma \sqrt {n}} \Big | > \epsilon \Big) \\ = & n \Big [ \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2} n} E \big \{(X _ {1} - \mu) ^ {2} I (| X _ {1} - \mu | > \epsilon \sigma \sqrt {n}) \big \} \Big ] \\ = & \sigma^ {- 2} E \big \{(X _ {1} - \mu) ^ {2} I (| X _ {1} - \mu | > \epsilon \sigma \sqrt {n}) \big \} \to 0 \quad \text {as} \quad n \to \infty , \end{array}
$$

by the DCT, since $E ( X _ { 1 } - \mu ) ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Thus, the triangular array $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq$ $j \leq n \}$ of (1.5) satisfies the Lindeberg condition (1.3). 

The main result of this section is the following CLT for scaled row sums of a triangular array of independent random variables. 

Theorem 11.1.1: (Lindeberg CLT). Let $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a triangular array of independent random variables satisfying (1.2) and the Lindeberg condition (1.3). Then, 

$$
\frac {S _ {n}}{s _ {n}} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, 1)\tag{1.6}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } X _ { n j } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { s _ { n } ^ { 2 } = V a r ( S _ { n } ) = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } \sigma _ { n j } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ 

As a direct consequence of Theorem 11.1.1 and Example 11.1.1, one gets the more familiar version of the CLT for the sample mean of iid random variables. 

Corollary 11.1.2: (CLT for iid random variables). Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables with $E X _ { 1 } ~ = ~ \mu$ and ${ \cal V } a r ( X _ { 1 } ) \ = \ \sigma ^ { 2 } \ \in$ $( 0 , \infty )$ . Then, 

$$
\sqrt {n} (\bar {X} _ {n} - \mu) \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma^ {2}),\tag{1.7}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { X } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { n j } , n \ge 1 } \end{array}$ 

For proving the theorem, the following simple inequality will be used. 

Lemma 11.1.3: For any $m \in \mathbb { N }$ and for any complex numbers $z _ { 1 } , \ldots , z _ { m }$ 2 $\omega _ { 1 } , \ldots , \omega _ { m }$ , with $\left| z _ { j } \right| \leq 1 , \left| \omega _ { j } \right| \leq 1$ for all $j = 1 , \ldots , m$ 

$$
\left| \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m} z _ {j} - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \omega_ {j} \right| \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} | z _ {j} - \omega_ {j} |.\tag{1.8}
$$

Proof: Inequality (1.8) follows from the identity 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m} z _ {j} - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \omega_ {j} & = & \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m} z _ {j} - \bigg (\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m - 1} z _ {j} \bigg) \omega_ {m} \\ & & + \bigg (\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m - 1} z _ {j} \bigg) \omega_ {m} - \bigg (\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m - 2} z _ {j} \bigg) \omega_ {m - 1} \omega_ {m} \\ & & + \dots + z _ {1} \prod_ {j = 2} ^ {m} \omega_ {j} - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {m} \omega_ {j}. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 11.1.1: W.l.o.g., suppose that $s _ { n } ^ { 2 } = 1$ for all $n \geq 1$ (Otherwise, setting $\tilde { X } _ { n j } \equiv X _ { n j } / s _ { n } , 1 \le j \le r _ { n } , n \ge 1$ , it is easy to check that for the triangular array $\{ \tilde { X } _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ , the variance of the nth row sum $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { s } _ { n } ^ { 2 } \equiv \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } \mathrm { V a r } ( \tilde { X } _ { n j } ) \stackrel {  } { = } 1 } \end{array}$ for all $n \geq 1$ , the Lindeberg condition holds, and $\begin{array} { r l } { \tilde { s } _ { n } ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } \tilde { X } _ { n j } \longrightarrow ^ { d } N ( 0 , 1 ) } & { { } } \end{array}$ if (1.6) holds.) Then, by Theorem 10.3.4, it is enough to show that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} E \exp (\iota t S _ {n}) = e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2} \quad \text { for   all } \quad t \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{1.9}
$$

For any $\epsilon > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \Delta_ {n} & \equiv & \max \left\{E X _ {n j} ^ {2}: 1 \leq j \leq r _ {n} \right\} \\ & \leq & \max \left\{E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon) + E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I (| X _ {n j} | \leq \epsilon): 1 \leq j \leq r _ {n} \right\} \\ & \leq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon) + \epsilon^ {2} \\ & = & o (1) + \epsilon^ {2} \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty , \text { by   the   Lindeberg   condition(1.3). } \end{array}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\Delta_ {n} \rightarrow 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\tag{1.10}
$$

Fix $t \in \mathbb { R }$ . Let $\phi _ { n j } ( \cdot )$ denote the characteristic function of $X _ { n j } , 1 \le j \le r _ { n }$ $n \geq 1$ . Note that by (1.10), there exists $n _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that for all $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ $I _ { 1 n } \equiv \operatorname* { m a x } \{ | 1 - t ^ { 2 } \sigma _ { n j } ^ { 2 } / 2 | : 1 \le j \le r _ { n } \} \le 1$ . Next, noting that $s _ { n } ^ { 2 } \ =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } \sigma _ { n j } ^ { 2 } = 1$ , by Lemma 11.1.3, for all $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & \left| E \exp (\iota t S _ {n}) - e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2} \right| \\ \leq & \left| \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \phi_ {n j} (t) - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \left(1 - \frac {t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2}}{2}\right) \right| \\ & + \left| \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \left(1 - \frac {t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2}}{2}\right) - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \exp (- t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} / 2) \right| \\ \leq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \left| \phi_ {n j} (t) - \left[ 1 - \frac {t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2}}{2} \right] \right| \\ & + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \left| \exp (- t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} / 2) - \left[ 1 - \frac {t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2}}{2} \right] \right| \\ \equiv & I _ {2 n} + I _ {3 n}, \quad \text {say.} \end{array}\tag{1.11}
$$

It will now be shown that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} I _ {k n} = 0 \quad \text { for } \quad k = 2, 3.
$$

First consider $I _ { 2 n }$ . Since $| \exp ( \iota x ) - [ 1 + \iota x + ( \iota x ) ^ { 2 } / 2 ] | \leq \operatorname* { m i n } \{ | x | ^ { 3 } / 3 ! , | x | ^ { 2 } \}$ for all $x \in \mathbb { R }$ **(cf. Lemma 10.1.5) and $E X _ { n j } = 0$ ** for all $1 \leq j \leq r _ { n }$ , for any $\epsilon > 0$ , by the Lindeberg condition, one gets 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} I _ {2 n} & \equiv & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \left| \phi_ {n j} (t) - \left[ 1 - \frac {t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2}}{2} \right] \right| \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \left| E \exp (\iota t X _ {n j}) - \left[ 1 + \iota t E X _ {n j} + \frac {(\iota t) ^ {2}}{2 !} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} \right] \right| \\ & \leq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E \min \left\{\frac {| t X _ {n j} | ^ {3}}{3 !}, | t X _ {n j} | ^ {2} \right\} \\ & \leq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E | t X _ {n j} | ^ {3} I (| X _ {n j} | \leq \epsilon) + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E (t X _ {n j}) ^ {2} I (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon) \\ & \leq & | t | ^ {3} \epsilon \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} + t ^ {2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon) \\ & \leq & | t | ^ {3} \epsilon + t ^ {2} \cdot o (1) \quad \text {as} \quad n \to \infty . \end{array}\tag{1.12}
$$

Since $\epsilon \in ( 0 , \infty )$ is arbitrary, $I _ { 2 n } \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ 

Next, consider $I _ { 3 n }$ . Note that for any $x \in \mathbb { R }$ 

$$
\left| e ^ {x} - 1 - x \right| = \left| \sum_ {k = 2} ^ {\infty} x ^ {k} / k! \right| \leq x ^ {2} \sum_ {k = 2} ^ {\infty} \frac {| x | ^ {k - 2}}{k !} \leq x ^ {2} e ^ {| x |}.
$$

Hence, using (1.10) and the fact that $s _ { n } ^ { 2 } = 1$ , one gets 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l}I _ {3 n}&\leq&\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \Big (\frac {t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2}}{2} \Big) ^ {2} \exp (t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} / 2)\\&\leq&t ^ {4} \exp (t ^ {2} \Delta_ {n} / 2) \bigg [ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} \cdot \Delta_ {n} \bigg ]\\&=&t ^ {4} \exp (t ^ {2} \Delta_ {n} / 2) \Delta_ {n}\\&&\rightarrow 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\end{array}\tag{1.13}
$$

Now (1.9) follows from (1.11), (1.12), and (1.13). This completes the proof of the theorem. ✷ 

Oftentimes, verification of the Lindeberg condition (1.3) becomes dificult as one has to find the truncated second moments of $X _ { n j } \mathrm { ' s }$ . A simpler suficient condition for the CLT is provided by Lyapounov’s condition. 

Definition 11.1.3: A triangular array $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ of independent random variables satisfying (1.2) is said to satisfy Lyapounov’s condition if there exists a $\delta \in ( 0 , \infty )$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} s _ {n} ^ {- (2 + \delta)} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E | X _ {n j} | ^ {2 + \delta} = 0,\tag{1.14}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { s _ { n } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } E X _ { n j } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ 

Note that by Markov’s inequality, if a triangular array $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq$ $r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ satisfies Lyapounov’s condition (1.14), then for any $\epsilon \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 

$$
s _ {n} ^ {- 2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon s _ {n})
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \leq & s _ {n} ^ {- 2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E | X _ {n j} | ^ {2} (| X _ {n j} | / \epsilon s _ {n}) ^ {\delta} \\ & \to 0 \quad \text {as} \quad n \to \infty . \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ satisfies the Lindeberg condition (1.3). This observation leads to the following result. 

Corollary 11.1.4: (Lyapounov’s CLT). Let $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a triangular array of independent random variables satisfying (1.2) and Lyapounov’s condition $( 1 . 1 4 )$ . Then, (1.6) holds, i.e., 

$$
\frac {S _ {n}}{s _ {n}} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, 1).
$$

It is clear that Lyapounov’s condition is only a suficient but not a necessary condition for the validity of the CLT. In contrast, under some regularity conditions on the triangular array $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ , which essentially says that the individual random variables $X _ { n j } \mathrm { { ' s } }$ are ‘uniformly small’, the Lindeberg condition is also a necessary condition for the CLT. This converse is due to W. Feller. 

Theorem 11.1.5: (Feller’s theorem). Let $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a triangular array of independent random variables satisfying (1.2) such that for any $\epsilon > 0$ 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \max _ {1 \leq j \leq r _ {n}} P (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon s _ {n}) = 0,\tag{1.15}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { s _ { n } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } E X _ { n j } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } X _ { n j } . ~ I f , } \end{array}$ in addition, 

$$
\frac {S _ {n}}{s _ {n}} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, 1),\tag{1.16}
$$

then $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ satisfies the Lindeberg condition. 

A triangular array $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ satisfying (1.15) is called a null array. Thus, the converse of Theorem 11.1.1 holds for null arrays. It may be noted that there exist non-null arrays for which (1.16) holds but the Lindeberg condition fails (Problem 11.9). 

Proof: W.l.o.g., suppose that $s _ { n } ^ { 2 } = 1$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Next fix $\epsilon \in ( 0 , \infty )$ Then, setting $t _ { 0 } = 4 / \epsilon$ , and noting that $\begin{array} { r } { 1 = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } E X _ { n j } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ and cos $x \ge$ 

$1 - x ^ { 2 } / 2$ for all $x \in \mathbb { R }$ , one gets 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \big (E \cos t _ {0} X _ {n j} - 1 \big) + \frac {t _ {0} ^ {2}}{2} \\ = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E \Big (\frac {t _ {0} ^ {2} X _ {n j} ^ {2}}{2} - 1 + \cos t _ {0} X _ {n j} \Big) \\ \geq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E \Big (\frac {t _ {0} ^ {2} X _ {n j} ^ {2}}{2} - 1 + \cos t _ {0} X _ {n j} \Big) I \big (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon \big) \\ \geq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E \Big (\frac {t _ {0} ^ {2} X _ {n j} ^ {2}}{2} - 2 \Big) I \big (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon \big) \\ \geq \Big (\frac {t _ {0} ^ {2}}{2} - \frac {2}{\epsilon^ {2}} \Big) \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I \big (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon \big) \\ = \frac {6}{\epsilon^ {2}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I \big (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon \big). \end{array}
$$

Hence, the Lindeberg condition would hold if it is shown that for all $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \left(E \cos t X _ {n j} - 1\right) + \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \rightarrow 0 \quad \text { as } \quad n \rightarrow \infty\\\Leftrightarrow \exp \left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \left(E \cos t X _ {n j} - 1\right)\right)\rightarrow e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2} \quad \text { as } \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\end{array}\tag{1.17}
$$

Let $\phi _ { n j } ( t ) = E \exp ( \iota t X _ { n j } ) , t \in \mathbb { R }$ denote the characteristic function of $X _ { n j }$ $1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } , n \geq 1$ . Note that E cos $t X _ { n j } = \operatorname { R e } ( \phi _ { n j } ( t ) )$ , where recall that for any complex number $z , \operatorname { R e } ( z )$ denotes the real part of $z , \mathrm { i . e . , R e } ( z ) = a$ if $z = a + \iota b , a , b \in \mathbb { R }$ . Since the function $h ( z ) = | z |$ is continuous on C and $| \exp ( \phi _ { n j } ( t ) ) | = \exp ( E \cos t X _ { n j } )$ , it follows that (1.17) holds if, for all $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 2 

$$
\exp \left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} (\phi_ {n j} (t) - 1)\right) \to e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2} \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty .
$$

However, by (1.16), E $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { g } \exp ( \iota t S _ { n } ) = \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { r _ { n } } \phi _ { n j } ( t ) \to e ^ { - t ^ { 2 } / 2 } } \end{array}$ for all $t \in \mathbb { R }$ Hence, it is enough to show that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} I _ {1 n} (t) & \equiv & \bigg [ \exp \bigg (\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} [ \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 ] \bigg) - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \phi_ {n j} (t) \bigg ] \\ & & \to 0 \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty \quad \text { for   all } \quad t \in \mathbb {R}. \end{array}\tag{1.18}
$$

Note that for any $\epsilon \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , by (1.15) and the inequality $| e ^ { \iota x } - 1 | \leq$ min $\{ 2 , | x | \}$ for all $x \in \mathbb { R }$ , one has 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} | \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 | & = & \left| E \big (\exp (\iota t X _ {n j}) - 1 \big) \right| \\ & \leq & E \min \{| t X _ {n j} |, 2 \} \\ & \leq & 2 P (| X _ {n j} | > \epsilon) + | t | \epsilon \end{array}
$$

uniformly in $j = 1 , \ldots , r _ { n }$ . Hence, letting $n \to \infty$ and then $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ , by (1.15), one gets 

$$
I _ {2 n} (t) \equiv \max _ {1 \leq j \leq r _ {n}} | \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 | = o (1) \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty\tag{1.19}
$$

for all $t \in \mathbb { R }$ . Further, by the inequality $| e ^ { \iota x } - 1 - \iota x | \leq | x | ^ { 2 } / 2 , x \in \mathbb { R }$ 27 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} | \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 | & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \big | E \exp (\iota t X _ {n j}) - 1 - E (\iota t X _ {n j}) \big | \\ & \leq & \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} = \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} s _ {n} ^ {2} = \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \end{array}\tag{1.20}
$$

uniformly in $t \in \mathbb { R } , n \geq 1$ . Now fix $t \in \mathbb R$ . Then, by (1.19), there exists $n _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that for all $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ , m $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { 1 a x } _ { 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } } | \phi _ { n } ( t ) - 1 | \leq 1 } \end{array}$ . Hence, by the arguments in the proof of Lemma $1 1 . 1 . 3 .$ , and by the inequalities $| e ^ { z } | \le$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { \infty } \bar { | z | ^ { k } } / k ! = e ^ { | z | } } \end{array}$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { | e ^ { z } - 1 - z | = \big | \sum _ { k = 2 } ^ { \infty } z ^ { k } / k ! \big | \le | z | ^ { 2 } \exp ( | z | ) , z \in \mathbb { C } } \end{array}$ 2 for all $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ , one has 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} I _ {1 n} (t) & = & \bigg | \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \exp \left([ \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 ]\right) - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \phi_ {n j} (t) \bigg | \\ & \leq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \big | \exp \left([ \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 ]\right) - \phi_ {n j} (t) \big | \cdot \prod_ {k = 1} ^ {r _ {n} - j} \big | \exp \left([ \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 ]\right) \big | \\ & \leq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \big | \exp \left([ \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 ]\right) - \phi_ {n j} (t) \big | \cdot \exp \left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \big | \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 \big |\right) \\ & \leq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \big | \exp \left([ \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 ]\right) - \phi_ {n j} (t) \big | \cdot \exp \left(\frac {t ^ {2}}{2}\right) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \big | \exp \left([ \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 ]\right) - 1 - [ \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 ] \big | \cdot \exp \left(\frac {t ^ {2}}{2}\right) \\ & \leq & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} \big | \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 \big | ^ {2} \cdot \exp \left(1 + \frac {t ^ {2}}{2}\right) \\ & \leq & \max _ {1 \leq j \leq r _ {n}} | \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 | \bigg (\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} | \phi_ {n j} (t) - 1 | \bigg) \exp \left(1 + \frac {t ^ {2}}{2}\right) \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \leq & I _ {2 n} (t) \cdot \left[ t ^ {2} \cdot \exp \left(1 + \frac {t ^ {2}}{2}\right) / 2 \right] \\ & \to 0 \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty , \end{array}
$$

by (1.19) and (1.20). Hence, (1.18) holds. This completes the proof of the theorem. ✷ 

The following example is an application of the Lindeberg CLT for proving asymptotic normality of the least squares estimator of a regression parameter. 

Example 11.1.2: Let 

$$
Y _ {j} = x _ {j} \beta + \epsilon_ {j}, \quad j = 1, 2, \ldots\tag{1.21}
$$

be a simple linear regression model, where $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a given sequence of real numbers, $\beta \in \mathbb { R }$ is the regression parameter and $\{ \epsilon _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ is a sequence of iid random variables with $E \epsilon _ { 1 } = 0$ and $E \epsilon _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \equiv \sigma ^ { 2 } \in ( \bar { 0 , } \infty )$ . The least squares estimator of $\beta$ based on $Y _ { 1 } , \dots , Y _ { n }$ is given by 

$$
\hat {\beta} _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} x _ {j} Y _ {j} / a _ {n} ^ {2}, \quad n \geq 1,
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { a _ { n } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { j } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . Suppose that the sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ satisfies 

$$
\max _ {1 \leq j \leq n} \left\{| x _ {j} | / a _ {n} \right\}\rightarrow 0 \quad \text { as } \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\tag{1.22}
$$

Then, 

$$
a _ {n} (\hat {\beta} _ {n} - \beta) \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma^ {2}).\tag{1.23}
$$

To prove (1.23), note that by (1.21), 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} a _ {n} (\hat {\beta} _ {n} - \beta) & = & a _ {n} \bigg [ \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} x _ {j} Y _ {j} - a _ {n} ^ {2} \beta \bigg ] \bigg / a _ {n} ^ {2} \\ & = & a _ {n} ^ {- 1} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} x _ {j} \epsilon_ {j} \equiv \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} X _ {n j}, \quad \text {say} \end{array}\tag{1.24}
$$

where $X _ { n j } = x _ { j } \epsilon _ { j } / a _ { n } , 1 \le j \le n , n \ge 1$ . Note that $E X _ { n j } = 0 , E X _ { n j } ^ { 2 } <$ and $\begin{array} { r } { s _ { n } ^ { \bar { 2 } } \equiv \bar { \sum } _ { j = 1 } ^ { \bar { n } } E X _ { n j } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { j } ^ { 2 } E \epsilon _ { j } ^ { 2 } / a _ { n } ^ { 2 } = \sigma ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ . Thus, $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq$ $j \le n \} _ { n \ge 1 }$  is a triangular array of independent random variables satisfying (1.2). Next, let $m _ { n } = \operatorname * { m a x } \{ | x _ { j } | / a _ { n } : 1 \leq j \leq n \} , n \geq 1$ . Then, by (1.22), for any $\delta \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , 

$$
s _ {n} ^ {- 2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} E X _ {n j} ^ {2} I \big (| X _ {n j} | > \delta s _ {n} \big)
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} {=} & {\sigma^ {- 2} a _ {n} ^ {- 2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} x _ {j} ^ {2} E \epsilon_ {j} ^ {2} I (| x _ {j} \epsilon_ {j} / a _ {n} | > \delta \sigma)} \\ {\leq} & {\sigma^ {- 2} a _ {n} ^ {- 2} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} x _ {j} ^ {2} \cdot E \epsilon_ {1} ^ {2} I (m _ {n} \cdot | \epsilon_ {1} | > \delta \sigma)} \\ {=} & {\sigma^ {- 2} E \epsilon_ {1} ^ {2} I \big (| \epsilon_ {1} | > \delta \sigma \cdot m _ {n} ^ {- 1} \big)} \\ & {\to 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \to \infty \mathrm{bytheDCT}.} \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq n \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ satisfies the Lindeberg condition (1.3) and hence, by Theorem 11.1.1, 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} X _ {n j}}{\sigma} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, 1),
$$

which, in view of (1.24), implies (1.23). 

The next result gives a multivariate generalization of Theorem 11.1.1. 

Theorem 11.1.6: (A multivariate version of the Lindeberg CLT). For each $n \geq 1$ , let $\{ X _ { n j } : 1 \leq j \leq r _ { n } \}$ be a collection of independent kdimensional random vectors satisfying 

$$
E X _ {n j} = 0, 1 \leq j \leq r _ {n} \quad a n d \quad \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E X _ {n j} ^ {\prime} X _ {n j} = \mathbb {I} _ {k},
$$

where $\mathbb { I } _ { k }$ denotes the identity matrix of order k and for any vector $x , x ^ { \prime }$ denotes its transpose. Suppose that for every $\epsilon \in ( 0 , \infty )$ ， 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} E \| X _ {n j} \| ^ {2} I (\| X _ {n j} \| > \epsilon) = 0.
$$

Then, 

$$
\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r _ {n}} X _ {n j} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \mathbb {I} _ {k}).
$$

The proof is a consequence of Theorem 11.1.1 and the Cramer-Wold device (cf. Theorem 10.4.5) and is left as an exercise (Problem 11.17). 

## 11.2 Stable distributions

If $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sequence of iid $N ( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ random variables, then for each $\begin{array} { r } { k \geq 1 , S _ { k } \equiv \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } X _ { i } } \end{array}$ has a $N ( k \mu , k \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ distribution. Similarly, if $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sequence of iid Cauchy $( \mu , \sigma )$ random variables, then for each $k \geq 1$ $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { k } \equiv \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } X _ { i } } \end{array}$ has a Cauchy $( k \mu , k \sigma )$ distribution. Thus, in both cases, for each $k \geq 1$ , there exist constants $a _ { k }$ and $b _ { k }$ such that $S _ { k }$ has the same distribution as $a _ { k } X _ { 1 } + b _ { k }$ (Problem 11.21). 

Definition 11.2.1: A nondegenerate random variable X is called stable if the above property holds, i.e., for each $k \in \mathbb N$ , there exist constants $a _ { k }$ and $b _ { k }$ such that 

$$
S _ {k} = ^ {d} a _ {k} X _ {1} + b _ {k},\tag{2.1}
$$

where $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots$ are iid random variables with the same distribution as $X$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { k } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } X _ { i } } \end{array}$ . In this case, the distribution $F _ { X }$ of X is called a stable distribution. 

There are two characterizations of stable distributions. 

Theorem 11.2.1: A nondegenerate distribution F is stable if there exists a sequence of iid random variable $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ and constants $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $\{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ such that $\textstyle { \bigl ( } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } Y _ { i } - b _ { k } { \bigr ) } / a _ { k } $ converges in distribution to $F$ . 

Theorem 11.2.2: A nondegenerate distribution $F$ is stable if its characteristic function φ(t) admits the representation 

$$
\phi (t) = \exp \left(\iota t c - b | t | ^ {\alpha} (1 + \iota \lambda s g n (t) \omega_ {\alpha} (t))\right)\tag{2.2}
$$

where $\iota = \sqrt { - 1 } , - 1 \leq \lambda \leq 1 , 0 < \alpha \leq 2 , 0 \leq b < \infty$ , and the functions $\omega _ { \alpha } ( t )$ and $s g n ( \cdot )$ are defined as 

$$
\omega_ {\alpha} (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \tan \frac {\pi \alpha}{2} & i f \quad \alpha \neq 1 \\ \frac {2}{\pi} \log | t | & i f \quad \alpha = 1 \end{array} \right.\tag{2.3}
$$

and 

$$
s g n (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & i f \quad t > 0 \\ - 1 & i f \quad t <   0 \\ 0 & i f \quad t = 0 \end{array} \right..
$$

Remark 11.2.1: When $\alpha = 2 , \phi ( t )$ in (2.2) reduces to $\exp ( \iota t c - b t ^ { 2 } )$ , which is the characteristic function of a normal random variable with mean c and variance 2b. 

Remark 11.2.2: When $\alpha = 1 , \lambda = 0 , \phi ( t )$ reduces to $\exp ( \iota t c - b | t | )$ , which is the characteristic function of a Cauchy $( c , b )$ distribution. 

Remark 11.2.3: Since $| \phi ( t ) |$ is integrable, the distribution F must be absolutely continuous. Apart from the normal and Cauchy distributions, for $\alpha = 1 / 2 , \lambda = 1$ , the density is given by 

$$
f (x) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi}} \frac {1}{x ^ {3 / 2}} \exp \Big (- \frac {1}{2 x} \Big), x > 0.\tag{2.4}
$$

For an explicit expression for the density of F, in other cases, see Feller (1966), Section 17.6. 

Definition 11.2.2: The parameter α in (2.2) is called the index of the stable distribution. 

Remark 11.2.4: The parameter λ is related to the behavior of the ratio of the right tail of the distribution to the left tail through the relation 

$$
\lim _ {x \to \infty} \frac {1 - F (x)}{F (- x)} = \frac {1 + \lambda}{(1 - \lambda)},\tag{2.5}
$$

where for $\lambda = 1$ , the ratio on the right side of (2.5) is defined to be $+ \infty$ 

Definition 11.2.3: A function $L : ( 0 , \infty ) \to ( 0 , \infty )$ is called slowly varying at $\infty$ if 

$$
\lim _ {x \to \infty} \frac {L (c x)}{L (x)} = 1 \quad \text { for   all } \quad 0 <   c <   \infty .\tag{2.6}
$$

A function $f : ( 0 , \infty ) \to ( 0 , \infty )$ is called regularly varying at with index $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ , α $\neq ~ 0$ if $f ( x ) ~ = ~ x ^ { \alpha } L ( x )$ for all $x \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( 0 , \infty )$ where $L ( \cdot )$ is slowly varying at . The functions $L _ { 1 } ( t ) = \log t , L _ { 2 } ( t ) = \log ( \log t )$ $L _ { 3 } ( t ) = ( \log t ) ^ { 2 }$ are slowly varying at but the function $L _ { 4 } ( t ) = t ^ { p }$ is not so for $p \neq 0 .$ 

There is a companion result to Theorem 11.2.1 giving necessary and suficient conditions for convergence of normalized sums of iid random variables to a stable distribution. 

Theorem 11.2.3: Let F be a nondegenerate stable distribution with index $\alpha , \ 0 \ < \ \alpha \ < \ 2$ . Then in order that a sequence $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ of iid random variables admits a sequence of constants $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $\{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ such that 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} - b _ {n}}{a _ {n}} \longrightarrow^ {d} F,\tag{2.7}
$$

it is necessary and suficient that 

$$
\lim _ {x \to \infty} \frac {P (Y _ {1} > x)}{P (| Y _ {1} | > x)} \equiv \theta \in [ 0, 1 ]\tag{2.8}
$$

exists and 

$$
P (| Y _ {1} | > x) = x ^ {- \alpha} L (x),\tag{2.9}
$$

where $L ( \cdot )$ is a slowly varying function at . $I f \left( 2 . 8 \right)$ and $( 2 . 9 )$ hold, then the normalizing constants $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $\{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ may be chosen to satisfy 

$$
n a _ {n} ^ {- \alpha} L (a _ {n}) \rightarrow 1 \quad a n d \quad b _ {n} = n E Y _ {1} I (| Y _ {1} | \leq a _ {n}).\tag{2.10}
$$

Remark 11.2.5: The analog of Theorem 11.2.3 for the case $\alpha = 2$ , i.e., for the normal distribution is the following. 

Theorem 11.2.4: Let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be iid random variables. In order that there exist constants $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $\{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ such that 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} - b _ {n}}{a _ {n}} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, 1),\tag{2.11}
$$

it is necessary and suficient that 

$$
\frac {x ^ {2} P (| Y _ {1} | > x)}{E Y _ {1} ^ {2} I (| Y _ {1} | \leq x)} \to 0 \quad a s \quad x \to \infty .\tag{2.12}
$$

Remark 11.2.6: Note that condition (2.12) holds if $E Y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . However, if $\textstyle P ( | Y _ { 1 } | > x ) \sim { \frac { C } { x ^ { 2 } } }$ as $x \to \infty$ , then $E Y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } = \infty$ and the classical CLT (cf. Corollary 11.1.2) fails. However, in this case, (2.12) holds and $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } Y _ { i }$ is asymptotically normal with a suitable centering and scaling (diferent from $\sqrt { n } )$ (Problem 11.20). 

Here, only the proof of Theorem 11.2.1 will be given. Further, a proof of Theorem 11.2.3, suficiency part, is also outlined. For the rest, see Feller (1966) or Gnedenko and Kolmogorov (1968). For proving Theorem 11.2.1, the following result is needed. 

Theorem 11.2.5: (Khinchine’s theorem on convergence of types). Let $\{ W _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a sequence of random variables such that for some sequences $\{ \alpha _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 } \subset [ 0 , \infty )$ and $\{ \beta _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 } \subset \mathbb { R }$ , both $W _ { n }$ and $\alpha _ { n } W _ { n } + \beta _ { n }$ converge in distribution to nondegenerate distributions G and H on R, respectively. Then li $\mathrm { n } _ { n \to \infty } \alpha _ { n } = \alpha$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \beta _ { n } = \beta } \end{array}$ exist with $0 < \alpha < \infty$ and $- \infty < \beta < \infty$ 

Proof: Let $\{ W _ { n } ^ { \prime } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a sequence of random variables such that for each $n \ \geq \ 1 , \ W _ { n }$ and $W _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ have the same distribution and $W _ { n }$ and $W _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ are independent. Then $Y _ { n } \equiv W _ { n } - W _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ and $Z _ { n } \equiv \alpha _ { n } ( W _ { n } - W _ { n } ^ { \prime } )$ both convergence in distribution to nondegenerate limits, say $\tilde { G }$ and $\ddot { H }$ . Indeed $\tilde { G } = \tilde { G * } G$ and $\tilde { H } = H * H$ , where denotes convolution. This implies that $\{ \alpha _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ cannot have 0 or $\infty$ as limit points. Also if $0 < \alpha \le \alpha ^ { \prime } < \infty$ are two limit points of $\{ \alpha _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { H } ( x ) = \tilde { G } ( \frac { x } { \alpha } ) = \tilde { G } ( \frac { x } { \alpha ^ { \prime } } ) } \end{array}$ for all $x .$ Since $\tilde { G } ( \cdot )$ is nondegenerate, α must equal $\alpha ^ { \prime }$ and so $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \alpha _ { n }$ exists in $( 0 , \infty )$ This implies that $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \beta _ { n }$ exists in R. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 11.2.1: The ‘only if’ part follows from the definition of $F$ being stable, since one can take $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ to be iid with distribution $F$ 

For the ‘if part,’ let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be iid random variables such that there exists constants $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $\{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ such that as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} - b _ {n}}{a _ {n}} \longrightarrow^ {d} F.
$$

To show that $F$ is stable, fix an integer $r \geq 1$ . Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be iid random variables with distribution $F .$ . Then as $k \to \infty$ ， 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k r} Y _ {i} - b _ {k r}}{a _ {k r}} \longrightarrow^ {d} X _ {1}.
$$

Also, the left side above equals 

$$
\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {r - 1} \left(\frac {\sum_ {i = j k + 1} ^ {(j + 1) k} Y _ {i} - b _ {k}}{a _ {k}}\right) \frac {a _ {k}}{a _ {k r}} + \frac {r b _ {k} - b _ {k r}}{a _ {k r}} = \alpha_ {k r} \left(\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {r - 1} \eta_ {j k}\right) + \beta_ {k r}, \quad \text { say. }
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \alpha _ { k r } = \frac { a _ { k } } { a _ { k r } } , \eta _ { j k } = \left( \frac { \sum _ { i = j k + 1 } ^ { ( j + 1 ) k } Y _ { i } - b _ { k } } { a _ { k } } \right) } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \beta _ { k r } = \frac { r b _ { k } - b _ { k r } } { a _ { k r } } } \end{array}$ . Since $\{ \eta _ { j k } :$ $j = 0 , 1 , \ldots , r - 1 \}$ are independent and for each j, $\eta _ { j k } \ \longrightarrow ^ { d } \ X _ { j + 1 }$ as $k \to \infty$ , it follows that as $k \to \infty$ 2 

$$
W _ {k} = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {r - 1} \eta_ {j k} \longrightarrow^ {d} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {r - 1} X _ {j + 1} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r} X _ {j}.
$$

Also, as $k \to \infty$ 

$$
\alpha_ {k r} W _ {k} + \beta_ {k r} \longrightarrow^ {d} X _ {1}.
$$

Since $F$ is nondegenerate, both $X _ { 1 }$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r } X _ { j }$ are nondegenerate random variables. Thus, as $k  \infty , W _ { k }$ and $\alpha _ { k r } \dot { W } _ { k } + \beta _ { k r }$ converge in distribution to nondegenerate random variables. Thus, by Khinchine’s theorem on convergence types proved above, it follows that $\alpha _ { k r } \ \to \ \alpha _ { r } ^ { \prime }$ and $\beta _ { k r } \ \to \ \beta _ { r } ^ { \prime }$ , $0 < \alpha _ { r } ^ { \prime } < \infty$ and $- \infty < \beta _ { r } ^ { \prime } < \infty$ . This yields that for each $r \in \mathbb N$ that $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { r } X _ { j }$ has the same distribution as $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { \alpha _ { r } ^ { \prime } } ( X _ { 1 } - \beta _ { r } ^ { \prime } ) } \end{array}$ , i.e., $X _ { 1 }$ is stable. ✷ 

Proof of the suficiency part of Theorem 11.2.3: (Outline). The proof is based on the continuity theorem. The characteristic function of $\begin{array} { r } { { \dot { T } } _ { n } \equiv \frac { S _ { n } - b _ { n } } { a _ { n } } } \end{array}$ is 

$$
\phi_ {n} (t) = E \Big (e ^ {\iota t \frac {S _ {n} - b _ {n}}{a _ {n}}} \Big) = \Big (\phi \Big (\frac {t}{a _ {n}} \Big) e ^ {- \iota t b _ {n} ^ {\prime} / a _ {n}} \Big) ^ {n} \equiv \Big (1 + \frac {1}{n} h _ {n} (t) \Big) ^ {n}
$$

where $b _ { n } ^ { \prime } = b _ { n } / n$ and $\begin{array} { r } { h _ { n } ( t ) = n \Big ( \phi ( \frac { t } { a _ { n } } ) e ^ { - \iota t b _ { n } ^ { \prime } / a _ { n } } - 1 \Big ) } \end{array}$ . Let $G ( \cdot )$ be the cdf of $Y _ { 1 }$ . Then 

$$
h _ {n} (t) = n \int \Bigl (e ^ {\iota t (y - b _ {n} ^ {\prime}) / a _ {n}} - 1 \Bigr) d G (y) = \int \bigl (e ^ {\iota t x} - 1 \bigr) \mu_ {n} (d x)
$$

where $\mu _ { n } ( A ) = n P ( Y _ { 1 } \in b _ { n } ^ { \prime } + a _ { n } A ) , A \in \mathcal { B } ( \mathbb { R } ) . \mathrm { ~ I f ~ } A = ( u , v ] , 0 < u < v <$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} n P \big (Y _ {1} \in b _ {n} ^ {\prime} + a _ {n} A \big) & = & n P \big (a _ {n} u + b _ {n} ^ {\prime} <   Y _ {1} \leq a _ {n} v + b _ {n} ^ {\prime} \big) \\ & = & n P \big (Y _ {1} > a _ {n} u + b _ {n} ^ {\prime} \big) - n P \big (Y _ {1} > a _ {n} v + b _ {n} ^ {\prime} \big). \end{array}
$$

By (2.8)–(2.10), 

$$
n P (Y _ {1} > a _ {n} x) = \left(\frac {P (Y _ {1} > a _ {n} x)}{P (Y _ {1} > a _ {n})}\right) n P (Y _ {1} > a _ {n}) \rightarrow \theta x ^ {- \alpha} \text {   for   } x > 0.
$$

By using (2.10), it can be show that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \frac {b _ {n} ^ {\prime}}{a _ {n}} & = & \frac {E Y _ {1} I (| Y _ {1} | \leq a _ {n})}{a _ {n}} \\ & = & O \Big (\frac {a _ {n} ^ {1 - \alpha} L (a _ {n})}{a _ {n}} \Big) \\ & = & o (1) \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \to \infty . \end{array}
$$

Hence, it follows that 

$$
n P (Y _ {1} > a _ {n} u + b _ {n} ^ {\prime}) - n P (Y _ {1} > a _ {n} v + b _ {n} ^ {\prime}) \rightarrow \theta (u ^ {- \alpha} - v ^ {- \alpha}).
$$

Similarly, for $A = \left( - v , - u \right]$ 2 

$$
n P (Y _ {1} \in b _ {n} ^ {\prime} + a _ {n} A) \rightarrow (1 - \theta) (u ^ {- \alpha} - v ^ {- \alpha}).
$$

This suggests that $h _ { n } ( t )$ should approach 

$$
\theta \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} (e ^ {\iota t x} - 1) x ^ {- (\alpha + 1)} d x + (1 - \theta) \alpha \int_ {- \infty} ^ {0} (e ^ {\iota t x} - 1) | x | ^ {- (\alpha + 1)} d x.
$$

But there are integrability problems for $| x | ^ { - ( \alpha + 1 ) }$ near 0 and so a more careful analysis is needed. It can be shown that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \lim _ {n \to \infty} h _ {n} (t) & = & \iota t c + \theta \alpha \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \left(e ^ {\iota t x} - 1 - \frac {\iota t x}{1 + x ^ {2}}\right) x ^ {(\alpha + 1)} d x \\ & & + (1 - \theta) \alpha \int_ {- \infty} ^ {0} \left(e ^ {\iota t x} - 1 - \frac {\iota t x}{1 + x ^ {2}}\right) | x | ^ {- (\alpha + 1)} d x \end{array}
$$

where $c$ is a constant. The right side is continuous at $t = 0$ and $\mathrm { s o } .$ , the result follows by the continuity theorem. For details, see Feller (1966). ✷ 

Remark 11.2.7: By the necessity part of Theorem 11.2.3, every stable distribution $F$ must satisfy 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} {1 - F (x)} & = & {\theta x ^ {- \alpha} L (x)} \\ {F (- x)} & = & {(1 - \theta) x ^ {- \alpha} L (x)} \end{array}
$$

for large x where $0 \leq \theta \leq 1$ and $L ( \cdot )$ is slowing varying at and $0 < \alpha < 2$ This implies that F has moments of order p such that $\alpha > p .$ . Distributions satisfying the above tail condition are called heavy tailed and arise in many applications. The Pareto distribution in economics is an example of a heavy tail distribution. 

Remark 11.2.8: One way to generate heavy tailed distributions is as follows. If Y is a positive random variable such that there exist $0 < c < \infty$ and $0 < p < \infty$ satisfying 

$$
P (Y <   y) \sim c y ^ {p} \quad \mathrm{as} \quad y \downarrow 0,
$$

then the random variable $X = Y ^ { - q }$ has the property 

$$
P (X > x) = P (Y <   x ^ {- 1 / q}) \sim c x ^ {- p / q} \quad \mathrm{as} \quad x \to \infty .
$$

If $p < 2 q$ , then X has heavy tails. Thus if $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ are iid Gamma(1,2), then $n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n ^ { - } } Y _ { i } ^ { - 1 }$ converges in distribution to a one sided Cauchy distribution (Problem 11.15). 

Definition 11.2.4: Let F and G be two probability distributions on R. Then G is said to belong to the domain of attraction of F if there exist a sequence of iid random variables $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ with distribution G and constants $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $\{ b _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ such that 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} - b _ {n}}{a _ {n}} \longrightarrow^ {d} F.
$$

Theorem 11.2.1 says that the only nondegenerate distributions F that admit a nonempty domain of attraction are the stable distributions. 

## 11.3 Infinitely divisible distributions

Definition 11.3.1: A random variable X (and its distribution) is called infinitely divisible if for each integer $k \in \mathbb N$ , there exist iid random variables $X _ { k 1 } , X _ { k 2 } , \ldots , X _ { k k }$ such that $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { k ^ { \bigcirc } } X _ { k j }$ has the same distribution as X. 

Examples include constants (degenerate distributions), normal, Poisson, Cauchy, and Gamma distributions. But distributions with bounded support cannot be infinitely divisible unless they are degenerate. In fact, if X is infinitely divisible satisfying $P ( | X | \leq M ) = 1$ for some $M < \infty$ , then the $X _ { k i } { } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s }$ in the above definition must satisfy $\begin{array} { r } { P \big ( | X _ { k 1 } | < \frac { M } { k } \big ) \ = \ 1 } \end{array}$ and so Var $\begin{array} { r } { ( X _ { k 1 } ) \le E X _ { k 1 } ^ { 2 } \le \frac { M ^ { 2 } } { k ^ { 2 } } } \end{array}$ implying $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { V a r } ( X ) = k \mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { k 1 } ) \le \frac { M ^ { 2 } } { k } } \end{array}$ for each $k \geq 1$ . Hence $\operatorname { V a r } ( X )$ must be zero, and the random variable X is a constant w.p. 1. 

The following results are easy to establish. 

Theorem 11.3.1: (a) If X and Y are independent and infinitely divisible, then $X + Y$ is also infinitely divisible. $( b ) \ J f \ X _ { n }$ is infinitely divisible for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and $X _ { n } \longrightarrow ^ { d } X$ , then X is infinitely divisible. 

Proof: (a) Follows from the definition. (b) For each $k \geq 1$ and $n \geq 1$ there exist iid random variables $X _ { n k 1 } , X _ { n k 2 } , . . . , X _ { n k k }$ such that $X _ { n }$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } X _ { n k j }$ have the same distribution. Now fix $k \geq 1$ . Then for any $y > 0$ 

$$
\left(P (X _ {n k 1} > y)\right) ^ {k} = P (X _ {n k j} > y \quad \text { for   all } \quad j = 1,..., k) \leq P (X _ {n} > k y)
$$

and similarly, 

$$
\left(P (X _ {n k 1} <   - y)\right) ^ {k} \leq P (X _ {n} \leq k y).
$$

Since $X _ { n } ~ \longrightarrow ^ { d } ~ X$ , the distributions of $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ are tight and so are $\{ X _ { n k 1 } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ . So if $F _ { k }$ is a weak limit point of $\{ X _ { n k 1 } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ and if $\{ Y _ { k j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { k }$ are iid with distribution $F _ { k }$ , then $X$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { k } Y _ { k j }$ have the same distribution and so X is infinitely divisible. ✷ 

A large class of infinitely divisible distributions are generated by the compound Poisson family. 

Definition 11.3.2: Let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be iid random variables and let N be a Poisson (λ) random variable, independent of the $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ . The random variable $\begin{array} { r } { X \equiv \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { N } Y _ { i } } \end{array}$ is said to have a compound Poisson distribution. 

Theorem 11.3.2: A compound Poisson distribution is infinitely divisible. 

Proof: Let X be a random variable as in Definition 11.3.2. For each $k \geq 1$ , let $\{ N _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { k }$ be iid Poisson random variables with mean $\frac { \lambda } { k }$ that are independent of $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ . Let 

$$
X _ {k j} = \sum_ {i = T _ {j} + 1} ^ {T _ {j + 1}} Y _ {i}, 1 \leq j \leq k
$$

where $T _ { 1 } = 0 , T _ { j } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { j - 1 } N _ { i } , 2 \leq j \leq k$ . Then $\{ X _ { k j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { k }$ are iid and $\sum _ { \stackrel { \scriptstyle j = 1 } { \scriptstyle \prod } } X _ { k j }$ and X are identically distributed and so X is infinitely divisible. 

Although the converse to the above is not valid, it is known that every infinitely divisible distribution is the limit of a sequence of centered and scaled compound Poisson distributions. This is a consequence of a deep result giving an explicit formula for the characteristic function of an infinitely divisible distribution which is stated below. For a proof of this result (stated below), see Feller (1966) and Chung (1974) or Gnedenko and Kolmogorov (1968). 

Theorem 11.3.3: (Levy-Khinchine representation theorem). Let X be an infinitely divisible random variable. Then its characteristic function $\phi ( t ) \equiv$ 

$E ( e ^ { \iota t X } )$ is of the form 

$$
\phi (t) = \exp \left(\iota t c - \beta \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} + \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \Bigl (e ^ {\iota t x} - 1 - \frac {\iota t x}{1 + x ^ {2}} \Bigr) \mu (d x)\right),
$$

where $c \in \mathbb { R } , \beta > 0$ and µ is a measure on $( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) )$ such that $\mu ( \{ 0 \} ) = 0$ and $\textstyle \int _ { | x | \leq 1 } x ^ { 2 } \mu ( d x ) < \infty$ and $\mu ( \{ x : | x | > 1 \} ) < \infty$ 

Corollary 11.3.4: Stable distributions are infinitely divisible. 

Proof: The normal distribution corresponds to the case $\mu ( \cdot ) \equiv 0$ and $\beta > 0$ . For nonnormal stable laws with index $\alpha < 2 .$ , set $\beta = 0$ and $\mu ( d x ) =$ $\theta x ^ { - ( \alpha + 1 ) } d x$ for $x > 0$ and $( 1 - \theta ) | x | ^ { - ( \alpha + 1 ) }$ dx for $x < 0$ ✷ 

Corollary 11.3.5: Every infinitely divisible distribution is the limit of centered and scaled compound Poisson distributions. 

Proof: Since the normal distribution can be obtained as a (weak) limit of centered and scaled Poisson distributions, it is enough to consider the case when $\beta = 0 , c = 0$ . Let $\mu _ { n } ( A ) = \mu ( A \cap \{ x : | x | > n ^ { - 1 } \} )$ ， $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } )$ and let 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \phi_ {n} (t) & = & \exp \left(\int \Bigl (e ^ {\iota t x} - 1 - \frac {\iota t x}{1 + x ^ {2}} \Bigr) \mu_ {n} (d x)\right) \\ & = & \exp \left(\lambda_ {n} \Bigl [ \int (e ^ {\iota t x} - 1) \tilde {\mu} _ {n} (d x) - \iota t c _ {n} \Bigr ]\right) \end{array}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \tilde {\mu} _ {n} (A) & = & \mu_ {n} (A) / \mu_ {n} (\mathbb {R}), A \in \mathcal {B} (\mathbb {R}), \lambda_ {n} = \mu_ {n} (\mathbb {R}), \text {and} \\ c _ {n} & = & \int \frac {x}{1 + x ^ {2}} \tilde {\mu} _ {n} (d x). \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\phi _ { n } ( \cdot )$ is a compound Poisson characteristic function centered at $c _ { n }$ with Poisson parameter $\lambda _ { n }$ and with the compounding distribution ${ \tilde { \mu } } _ { n }$ By the DCT, $\phi _ { n } ( t )  \phi ( t )$ for each $t \in \mathbb R$ . Hence by the Levy-Cramer continuity theorem, the result follows. ✷ 

Another characterization of infinitely divisible distributions is similar to that of stable distributions. Recall that a stable distribution is one that is the limit of normalized sums of iid random variables and conversely. 

Theorem 11.3.6: A random variable X is infinitely divisible if it is the limit in distribution of a sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ where for each $n , \ X _ { n }$ is the sum of n iid random variables $\{ X _ { n j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ 

Thus X is infinitely divisible if it is the limit in distribution of the row sums of a triangular array of random variables where in each row, all the random variables are iid. 

Proof: The ‘only $\mathrm { i f } ^ { \prime }$ part follows from the definition. For the $ { \mathrm { \Omega } } _ { \mathrm { i f } }  { \mathrm { \Omega } } _ { }$ part, fix $k \geq 1$ . Then $X _ { k \cdot n }$ can be written as 

$$
X _ {k \cdot n} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} Y _ {j n},
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { Y _ { j n } = \sum _ { r = ( j - 1 ) n + 1 } ^ { j n } X _ { k \cdot n , r } \ j = 1 , 2 , \ldots , k } \end{array}$ . By hypothesis, $X _ { k \cdot n } \longrightarrow ^ { d }$ X. Now, $\{ Y _ { j n } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { k }$ are iid and it can be shown, as in the proof of Theorem 11.3.1, that for each $i = 1 , \ldots , k , \{ Y _ { i n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ are tight and hence, converges in distribution to a limit $Y _ { i }$ through a subsequence, and that X and $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } Y _ { i }$ have the same distribution. Thus, X is infinitely divisible. ✷ 

## 11.4 Refinements and extensions of the CLT

This section is devoted to studying some refinements and generalizations of the basic CLT results, such as the rate of convergence in the CLT, Edgeworth expansions and large deviations for sums of iid random variables, and also a generalization of the basic CLT to a functional version. 

## 11.4.1 The Berry-Esseen theorem

Let $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be a sequence of iid random variables with $E X _ { 1 } = \mu$ and $\operatorname { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Then, Corollary 11.1.2 and Poly¯a’s theorem imply that 

$$
\Delta_ {n} \equiv \sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} \left| P \Big (\frac {S _ {n} - n \mu}{\sigma \sqrt {n}} \leq x \Big) - \Phi (x) \right| \to 0 \quad \text {as} \quad n \to \infty ,\tag{4.1}
$$

where $S _ { n } = X _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + X _ { n } , n \geq 1$ , and $\Phi ( \cdot )$ is the cdf of the $N ( 0 , 1 )$ distribution. A natural question that arises in this context is “how fast does $\Delta _ { n } \ \mathrm { g o }$ to zero?” Berry (1941) and Esseen (1942) independently proved that $\Delta _ { n } = O ( n ^ { - 1 / 2 } )$ as $n  \infty$ , provided $E | \dot { X } _ { 1 } | ^ { 3 } < \infty$ . This result is referred to as the Berry-Esseen theorem. 

Theorem 11.4.1: (The Berry-Esseen theorem). Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables with $E X _ { 1 } = \mu$ 2 ${ \cal V } a r ( X _ { 1 } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } \in \overline { { { ( 0 , \infty ) } } }$ and $E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 3 } < \infty$ . Then, for all $n \geq 1$ 

$$
\Delta_ {n} \equiv \sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} \left| P \left(\frac {S _ {n} - n \mu}{\sigma \sqrt {n}} \leq x\right) - \Phi (x) \right| \leq C \cdot \frac {E | X _ {1} - \mu | ^ {3}}{\sigma^ {3} \sqrt {n}}\tag{4.2}
$$

where $C \in ( 0 , \infty )$ is a constant. 

The value of the constant $C \in ( 0 , \infty )$ does not depend on n and on any characteristics of the distribution of $X _ { 1 }$ . Indeed, the proof of Theorem 11.4.1 below shows that $C \leq \sqrt { \frac { 2 } { \pi } } \cdot \left[ \frac { 5 } { 2 } + \frac { 1 2 } { \pi } \right] < 5 . 0 5$ 

The following result plays an important role in the proof of Theorem 11.4.1. 

Lemma 11.4.2: (A smoothing inequality). Let F be a cdf on R with xd $F ( x ) = 0$ and characteristic function $\begin{array} { r } { \zeta ( t ) = \int \exp ( \iota t x ) d F ( x ) , t \in \mathbb { R } } \end{array}$ Let $G : \mathbb { R } $ R be a diferentiable function with derivative g such that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { | x | \to \infty } \left( F ( x ) - G ( x ) \right) \ = \ 0 } \end{array}$ . Suppose that $\begin{array} { r } { \int ( 1 + | x | ) | g ( x ) | d x < \infty } \end{array}$ $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } x ^ { r } g ( x ) d x = 0 \ f o r \ r = 0 , 1 } \end{array}$ and $| g ( x ) | \leq C _ { 0 }$ for all $x \in \mathbb { R }$ , for some $C _ { 0 } \stackrel { \_ } { \in } ( 0 , \infty )$ . Then, for any $T \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 

$$
\sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} \left| F (x) - G (x) \right| \leq \frac {1}{\pi} \int_ {- T} ^ {T} \frac {| \zeta (t) - \xi (t) |}{| t |} d t + \frac {2 4 C _ {0}}{\pi T}\tag{4.3}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \xi ( t ) = \int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } \exp ( \iota t x ) g ( x ) d x , t \in \mathbb { R } } \end{array}$ 

For a proof of Lemma 11.4.2, see Feller (1966). 

The next lemma deals with an expansion of the logarithm of the characteristic function of X, in a neighborhood of zero. Let $z = r e ^ { i \theta } , r \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 2 $\theta \in [ 0 , 2 \pi )$ be the polar representation of a nonzero complex number z. Then, the (principal branch of the) complex logarithm of z is defined as 

$$
\log z = \log r + i \theta .\tag{4.4}
$$

The function log z is infinitely diferentiable on the set $\{ z \in \mathbb { C } : z = r e ^ { i \theta } , r \in$ $( 0 , \infty ) , 0 \leq \theta < 2 \pi \}$ and has a convergent Taylor’s series expansion around 1 on the unit disc: 

$$
\log (1 + z) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} z ^ {k} / k \quad \text { for } \quad | z | <   1.\tag{4.5}
$$

Lemma 11.4.3: Let Y be a random variable with $E Y = 0 , \tilde { \sigma } ^ { 2 } = E Y ^ { 2 } \in$ $( 0 , \infty ) , \tilde { \rho } = E | Y | ^ { 3 } < \infty$ and characteristic function $\phi _ { Y } ( t ) = E \exp ( \iota t Y )$ $t \in \mathbb { R }$ . Then, for all $\textstyle t \in \left[ - \frac { 1 } { \tilde { \sigma } } , \frac { 1 } { \tilde { \sigma } } \right]$ 2 

$$
\left| \log \phi_ {Y} (t) + \frac {t ^ {2} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {2}}{2} \right| \leq \frac {5}{1 2} | t | ^ {3} \tilde {\rho}\tag{4.6}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \log \phi_ {Y} (t) - \left[ \frac {(\iota t) ^ {2}}{2 !} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {2} + \frac {(\iota t) ^ {3}}{3 !} E Y ^ {3} \right] \right| \\ \leq E \bigg (\min \left\{\frac {| t Y | ^ {3}}{3}, \frac {(t Y) ^ {4}}{2 4} \right\} \bigg) + \frac {t ^ {4} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {4}}{4}. \end{array}\tag{4.7}
$$

Proof: Note that by Lemma 10.1.5, 

$$
\left| \phi_ {Y} (t) - 1 \right| = \left| E \big (\exp (\iota t Y) - 1 - \iota t Y \big) \right| \leq \frac {t ^ {2} E Y ^ {2}}{2} \leq \frac {1}{2}\tag{4.8}
$$

whenever $| t | \le \tilde { \sigma } ^ { - 1 }$ . In particular, log $\phi _ { Y } ( t )$ is well defined for all $t \in$ $\big \lceil - \tilde { \sigma } ^ { - 1 } , \tilde { \sigma } ^ { - \mathrm { i } } \big \rceil$ 

#By (4.5), (4.8), and Lemma 10.1.5, for $| t | \leq \tilde { \sigma } ^ { - 1 }$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \left| \log \phi_ {Y} (t) + \frac {t ^ {2} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {2}}{2} \right| \\ = & \left| \log \left[ 1 + \left(\phi_ {Y} (t) - 1\right) \right] + \frac {t ^ {2} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {2}}{2} \right| \\ \leq & \left| \phi_ {Y} (t) - \left[ 1 - \frac {t ^ {2} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {2}}{2} \right] \right| + \sum_ {k = 2} ^ {\infty} \left| \phi_ {Y} (t) - 1 \right| ^ {k} / k \\ \leq & E \Big | (t Y) ^ {2} \wedge \frac {| t Y | ^ {3}}{3 !} \Big | + \frac {1}{2} \Big (\frac {t ^ {2} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {2}}{2} \Big) ^ {2} \sum_ {k = 2} ^ {\infty} \Big (\frac {1}{2} \Big) ^ {k - 2} \\ \leq & \frac {| t | ^ {3} \rho}{6} + \frac {t ^ {4} \tilde {\sigma} ^ {4}}{4}. \end{array}
$$

Now using the bounds $| t \tilde { \sigma } | \leq 1$ and $\tilde { \sigma } ^ { 3 } = ( E Y ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 3 / 2 } \leq E | Y | ^ { 3 } = \tilde { \rho } ,$ , one gets (4.6). The proof of (4.7) is similar and hence, it is left as an exercise (Problem 11.27). ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 11.4.1: W.l.o.g., set $\mu ~ = ~ 0$ and $\sigma = 1$ . Then, $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , . . .$ . are iid zero mean, unit variance random variables. Let $X = ^ { d } X _ { 1 }$ 2 $\rho = E | X | ^ { 3 }$ and $\phi _ { X } ( \cdot )$ denote the characteristic function of X. It is easy to check that the conditions of Lemma 11.4.2 hold with $\begin{array} { r } { F ( x ) = P \big ( \frac { S _ { n } } { \sqrt { n } } \leq x \big ) } \end{array}$ ， $G ( x ) \ = \ \Phi ( x ) , \ x \ \in \ \mathbb { R }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { C _ { 0 } \ = \ \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi } } } \end{array}$ . Hence, by Lemma 11.4.2, with $T = { \sqrt { n } } / \rho _ { ; }$ 

$$
\Delta_ {n} \leq \frac {1}{\pi} \int_ {- T} ^ {T} \frac {\left| \phi_ {X} ^ {n} (\frac {t}{\sqrt {n}}) - e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2} \right|}{| t |} d t + \frac {2 4 \rho}{\pi \sqrt {2 \pi n}}.\tag{4.9}
$$

By Lemma 11.4.3 (with $\begin{array} { r } { Y = \frac { X _ { 1 } - \mu } { \sigma } } \end{array}$ and t replaced by $\textstyle { \frac { t } { \sqrt { n } } } )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} r _ {n} (t) & \equiv & \left| n \log \phi_ {X} \Big (\frac {t}{\sqrt {n}} \Big) + \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \right| \\ & = & n \Big | \log \phi_ {X} \Big (\frac {t}{\sqrt {n}} \Big) + \Big (\frac {t}{\sqrt {n}} \Big) ^ {2} \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{2} \Big | \\ & \leq & \frac {5}{1 2} \cdot \frac {\rho | t | ^ {3}}{\sqrt {n}} \end{array}\tag{4.10}
$$

for all $| t | \leq { \sqrt { n } } , n \geq 1$ 

Since $\rho = E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 3 } \ge ( E X _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 3 / 2 } = \sigma ^ { 3 } = 1 , | T | \le \sqrt { n }$ . Hence, using the inequality $| e ^ { z } - 1 | \leq | z | e ^ { | z | }$ for all $z \in \mathbb { C }$ and (4.10), one gets 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left| \phi_ {X} ^ {n} \left(\frac {t}{\sqrt {n}}\right) - e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2} \right|} \\ {=} & {\left| \exp \left(n \cdot \log \phi_ {X} \left(\frac {t}{\sqrt {n}}\right) + \frac {t ^ {2}}{2}\right) - 1 \right| \cdot \exp \left(- \frac {t ^ {2}}{2}\right)} \\ {\leq} & {| r _ {n} (t) | \exp \left(| r _ {n} (t) |\right) \cdot \exp \left(- \frac {t ^ {2}}{2}\right)} \\ {\leq} & {\frac {5 \rho}{1 2 \sqrt {n}} | t | ^ {3} \exp \left(- \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \left[ 1 - \frac {5 \rho | t |}{6 \sqrt {n}} \right]\right)} \\ {\leq} & {\frac {5 \rho}{1 2 \sqrt {n}} | t | ^ {3} \exp \left(- \frac {t ^ {2}}{1 2}\right)} \end{array}\tag{4.11}
$$

for all ${ \frac { \rho | t | } { \sqrt { n } } } \leq 1 , { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ ., for all $| t | \leq T , n \geq 1$ . Since $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } t ^ { 2 } \exp { \left( - \frac { t ^ { 2 } } { 1 2 } \right) } d t = 6 \sqrt { 2 \pi } } \end{array}$ 2 the theorem follows from (4.9) and (4.11) with $\begin{array} { r } { C = \sqrt { \frac { 2 } { \pi } } \bigl [ \frac { 5 } { 2 } + \frac { 1 2 } { \pi } \bigr ] } \end{array}$ ✷ 

A striking feature of Theorem 11.4.1 is that the upper bound on $\Delta _ { n }$ in (4.2) is valid for all $n \geq 1$ . Also, under the conditions of Theorem 11.4.1, the rate $O ( \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { n } } } )$ in (4.2) is the best possible in the sense that there exist random variables for which $\Delta _ { n }$ is bounded below by a constant multiple of $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { n } } }$ (cf. Problem 11.29). Edgeworth expansions of the cdf of $\frac { S _ { n } - n \mu } { \sigma { \sqrt { n } } }$ , to be developed in the next section, can be used to show that for certain random variables $X _ { 1 }$ satisfying additional moment and symmetry conditions, $\Delta _ { n }$ may go to zero at a faster rate. (For example, consider $X _ { 1 } \sim N ( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } ) .$ ) 

For iid sequences $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ with $E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 2 + \delta } < \infty$ for some $\delta \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( 0 , 1 ]$ Theorem 11.4.1 can be strengthened to show that $\Delta _ { n }$ decreases at the rate $O ( n ^ { - \delta / 2 } )$ as $n \to \infty$ (cf. Chow and Teicher (1997), Chapter 9). 

## 11.4.2 Edgeworth expansions

Recall from Chapter 10 that a random variable $X _ { 1 }$ is called lattice if there exist $a \in \mathbb { R }$ and $h \in ( 0 , \infty )$ such that 

$$
P \big (X _ {1} \in \{a + i h: i \in \mathbb {Z} \} \big) = 1.\tag{4.12}
$$

The largest h satisfying (4.12) is called the span of (the distribution of) $X _ { 1 }$ . A random variable $X _ { 1 }$ is called nonlattice if it is not a lattice random variable. From Proposition 10.1.1, it follows that $X _ { 1 }$ is nonlattice if 

$$
\left| E \exp (\iota t X _ {1}) \right| <   1 \quad \text { for   all } \quad t \neq 0.\tag{4.13}
$$

The next result gives an Edgeworth expansion for the cdf of $\frac { S _ { n } - n \mu } { \sigma { \sqrt { n } } }$ with an error of order $o ( n ^ { - 1 / 2 } )$ for nonlattice random variables. 

Theorem 11.4.4: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables with $E X _ { 1 } = \mu , \ V a r ( X _ { 1 } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \overline { { \infty } } )$ and $E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 3 } < \infty$ . Suppose, in addition, that $X _ { 1 }$ is nonlattice, i.e., it satisfies $\left( 4 . 1 3 \right)$ . Then, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} \bigg | P \Big (\frac {S _ {n} - n \mu}{\sigma \sqrt {n}} \leq x \Big) - \Big [ \Phi (x) - \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \cdot \frac {\mu_ {3}}{6 \sigma^ {3}} (x ^ {2} - 1) \phi (x) \Big ] \bigg | \\ = o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \quad a s \quad n \to \infty , \end{array}\tag{4.14}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \phi ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi } } e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } / 2 } , x \in \mathbb { R } \ a n d \ \mu _ { 3 } = E ( X _ { 1 } - \mu ) ^ { 3 } . } \end{array}$ 

The function 

$$
e _ {n, 2} (x) \equiv \Phi (x) - \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \cdot \frac {\mu_ {3}}{6 \sigma^ {3}} (x ^ {2} - 1), x \in \mathbb {R}\tag{4.15}
$$

is called a second order Edgeworth expansion for $\begin{array} { r } { T _ { n } \equiv \frac { S _ { n } - n \mu } { \sigma \sqrt { n } } } \end{array}$ . The above theorem shows that the cdf of the normalized sum $T _ { n }$ can be approximated by the second order Edgeworth expansion with accuracy $o ( n ^ { - 1 / 2 } )$ . It can be shown that if $E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 4 } < \infty$ and $X _ { 1 }$ satisfies Cramer’s condition: 

$$
\limsup _ {| t | \to \infty} \left| E \exp (\iota t X _ {1}) \right| <   1,\tag{4.16}
$$

then the bound on the right side of (4.14) can be improved to $O ( n ^ { - 1 } )$ . Note that for a symmetric random variable $X _ { 1 }$ , having a finite fourth moment and satisfying (4.16), the second term in $e _ { n , 2 } ( x )$ is zero and the rate of normal approximation becomes $O ( n ^ { - 1 } )$ . Higher order Edgeworth expansions for $T _ { n }$ can be derived using (4.16) and arguments similar to those in the proof of Theorem 11.4.4, but the form of the expansion becomes more complicated. See Petrov (1975), Bhattacharya and Rao (1986), and Hall (1992) for detailed accounts of the Edgeworth expansion theory.

This section concludes with an analog of Theorem 11.4.4 for lattice random variables. Note that for $X _ { 1 }$ satisfying $P ( X _ { 1 } \in \{ a + j h : j \in \mathbb { Z } \} ) = 1$ , the normalized sample sum $T _ { n }$ takes values in the lattice $\begin{array} { r } { \left\{ \frac { n a - n \mu } { \sigma \sqrt { n } } + j h / \sigma \sqrt { n } \right. } \end{array}$ $j \in \mathbb { Z } \}$ . Hence, the cdf of $T _ { n }$ is a step function. The second order Edgeworth expansion for $T _ { n }$ is no longer a smooth function — the efect of the jumps of the cdf of $T _ { n }$ is now accounted for by adding a discontinuous function to the expansion $e _ { n , 2 }$ . Let 

$$
Q (x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor - \frac {1}{2}, x \in \mathbb {R}\tag{4.23}
$$

where $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the largest integer not exceeding $x , x \in \mathbb { R }$ . It is easy to check that $Q ( x )$ is a periodic function of period 1 with values in $[ - \ \frac { 1 } { 2 } , \ \frac { 1 } { 2 } ]$ 2 $Q ( x )$ " # is right continuous, and it has jumps of size 1 at the integer values. The second order Edgeworth expansions for $T _ { n }$ in the lattice case involves the function $Q$ , as shown below. 

Theorem 11.4.5: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of lattice random variables with span $h > 0$ . Suppose that ${ \mathrm { { \bar { E } } } } | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 3 } < \infty$ and $\sigma ^ { 2 } = V a r ( X _ { 1 } ) \in ( 0 , \infty )$ Then, 

$$
\sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} \left| P \Big (\frac {S _ {n} - n \mu}{\sigma \sqrt {n}} \leq x \Big) - \tilde {e} _ {n, 2} (x) \right| = o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \quad a s \quad n \to \infty\tag{4.24}
$$

where $\mu = E X _ { 1 } , S _ { n } = X _ { 1 } + \dots + X _ { n } , n \geq 1$ 

$$
\tilde {e} _ {n, 2} (x) = \Phi (x) - \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \biggl [ \frac {\mu_ {3}}{6 \sigma^ {3}} (x ^ {2} - 1) + \frac {h}{\sigma} Q \biggl (\frac {\sqrt {n} [ n x \sigma - n x _ {0} ]}{h} \biggr) \biggr ] \phi (x),\tag{4.25}
$$

$x \in \mathbb { R } , Q ( x )$ is as in $\begin{array} { r } { ( \mathscr { 4 . 2 3 } ) , \phi ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi } } \exp ( - x ^ { 2 } / 2 ) , x \in \mathbb { R } } \end{array}$ and $x _ { 0 }$ is a real number satisfying $P ( X _ { 1 } = \mu + x _ { 0 } ) > 0$ 

For a proof of Theorem 11.4.5 and for related results, see Esseen (1945) and Bhattacharya and Rao (1986). 

## 11.4.3 Large deviations

Let $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be iid random variables with $E X _ { 1 } = \mu$ . The SLLN implies that for any $x > \mu ,$ 2 

$$
P (\bar {X} _ {n} > x) \rightarrow 0 \quad \text { as } \quad n \rightarrow \infty ,\tag{4.26}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { X } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } , n \ge 1 } \end{array}$ . If $X _ { i }$ ’s were distributed as $N ( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ for some $\mu \in \mathbb { R }$ and $\sigma ^ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , then the left side of (4.26) equals $\Phi \Big ( \frac { \sqrt { n } ( x - \mu ) } { \sigma } \Big )$ Now note that 

$$
- \log \Phi \bigg (\frac {\sqrt {n} (x - \mu)}{\sigma} \bigg) \sim - \log \big [ \exp (- n c _ {1} ^ {2}) / (\sqrt {n} c _ {1} \sqrt {2 n}) \big ] \sim n c _ {1} ^ {2},
$$

where $c _ { 1 } = ( x - \mu ) / \sigma \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Large deviation bounds on the probability $P ( { \bar { X } } _ { n } \ > \ x )$ assert that a similar behavior holds for many distributions other than the normal distribution on the (negative) logarithmic scale. 

The main result of this section is the following. 

Theorem 11.4.6: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid nondegenerate random variables with 

$$
\phi (t) \equiv E e ^ {t X _ {1}} <   \infty \quad f o r a l l \quad t > 0.\tag{4.27}
$$

Let $\mu = E X _ { 1 }$ . Then, for all $x \in \left( \mu , \theta \right)$ 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq x) = - \gamma (x),\tag{4.28}
$$

where 

$$
\gamma (x) = \sup _ {t > 0} \{t x - \log \phi (t) \} a n d \theta = \sup \{x \in \mathbb {R}: P (X _ {1} \leq x) <   1 \}.\tag{4.29}
$$

Note that under (4.27), $E X _ { 1 } ^ { + } < \infty$ and hence, $\mu \equiv E X _ { 1 }$ is well defined, and $\mu \in [ - \infty , \infty )$ 

For proving the theorem, the following results are needed. 

Lemma 11.4.7: Let $X _ { 1 }$ be a nondegenerate random variable satisfying $( 4 . 2 7 )$ . Let $\mu = E X _ { 1 }$ and let $\gamma ( x )$ , θ be as in $\left( 4 . 2 9 \right)$ . Then, 

(i) the function $\phi ( t )$ is infinitely diferentiable on $( 0 , \infty )$ with $\phi ^ { ( r ) } ( t )$ , the rth derivative $o f \phi ( t )$ being given by 

$$
\phi^ {(r)} (t) = E \left(X _ {1} ^ {r} e ^ {t X _ {1}}\right), t \in (0, \infty), r \in \mathbb {N},\tag{4.30}
$$

(ii) $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { t \downarrow 0 } \phi ( t ) = 1 , \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t \downarrow 0 } \phi ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) = \mu , a n d \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t  \infty } \frac { \phi ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) } { \phi ( t ) } = \theta ,$ 

(iii) for every $x \in \left( \mu , \theta \right)$ , there exists a unique solution $a _ { x } \in \mathbb { R }$ to the equation 

$$
x = \phi^ {\prime} (a _ {x}) / \phi (a _ {x})\tag{4.31}
$$

such that $\gamma ( x ) = x a _ { x } - \log \phi ( a _ { x } )$ 

Proof: Let F denote the cdf of $X _ { 1 } . ~ ( \mathrm { i } )$ Note that for any $h \neq 0$ 2 

$$
h ^ {- 1} \big [ \phi (t + h) - \phi (t) \big ] = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \frac {e ^ {h x} - 1}{h} \cdot e ^ {t x} d F (x).
$$

As $h \  \ 0$ , the integrand converges $x e ^ { t x }$ for all $x , t .$ . Also, $| \frac { e ^ { h s } - 1 } { h } | \leq$ $\textstyle \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } { \left| h ^ { k - 1 } x ^ { k } \right| } / { k ! } \leq | x | e ^ { | h x | }$ for all $h , x$ . Hence, for any $x \in \mathbb { R } , t \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 2 and $0 < | h | < \dot { t } / 2$ , the integrand is bounded above by 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} | x | e ^ {| h x |} e ^ {t x} & = & | x | e ^ {(t - | h |) x} I _ {(- \infty , 0)} (x) + | x | e ^ {(t + | h |) x} I (x > 0) \\ & \leq & | x | e ^ {- t | x | / 2} I _ {(- \infty , 0)} (x) + | x | e ^ {3 t x} I _ {(0, \infty)} (x) \\ & \equiv & g (x), \text {say.} \end{array}\tag{4.32}
$$

Since $\textstyle \int g ( x ) d F ( x ) < \infty$ , by the DCT, it follows that 

$$
\lim _ {h \to 0} \frac {\phi (t + h) - \phi (t)}{h} \quad \text { exists   and   equals } \quad \int x e ^ {t x} d F (x)
$$

for all $t \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( 0 , \infty )$ . Thus, $\phi ( t )$ is diferentiable on $( 0 , \infty )$ with $\phi ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) =$ $E X _ { 1 } e ^ { t X _ { 1 } } , t \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Now, using induction and similar arguments, one can complete the proof of part (i) (Problem 11.34). 

Next consider (ii). Since $e ^ { t x } \leq I _ { ( - \infty , 0 ] } ( x ) + e ^ { x } I _ { ( 0 , \infty ) } ( x )$ for all $x \in \mathbb { R }$ 2 $t \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , by the DCT, the first relation follows. For the second, note that 

$$
| x | e ^ {t x} I _ {(- \infty , 0)} (x) \uparrow | x | I _ {(- \infty , 0 ]} (x) \quad \text { as } \quad t \downarrow 0\tag{4.33}
$$

and $| x | e ^ { t x } \leq | x | e ^ { x }$ for all $0 < t \leq 1 , x > 0$ . Hence, applying the MCT for $x \in ( - \infty , 0 ]$ and the DCT for $x \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , one obtains the second limit. Derivation of the third limit is left as an exercise (Problem 11.35). 

To prove part (iii), fix $x \in \left( \mu , \theta \right)$ and let $\gamma ( t ) = t x - \log { \phi ( t ) } , t \geq 0$ . Then, for $t \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \gamma^ {(1)} (t) & = & x - \frac {\phi^ {(1)} (t)}{\phi (t)} \\ \gamma^ {(2)} (t) & = & \frac {\phi^ {(2)} (t)}{\phi (t)} - \Big (\frac {\phi^ {(1)} (t)}{\phi (t)} \Big) ^ {2} = \mathrm{Var} (Y _ {t}), \end{array}\tag{4.34}
$$

where $Y _ { t }$ is a random variable with cdf $\begin{array} { r } { P ( Y _ { t } \leq y ) = \int _ { - \infty } ^ { y } e ^ { t u } d F ( x ) / \phi ( t ) } \end{array}$ $y \in \mathbb { R }$ . Since $X _ { 1 }$ is nondegenerate, so is $Y _ { t } ~ \mathrm { ( f o r }$ any $t \geq 0 )$ and hence, $\mathrm { V a r } ( Y _ { t } ) > 0$ . As a consequence, the second derivative of the function $\gamma ( t )$ is positive. And the minimum of $\gamma ( t )$ over $( 0 , \infty )$ is attained by a solution to the equation $\gamma ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) = 0 , \mathrm { i . e . }$ , by $t = a _ { x }$ satisfying (4.30). That such a solution exists and is unique follows from part (ii) and the facts that $x > \mu ,$ $\frac { \phi ^ { ( 1 ) } ( 0 + ) } { \phi ( 0 ) } = \mu ~ ( \mathrm { b y ~ ( i i ) } )$ , and that $\frac { \phi ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) } { \phi ( t ) }$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $( 0 , \infty )$ (as for any $t \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , the derivative of $\frac { \phi ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) } { \phi ( t ) }$ coincides with $\gamma ^ { ( 2 ) } ( t )$ , which is positive by (4.34)). This proves part (iii). ✷ 

Lemma 11.4.8: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be as in Theorem $1 1 . 4 . 6 .$ . For $t \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 2 let $\{ Y _ { t , n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables with cdf 

$$
P (Y _ {t, 1} \leq y) = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {y} e ^ {t u} d F (u) / \phi (t), y \in \mathbb {R},
$$

where $F$ is the cdf $o f X _ { 1 }$ . Let $\nu _ { n }$ and $\lambda _ { n }$ denote the probability distributions of $S _ { n } \equiv X _ { 1 } + \cdots + X _ { n }$ and $T _ { n , t } = Y _ { t , 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + Y _ { t , n } , n \geq 1$ . Then, for each $n \geq 1$ 2 

$$
\nu_ {n} \ll \lambda_ {n} \quad a n d \quad \frac {d \nu_ {n}}{d \lambda_ {n}} (x) = e ^ {- t x} \phi (t) ^ {n}, x \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{4.35}
$$

Proof: The proof is by induction. Clearly, the assertion holds for $n = 1$ Next, suppose that (4.35) is true for some $r \in \mathbb N$ and let $n = r + 1$ . Then, for any $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \nu_ {n} (A) & = & P \big (X _ {1} + \dots + X _ {n} \in A \big) \\ & = & \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} P \big (X _ {1} + \dots + X _ {n - 1} \in A - x \big) d F (x) \\ & = & \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \int_ {A - x} \Big [ \frac {d \nu_ {n - 1}}{d \lambda_ {n - 1}} (u) \Big ] d \lambda_ {n - 1} (u) d F (x) \\ & = & \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \int_ {A - x} e ^ {- t u} \phi (t) ^ {n - 1} d \lambda_ {n - 1} (u) d F (x) \\ & = & [ \phi (t) ] ^ {n} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \int_ {A - x} e ^ {- t (u + x)} d \lambda_ {n - 1} (u) d \lambda_ {1} (x) \\ & = & [ \phi (t) ] ^ {n} \int_ {A} e ^ {- t u} \big (\lambda_ {n - 1} * \lambda_ {1} \big) (d \nu), \end{array}
$$

where denotes convolution. Since $\lambda _ { n - 1 } * \lambda _ { 1 } = \lambda _ { n }$ , the result follows. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 11.4.6: Fix $x \in \left( \mu , \theta \right)$ . Note that by Markov’s inequality, for any $t > 0 , n \geq 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq x) & = & P \Big (e ^ {t \bar {X} _ {n}} \geq e ^ {t x} \Big) \\ & \leq & e ^ {- t x} E \Big (e ^ {t \bar {X} _ {n}} \Big) \\ & = & \exp \big (- t x + n \log \phi (t / n) \big). \end{array}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} n ^ {- 1} \log P \big (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq x \big) \leq - x \cdot \frac {t}{n} + \log \phi \big (\frac {t}{n} \big) \quad \text { for   all } \quad t > 0, n \geq 1 \\ \Rightarrow \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \big (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq x \big) \leq \inf _ {t > 0} \{- x t + \log \phi (t) \} = - \gamma (x). \end{array}\tag{4.36}
$$

This yields the upper bound. Next it will be shown that 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \big (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq x \big) \geq - \gamma (x).\tag{4.37}
$$

To that end, let $\{ Y _ { t , n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } , \nu _ { n }$ , and $\lambda _ { n }$ be as in Lemma 11.4.8. Also, let $a _ { x }$ be as in (4.30). Then, for any $y > x , t \in ( a _ { x } , \infty )$ , and $n \geq 1$ , by Lemma 11.4.8, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P \big (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq x \big) & = & \nu_ {n} \big ([ n x, \infty) \big) \\ & = & \int_ {[ n x, \infty)} e ^ {- t u} \phi (t) ^ {n}   d u \\ & \geq & \int_ {[ n x, n y ]} e ^ {- t u} \phi (t) ^ {n}   d u \\ & \geq & \phi (t) ^ {n} e ^ {- t n y} \lambda_ {n} \big ([ n x, n y ] \big). \end{array}\tag{4.38}
$$

Note that $\begin{array} { r } { E Y _ { t , 1 } = \int u d \lambda _ { 1 } ( u ) = \phi ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) / \phi ( t ) } \end{array}$ . Since $\phi ^ { ( 1 ) } ( \cdot ) / \phi ( \cdot )$ is strictly increasing and continuous on $( 0 , \infty )$ , given $y > x$ , there exists a $t = t _ { y } \in$ $( a _ { x } , \infty )$ such that 

$$
y > \frac {\phi^ {(1)} (t)}{\phi (t)} > \frac {\phi^ {(1)} (a _ {x})}{\phi (a _ {x})} = x.\tag{4.39}
$$

By the WLLN, for any $y > x$ and t satisfying (4.39), 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l}\lambda_ {n} ([ n x, n y ])&=&P \bigg (x \leq \frac {Y _ {t , 1} + \cdots + Y _ {t , n}}{n} \leq y \bigg)\\&&\rightarrow 1 \quad \text { as } \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\end{array}
$$

Hence, from (4.38), it follows that 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \big (\bar {X} _ {n} \geq x \big) \geq - t y + \log \phi (t)
$$

for all $y \ > \ x$ and all $t \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( a _ { x } , \infty )$ satisfying (4.39). Now, letting $t \downarrow a _ { x }$ first and then $y \downarrow x .$ , one gets $( 4 . 3 7 )$ . This completes the proof of Theorem 11.4.6. ✷ 

Remark 11.4.1: If (4.27) holds and $\theta < \infty$ , then
