# Discrete Parameter Martingales

## 13.1 Definitions and examples

This section deals with a class of stochastic processes called martingales. Martingales arise in a natural way in many problems in probability and statistics. It provides a more general framework than the case of independent random variables where results, like the SLLN, the CLT, and other convergence theorems, can be established. Much of the discrete parameter martingale theory was developed by the great American mathematician J. L. Doob, whose book (Doob (1953)) has been very influential. 

Definition 13.1.1: Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ be a probability space and let $N =$ $\{ 1 , \ldots , n _ { 0 } \}$ be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb { N } = \{ 1 , 2 , . . . \} , n _ { 0 } \leq \infty$ 

(a) A collection $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ of sub-σ-algebras of $\mathcal { F }$ is called a filtration if ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \subset { \mathcal { F } } _ { n + 1 }$ for all $1 \leq n < n _ { 0 }$ 

(b) A collection of random variables $\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \}$ is said to be adapted to the filtration $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ if $X _ { n }$ is -measurable for all $n \in N$ 

(c) Given a filtration $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ and random variables $\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \}$ ， the collection $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ is called a martingale if 

(i) $\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \}$ is adapted to $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ 2 

(ii) $E | X _ { n } | < \infty$ for all $n \in N$ , and 

(iii) for all $1 \leq n < n _ { 0 }$ 

$$
E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) = X _ {n}.\tag{1.1}
$$

When $N = \mathbb { N }$ , there is no maximum element in N. In this case, Definition 13.1.1 is to be interpreted by setting $n _ { 0 } = + \infty$ in parts (a) and (c) (iii). A similar convention applies to Definition 13.1.2 below. Also, recall that equalities and inequalities involving conditional expectations are interpreted as being valid events w.p. 1. 

If $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ is a martingale, then $\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \}$ is also said to be a martingale w.r.t. (the filtration) $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ . Also $\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \}$ is called a martingale if it is a martingale w.r.t. some filtration. Observe that if $\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \}$ is a martingale w.r.t. any given filtration $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ 2 it is also a martingale w.r.t. the natural filtration $\{ { \mathcal { X } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ , where $\mathcal { X } _ { n } = \sigma \langle \{ X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } \} \rangle , n \in N$ . Clearly, $\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \}$ is adapted to $\{ \mathcal { X } _ { n }$ $n \in N \}$ . To see that $E ( X _ { n + 1 } | { \mathcal { X } } _ { n } ) = X _ { n }$ for all $1 \leq n < n _ { 0 }$ , note that $\mathcal { X } _ { n } \subset \mathcal { F } _ { n }$ for all $n \in N$ and hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {X} _ {n}) & = & E (E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \mid \mathcal {X} _ {n}) \\ & = & E (X _ {n} | \mathcal {X} _ {n}) = X _ {n}. \end{array}\tag{1.2}
$$

Thus, $\left\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { X } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \right\}$ is a martingale. 

A classic interpretation of martingales in the context of gambling is given as follows. Let $X _ { n }$ represent the fortune of a gambler at the end of the nth play and let ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ be the information available to the gambler up to and including the nth play. Then, ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ contains the knowledge of all events like $\{ X _ { j } \ \leq \ r \}$ for $r \in \mathbb { R } , j \leq n$ , making $X _ { n }$ measurable w.r.t. ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ . And Condition (iii) in Definition 13.1.1 (c) says that given all the information up until the end of the nth play, the expected fortune of the gambler at the end of the $( n + 1 )$ th play remains unchanged. Thus a martingale represents a fair game. In situations where the game puts the gambler in a favorable or unfavorable position, one may express that by suitably modifying condition (iii), yielding what are known as sub- and super-martingales, respectively. 

Definition 13.1.2: Let $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ be a filtration and $\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \}$ be a collection of random variables in $L ^ { 1 } ( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ adapted to $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } : n \in N \}$ Then $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ is called a sub-martingale if 

$$
E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \geq X _ {n} \quad \text { for   all } \quad 1 \leq n <   n _ {0},\tag{1.3}
$$

and a super-martingale 

$$
E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \leq X _ {n} \quad \text { for   all } \quad 1 \leq n <   n _ {0}.\tag{1.4}
$$

Suppose that $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ is a sub-martingale. Then $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ implies that $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n + 1 } \subset \ldots \subset { \mathcal { F } } _ { n + k }$ for every $k \geq 1 , n + k \in N$ and hence, by (1.3), 

$$
\int_ {A} X _ {n} d P \leq \int_ {A} E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) d P = \int_ {A} X _ {n + 1} d P
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \vdots \\ \leq & \int_ {A} X _ {n + k} d P. \end{array}\tag{1.5}
$$

Therefore, $E ( X _ { n + k } | { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) \geq X _ { n }$ and, by taking $A = \Omega$ in (1.5), $E X _ { n + k } \ \geq$ $E X _ { n }$ . Thus, the expected values of a sub-martingale is nondecreasing. For a martingale, by (1.2), equality holds at every step of (1.5) and hence, 

$$
E (X _ {n + k} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) = X _ {n}, E X _ {n + k} = E X _ {n}\tag{1.6}
$$

for all $k \geq 1 , n , n + k \in N$ . Thus, in a fair game, the expected fortune of the gambler remains constant over time. 

Here are some examples. 

Example 13.1.1: (Random walk). Let $Z _ { 1 } , Z _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be a sequence of iid random variables on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ with finite mean $\mu = E Z _ { 1 }$ and let $\mathcal { F } _ { n } = \sigma \langle Z _ { 1 } , \ldots , Z _ { n } \rangle , n \geq 1$ . Let $X _ { n } = Z _ { 1 } + \ldots Z _ { n } , n \geq 1$ . Then, for all $n \geq 1 , \sigma \langle X _ { n } \rangle \subset \mathcal { F } _ { n }$ and $E | X _ { n } | < \infty$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Also, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) & = & E \big ((Z _ {1} + \ldots + Z _ {n + 1}) \mid Z _ {1}, \ldots , Z _ {n} \big) \\ & = & Z _ {1} + \ldots + Z _ {n} + E Z _ {n + 1} \quad (\text { by   independence }) \\ & = & X _ {n} + \mu , \end{array}
$$

so that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l r c l} E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) & = & X _ {n} & \text {if} & \mu = 0 \\ & > & X _ {n} & \text {if} & \mu > 0 \\ & <   & X _ {n} & \text {if} & \mu <   0. \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ is a martingale if $\mu = 0$ , a sub-martingale if $\mu \geq 0$ and a super-martingale if $\mu \leq 0$ 

Example 13.1.2: (Random walk continued). Let $\{ Z _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be as in Example 13.1.1 and let $E Z _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { Y _ { n } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n ^ { - } } ( Z _ { i } - \mu ) ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ and $\tilde { Y } _ { n } = Y _ { n } - n \sigma ^ { 2 }$ , where $\sigma ^ { 2 } = V a r ( Z _ { 1 } )$ . Then, check that $\{ ( Y _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ is a sub-martingale and $\{ ( \tilde { Y } _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ is a martingale (Problem 13.3). 

Example 13.1.3: (Doob’s martingale). Let Z be an integrable random variable and let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } : n \geq 1 \}$ be a filtration both defined on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ . Define 

$$
X _ {n} = E (Z | \mathcal {F} _ {n}), n \geq 1.\tag{1.7}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) & = & E (E (Z | \mathcal {F} _ {n + 1}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \\ & = & E (Z | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) = X _ {n}. \end{array}
$$

Then, clearly, $X _ { n }$ is integrable and ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ -measurable for all $n \geq 1$ . Also, 

Thus, $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ is a martingale. 

Example 13.1.4: (Generation of a martingale from a given sequence of random variables). Let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 } \subset L ^ { 1 } ( \Omega , \mathcal { F } , P )$ be an arbitrary collection of integrable random variables and let $\mathcal { F } _ { n } = \sigma \langle Y _ { 1 } , \ldots , Y _ { n } \rangle , n \geq 1$ . For $n \geq 1$ 2 define 

$$
X _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \left\{Y _ {j} - E \left(Y _ {j} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {j - 1}\right) \right\}\tag{1.8}
$$

where ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { 0 } \equiv \{ \emptyset , \Omega \}$ 

Then, for each $n \geq 1 , X _ { n }$ is integrable and ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ -measurable. Also, for $n \geq 1$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n + 1} E ([ Y _ {j} - E (Y _ {j} | \mathcal {F} _ {j - 1}) ] \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} [ Y _ {j} - E (Y _ {j} | \mathcal {F} _ {j - 1}) ] + [ E (Y _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) - E (Y _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) ] \\ & = & X _ {n}. \end{array}
$$

Hence $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ is a martingale. Thus, one can construct a martingale sequence starting from any arbitrary sequence of integrable random variables. When $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ are iid with $E Y _ { 1 } = 0 , ( 1 . 8 )$ yields $\textstyle X _ { n } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } Y _ { j }$ and one gets the martingale sequence of Example 13.1.1. 

Example 13.1.5: (Branching process). Let $\{ \xi _ { n k } : n \ge 1 , k \ge 1 \}$ be a double array of iid nonnegative integer valued random variables with $E \xi _ { n k } = \mu \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . One may think of $\xi _ { n k }$ as the number of ofspring of the kth individual at time n in an evolving population. Let $Z _ { n }$ denote the size of the population at time $n , n \geq 0$ . If one considers the evolution of the population starting with a single individual at time $n = 0$ , then 

$$
Z _ {0} = 1 \quad \text { and } \quad Z _ {n} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {Z _ {n - 1}} \xi_ {n k}, n \geq 1.
$$

The sequence $Z _ { 0 } , Z _ { 1 } , \ldots$ . is called a branching process (cf. Chapter 18). 

Let $\mathcal { F } _ { n } = \sigma \langle Z _ { 1 } , \ldots , Z _ { n } \rangle , n \geq 1$ . Then, for $n \geq 1$ 

$$
E (Z _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) = E \bigg (\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {Z _ {n}} \xi_ {n + 1, k} \mid Z _ {n} \bigg) = \mu Z _ {n}\tag{1.9}
$$

and therefore, $\{ ( Z _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ is a martingale, sub-martingale or supermartingale according as $\mu = 1 , \mu \geq 1$ or $\mu \leq 1$ . One can define a new sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ from $\{ Z _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ such that $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale w.r.t. ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ for all values of $\mu \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Let 

$$
X _ {n} = \mu^ {- n} Z _ {n}, n \geq 1.\tag{1.10}
$$

Then, using (1.9), it is easy to check that $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ is a martingale. 

Example 13.1.6: (Likelihood ratio). Let $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be a collection of random variables on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ and let $\mathcal { F } _ { n } = \sigma \langle Y _ { 1 } , \ldots , Y _ { n } \rangle$ 2 $n \geq 1$ . Let $Q$ be another probability measure on $\mathcal { F }$ . Suppose that under both $P$ and $Q ,$ the joint distributions of $( Y _ { 1 } , \ldots , Y _ { n } )$ are absolutely continuous w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure $\lambda _ { n } \mathrm { o n } \mathbb { R } ^ { n } , n \geq 1$ . Denote the corresponding densities by $p _ { n } ( y _ { 1 } , \ldots , y _ { n } )$ and $q _ { n } ( y _ { 1 } , \ldots , y _ { n } ) , n \geq 1$ and for simplicity, suppose that $p _ { n } ( y _ { 1 } , \ldots , y _ { n } )$ is everywhere positive. Then, a likelihood ratio for discriminating between the probability measures $P$ and $Q$ on the basis of the observations $Y _ { 1 } , \dots , Y _ { n }$ , is given by 

$$
X _ {n} = q _ {n} (Y _ {1}, \ldots , Y _ {n}) / p _ {n} (Y _ {1}, \ldots , Y _ {n}), n \geq 1.
$$

A higher value of $X _ { n }$ is supposed to provide “evidence” in favor of $Q$ (over $P )$ as the “true” probability measure determining the distribution of $( Y _ { 1 } , \ldots , Y _ { n } )$ . It will now be shown that $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale w.r.t. ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ $n \geq 1$ under P. Clearly, $X _ { n }$ is ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n } .$ -measurable for all $n \geq 1$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int | X _ {n} | d P & = & \int_ {\Omega} \frac {q _ {n} (Y _ {1} , \ldots , Y _ {n})}{p _ {n} (Y _ {1} , \ldots , Y _ {n})} d P \\ & = & \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {n}} \frac {q _ {n} (y _ {1} , \ldots , y _ {n})}{p _ {n} (y _ {1} , \ldots , y _ {n})} p _ {n} (y _ {1}, \ldots , y _ {n}) d \lambda_ {n} \\ & = & \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {n}} q _ {n} (y _ {1}, \ldots , y _ {n}) d \lambda_ {n} = Q (\Omega) = 1 <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

so that $X _ { n }$ is integrable (w.r.t. P) for all $n \geq 1$ . Noting that the sets in the σ-algebra ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ are given by $\{ ( Y _ { 1 } , \dots , Y _ { n } ) \in B \}$ for $B \in B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { n } )$ , one has, for any $n \geq 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int_ {\{(Y _ {1}, \ldots , Y _ {n}) \in B \}} X _ {n + 1} d P & = & \int_ {\{(Y _ {1}, \ldots , Y _ {n + 1}) \in B \times \mathbb {R} \}} \frac {q _ {n + 1} (Y _ {1} , \ldots , Y _ {n + 1})}{p _ {n + 1} (Y _ {1} , \ldots , Y _ {n + 1})} d P \\ & = & \int_ {B \times \mathbb {R}} \frac {q _ {n + 1} (y _ {1} , \ldots , y _ {n + 1})}{p _ {n + 1} (y _ {1} , \ldots , y _ {n + 1})} \\ & & p _ {n + 1} (y _ {1}, \ldots , y _ {n + 1}) d \lambda_ {n + 1} \\ & = & \int_ {B} q _ {n} (y _ {1}, \ldots , y _ {n}) d \lambda_ {n} \\ & = & \int_ {B} \frac {q _ {n} (y _ {1} , \ldots , y _ {n})}{p _ {n} (y _ {1} , \ldots , y _ {n})} p _ {n} (y _ {1}, \ldots , y _ {n}) d \lambda_ {n} \end{array}
$$

$$
= \int_ {\left\{\left(Y _ {1}, \dots , Y _ {n}\right) \in B \right\}} X _ {n} d P,
$$

implying that $E ( X _ { n + 1 } | \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) = X _ { n } , n \ge 1$ . This shows that $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \geq$ 1 is a martingale for any arbitrary sequence of random variables $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ under P. However, $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ may not be a martingale under Q. 

Example 13.1.7: (Radon-Nikodym derivatives). Let $\Omega = ( 0 , 1 ] , \mathcal { F } =$ $B ( 0 , 1 ]$ , the Borel σ-algebra on (0, 1] and let $P$ denote the Lebesgue measure on (0, 1]. For $n \geq 1$ , let ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ be the σ-algebra generated by the partition $\{ ( ( k - 1 ) 2 ^ { - n } , k 2 ^ { n } ] , k = 1 , \ldots , 2 ^ { n } \}$ of (0, 1] by dyadic intervals. Let ν be a finite measure on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ . Let $\nu _ { n }$ be the restriction of ν to ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ and $P _ { n }$ be the restriction of P to ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ , for each $n \geq 1$ . As ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ consists of all disjoint unions of the intervals $( ( k - 1 ) 2 ^ { - n } , k 2 ^ { - n } ] , 1 \leq k \leq 2 ^ { n } , P _ { n } ( A ) = 0$ for some $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { n }$ if $A = \emptyset$ . Consequently, $\nu _ { n } ( A ) = 0$ whenever $P _ { n } ( A ) = 0 , A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } .$ $\mathrm { i . e . , } \nu _ { n } \ll P _ { n }$ . Let $X _ { n }$ denote the Radon-Nikodym derivative of $\nu _ { n }$ w.r.t. $P _ { n }$ , given by 

$$
X _ {n} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {2 ^ {n}} \left[ \nu \left(\left((k - 1) 2 ^ {- n}, k 2 ^ {- n} \right]\right) 2 ^ {n} \right] I _ {\left((k - 1) 2 ^ {- n}, k 2 ^ {- n} \right]}.\tag{1.11}
$$

Clearly, $X _ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { n } { \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l { \epsilon } } }$ e and P-integrable. It is easy to check that $E ( X _ { n + 1 } | \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) = X _ { n }$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Hence $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \geq 1 \}$ is a martingale on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ . Note that the absolute continuity of $\nu _ { n }$ w.r.t. $P _ { n }$ (on $\mathcal { F } _ { n } )$ holds for each $1 \leq n < \infty$ even though the measure ν may not be absolutely continuous w.r.t. P on $\mathcal { F } = B ( ( 0 , 1 ] )$ . 

Proposition 13.1.1: (Convex functions of martingales and submartingales). Let $\phi ~ : ~ \mathbb { R } ~ \to ~ \mathbb { R }$ be a convex function and let $N \_ =$ $\{ 1 , 2 , \dots n _ { 0 } \} \subset \mathbb { N }$ be a nonempty subset. 

(i) If $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ is a martingale with $E | \phi ( X _ { n } ) | < \infty$ for all $n \in N$ , then $\{ ( \phi ( X _ { n } ) , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ is a sub-martingale. 

(ii) $I f \left\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \right\}$ is a sub-martingale, $E | \phi ( X _ { n } ) | < \infty$ for all $n \in$ N, and in addition, φ is nondecreasing, then $\{ ( \phi ( X _ { n } ) , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ is a sub-martingale. 

Proof: By the conditional Jensen’s inequality (Theorem 12.2.4) for all $1 \leq n < n _ { 0 }$ 2 

$$
E (\phi (X _ {n + 1}) | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \geq \phi (E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n})).\tag{1.12}
$$

Parts (i) and (ii) follow from (1.12) on using the martingale and submartingale properties of $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \in N }$ , respectively. ✷ 

Proposition 13.1.2: (Doob’s decomposition of a sub-martingale). Let $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ be a sub-martingale for some $N = \{ 1 , \dots , n _ { 0 } \} \subset \mathbb { N }$ Then, there exist two sets of random variables $\{ Y _ { n } : n \in N \}$ and $\{ Z _ { n } : n \in$ N satisfying $X _ { n } = Y _ { n } + Z _ { n } , n \in N$ such that 

(i) $\{ ( Y _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) : n \in N \}$ is a martingale 

(ii) For all $n \in N , Z _ { n + 1 } \geq Z _ { n } \geq 0 \ w . p$ . 1 and $Z _ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 } { - } m e a s u r a b l e .$ where $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 } = \{ \emptyset , \Omega \}$ 

(iii) $I f \left\{ X _ { n } : n \in N \right\}$ are L<sup>1</sup>-bounded, i.e., $M \equiv \operatorname * { m a x } \{ E | X _ { n } | : n \in N \} <$ , then so are $\{ Y _ { n } : n \in N \}$ and $\{ Z _ { n } : n \in N \}$ 

Proof: Define the diference variables $\Delta _ { n } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ by 

$$
\Delta_ {1} = X _ {1}, \quad \text { and } \quad \Delta_ {n} = X _ {n} - X _ {n - 1}, n \geq 2, n \in N.
$$

Note that $\begin{array} { r } { X _ { n } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \Delta _ { j } , n \in N } \end{array}$ , and $E ( \Delta _ { n } | \mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 } ) \ge 0$ for all $n \geq 2$ 7 $n \in N$ . Now, set 

$$
Y _ {1} = \Delta_ {1}, Y _ {n} = X _ {n} - \sum_ {j = 2} ^ {n} E (\Delta_ {j} | \mathcal {F} _ {j - 1}), n \geq 2, n \in N
$$

and 

$$
Z _ {1} = 0, Z _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 2} ^ {n} E (\Delta_ {j} | \mathcal {F} _ {j - 1}), n \geq 2, n \in N.
$$

Check that the requirements (i) and (ii) above hold. To prove the $L ^ { 1 } \mathbf { - }$ boundedness, notice that by (ii), for any $n \geq 2 , n \in N$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E | Z _ {n} | & = & E Z _ {n} = E \bigg [ \sum_ {j = 2} ^ {n} E (\Delta_ {j} | \mathcal {F} _ {j - 1}) \bigg ] = \sum_ {j = 2} ^ {n} E (\Delta_ {j}) \\ & = & E X _ {n} - E X _ {1} \leq 2 M. \end{array}\tag{1.13}
$$

Also, $X _ { n } = Y _ { n } + Z _ { n }$ for all $n \in N$ implies that 

$$
\left| Y _ {n} \right| \leq \left| X _ {n} \right| + \left| Z _ {n} \right|, n \in N.\tag{1.14}
$$

Hence, (iii) follows. 

## 13.2 Stopping times and optional stopping theorems

In the following (and elsewhere), $\cdot _ { n } \geq 1 ^ { \prime }$ is used as an alternative for the statement $\textstyle \cdot _ { n } \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \prime }$ or equivalently for $1 \leq n < \infty$ 

Definition 13.2.1: Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ be a probability space, $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration and T be a -measurable random variable taking values in the set $\bar { \mathbb { N } } \equiv \mathbb { N } \cup \{ \infty \} = \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , \} \cup \{ \infty \}$ 

(a) $T$ is called a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ if 

$$
\{T = n \} \in \mathcal {F} _ {n} \quad \text { for   all } \quad n \geq 1.\tag{2.1}
$$

(b) $T$ is called a finite or proper stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ (under P) if 

$$
P (T <   \infty) = 1.\tag{2.2}
$$

Given a filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ , define the σ-algebra 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {\infty} = \sigma \langle \bigcup_ {n \geq 1} \mathcal {F} _ {n} \rangle .\tag{2.3}
$$

Since $\{ T = + \infty \} ^ { c } = \bigcup _ { n > 1 } \{ T = n \} \in \mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ , (2.1) is equivalent to $\mathbf { \nabla } \cdot \{ T =$ $n \} \in \mathcal { F } _ { n }$ for all $1 \leq n \leq \infty ^ { \bar { } }$ . It is also easy to check (Problem 13.7) that $T$ is a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ if 

$$
\{T \leq n \} \in \mathcal {F} _ {n} \quad \text { for   all } \quad n \geq 1\tag{2.4}
$$

if $\{ T > n \} \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ for all $n \geq 1$ . However, the condition 

$$
\left. ^ {\prime} \{T \geq n \} \in \mathcal {F} _ {n} \quad \text { for   all } \quad n \geq 1 ^ {\prime} \right.\tag{2.5}
$$

does not always imply that $T$ is a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ (cf. Problem 13.7). Note that for a stopping time T w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ 

$$
\{T \geq n \} = \{T \leq n - 1 \} ^ {c} \in \mathcal {F} _ {n - 1} \quad \text { for } \quad n \geq 2,
$$

and $\{ T \geq 1 \} = \Omega$ . Since $\mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 } ~ \subset ~ \mathcal { F } _ { n }$ for all $n \geq 2$ , (2.5) is a weaker requirement than T being a stopping time w.r.t $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ 

Proposition 13.2.1: Let T be a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ and let $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ be as in (2.3). Define 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {T} = \left\{A \in \mathcal {F} _ {\infty}: A \cap \{T = n \} \in \mathcal {F} _ {n} \quad f o r a l l \quad n \geq 1 \right\}.\tag{2.6}
$$

Then, $\mathcal { F } _ { T }$ is a σ-algebra. 

Proof: Left as an exercise (Problem 13.8). 

If T is a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ , then for any $m \in \mathbb { N } , \{ T = m \} \cap$ $\{ T = n \} = \emptyset \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ for all $n \neq$ m and $\{ \bar { T } = m \} \cap \{ T = n \} = \{ T = m \} \in \mathcal { F } _ { m }$ for $n = m$ . Thus, $\{ T = m \} \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { T }$ for all $m \geq 1$ and hence, $\sigma \langle T \rangle \subset \mathcal { F } _ { T }$ . But the reverse inclusion may not hold as shown below. 

Example 13.2.1: Let $T \equiv m$ for some given integer $m \geq 1$ . Then, $T$ is a stopping time w.r.t. any filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ . For this $T _ { \cdot }$ 

$$
A \in \mathcal {F} _ {T} \Rightarrow A \cap \{T = m \} \in \mathcal {F} _ {m} \Rightarrow A \in \mathcal {F} _ {m},
$$

so that $\mathcal { F } _ { T } \subset \mathcal { F } _ { m }$ . Conversely, suppose $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { m }$ . Then, $A \cap \left\{ T = n \right\} = \emptyset \in$ ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ for all $n \neq m$ , and $A \cap \left\{ T = m \right\} = A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { m }$ for $n = m$ . Thus, $\mathcal { F } _ { m } = \mathcal { F } _ { T }$ But $\sigma \langle T \rangle = \{ \Omega , \emptyset \}$ 

Example 13.2.2: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of random variables adapted to a filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ and let $\{ B _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of Borel sets in R. Define the random variable 

$$
T = \inf \left\{n \geq 1: X _ {n} \in B _ {n} \right\}.\tag{2.7}
$$

Then, $T ( \omega ) < \infty$ if $X _ { n } ( \omega ) ~ \in ~ B _ { n }$ for some $n \in \mathbb N$ and $T ( \omega ) ~ = ~ + \infty$ if $X _ { n } ( \omega ) \not \in B _ { n }$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Since, for any $n \geq 1$ 2 

$$
\{T = n \} = \left\{X _ {1} \notin B _ {1}, \dots , X _ {n - 1} \notin B _ {n - 1}, X _ {n} \in B _ {n} \right\} \in \mathcal {F} _ {n},
$$

T is a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ . Now, define a new random variable $X _ { T }$ by 

$$
X _ {T} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} X _ {m} & \text { if } \quad T = m \\ \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} X _ {n} & \text { if } \quad T = \infty . \end{array} \right.\tag{2.8}
$$

The, $X _ { T } \in \bar { \mathbb { R } }$ and for any $n \geq 1$ and $r \in \mathbb { R }$ 2 

$$
\left\{X _ {T} \leq r \right\} \cap \left\{T = n \right\} = \left\{X _ {n} \leq r \right\} \cap \left\{T = n \right\} \in \mathcal {F} _ {n}.
$$

Also, $\left\{ X _ { T } = \pm \infty \right\} \cap \left\{ T = n \right\} = \left\{ X _ { n } = \pm \infty \right\} \cap \left\{ T = n \right\} = \emptyset$ for all $n \geq 1$ Hence, it follows that $X _ { T }$ is $\langle \mathcal { F } _ { T } , B ( \bar { \mathbb { R } } ) \rangle$ -measurable. 

Example 13.2.3: Let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables with $E Y _ { 1 } = \mu$ . Let $X _ { n } = ( Y _ { 1 } + \bar { . . . } + Y _ { n } ) , n \geq 1$ denote the random walk corresponding to $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ . For $x > 0$ , let 

$$
T _ {x} = \inf \left\{n \geq 1: X _ {n} > n \mu + x \sqrt {n} \right\}.\tag{2.9}
$$

Then, $T _ { x }$ is the first time the sequence of partial sums $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ exceeds the level $n \mu + x { \sqrt { n } }$ and is a special case of (2.7) with $B _ { n } = ( n \mu + x { \sqrt { n } } , \infty )$ 2 $n \geq 1$ . Consequently, $T _ { x }$ is a stopping time w.r.t. $\mathcal { F } _ { n } = \sigma \langle Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , . . . , Y _ { n } \rangle$ 2 $n \geq 1$ . Note that if $E Y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , by the law of iterated logarithm (cf. 8.7), 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} \frac {X _ {n} - n \mu}{\sqrt {2 \sigma^ {2} n \log \log n}} = 1 \quad \text {w.p.} 1,
$$

$$
\text { i.e., } \quad X _ {n} > n \mu + C \sqrt {n \log \log n} \quad \text { infinitely   often   w.p. } 1
$$

for some constant $C > 0$ . Thus, $P ( T _ { x } < \infty ) = 1$ and hence, $T _ { x }$ is a finite stopping time. This random variable $T _ { x }$ arises in sequential probability ratio tests (SPRT) for testing hypotheses on the mean of a (normal) population. See Woodroofe (1982), Chapter 3. 

Definition 13.2.2: Let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be a filtration in a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ . A betting sequence w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ is a sequence $\{ H _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ of nonnegative random variables such that for each $n \geq 1 , H _ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 }$ measurable. The following result says that there is no betting scheme that can beat a gambling system, i.e., convert a fair one into a favorable one or the other way around. 

Theorem 13.2.2: (Betting theorem). Let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be a filtration in a probability space. Let $\{ H _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be a betting sequence w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ . For an adapted sequence $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be defined by $Y _ { 0 } ~ = ~ X _ { 0 }$ $\begin{array} { r } { Y _ { n } \ = \ Y _ { 0 } + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( X _ { j } - X _ { j - 1 } ) \bar { H _ { j } } , \ n \ \ge \ 1 } \end{array}$ . Let $E | ( X _ { j } - X _ { j - 1 } ) H _ { j } | < \infty$ for $j \geq 1$ . Then, 

(i) $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ a martingale $\Rightarrow \{ Y _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is also a martingale, 

(ii) $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 } \quad a$ sub-martingale $\begin{array} { r l } { \Rightarrow } & { { } \{ Y _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 } } \end{array}$ is also a submartingale, 

Proof: Clearly, for all $n \ge 1 , E | Y _ { n } | < \infty$ and $Y _ { n }$ is ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ -measurable. Further, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E \big (Y _ {n + 1} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {n} \big) & = & Y _ {n} + E \big ((X _ {n + 1} - X _ {n}) H _ {n + 1} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n} \big) \\ & = & Y _ {n} + H _ {n + 1}   E \big ((X _ {n + 1} - X _ {n}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n} \big) \end{array}
$$

since $H _ { n + 1 }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { n + 1 } . . . \mathrm { m e a s u r a b l e }$ . Now the theorem follows from the defining properties of $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ ✷ 

The above theorem leads to the following results known as Doob’s optional stopping theorems. 

Theorem 13.2.3: (Doob’s optional stopping theorem I). Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be a sub-martingale. Let T be a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ . Let ${ \tilde { X } } _ { n } \equiv$ $X _ { T \wedge n } , \ n \ \geq \ 0$ . Then $\{ \tilde { X } _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ is also a sub-martingale and hence $E \tilde { X } _ { n } \geq E X _ { 0 }$ for all $n \geq 1$ 

Proof: For any $A \in B ( \mathbb { R } )$ and $n \geq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \tilde {X} _ {n} ^ {- 1} (A) & = & \{\omega : \tilde {X} _ {n} \in A \} \\ & = & \bigg (\bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \{\omega : X _ {j} \in A, T = j \} \bigg) \cup \{\omega : X _ {n} \in A, T > n \}. \end{array}
$$

Since $T$ is a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ the right side above belongs to ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ for each $n \geq 0$ . Next, $\begin{array} { r } { | \tilde { X } _ { n } | \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } | \bar { X } _ { j } | } \end{array}$ and hence $E | \tilde { X } _ { n } | < \infty$ Finally, let $H _ { j } ~ = ~ 1 ~ \mathrm { i f } ~ j ~ \le ~ T$ and 0 if $j ~ > ~ T$ . Since for all $j ~ \geq ~ 1$ $\{ \omega : H _ { j } = 1 \} = \{ \omega : T \le j - 1 \} ^ { c } \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { j - 1 } , \{ H _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ is a betting sequence w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ . Also, $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { X } _ { n } = X _ { 0 } + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( X _ { j } - X _ { j - 1 } ) H _ { j } } \end{array}$ . Now the betting theorem (Theorem 13.2.2) implies the present theorem. ✷ 

Remark 13.2.1: If $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a martingale, then both $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ and $\{ - X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ are sub-martingales, and hence the above theorem implies that if $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a martingale, then so is $\{ \tilde { X } _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ , and hence $E \tilde { X } _ { n } = E X _ { T \wedge n } = E X _ { 0 } = E X _ { n }$ for all $n \geq 1$ 

This suggests the question that if $P ( T < \infty ) = 1$ , then on letting $n \to \infty$ ， does $E \tilde { X } _ { n }  E X _ { T } ?$ Consider the following example. Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ denote the symmetric simple random walk on the integers with $X _ { 0 } = 0$ . Let $T =$ inf $\{ n : n \geq 1 , X _ { n } = 1 \}$ . Then $P ( T < \infty ) = 1$ and $E \tilde { X } _ { n } = E X _ { T \wedge n } =$ $E X _ { 0 } = 0$ but $X _ { T } = 1 \mathrm { w . p }$ . 1 and hence $E \tilde { X } _ { n } \not \to E X _ { T } = 1$ . So, clearly some additional hypothesis is needed. 

Theorem 13.2.4: (Doob’s optional stopping theorem II). Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be a martingale. Let T be a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ Suppose $P ( T < \infty ) = 1$ and there is a $0 < K < \infty$ such that for all $n \geq 0$ 

$$
\left| X _ {T \wedge n} \right| \leq K w. p. 1.
$$

Then $E X _ { T } = E X _ { 0 }$ 

Proof: Since $P ( T < \infty ) = 1 , X _ { T \wedge n }  X _ { T } \ \mathrm { w . p . }$ 1 and $| X _ { T } | \le K < \infty$ and hence $E | X _ { T } | < \infty$ . Thus, $E | X _ { T } - X _ { T \wedge n } | \leq 2 K P ( T > n ) \to 0 .$ ✷ 

## Remark 13.2.2: Since

$$
X _ {T} = X _ {T} I _ {(T \leq n)} + X _ {n} I _ {(T > n)}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E X _ {T} I _ {(T \leq n)} & = & \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} E (X _ {j}: T = j) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n} E (X _ {0}: T = j) = E (X _ {0}: T \leq n) \end{array}
$$

it follows that if $E { \big ( } | X _ { n } | I _ { ( T > n ) } { \big ) } \to 0 { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } n \to \infty$ and $P ( T < \infty ) = 1$ then $E X _ { T } = E X _ { 0 }$ 

A stronger version of Doob’s optional stopping theorem is given below in Theorem 13.2.6. 

Proposition 13.2.5: Let S and $T$ be two stopping times w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ with $S \leq T$ . Then, $\mathcal { F } _ { S } \subset \mathcal { F } _ { T }$ 

Proof: For any $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { S }$ and $n \geq 1$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} A \cap \{T = n \} & = & A \cap \{T = n \} \cap \{S \leq n \} \\ & = & \left[ \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {n} A \cap \{S = k \} \right] \cap \{T = n \} \\ & \in & \mathcal {F} _ {n}, \end{array}
$$

since $A \cap \{ S = k \} \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { k }$ for all $1 \leq k \leq n$ . Thus, $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { T }$ , proving the result. ✷ 

Theorem 13.2.6: (Doob’s optional stopping theorem III). Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale and S and T be two finite stopping times w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ such that $S \leq T$ . If $X _ { S }$ and $X _ { T }$ are integrable and if 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} E | X _ {n} | I (| X _ {n} | > T) = 0,\tag{2.10}
$$

then 

$$
E (X _ {T} | \mathcal {F} _ {S}) \geq X _ {S} \quad a. s.\tag{2.11}
$$

$H ,$ in addition, $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale, then equality holds in $\it { ( 2 . 1 1 ) }$ 

Thus, Theorem 13.2.6 shows that if a martingale (or a sub-martingale) is stopped at random time points S and T with $S \leq T$ , then under very mild conditions, $\big \{ ( X _ { S } , \mathcal { F } _ { S } ) , ( X _ { T } , \mathcal { F } _ { T } ) \big \}$ continues to have the martingale  (sub-martingale, respectively) property. 

Proof: To show (2.11), it is enough to show that 

$$
\int_ {A} (X _ {T} - X _ {S}) d P \geq 0 \quad \text { for   all } \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {S}.\tag{2.12}
$$

Fix $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { S }$ . Let $\{ n _ { k } \} _ { k \ge 1 }$ be a subsequence along which the “lim inf” is attained in (2.10). Let $\bar { T _ { k } } = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ T , n _ { k } \}$ and $S _ { k } = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ S , n _ { k } \} , k \geq 1$ . The proof of (2.12) involves showing that 

$$
\int_ {A} (X _ {T _ {k}} - X _ {S _ {k}}) d P \geq 0 \quad \text { for   all } \quad k \geq 1\tag{2.13}
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {A} \left[ (X _ {T} - X _ {S}) - (X _ {T _ {k}} - X _ {S _ {k}}) \right] d P = 0.\tag{2.14}
$$

Consider (2.13). Since $S _ { k } \le T _ { k } \le n _ { k }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} X _ {T _ {k}} - X _ {S _ {k}} & = & \sum_ {n = S _ {k} + 1} ^ {T _ {k}} (X _ {n} - X _ {n - 1}) \\ & = & \sum_ {n = 2} ^ {n _ {k}} (X _ {n} - X _ {n - 1}) I (S _ {k} + 1 \leq n \leq T _ {k}). \end{array}\tag{2.15}
$$

Note that for all $2 \leq n \leq n _ { k } , \{ T _ { k } \geq n \} = \{ T _ { k } \leq n - 1 \} ^ { c } = \{ T \leq n - 1 \} ^ { c } \in$ $\mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 }$ and $\left\{ S _ { k } + 1 \le n \right\} = \left\{ S _ { k } \le n - 1 \right\} = \left\{ S \le n - 1 \right\} \in \mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 }$ . Also, since $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { S } , B _ { n } \equiv A \cap \left\{ S _ { k } + 1 \leq n \leq T _ { k } \right\} = \left( A \cap \left\{ S _ { k } + 1 \leq n \right\} \right) \cap \left\{ T _ { k } \geq 1 \right\} \subsetneq \left( A \cap \left\{ S _ { k } + 1 \leq n \right\} \right) .$ $n \} \in \mathcal F _ { n - 1 }$ for all $2 \leq n \leq n _ { k }$ . Hence, by the sub-martingale property of 

$\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ , from (2.15), 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int_ {A} (X _ {T _ {k}} - X _ {S _ {k}}) d P & = & \sum_ {n = 2} ^ {n _ {k}} \int_ {A \cap \{S _ {k} + 1 \leq n \leq T _ {k} \}} (X _ {n} - X _ {n - 1}) d P \\ & = & \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {n _ {k}} \int_ {B _ {n}} \big [ E (X _ {n} | \mathcal {F} _ {n - 1}) - X _ {n - 1} \big ] d P \\ & \geq & 0. \end{array}\tag{2.16}
$$

This proves (2.13). To prove (2.14), note that by (2.10) and the integrability of $X _ { S }$ and $X _ { T }$ and the DCT, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \Big | \int_ {A} \big [ (X _ {T} - X _ {S}) - (X _ {T _ {k}} - X _ {S _ {k}}) \big ] d P \Big | \\ \leq \lim _ {k \to \infty} \int \big [ | X _ {T} - X _ {T _ {k}} | + | X _ {S} - X _ {S _ {k}} | \big ] d P \\ \leq \lim _ {k \to \infty} \Big [ \int_ {\{T > n _ {k} \}} (| X _ {T} | + | X _ {n _ {k}} |) d P + \int_ {\{S > n _ {k} \}} (| X _ {S} | + | X _ {n _ {k}} |) d P \Big ] \\ \leq \lim _ {k \to \infty} \Big [ \int_ {\{T > n _ {k} \}} | X _ {T} | d P + 2 \int_ {\{T > n _ {k} \}} | X _ {n _ {k}} | d P + \int_ {\{S > n _ {k} \}} | X _ {S} | d P \Big ] \\ = 0, \end{array}
$$

since $\{ S > n _ { k } \} \subset \{ T > n _ { k } \}$ and $\{ T > n _ { k } \} \downarrow \emptyset$ as $k  \infty$ . This proves the theorem for the case when $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sub-martingale. When $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale, equality holds in the last line of (2.16), which implies equality in (2.13) and hence, in (2.12). This completes the proof. ✷ 

Remark 13.2.3: If there exists a $t _ { 0 } < \infty$ such that $P ( T \leq t _ { 0 } ) = 1$ , then (2.10) holds. 

Corollary 13.2.7: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale and let T be a finite stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ such that $E | X _ { T } | < \infty$ and $( 2 . 1 0 )$ holds. Then,

E X _ {T} \geq E X _ {1}.\tag{2.17}
$$

If, in addition, $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale, then equality holds in $( 2 . 1 7 )$ 

Proof: Follows from Theorem 13.2.6 by setting $S \equiv 1$ 

Corollary 13.2.8: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale. Let $\{ T _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of stopping times such that 

(i) for all $n \geq 1 , T _ { n } \leq T _ { n + 1 } \ w . p .$ 1, 

(ii) for all $n \geq 1$ , there exist a nonrandom $t _ { n } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ such that $P ( T _ { n } \leq$ $t _ { n } ) = 1$ 

Let $\mathcal { G } _ { n } \equiv \mathcal { F } _ { T _ { n } } , Y _ { n } \equiv X _ { T _ { n } } , n \geq 1$ . Then $\{ Y _ { n } , { \mathcal { G } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sub-martingale. If $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale, then $\{ Y _ { n } , { \mathcal { G } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale. 

Proof: Use Theorem 13.2.6 and Remark 13.2.3. 

Corollary 13.2.9: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale. Let T be a stopping time. Let 

$$
T _ {n} = \min \{T, n \}, n \geq 1.
$$

Then $\{ X _ { T _ { n } } , \mathcal { F } _ { T _ { n } } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sub-martingale. 

Note that this is a stronger version of Theorem 13.2.3 as $\mathcal { F } _ { T _ { n } } \subset \mathcal { F } _ { n }$ for all $n \geq 1$ 

Theorem 13.2.10: (Doob’s maximal inequality). Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale and let $M _ { m } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ X _ { 1 } , \dots , X _ { m } \}$ , m  N. Then, for any $m \in \mathbb { N }$ and $x \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 

$$
P (M _ {m} > x) \leq \frac {E X _ {m} ^ {+} I (M _ {m} > x)}{x} \leq \frac {E X _ {m} ^ {+}}{x}.\tag{2.18}
$$

Proof: Fix $m \geq 1 , x > 0$ . Define a random variable S by 

$$
S = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \inf \{k: 1 \leq k \leq m, X _ {k} > x \} & \text { on } \quad A \\ m & \text { on } \quad A ^ {c} \end{array} \right.
$$

where $A = \left\{ X _ { k } > x \right.$ for some $1 \leq k \leq m \} = \{ M _ { m } > x \}$ . Then it is easy to check that S is a stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ and $S \leq m$ . Set $T \equiv m$ Then (2.10) holds and hence, by Theorem 13.2.6, 

$$
\left\{\left(X _ {S}, \mathcal {F} _ {S}\right), \left(X _ {m}, \mathcal {F} _ {m}\right) \right\} \quad \text { is   a   sub - martingale. }
$$

Note that $\begin{array} { r } { A = \{ M _ { m } > x \} = \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { m } \{ M _ { m } > x , S = k \} = \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { m } \{ X _ { S } > x , S = } \end{array}$ $k \} = \{ X _ { S } > x \} \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { S }$ . Hence, by Markov’s inequality, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P (A) & = & P (X _ {S} > x) \leq \frac {1}{x} \int_ {\{X _ {S} > x \}} X _ {S} d P \leq \frac {1}{x} \int_ {A} X _ {m} d P \\ & \leq & \frac {1}{x} \int_ {A} X _ {m} ^ {+} d P \leq \frac {E X _ {m} ^ {+}}{x}. \end{array}
$$

Remark 13.2.4: An alternative proof of (2.18) is as follows. Let $A _ { 1 } =$ $\{ X _ { 1 } \ > \ x \} , \ A _ { k } \ = \ \{ X _ { 1 } \ \leq \ x , X _ { 2 } \ \leq \ x , \ldots , X _ { k - 1 } \ \leq \ x , X _ { k } \ > \ x \}$ for $k =$ $2 , \ldots , m$ . Then $\bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } A _ { i } = A \equiv \{ M _ { m } > x \}$ and $A _ { k } \in \mathcal { F } _ { k }$ for all k. Now for $x > 0$ 2 

$$
P (M _ {m} > x) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} P (A _ {k}) \leq \frac {1}{x} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} E (X _ {k} I _ {A _ {k}}).
$$

By the sub-martingale property of $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ 

$$
E (X _ {k} I _ {A _ {k}}) \leq E (X _ {m} I _ {A _ {k}}) \quad \text { for } \quad k \leq m.
$$

Thus 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P (M _ {m} > x) & \leq & \frac {1}{x}   E \bigg (X _ {m} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} I _ {A _ {k}} \bigg) \\ & \leq & \frac {1}{x}   E (X _ {m} I _ {A}) \\ & \leq & \frac {1}{x}   E (X _ {m} ^ {+} I _ {A}) \leq \frac {1}{x}   E (X _ {m} ^ {+}). \end{array}
$$

Theorem 13.2.11: (Doob’s L<sup>p</sup>-maximal inequality for sub-martingales). Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale and let $M _ { n } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ X _ { j } : 1 \leq j \leq n \}$ Then, for any $p \in ( 1 , \infty )$ ), 

$$
E (M _ {n} ^ {+}) ^ {p} \leq \left(\frac {p}{p - 1}\right) ^ {p} E (X _ {n} ^ {+}) ^ {p} \leq \infty .\tag{2.19}
$$

Proof: If $E ( X _ { n } ^ { + } ) ^ { p } = \infty$ , then (2.19) holds trivially. Let $E ( X _ { n } ^ { + } ) ^ { p } \ < \infty$ Since for $p > 1 , \phi ( x ) = ( x ^ { + } ) ^ { p }$ is a convex nondecreasing function on R. Hence, $\{ ( X _ { n } ^ { + } ) ^ { p } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sub-martingale and $E ( X _ { i } ^ { + } ) ^ { p } \leq E ( X _ { n } ^ { + } ) ^ { p } < \infty$ for all $j \leq n$ . Since $\begin{array} { r } { ( M _ { n } ^ { + } ) ^ { p } \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( X _ { j } ^ { + } ) ^ { p } } \end{array}$ , this implies that $E ( M _ { n } ^ { + } ) ^ { p } < \infty$ For any nonnegative random variable Y and $p > 0$ , by Tonelli’s theorem, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E Y ^ {p} & = & p E \bigg (\int_ {0} ^ {Y} x ^ {p - 1} d x \bigg) \\ & = & p E \bigg (\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} x ^ {p - 1} I (Y > x) d x \bigg) \\ & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} p x ^ {p - 1} P (Y > x) d x. \end{array}
$$

Thus, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (M _ {n} ^ {+}) ^ {p} & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} p x ^ {p - 1} P (M _ {n} ^ {+} > x) d x \\ & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} p x ^ {p - 1} P (M _ {n} > x) d x. \end{array}
$$

By Theorem 13.2.10, for $x > 0$ 

$$
P (M _ {n} > x) \leq \frac {1}{x} E (X _ {n} ^ {+} I (M _ {n} > x)),
$$

and hence 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (M _ {n} ^ {+}) ^ {p} & \leq & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} p x ^ {p - 2} E (X _ {n} ^ {+} I (M _ {n} > x)) d x \\ & = & \frac {p}{(p - 1)}   E (X _ {n} ^ {+} M _ {n} ^ {p - 1}) \\ & \leq & \bigg (\frac {p}{p - 1} \bigg) (E (X _ {n} ^ {+}) ^ {p}) ^ {1 / p} (E (M _ {n} ^ {(p - 1) q}) ^ {1 / q} \end{array}
$$

(by Holder’s inequality) where $q$ is the conjugate of $p ,$ i.e. $\begin{array} { r } { q = \frac { p } { ( p - 1 ) } } \end{array}$ Thus, 

$$
\left(E (M _ {n} ^ {+}) ^ {p}\right) ^ {1 / p} \leq \left(\frac {p}{p - 1}\right) \left(E (X _ {n} ^ {+}) ^ {p}\right) ^ {1 / p},
$$

proving (2.19). 

Corollary 13.2.12: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a martingale and let $\tilde { M } _ { n } \ =$ sup $\{ | X _ { j } | : 1 \leq j \leq n \}$ . Then, for $p \in ( 1 , \infty )$ 

$$
E \tilde {M} _ {n} ^ {p} \leq \left(\frac {p}{p - 1}\right) ^ {p} E \Big (| X _ {n} | ^ {p} \Big).
$$

Proof: Since $\{ | X _ { n } | , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sub-martingale, this follows from Theorem 13.2.11. ✷ 

Theorem 13.2.13: (Doob’s L log L maximal inequality for submartingales). Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale and $M _ { n } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ X _ { j }$ $1 \leq j \leq n \}$ . Then 

$$
E M _ {n} ^ {+} \leq \left(\frac {e}{e - 1}\right) \left(1 + E (X _ {n} ^ {+} \log X _ {n} ^ {+})\right),\tag{2.20}
$$

where 0 log 0 is interpreted as 0. 

Proof: As in the proof of Theorem 13.2.11, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E M _ {n} ^ {+} & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P (M _ {n} ^ {+} > x) d x \\ & \leq & 1 + \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{x} E (X _ {n} ^ {+} I (M _ {n} ^ {+} > x)) d x \\ & = & 1 + E (X _ {n} ^ {+} \log M _ {n} ^ {+}) . \end{array}\tag{2.21}
$$

For $x > 0 , y > 0$ 2 

$$
x \log y = x \log x + x \log {\frac {y}{x}}.
$$

Now x log $\begin{array} { r } { { \frac { y } { x } } = y \phi ( { \frac { x } { y } } ) } \end{array}$ where $\phi ( t ) \equiv - t \log t , t > 0$ . It can be verified $\phi ( t )$ attains its maximum $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { e } }$ at $\textstyle t = { \frac { 1 } { e } }$ . Thus 

$$
x \log y \leq x \log x + \frac {y}{e}.
$$

So 

$$
E X _ {n} ^ {+} \log M _ {n} ^ {+} \leq E X _ {n} ^ {+} \log X _ {n} ^ {+} + \frac {E M _ {n} ^ {+}}{e}.\tag{2.22}
$$

If $E X _ { n } ^ { + }$ log $X _ { n } ^ { + } = \infty$ , (2.20) is trivially true. If $E X _ { n } ^ { + }$ log $X _ { n } ^ { + } < \infty$ , then as in the proof of Theorem 13.2.11, it can be shown that $E M _ { n } ^ { + } < \infty$ . Hence, the theorem follows from (2.21) and (2.22). ✷ 

A special case of Theorem 13.2.10 is the maximal inequality of Kolmogorov (cf. Section 8.3) as shown by the following example. 

Example 13.2.4: Let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a sequence of independent random variables with $E Y _ { n } = 0$ and $E | Y _ { n } | ^ { \alpha } < \infty$ for all $n \geq 1$ for some $\alpha \in ( 1 , \infty )$ Let $S _ { n } = Y _ { 1 } + . . . + Y _ { n } , n \geq 1$ . Then, $\phi ( x ) \equiv | x | ^ { \alpha } , x > 0$ is a convex function, and hence, by Proposition 13.1.1, $X _ { n } \equiv \phi ( \vert S _ { n } \vert )$ , n  1 is a sub-martingale w.r.t. $\mathcal { F } _ { n } = \sigma \langle \{ Y _ { 1 } , \ldots , Y _ { n } \} \rangle$ , $n \geq 1$ . Now, by Theorem 13.2.10, for any $x > 0$ and $m \geq 1$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P \Big (\max _ {1 \leq n \leq m} | S _ {n} | > x \Big) & = & P \Big (\max _ {1 \leq n \leq m} X _ {n} > x ^ {\alpha} \Big) \\ & \leq & x ^ {- \alpha} E X _ {m} ^ {+} \\ & \leq & x ^ {- \alpha} E | S _ {m} | ^ {\alpha}. \end{array}\tag{2.23}
$$

Kolmogorov’s inequality corresponds to the case where $\alpha = 2$ 

Another application of the optimal stopping theorem yields the following useful result. 

Theorem 13.2.14: (Wald’s lemmas). Let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables and let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration such that 

(i) $Y _ { n }$ is $F _ { n }$ -measurable and (ii) $F _ { n }$ and $\sigma \langle \{ Y _ { k } : k \geq n + 1 \} \rangle$ are independent for all $n \geq 1$ (2.24) 

Also, let $T$ be a finite stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ and $E | T | < \infty$ . Let $S _ { n } = Y _ { 1 } + . . . + Y _ { n } , n \geq 1$ . Then, 

(a) $E | Y _ { 1 } | < \infty$ implies 

$$
E S _ {T} = (E Y _ {1}) (E T).\tag{2.25}
$$

(b) $E Y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ implies 

$$
E (S _ {T} - T E Y _ {1}) ^ {2} = \operatorname{Var} (Y _ {1}) E (T).\tag{2.26}
$$

Proof: W.l.o.g., suppose that $E Y _ { 1 } = 0$ . Then, $\{ S _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale. By Corollary 13.2.7, (2.25) would follow if one showed that (2.10) holds with $X _ { n } = S _ { n }$ and that $E | S _ { T } | < \infty$ . Since $\begin{array} { r } { | S _ { n } | \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } | Y _ { i } | \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { T } | Y _ { i } | } \end{array}$ on the set $\{ T \geq n \}$ , both these conditions would hold if $E ( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { T } | Y _ { i } | ) < \infty$ . Now, by the MCT and the independence of $Y _ { i }$ and $\{ T \geq i \} = \{ T \leq i - 1 \} ^ { c } \in \mathcal { F } _ { i - 1 }$ for $i \geq 2$ and the fact that $\{ T \geq 1 \} = \Omega$ , it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {T} | Y _ {i} | & = & E \bigg (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} | Y _ {i} | I (i \leq T) \bigg) \\ & = & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} E | Y _ {i} | I (i \leq T) \\ & = & E | Y _ {1} | \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} P (T \geq i) \\ & = & E | Y _ {1} | E | T | <   \infty . \end{array}\tag{2.27}
$$

This proves (a). 

To prove (b), set $\sigma ^ { 2 } ~ = ~ \mathrm { V a r } ( Y _ { 1 } )$ and note that $E Y _ { 1 } ~ = ~ 0 \Rightarrow ~ \{ S _ { n } ^ { 2 } ~ -$ $n \sigma ^ { 2 } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ is a martingale. Let $T _ { n } = T \wedge n , n \geq 1$ . Then, $T _ { n }$ is a bounded stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ and hence, by Theorem 13.2.6, 

$$
E [ S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {2} - (E T _ {n}) \sigma^ {2} ] = E (S _ {1} ^ {2} - \sigma^ {2}) = 0 \text {   for   all   } n \geq 1.\tag{2.28}
$$

Thus, (2.26) holds with T replaced by $T _ { n }$ . Since $T$ is a finite stopping time, $T _ { n } \uparrow T < \infty \mathrm { w . p . }$ . 1 and therefore, $S _ { T _ { n } } \  \ S _ { T }$ as $n  \infty$ , w.p. 1. Now applying Fatou’s lemma and the MCT, from (2.28), one gets 

$$
E S _ {T} ^ {2} \leq \liminf _ {n \to \infty} E S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {2} = \liminf _ {n \to \infty} (E T _ {n}) \sigma^ {2} = (E T) \sigma^ {2}.\tag{2.29}
$$

Also, note that for any $n \geq 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (S _ {T} ^ {2} - S _ {T _ {n}} ^ {2}) & = & E (S _ {T} ^ {2} - S _ {n} ^ {2}) I (T > n) \\ & = & E [ (S _ {T} - S _ {n}) ^ {2} + 2 S _ {n} (S _ {T} - S _ {n}) ] I (T > n) \\ & \geq & 2 E S _ {n} (S _ {T} - S _ {n}) I (T > n) \\ & = & 2 E S _ {n} (S _ {T _ {1 n}} - S _ {n}) \\ & = & 2 E [ S _ {n} \cdot E \{(S _ {T _ {1 n}} - S _ {n}) | \mathcal {F} _ {n} \} ], \end{array}\tag{2.30}
$$

where $T _ { 1 n } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ T , n \}$ . Since $E T _ { 1 n } \ \leq \ E T + n < \infty$ , and $\{ T _ { 1 n } > k \} =$ $\{ T > k \}$ for all $k > n$ , the conditions of Theorem 13.2.6 hold with $X _ { n } =$ $S _ { n } , S = n$ and $T = T _ { 1 n }$ . Hence, $E ( S _ { T _ { 1 n } } - S _ { n } | F _ { n } ) = 0 ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . and by (2.30), $E S _ { T } ^ { 2 } \geq E S _ { T } ^ { 2 }$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Now letting $n \to \infty$ and using (2.28), one gets $E S _ { T } ^ { \bar { 2 } } \geq ( E T ) \sigma ^ { 2 }$ , as in (2.29). This completes the proof of (b). ✷ 

This section is concluded with the statement of an inequality relating the pth moment of a martingale to the $\left( { p / 2 } \right)$ th moment of its squared variation. 

Theorem 13.2.15: (Burkholder’s inequality). Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a martingale sequence. Let $\xi _ { j } = X _ { j } - X _ { j - 1 } , \alpha \geq 1$ , with $X _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then for any $p \in [ 2 , \infty )$ , there exist positive constants $A _ { p }$ and $B _ { p }$ such that 

$$
E | X _ {n} | ^ {p} \leq A _ {p} E \bigg (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \xi_ {i} ^ {2} \bigg) ^ {p / 2}
$$

and 

$$
E | X _ {n} | ^ {p} \leq B _ {p} \bigg \{E \bigg (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} E \big (\xi_ {i} ^ {2} | \mathcal {F} _ {i - 1} \big) \bigg) ^ {p / 2} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} E | \xi_ {i} | ^ {p} \bigg \}.
$$

For a proof, see Chow and Teicher (1997). 

## 13.3 Martingale convergence theorems

The martingale (or sub- or super-martingale) property of a sequence of random variables $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ implies, under some mild additional conditions, a remarkable regularity, namely, that $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converges w.p. 1 as $n $ $\infty$ . For example, any nonnegative super-martingale converges w.p. 1. Also any sub-martingale $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ for which $\{ E | X _ { n } | \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is bounded converges w.p. 1. Further, if $\{ E | X _ { n } | ^ { p } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is bounded for some $p \in ( 1 , \infty )$ , then $X _ { n }$ converges w.p. 1 and in $L ^ { p }$ as well. 

The proof of these assertions depend crucially on an ingenious inequality due to Doob. Recall that one way to prove that a sequence of real numbers $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converges as $n \to \infty$ is to show that it does not oscillate too much as $n  \infty$ . That is, for all $a < b$ , the number of times the sequence goes from below a to above b is finite. This number is referred to as the number of upcrossings from a to b. Doob’s upcrossing lemma (see Theorem 13.3.1 below) shows that for a sub-martingale, the mean of the upcrossings can be bounded above. First, a formal definition of upcrossings of a given sequence $\{ x _ { j } : 1 \leq j \leq n \}$ of real numbers from level $a$ to level $b$ with $a < b$ is given. Let 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} N _ {1} & = & \min \{j: 1 \leq j \leq n, x _ {j} \leq a \} \\ N _ {2} & = & \min \{j: N _ {1} <   j \leq n, x _ {j} \geq b \} \end{array}
$$

and, define recursively, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} N _ {2 k - 1} & = & \min \{j: N _ {2 k - 2} <   j \leq n, x _ {j} \leq a \} \\ N _ {2 k} & = & \min \{j: N _ {2 k - 1} <   j \leq n, x _ {j} \geq b \}. \end{array}
$$

If any of these sets on the right side is empty, all subsequent ones will be empty as well and the corresponding $N _ { k } { } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s }$ will not be well defined. If $N _ { 1 }$ or $N _ { 2 }$ is not well defined, then set $U \{ \{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ; a , b \}$ , the number of upcrossings of the interval $( a , b )$ by $\{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 }$  equal to zero. Otherwise let $N _ { \ell }$ be the last one that is well defined. Set $\begin{array} { r } { U \big \{ \{ x _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ; a , b \big \} = \frac { \ell } { 2 } } \end{array}$ if  is even and $\frac { \ell - 1 } { 2 }$ if  is odd. 

Theorem 13.3.1: (Doob’s upcrossing lemma). Let $\{ X _ { j } , \mathcal { F } _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ be a submartingale and let $a \ < \ b$ be real numbers. Let $U _ { n } \equiv U \{ \{ \bar { X } _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ; a , b \}$ Then 

$$
E U _ {n} \leq \frac {E (X _ {n} - a) ^ {+} - E (X _ {1} - a) ^ {+}}{(b - a)} \leq \frac {E X _ {n} ^ {+} + | a |}{(b - a)}.\tag{3.1}
$$

Proof: Consider first the special case when $X _ { j } \ \geq \ 0 \ \mathrm { w . p }$ . 1 for all $j \geq 1$ and $a = 0$ . Let $\tilde { N } _ { 0 } = 1$ . Let 

$$
\tilde {N} _ {j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} N _ {j} & \text { if } j = 2 k, k \leq U _ {n} \text { or   if } \\ & j = 2 k - 1, k \leq U _ {n}, \\ n & \text { otherwise. } \end{array} \right.
$$

If $j$ is odd and $j + 1 \leq 2 U _ { n }$ , then 

$$
X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j + 1}} \geq b > 0.
$$

If $j$ is odd and $j + 1 \ge 2 U _ { n } + 2$ , then 

$$
X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j + 1}} = X _ {n} = X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j}}.
$$

Thus $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j \mathrm { o d d } } ( X _ { \tilde { N } _ { i + 1 } } - X _ { \tilde { N } _ { i } } ) \geq b U _ { n } } \end{array}$ . It is easy to check that $\{ \tilde { N } _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ are stopping times. By Theorem 13.2.6, 

$$
E (X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j + 1}} - X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j}}) \geq 0 \quad \text { for } \quad j = 1, 2, \dots , n.
$$

Thus, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (X _ {n} - X _ {1}) & = & E \bigg (\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {n - 1} (X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j + 1}} - X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j}}) \bigg) \\ & \geq & b E U _ {n} + E \Big (\sum_ {j \text {   even }} (X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j + 1}} - X _ {\tilde {N} _ {j}}) \Big) \\ & \geq & b E U _ {n}. \end{array}\tag{3.2}
$$

Hence, both inequalities of (3.1) hold for the special case. 

Now for the general case, let $Y _ { j } ~ \equiv ~ ( X _ { j } ~ - ~ a ) ^ { + } , ~ 1 ~ \le ~ j ~ \le ~ n$ . Then $\{ Y _ { j } , \mathcal { F } _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n }$ is a nonnegative sub-martingale and $U _ { n } \{ \{ Y _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } , 0 , b - a \} \equiv$ $U _ { n } \{ \{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } , a , b \}$ . Thus, from (3.2) 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E U _ {n} & \leq & \frac {E (Y _ {n} - Y _ {1})}{(b - a)} \\ & = & \frac {E ((X _ {n} - a) ^ {+}) - E ((X _ {1} - a) ^ {+})}{(b - a)}  , \end{array}
$$

proving the first inequality of (3.1). The second inequality follows by noting that $( x - a ) ^ { + } \leq x ^ { + } + | a |$ for any x, $a \in \mathbb { R }$ ✷ 

The first convergence theorem is an easy consequence of the above theorem. 

Theorem 13.3.2: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale such that 

$$
\sup _ {n \geq 1} E X _ {n} ^ {+} <   \infty .
$$

Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converges to a finite limit $X _ { \infty } \ w . p .$ 1 and $E | X _ { \infty } | < \infty$ 

Proof: Let 

$$
A = \{\omega : \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} X _ {n} <   \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} X _ {n} \},
$$

and for $a < b$ , let 

$$
A (a, b) = \{\omega : \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} X _ {n} <   a <   b <   \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} X _ {n} \}.
$$

Then, $A = \cup A ( a , b )$ where the union is taken over all rationals $a , b$ such that $a < b$ . To establish convergence of $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ it sufices to show that $P ( A ( a , b ) ) = 0$ for each $a < b .$ , as this implies $P ( A ) = 0$ . Fix $a < b$ and let $U _ { n } = U \{ \{ X _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ; \ a , b \}$ . For $\omega \in A ( a , b ) , U _ { n } \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ . On the  other hand, by the upcrossing lemma 

$$
E U _ {n} \leq \frac {E X _ {n} ^ {+} + | a |}{(b - a)}
$$

and by hypothesis, $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { n \geq 1 } E X _ { n } ^ { + } < \infty$ , implying that 

$$
\sup _ {n \geq 1} E U _ {n} <   \infty .
$$

By the MCT, $\begin{array} { r } { E \big [ \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } U _ { n } \big ] = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } E U _ { n } } \end{array}$ , and hence 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} U _ {n} <   \infty \quad \text { w   .   p   . } 1.
$$

Thus, $P ( A ( a , b ) ) = 0$ for all $a < b$ , and hence $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n } = X _ { \infty } } \end{array}$ exists w.p. 1. By Fatou’s lemma 

$$
E | X _ {\infty} | \leq \lim _ {n \to \infty} E | X _ {n} | \leq \sup _ {n \geq 1} E | X _ {n} |.
$$

But $E | X _ { n } | ~ = ~ 2 E ( X _ { n } ^ { + } ) - E X _ { n } ~ \le ~ 2 E X _ { n } ^ { + } - E X _ { 1 }$ , as $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ a sub-martingale implies $E X _ { n } \ \geq \ E X _ { 1 }$ . Thus, $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n > 1 } E X _ { n } ^ { + } < \infty } \end{array}$ implies $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { n \geq 1 } E | X _ { n } | < \infty$ . So, $E | X _ { \infty } | < \infty$ and hence $| X _ { \infty } ^ { - } | < \infty \ \mathrm { w . p . \ 1 }$ ✷ 

Corollary 13.3.3: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a nonnegative super-martingale. Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converges to a finite limit w.p. 1. 

Proof: Since $\{ - X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a nonpositive sub-martingale, $\mathrm { { s u p } } _ { n \geq 1 }$ $E ( - X _ { n } ) ^ { + } ~ = ~ 0 ~ < ~ \infty$ . By Theorem 13.3.2, $\{ - X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converges to a finite limit w.p. 1. ✷ 

Corollary 13.3.4: Every nonnegative martingale converges w.p. 1. 

A natural question is that if a sub-martingale converges w.p. 1 to a finite limit, does it do so in $L ^ { 1 }$ or in $L ^ { p }$ for $p > 1$ . It turns out that if a submartingale is $L ^ { p }$ bounded for some $p > 1$ , then it converges in $L ^ { p }$ . But this is false for $p = 1$ as the following examples show. 

Example 13.3.1: (Gambler’s ruin problem). Let $\{ S _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be the simple symmetric random walk, i.e., $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \xi _ { i } , n \ge 1 } \end{array}$ , where $\{ \xi _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ is a sequence of iid random variables with $\begin{array} { r } { \dot { P } ( \xi _ { 1 } = 1 ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } = P ( \xi _ { 1 } = - 1 ) } \end{array}$ . Let 

$$
N = \inf \{n: n \geq 1, S _ {n} = 1 \}.
$$

As noted earlier, N is a finite stopping time and that $\{ S _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ is a martingale. Let $X _ { n } = S _ { N \wedge n } , n \geq 1$ . Then by the optional sampling theorem, $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale. Clearly, $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n } \equiv X _ { \infty } = S _ { N } = 1 } \end{array}$ exists w.p. 1. But $E X _ { n } \equiv 0$ while $E X _ { \infty } = 1$ and so $X _ { n }$ does not converge to $X _ { \infty }$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ 

Example 13.3.2: Suppose that $\{ \xi _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ is a sequence of iid nonnegative random variables with $E \xi _ { 1 } = 1$ . Let $X _ { n } = \Pi _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \xi _ { i } , n \geq 1$ . Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a nonnegative martingale and hence converges w.p. 1 to $X _ { \infty } .$ , say. If $P ( \xi _ { 1 } = 1 ) < 1$ , it can be shown that $X _ { \infty } = 0 ~ \mathrm { w . p }$ . 1. Thus, $X _ { n } \not \to X _ { \infty }$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ . In particular, $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is not UI (Problem 13.19). 

Example 13.3.3: If $\{ Z _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a branching process with ofspring distribution $\{ p _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 0 }$ and mean $\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \boldsymbol { m } } } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } j p _ { j } } \end{array}$ then $X _ { n } \equiv Z _ { n } / m ^ { n }$ (cf. 1.9) is a nonnegative martingale and hence $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n } X _ { n } = X _ { \infty }$ exists w.p. 1. It is known that $X _ { n }$ converges to $X _ { \infty }$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ if $m > 1$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } j \log p _ { j } < \infty$ (cf. Chapter 18). See also Athreya and Ney (2004). 

Theorem 13.3.5: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sub-martingale. Then the following are equivalent: 

(i) There exists a random variable $X _ { \infty }$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ such that $X _ { n }  X _ { \infty }$ in $L ^ { 1 }$

Remark 13.3.1: Let (ii) of Theorem 13.3.5 hold. For any $A \in \mathcal F _ { n }$ and $m > n$ , by the sub-martingale property

By uniform integrability, for any $A \in { \mathcal { F } }$

This implies that $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \cup \{ X _ { \infty } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty } \}$ is a sub-martingale, where $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } = \sigma \langle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } \mathcal { F } _ { n } \rangle } \end{array}$ . That is, the sub-martingale is closable at right. Further, $E X _ { n } \to E X _ { \infty } ^ { - }$ . Conversely, it can be shown that if there exists a random variable $X _ { \infty }$ , measurable w.r.t. $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ , such that

(b) $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \cup \{ X _ { \infty } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty } \}$ is a sub-martingale, and 

(c) $E X _ { n } \to E X _ { \infty }$ 

then by (a) and (b), $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is uniformly integrable and (i) of Theorem 13.3.5 holds. 

Corollary 13.3.6: $I f \left\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \right\} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale, then it is closable at right if $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is uniformly integrable $i f X _ { n }$ converges in $L ^ { 1 }$ 

This follows from the previous remark since for a martingale, $E X _ { n }$ is constant for $1 \leq n \leq \infty$ 

Remark 13.3.2: A suficient condition for a sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } ^ { \infty }$ of random variables to be uniformly integrable is that there exists a random variable M such that $E M ~ < ~ \infty$ and $| X _ { n } | ~ \leq ~ M$ w.p. 1 for all $n \ \geq \ 1$ . for all $n \geq 1$ . ## $L ^ { 1 }$ Convergence of the Doob Martingale

Definition 13.3.1: Let X be a random variable on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ and $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ a filtration in $\mathcal { F }$ . Let $E | X | \ < \ \infty$ and $\begin{array} { l l } { X _ { n } } & { \equiv } \end{array}$ 

$E ( X | \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) , n \geq 1$ . Then $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is called a Doob martingale (cf. Example 13.1.3). 

For a Doob martingale, $E | X _ { n } | \leq E | X |$ and it can be shown that $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is uniformly integrable (Problem 13.20). Hence, $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n }$ exists w.p. 1 and in $L ^ { 1 }$ , and equals $E ( X | \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } )$ , where $\textstyle { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty } = \sigma \langle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \rangle$ . This may be summarized as: 

Theorem 13.3.7: Let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration and let X be an ${ \mathcal F } _ { \infty } .$ measurable with $E | X | < \infty$ . Then 

$$
E (X | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \to X \quad w. p. 1 a n d i n L ^ {1}.
$$

Corollary 13.3.8: Let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } = \sigma \langle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } \mathcal { F } _ { n } \rangle } \end{array}$ 

(i) For any $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty }$ , one has 

$$
P (A | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \to I _ {A} \quad w. p. 1.
$$

(ii) For any random variable X with $E | X | < \infty$ 2 

$$
E (X | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \to E (X | \mathcal {F} _ {\infty}) w. p. 1.
$$

Proof: Take $X = I _ { A }$ for (i) and in Theorem 13.3.7, replace X by $E ( X | \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } )$ for (ii). ✷ 

Kolmogorov’s zero-one law (Theorem 7.2.4) is an easy consequence of this. If $\{ \xi _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ are independent random variables and A is a tail event and $\mathcal { F } _ { n } \equiv \sigma \langle \bar { \xi _ { j } } : 1 \leq j \leq n \rangle$ , then $P ( A | \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) = P ( A )$ for each n and hence $P ( A ) = I _ { A } { \mathrm { ~ w . p . ~ } } 1 , { \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } } P ( A ) = 0 { \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } } 1$ 

Theorem 13.3.9: $( L ^ { p }$ convergence of sub-martingales, $p \ > \ 1 )$ Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a nonnegative sub-martingale. Let $1 ~ < ~ p ~ < ~ \infty$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n > 1 } E | X _ { n } | ^ { p } < \infty } \end{array}$ . Then lim $\mathfrak { l } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n } = X _ { \infty }$ exists w.p. 1 and in L<sup>p</sup>, and $\{ ( X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) \} _ { n \geq 1 } \cup \{ X _ { \infty } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty } \}$ is a L<sup>p</sup>-bounded sub-martingale. 

Proof: By Doob’s maximal $L ^ { p }$ inequality (Theorem 13.2.11), for any $n \geq$ 1, 

$$
E M _ {n} ^ {p} \leq \left(\frac {p}{p - 1}\right) ^ {p} E X _ {n} ^ {p} \leq \left(\frac {p}{p - 1}\right) ^ {p} \sup _ {m \geq 1} E X _ {m} ^ {p},\tag{3.3}
$$

where $M _ { n } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ X _ { j } : 1 \leq j \leq n \}$ . Let $M = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } M _ { n }$ . Then (3.3) yields 

$$
E M ^ {p} <   \infty .
$$

This makes $\{ | X _ { n } | ^ { p } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ uniformly integrable. Also su $\log _ { n \geq 1 } E | X _ { n } | ^ { p } < \infty$ and $p > 1 \Rightarrow \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } E | X _ { n } | < \infty$ and hence, $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } X _ { n } = X _ { \infty } ^ { - } } \end{array}$ exists w.p. 1 as a finite limit. The uniform integrability of $\{ | X _ { n } | ^ { p } \} _ { n \geq p }$ implies $L ^ { p }$ convergence (cf. Problem 2.36). The closability also follows as in Remark 13.3.1. ✷ 

Corollary 13.3.10: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a martingale. Let $1 < p < \infty$ and $\mathrm { s u p } _ { n \geq 1 } E | X _ { n } | ^ { p } < \infty$ . Then the conclusions of Theorem 13.3.9 hold.
