## Reversed Martingales

Definition 13.3.2: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \leq - 1 }$ be an adapted family with $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ as the underlying probability space, i.e., for $n < m , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \subset { \mathcal { F } } _ { m } \subset { \mathcal { F } }$ and $X _ { n }$ is ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ -measurable for each $n \leq - 1$ . Such a sequence is called a reversed martingale if 

(i) $E | X _ { n } | < \infty$ for all $n \leq - 1$ ， 

(ii) $E ( X _ { n + 1 } | { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) = X _ { n }$ for all $n \leq - 1$ 

The definitions of reversed sub- and super-martingales are similar. 

Reversed martingales are well behaved since they are closed at right. 

Theorem 13.3.11: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \leq - 1 }$ be a reversed martingale. Then 

(a) $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to - \infty } X _ { n } = X _ { - \infty }$ exists w.p. 1 and in $L ^ { 1 }$ , 

(b) $X _ { - \infty } = E ( X _ { - 1 } | \mathcal { F } _ { - \infty } )$ , where ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { - \infty } \equiv \bigcap _ { n \leq - 1 } { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } .$ 

Proof: Fix $a < b$ . For $n \leq - 1$ , let $U _ { n }$ be the number of $( a , b )$ upcrossings of $\{ X _ { j } : n \leq j \leq - 1 \}$ . Then by Doob’s upcrossing lemma (Theorem 13.3.1), 

$$
E U _ {n} \leq \frac {E (X _ {1} - a) ^ {+}}{(b - a)}.
$$

Let $U = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to - \infty } U _ { n }$ . Letting $n \to - \infty$ , by the MCT, it follows that 

$$
E U <   \infty .
$$

Thus, $U < \infty \mathrm { \bf ~ w . p . ~ } ]$ 1. This being true for every $a \ < \ b ,$ , one may conclude as in Theorem 13.3.2 that $\begin{array} { r } { P ( \varlimsup _ { n \to - \infty } X _ { n } > \varliminf _ { n \to - \infty } X _ { n } ) = 0 } \end{array}$ . So $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to - \infty } X _ { n } = X _ { - \infty }$ exists w.p. 1. Also, by Jensen’s inequality, $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \leq - 1 }$ is uniformly integrable. So $X _ { n }  X _ { - \infty }$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ , proving (a). 

To prove (b), note that for any $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { - \infty }$ , by uniform integrability, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int_ {A} X _ {- \infty} d P & = & \lim _ {n \to - \infty} \int_ {A} X _ {- n} d P \\ & = & \int_ {A} X _ {- 1} d P, \quad \text { by   the   martingale   property. } \end{array}
$$

Corollary 13.3.12: (The Strong Law of Large Numbers for iid random variables). Let $\{ \xi _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables with $E | \xi _ { 1 } | <$ . Then, $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \bar { \xi _ { i } } \to E \xi _ { 1 } } \end{array}$ as $n \to \infty$ , w.p. 1. 

Proof: For $k \geq 1$ , let $S _ { k } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { k }$ and 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {- k} = \sigma \langle \{S _ {k}, \xi_ {k + 1}, \xi_ {k + 2}, \dots \} \rangle .
$$

Let $X _ { n } \equiv E ( \xi _ { 1 } | \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) _ { n \leq - 1 }$ . By the independence of $\{ \xi _ { i } \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ , for any $n \leq - 1$ 2 with $k = - n$ 

$$
X _ {n} = E (\xi_ {1} | \sigma \langle S _ {k} \rangle).
$$

Also, by symmetry, for any $k \geq 1$ 

$$
E (\xi_ {1} | \sigma \langle S _ {k} \rangle) = E (\xi_ {j} | \sigma \langle S _ {k} \rangle) \text {   for   } 1 \leq j \leq k.
$$

Thus, $\begin{array} { r } { X _ { n } \ = \ \frac { 1 } { k } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } E ( \xi _ { j } | \sigma \langle S _ { k } \rangle ) \ = \ \frac { S _ { k } } { k } } \end{array}$ , for all $k = - n \ge 1$ . It is easy to check that $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \leq - 1 }$ is a reversed martingale and so by Theorem 13.3.11, 

$$
\lim _ {n \to - \infty} X _ {n} = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {S _ {k}}{k} \quad \text { exists   w.p.   1   and   in } \quad L ^ {1}.
$$

By Kolmogorov’s zero-one law, lim $\scriptstyle { \mathsf { i } } _ { k \to \infty } { \frac { S _ { k } } { k } }$ is a tail random variable, and so a constant, which by $L ^ { 1 }$ convergence must equal $E \xi _ { 1 }$ ✷ 

## 13.4 Applications of martingale methods

## 13.4.1 Supercritical branching processes

Recall Example 13.1.5 on branching processes. Assume that it is supercritical, i.e., $\mu = E \xi _ { 1 1 } > 1$ and that $\sigma ^ { 2 } = \mathrm { V a r } ( \xi _ { 1 1 } ) < \infty$ 

Proposition 13.4.1: Let $X _ { n } = \mu ^ { - n } Z _ { n }$ be the martingale defined in $( 1 . 9 )$ Then, $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is an L<sup>2</sup>-bounded martingale. 

Proof: Let $v _ { n } = \mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { n } ) , n \geq 1$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} v _ {n + 1} & = & \operatorname{Var} (E (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n})) + E (\operatorname{Var} (X _ {n + 1} | \mathcal {F} _ {n})) \\ & = & \operatorname{Var} (X _ {n}) + \frac {E (Z _ {n} \sigma^ {2})}{\mu^ {2 (n + 1)}} \\ & = & v _ {n} + \sigma^ {2} \mu^ {- 2} \mu^ {- n}, n \geq 1. \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\begin{array} { r } { v _ { n + 1 } = \sigma ^ { 2 } \mu ^ { - 2 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \mu ^ { - j } } \end{array}$ . Since $\mu > 1 , \{ v _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is bounded. Now since $E X _ { n } \equiv 1 , \{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is L -bounded. ✷ 

A direct consequence of Proposition 13.4.1 and Theorem 13.3.8 is that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n } = X _ { \infty } } \end{array}$ exists w.p. 1 and in mean-square. 

## 13.4.2 Investment sequences

Let $X _ { n }$ be the value of a portfolio at (the end of) the nth period. Suppose the returns on the investment are random and satisfy 

$$
E (X _ {n + 1} | X _ {0}, X _ {1}, \dots , X _ {n}) \leq \rho_ {n + 1} X _ {n}, n \geq 1
$$

where $\rho _ { n + 1 }$ is a strictly positive random variable that is ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n } { \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e } } .$ where $\mathcal { F } _ { n } \equiv \sigma \langle X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , . . . , X _ { n } \rangle$ . Let $\rho _ { 1 } \equiv 1$ and 

$$
Z _ {n} = \frac {X _ {n}}{\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \rho_ {j}}, n \geq 1.
$$

Then, $\{ Z _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a nonnegative super-martingale and hence, it converges w.p. 1 to a limit $Z$ , with $E Z \le E Z _ { 1 } = E X _ { 1 }$ . This implies that $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converges w.p. 1 on the event $\begin{array} { r } { A \equiv \left\{ \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \rho _ { j } \right. } \end{array}$ converges . 

## 13.4.3 A conditional Borel-Cantelli lemma

Let $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of events in a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ and let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration in ${ \mathcal F } .$ . Let $A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ for all $n \geq 1$ and $\begin{array} { l l } { p _ { n } } & { = } \end{array}$ $P ( A _ { n } | \mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 } ) , n \geq 1$ , where $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ is the trivial $\boldsymbol { \sigma } \mathrm { - a l g e b r a } \equiv \left\{ \Omega , \emptyset \right\}$ . Let $\delta _ { n } =$ $I _ { A _ { n } }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { X _ { n } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ( \delta _ { j } - p _ { j } ) , n \geq 1 } \end{array}$ . Then 

$$
\{X _ {n}, \mathcal {F} _ {n} \} _ {n \geq 1}
$$

is a martingale. Let $\begin{array} { r } { V _ { j } = \mathrm { V a r } ( \delta _ { j } | \mathcal { F } _ { j - 1 } ) = p _ { j } ( 1 - p _ { j } ) , j \ge 1 , s _ { n } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } V _ { j } } \end{array}$ and $\tilde { s } _ { n } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ s _ { n } , 1 \} , n \geq 1$ . Since $V _ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 ^ { - 1 } }$ measurable, so are $s _ { n }$ and $\tilde { s } _ { n }$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { Y _ { n } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( \delta _ { j } - p _ { j } ) / \tilde { s } _ { j } , n \geq 1 } \end{array}$ . Then, $\{ Y _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale. Clearly, $E Y _ { n } = { \mathrm { { 0 } } }$ and by the martingale property 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E Y _ {n} ^ {2} = \mathrm{Var} (Y _ {n}) & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \mathrm{Var} \left(\frac {\delta_ {j} - p _ {j}}{\tilde {s} _ {j}}\right) \\ & = & \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} E \bigg (\frac {V _ {j}}{\tilde {s} _ {j} ^ {2}} \bigg) \\ & = & E \bigg (\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \frac {V _ {j}}{\tilde {s} _ {j} ^ {2}} \bigg). \end{array}
$$

But $V _ { 1 } = s _ { 1 }$ and $V _ { j } = s _ { j } - s _ { j - 1 }$ for $j \geq 2$ and so $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { V _ { j } } { \tilde { s } _ { j } ^ { 2 } } \leq \int _ { s _ { j - 1 } } ^ { s _ { j } } \frac { 1 } { t ^ { 2 } } d t } \end{array}$ and hence, 

$$
\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {V _ {j}}{\tilde {s} _ {j} ^ {2}} \leq \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{t ^ {2}} d t = 1.
$$

So $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n \geq 1 } E Y _ { n } ^ { 2 } \leq 1 } \end{array}$ . Thus, $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ converges to some $Y$ w.p. 1 and in $L ^ { 2 }$ 

If $s _ { n } \to \infty$ , then by Kronecker’s lemma (cf. Lemma 8.4.2). 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{s _ {n}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} (\delta_ {j} - p _ {j}) \to 0 \\ \Rightarrow \left(\frac {\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \delta_ {j}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j}} - 1\right) \frac {\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j}}{s _ {n}} \to 0. \end{array}
$$

But $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } p _ { j } \geq s _ { n }$ and hence 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \delta_ {j}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j}} \to 1 \quad \text { w   .   p   . } 1 \text { on   the   event } \quad B \equiv \left\{s _ {n} \to \infty \right\}.\tag{4.1}
$$

Next it is claimed that on $B ^ { c } \equiv \{ \operatorname * { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } s _ { n } < \infty \}$ , li $\quad \operatorname* { m } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n } = X$ exists and is finite w.p. 1. To prove the claim, fix $0 < t < \infty$ . Let $N _ { t } =$ inf $\{ n : s _ { n + 1 } > t \}$ . Since $s _ { n + 1 }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { n } { \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e } }$ $N _ { t }$ is a stopping time and by the optional stopping theorem I (Theorem 13.2.3), $\{ Z _ { n } \equiv X _ { N _ { t } \wedge n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale. By Doob’s $L ^ { 2 } .$ -maximal inequality, 

$$
E \Big (\sup _ {1 \leq j \leq n} Z _ {j} ^ {2} \Big) \leq 4 E (Z _ {n} ^ {2}).
$$

Also it is easy to verify that $\{ X _ { n } ^ { 2 } - s _ { n } ^ { 2 } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale and by the optional sampling theorem (Theorem 13.2.4), 

$$
E (X _ {n \wedge N _ {t}} ^ {2} - s _ {n \wedge N _ {t}} ^ {2}) = 0.
$$

Thus, $E Z _ { n } ^ { 2 } = E s _ { n \wedge N _ { t } } ^ { 2 } \leq t$ and hence for each t, $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } Z _ { n }$ exists w.p. 1 and in $L _ { 2 }$ . Thus, lim $_ { \cdot n  \infty } X _ { N _ { t } \wedge n }$ exists w.p. 1 for each t. But, on $B ^ { c }$ $N _ { t } ~ = ~ \infty$ for all large t. So $\quad \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n } \ = \ X$ exists w.p. 1 on $B ^ { c }$ . This proves the claim. 

It follows that on $\begin{array} { r } { B ^ { c } \cap \{ \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } p _ { j } = \infty \} } \end{array}$ 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \delta_ {j}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j}} - 1 = \frac {X _ {n}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j}} \to 0.
$$

Also, since $B \equiv \{ s _ { n } \to \infty \}$ is a subset of $\textstyle \{ \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } p _ { j } = \infty \}$ and it has been shown in (4.1) that 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \delta_ {j}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j}} \to 1 \quad \text { w.p.   1   on } \quad B,
$$

it follows that 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \delta_ {j}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j}} \rightarrow 1 \quad \text { w   .   p   . } 1 \text { o   n } \quad \left\{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} p _ {j} = \infty \right\}.
$$

Summarizing the above, one gets the following result. 

Theorem 13.4.2: (A conditional Borel-Cantelli lemma). Let $\{ A _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of events in a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ and $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration such that $A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ , for all $n \geq 1$ . Let $p _ { n } = P ( A _ { n } | \mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 } )$ for $n \geq 2 , p _ { 1 } = P ( A _ { 1 } )$ . Then on the event $\begin{array} { r } { B _ { 0 } \equiv \{ \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } p _ { j } = \infty \} } \end{array}$ 

$$
\frac {\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} I _ {A _ {j}}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j}} \to 1 \quad w. p. 1,
$$

and in particular, infinitely many $A _ { n }$ ’s happen w.p. 1 on $B _ { 0 }$ . 

## 13.4.4 Decomposition of probability measures

The almost sure convergence of a nonnegative martingale yields the following theorem on the Lebesgue decomposition of two probability measures on a given measurable space. 

Theorem 13.4.3: Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ be a measurable space and $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration with $\mathcal { F } _ { n } ~ \subset ~ \mathcal { F } ~ f o r$ all $n \geq 1$ . Let P and Q be two probability measures on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ such that for each $n \geq 1 , P _ { n } \equiv t h $ e restriction of P to ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ is absolutely continuous w.r.t. $Q _ { n } \equiv o n$ the restriction of Q to ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ , with the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\begin{array} { r } { X _ { n } = \frac { d P _ { n } } { d Q _ { n } } } \end{array}$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } \equiv \sigma \langle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } \mathcal { F } _ { n } \rangle } \end{array}$ and $X \equiv { \overline { { \operatorname { l i m } } } } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n }$ . Then for any $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P (A) & = & \int_ {A} X d Q + P (A \cap (X = \infty)) \\ & \equiv & P _ {a} (A) + P _ {s} (A), s a y, \end{array}\tag{4.2}
$$

and $P _ { a } \ll Q$ and $P _ { s } \perp Q$ 

Proof: For $\begin{array} { l l l l l } { 1 } & { \leq } & { k } & { \leq } & { n } \end{array}$ , let $\begin{array} { r c l } { M _ { k , n } } & { = } & { \operatorname* { m a x } _ { k \leq j \leq n } X _ { j } } \end{array}$ . Let $\begin{array} { r l } { M _ { k } } & { { } = } \end{array}$ $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n > k } M _ { k , n } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } M _ { k , n } } \end{array}$ . Then $\begin{array} { r } { X \equiv \varlimsup _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n } = \varliminf _ { k \to \infty } M _ { k } } \end{array}$ . Fix $1 \le \bar { k } _ { 0 } , N < \infty$ and $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { k _ { 0 } }$ . Then for $n \geq k \geq k _ { 0 } , B _ { k , n } \equiv A \cap \{ M _ { k , n } \leq$ $N \} \in \mathcal { F } _ { n }$ and hence 

$$
P (B _ {k, n}) = \int X _ {n} I _ {B _ {k, n}} d Q.\tag{4.3}
$$

As $n  \infty , M _ { k , n } \uparrow M _ { k }$ and so $I _ { B _ { k , n } } \downarrow I _ { B _ { k } }$ , where $B _ { k } \equiv A \cap \{ M _ { k } \leq N \} =$ $\cap _ { n > k } B _ { k , n }$ . Also, since $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a nonnegative martingale under the probability measure Q, $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } X _ { n }$ exists w.p. 1 and hence coincides with X. Thus, by the bounded convergence theorem applied to (4.3), 

$$
P (B _ {k}) = \int X I _ {B _ {k}} d Q.
$$

Now let $N \to \infty$ and use the MCT to conclude that 

$$
P (A \cap (M _ {k} <   \infty)) = \int X I _ {\{M _ {k} <   \infty \}} d Q.
$$

Since $\left\{ M _ { k } < \infty \right\} \uparrow \left\{ X < \infty \right\}$ , another application of the MCT yields 

$$
P (A \cap \{X <   \infty \}) = \int X I _ {\{X <   \infty \}} d Q.\tag{4.4}
$$

Since $Q ( X < \infty ) = 1$ and 

$$
P (A) = P (A \cap (X <   \infty)) + P (A \cap (X = \infty)),
$$

(4.2) is proved for all $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { k _ { 0 } }$ and hence, also for all $A \in \textstyle \bigcup _ { k > 1 } { \mathcal { F } } _ { k }$ . Since $\textstyle \bigcup _ { k > 1 } { \mathcal { F } } _ { k }$ is an algebra, (4.2) holds for all $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } \equiv \sigma \langle \bigcup _ { k > 1 } \overleftarrow { \mathcal { F } _ { k } } \rangle$ 

To prove the second part, simply note that $Q ( A ) = 0$  implies $P _ { a } ( A ) = 0$ and $Q ( X = \infty ) = 0$ ✷ 

Remark 13.4.1: The right side of (4.2) provides the Lebesgue decomposition of P w.r.t. Q. 

Corollary 13.4.4: 

(i) $P \ll Q \ i f \ E _ { Q } X = 1 \ i f \ P ( X = \infty ) = 0 .$ 

(ii) $P \perp Q \ i f f Q ( X = 0 ) = 1 \ i f f \ P ( X = \infty ) = 1 .$ 

Proof: Follows easily from (4.2). 

For some applications of Corollary 13.4.4 to branching processes see Athreya (2000). 

Corollary 13.4.5: Let $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a nonnegative martingale on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , Q )$ , with $E _ { Q } X _ { 1 } = 1$ . Let P be defined on $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n > 1 } { \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ by $P ( A ) = E _ { Q } X _ { n } I _ { A } i f A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ . Then P is well defined. Suppose further that P admits an extension to a probability measure on $\left( \Omega , \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } \right)$ where $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } \equiv \sigma ( \bigcup _ { n > 1 } \mathcal { F } _ { n } ) } \end{array}$ . Then (4.2) holds. 

Proof: If $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { n }$ , then $A \in \mathcal { F } _ { m }$ for any $m > n$ . But $E _ { Q } X _ { m } I _ { A } = E _ { Q } X _ { n } I _ { A }$ by the martingale property, and so P is well defined on $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } { \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ . The rest of the corollary follows from the theorem. ✷ 

Remark 13.4.2: It can be shown that if $\mathcal { F } _ { n } \equiv \sigma \langle X _ { j } : 1 \leq j \leq n \rangle$ , then P does admit an extension to $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ (cf. see Athreya (2000)). 

Corollary 13.4.6: Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ be a measurable space. Let for each $n \geq 1$ $\mathcal { A } _ { n } \equiv \{ A _ { n 1 } , A _ { n 2 } , . . . , A _ { n k _ { n } } \} \subset \mathcal { F }$ be a partition of Ω. Let $\mathcal { A } _ { n } \subset \sigma \langle \mathcal { A } _ { n + 1 } \rangle$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Let P and Q be two probability measures on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ . Let Q be such that $Q ( A _ { n i } ) > 0$ for all n and i. Let $\textstyle { \mathcal { F } } = \sigma \langle \bigcup _ { n \geq 1 } { \mathcal { A } } _ { n } \rangle$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { X _ { n } \equiv \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k _ { n } } \frac { P ( A _ { n i } ) } { Q ( A _ { n i } ) } I _ { A _ { n i } } } \end{array}$ . Then $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a martingale on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , Q )$ and $P$ satisfies the decomposition $( 4 . 2 )$ 

The proof of Corollary 13.4.6 is left as an exercise (Problem 13.22). 

Remark 13.4.3: This yields the Lebesgue decomposition of $P { \mathrm { ~ w . r . t . ~ } } Q$ when $\mathcal { F }$ is countably generated, i.e., when there exists a countable collection $\mathcal { A }$ of subsets of Ω such that ${ \mathcal { F } } = \sigma { \langle \mathcal { A } \rangle }$ . In particular, this holds if $\Omega = \mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ and $\mathcal { F } \equiv B \big ( ( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } ) \big )$ for $k \in \mathbb N$ 

## 13.4.5 Kakutani’s theorem

Theorem 13.4.7: (Kakutani’s theorem). Let $P$ and $Q$ be the probability distributions on $\left( \mathbb { R } ^ { \infty } , B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { \infty } ) \right)$ of the sequences of independent random variables $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ and $\{ Y _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ -, respectively. Let for each $j \geq 1$ , the distribution of $X _ { j }$ be dominated by that of $Y _ { j }$ . Then 

$$
e i t h e r \quad P \ll Q \quad o r \quad P \perp Q.\tag{4.5}
$$

Proof: Let $f _ { j }$ be the density of $\lambda _ { j } ~ \mathrm { w . r . t . } ~ \mu _ { j }$ where $\lambda _ { j } ( \cdot ) = P ( X _ { j } \in \cdot )$ and $\mu _ { j } ( \cdot ) = Q ( Y _ { j } \in \cdot )$ . Let $\Omega = \mathbb { R } ^ { \infty } , \mathcal { F } = ( \mathcal { B } ( \bar { \mathbb { R } } ) ) ^ { \infty }$ . Then $P = \Pi _ { j \geq 1 } \lambda _ { j } , Q =$ $\Pi _ { j \geq 1 } \mu _ { j }$ . Let $\xi _ { n } ( \omega ) \equiv \omega ( n )$ , the nth co-ordinate of ${ \boldsymbol { \omega } } = ( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } , \ldots ) \in \Omega$ and $\mathcal { F } _ { n } \equiv \sigma \langle \xi _ { j } : 1 \leq j \leq n \rangle$ . Also let $P _ { n }$ be the restriction of $P$ to ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ and $Q _ { n }$ be that of Q to ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ . Then $P _ { n } \ll Q _ { n }$ with probability density 

$$
L _ {n} = \frac {d P _ {n}}{d Q _ {n}} = \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {n} f _ {j} (\xi_ {j}).
$$

Since $\{ \overline { { \operatorname* { l i m } } } _ { n \to \infty } L _ { n } < \infty \}$ is a tail event, by the independence of $\{ \xi _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ under $P$ and the Kolmogorov’s zero-one law, $P ( \overline { { \mathrm { l i m } } } _ { n  \infty } L _ { n } < \infty ) = 0$ or 1. Now, by Corollary 13.4.4, (4.5) follows. ✷ 

Remark 13.4.4: It can be shown that $P \ll Q$ or $P \perp Q$ according as $\begin{array} { r } { \prod _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } E \sqrt { f _ { j } ( Y _ { j } ) } > 0 \mathrm { ~ o r = 0 ~ } } \end{array}$ . For a proof, see Durrett (2004). 

Remark 13.4.5: If $\{ X _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ are iid and $\{ Y _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ are also iid, then $P = Q$ or $P \perp Q$ . This is because $f _ { j } = f _ { 1 }$ for all $j$ and $E _ { Q } \sqrt { f _ { 1 } } \leq ( E _ { Q } f _ { 1 } ) ^ { 1 / 2 } \leq 1$ and so either $E _ { Q } \sqrt { f _ { 1 } } < 1$ or $E _ { Q } \sqrt { f _ { 1 } } = 1$ . In the latter case $f _ { 1 } \equiv 1$ , since $E _ { Q } ( \sqrt { f _ { 1 } } ) ^ { 2 } = 1 = E _ { Q } ( \sqrt { f _ { 1 } } ) \Rightarrow \mathrm { V a r } _ { Q } ( \sqrt { f _ { 1 } } ) = 0$ 

Remark 13.4.6: The above result can be extended to Markov chains. Let P and $Q$ be two irreducible stochastic matrices on a countable set and let $Q$ be positive recurrent. Also, let $P _ { x _ { 0 } }$ denote the distribution of a Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ starting at $x _ { 0 }$ and with transition probability P, and similarly, let $Q _ { y _ { 0 } }$ denote the distribution of a Markov chain $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ starting at $y _ { 0 }$ and with transition probability Q. Then 

$$
\text { either } \quad P _ {x _ {0}} \perp Q _ {y _ {0}} \quad \text { or } \quad P = Q.\tag{4.6}
$$

The proof of this is left as an exercise (Problem 13.23). 

## 13.4.6 de Finetti’s theorem

Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of exchangeable random variables on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ , i.e., for each $n \ \geq \ 1$ , the distribution of $( X _ { \sigma ( 1 ) } , X _ { \sigma ( 2 ) } , . . . , X _ { \sigma ( n ) } )$ is the same as that of $( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n } )$ where $( \sigma ( 1 ) , \sigma ( 2 ) , \ldots , \sigma ( n ) )$ is a permutation of $( 1 , 2 , \ldots , n )$ . Then there is a $\sigma -$ algebra $\mathcal { G } \subset \mathcal { F }$ such that for each $n \geq 1$ ， 

$$
P (X _ {i} \in B _ {i}, i = 1, 2, \dots , n \mid \mathcal {G}) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} P (X _ {i} \in B _ {i} \mid \mathcal {G})\tag{4.7}
$$

for all $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } \in B ( \mathbb { R } )$ 

This is known as de Finetti’s theorem. For a proof, see Durrett (2004) and Chow and Teicher (1997). This theorem says that conditioned on the $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \ge 1 }$ are iid random variables with distribution $P ( X _ { 1 } \in \cdot \mid { \mathcal { G } } )$ . The converse to this result, i.e., if for some σ-algebra $\mathcal { G } \subset \mathcal { F } \left( 4 . 7 \right)$ holds, then the sequence $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \ge 1 }$ is exchangeable is not dificult to verify (Problem 13.26).
