## 14.1 Markov chains: Countable state space

## 14.1.1 Definition

Let $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbb { S } = \{ a _ { j } : j = 1 , 2 , \ldots , K \} , K \leq \infty } \end{array}$ be a finite or countable set. Let $P = ( ( p _ { i j } ) ) _ { K \times K }$ be a stochastic matrix, i.e., $p _ { i j } ~ \geq ~ 0 _ { \mathrm { { \scriptsize ~ \cdot ~ } } }$ , for every $i ,$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { K } p _ { i j } = 1 } \end{array}$ and $\mu = \{ \mu _ { j } : 1 \leq j \leq K \}$ be a probability distribution, i.e., $\mu _ { j } \geq 0$ for all j and $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { K } \mu _ { j } = 1 } \end{array}$ 

Definition 14.1.1: A sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ of S-valued random variables on some probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ is called a Markov chain with stationary transition probabilities $P = \left( \left( p _ { i j } \right) \right)$ , initial distribution $\mu _ { : }$ , and state space S if 

(i) $X _ { 0 } \sim \mu , \mathrm { i . e . , } P ( X _ { 0 } = a _ { j } ) = \mu _ { j }$ for all j, and 

(ii) $P { \big ( } X _ { n + 1 } = a _ { j } \mid X _ { n } = a _ { i } , X _ { n - 1 } = a _ { i _ { n - 1 } } , \ldots , X _ { 0 } = a _ { i _ { 0 } } { \big ) } = p _ { i j }$ for all $a _ { i } , a _ { j } , a _ { i _ { n - 1 } } , \ldots , a _ { i _ { 0 } } \in \mathbb { S } { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } n = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots ,$ 

i.e., the sequence is memoryless. Given $X _ { n } , X _ { n + 1 }$ is independent of $\{ X _ { j }$ $j \le n - 1 \}$ . More generally, given the present $( X _ { n } )$ , the past $( \{ X _ { j } : j \leq$ $n - 1 \}$ and the future $( \{ X _ { j } ~ : ~ j ~ > ~ n \} )$ are stochastically independent (Problem 14.1). 

A few questions arise: 

Question 1: Does such a sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ exist for every $\mu$ and $P _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and 

if so, how does one generate them? 

The answer is yes. There are two approaches, namely, (i) using Kolmogorov’s consistency theorem and (ii) an iid random iteration scheme. 

Question 2: How does one describe the finite time behavior, i.e., the joint distribution of $( X _ { 0 } , X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } )$ for any $n \in \mathbb { N } ?$ 

One may use the Markov property repeatedly to obtain the joint distribution. 

Question 3: What can one say about the long-term behavior? One can ask questions like: 

(a) Does the trajectory $n  X _ { n }$ converge as $n \to \infty ?$ 

(b) Does the distribution of $X _ { n }$ converge as $n  \infty ?$ 

(c) Do the laws of large numbers hold for a suitable class of functions $f ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s } , \mathrm { i . e . }$ , do the limits $\begin{array} { r l } { } & { { } \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f ( X _ { j } ) } \end{array}$ exist w.p. 1? 

(d) Do stationary distributions exist? (A probability distribution $\pi =$ $\{ \pi _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { S } }$ is called a stationary distribution for a Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ if $X _ { 0 }$ has distribution π, then $X _ { n }$ also has distribution π for all $n \geq 1 . )$ 

The key to answering these questions are the concepts of communication, irreducibility, aperiodicity, and most importantly recurrence. The main tools are the laws of large numbers, renewal theory, and coupling. 

## 14.1.2 Examples

Example 14.1.1: (IID sequence). Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ be a sequence of iid $\mathbb { S } _ { - }$ valued random variables with distribution $\mu = \{ \mu _ { j } \}$ . Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ is a Markov chain with initial distribution $\mu$ and transition probabilities given by $p _ { i j } = \mu _ { j }$ for all i, i.e., all rows of P are identical. It is also easy to prove the converse, i.e., if all rows of $_ { P }$ are identical, then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ are iid and independent of $X _ { 0 }$ 

To answer Question 3 in this case, note that $P [ X _ { n } = j ] = \mu _ { j }$ for all n and thus $X _ { n }$ converges in distribution. But the trajectories do not converge. However, the law of large numbers holds and $\mu$ is the unique stationary distribution. 

Example 14.1.2: (Random walks). Let $\mathbb { S } = \mathbb { Z }$ , the set of integers. Let $\{ \epsilon _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be iid with distribution $\{ p _ { j } \} _ { j \in \mathbb { Z } }$ , i.e., $P [ \epsilon _ { 1 } = j ] = p _ { j }$ for $j \in$ Z and $\{ \epsilon _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ are independent. Let $X _ { 0 }$ be a Z-valued random variable independent of $\{ \epsilon _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ . Then, define for $n \geq 0$ , 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = X _ {n} + \epsilon_ {n + 1} = X _ {n - 1} + \epsilon_ {n} + \epsilon_ {n - 1} = \dots = X _ {0} + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n + 1} \epsilon_ {j}.
$$

In this case, with probability one, the trajectories of $X _ { n }$ go to $+ \infty$ (respectively, $- \infty )$ , if $E ( \epsilon _ { 1 } ) > 0$ (respectively $< 0 )$ . If $E ( \epsilon _ { 1 } ) = 0$ , then the trajectories fluctuate infinitely often provided $p _ { 0 } \neq 1$ 

Example 14.1.3: (Branching processes). Let $\mathbb { S } = \mathbb { Z } _ { + } = \{ 0 , 1 , 2 , . . . \}$ Let $\{ p _ { j } \} _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ be a probability distribution. Let $\{ \xi _ { n i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { N } , n \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + } }$ be iid random variables with distribution $\{ p _ { j } \} _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ . Let $Z _ { 0 }$ be a $\mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ -valued random variable independent of $\left\{ \xi _ { n i } \right\}$ . Let 

$$
Z _ {n + 1} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {Z _ {n}} \xi_ {n i} \quad \text { for } \quad n \geq 0.
$$

If $p _ { 0 } = 0$ and $p _ { 1 } < 1$ , then $Z _ { n } \to \infty \mathrm { ~ w . p . ~ } 1$ . If $p _ { 0 } > 0$ , then $P [ Z _ { n } $ $\infty ] + P [ Z _ { n }  0 ] = 1$ . Also, $P [ Z _ { n } \to 0 \mid Z _ { 0 } = 1 ] = q$ is the smallest solution in [0,1] to the equation 

$$
q = f (q) = \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} p _ {j} q ^ {j}.
$$

So $\begin{array} { r } { q = 1 \mathrm { i f f } m \equiv \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } j p _ { j } ( 1 ) \leq 1 } \end{array}$ (see Chapter 18 also). 

Example 14.1.4: (Birth and death chains). Again take $\mathbb { S } = \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ . Define P by 

$$
\begin{array}{c c} p _ {i, i + 1} = \alpha_ {i}, & p _ {i, i - 1} = \beta_ {i} = 1 - \alpha_ {i}, \text {   for   } i \geq 1, \\ p _ {0, 1} = \alpha_ {0}, & p _ {0, 0} = \beta_ {0} = 1 - \alpha_ {0}. \end{array}
$$

The population increases at rate $\alpha _ { i }$ and decreases at rate $1 - \alpha _ { i }$ 

Example 14.1.5: (Iterated function systems). Let $G : = \{ h _ { i } : h _ { i } : \mathbb { S } \to $ S, $i = 1 , 2 , \ldots , L \} , L \leq \infty$ . Let $\mu = \{ p _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { L }$ be a probability distribution. Let $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ be iid, such that $P ( f _ { n } = h _ { i } ) = p _ { i } , 1 \leq i \leq L$ . Let $X _ { 0 }$ be a S-valued random variable independent of $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ . Then, the iid random iteration scheme 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} X _ {1} & = & f _ {1} (X _ {0}) \\ X _ {2} & = & f _ {2} (X _ {1}) \\ & \vdots \\ X _ {n + 1} & = & f _ {n + 1} (X _ {n}) = f _ {n + 1} \big (f _ {n} (\dots (f _ {1} (X _ {0})) \dots) \big) \end{array}
$$

is a Markov chain with transition probability matrix 

$$
p _ {i j} = P (f _ {1} (i) = j) = \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {L} p _ {r} I \big (h _ {r} (i) = j \big).
$$

Remark 14.1.1: Any discrete state space Markov chain can be generated in this way (see II in 14.1.3 below). 

## 14.1.3 Existence of a Markov chain

I. Kolmogorov’s approach. Let $\Omega = \mathbb { S } ^ { \mathbb { Z } _ { + } } = \{ \omega : \omega \equiv \{ x _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } , x _ { n } \in$ S for all $n \}$ be the set of all sequences $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ with values in S. Let $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ consist of all finite dimensional subsets of Ω of the form 

$$
A = \left\{\omega : \omega = \{x _ {n} \} _ {n = 0} ^ {\infty}, x _ {j} = a _ {j}, 0 \leq j \leq m \right\},
$$

where $m \ < \ \infty$ and $a _ { j } ~ \in ~ \mathbb { S }$ for all $j = 0 , 1 , \ldots , m$ . Let $\mathcal { F }$ be the σ-algebra generated by $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ . Fix $\mu$ and P . For A as above let 

$$
\lambda_ {\mu , \boldsymbol {P}} (A) := \mu_ {a _ {0}} p _ {a _ {0} a _ {1}} p _ {a _ {1} a _ {2}} \dots p _ {a _ {m - 1} a _ {m}}.
$$

Then it can be shown, using the extension theorem from Chapter 2 or Kolmogorov’s consistency theorem of Chapter 6, that $\lambda _ { \mu , P }$ can be extended to be a probability measure on $\mathcal { F }$ . Let $X _ { n } ( \omega ) \stackrel { \cdot \cdot } { = } x _ { n }$ , if $\omega = \{ x _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ , be the coordinate projection. Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ will be a sequence of S-valued random variables on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \lambda _ { \mu , P } )$ , such that it is a Markov chain with initial distribution $\mu$ and transition probability P. A typical element $\omega = \{ x _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ of $\Omega$ is called a sample path or a sample trajectory. 

The following are examples of events (sets) in ${ \mathcal F }$ which are not finitedimensional: 

$$
A _ {1} = \left\{\omega : \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} h (x _ {j}) \text {exists} \right\} \text {for a given} h: \mathbb {S} \rightarrow \mathbb {R},
$$

$$
A _ {2} = \left\{\omega : \text { the   set   of   limit   points   of } \{x _ {n} \} _ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} = \{a, b \} \right\}
$$

Thus, it is essential to go to $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , \lambda _ { \mu , P } )$ to discuss the events involving asymptotic (long term) behavior, i.e., as $n \to \infty$ 

II. IIIDRM approach (iteration of iid random maps). Let $\begin{array} { r l } { \pmb { P } } & { { } = } \end{array}$ $\left( ( p _ { i j } ) \right) _ { K \times K }$ be a stochastic matrix. Let $f : \mathbb { S } \times [ 0 , 1 ] \to \mathbb { S }$ be 

$$
f (a _ {i}, u) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} a _ {1} & \text { if } \quad 0 \leq u <   p _ {i 1} \\ a _ {2} & \text { if } \quad p _ {i 1} \leq u <   p _ {i 1} + p _ {i 2} \\ \vdots \\ a _ {j} & \text { if } \quad p _ {i 1} + p _ {i 2} + \dots + p _ {i (j - 1)} \leq u <   p _ {i 1} + p _ {i 2} \\ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad + \dots + p _ {i j} \\ \vdots \\ a _ {K} & \text { if } \quad p _ {i 1} + p _ {i 2} + \dots + p _ {i (K - 1)} \leq u <   1. \end{array} \right.\tag{1.1}
$$

Let $U _ { 1 } , U _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be iid Uniform [0, 1] random variables. Let $f _ { n } ( \cdot ) : =$ $f ( \cdot , U _ { n } )$ . Then for each n, $f _ { n }$ maps S to S. Also $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ are iid. 

Let $X _ { 0 }$ be independent of $\{ U _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ and $X _ { 0 } \sim \mu$ . Then the sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ defined by 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = f _ {n + 1} (X _ {n}) = f (X _ {n}, U _ {n + 1})
$$

is a Markov chain with initial distribution $\mu$ and transition probability P. The underlying probability space on which $X _ { 0 }$ and $\{ U _ { i } \} _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty }$ are defined can be taken to be the Lebesgue space $( [ 0 , 1 ] , B ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) , m )$ 2 where m is the Lebesgue measure. 

## Finite Time Behavior of $\{ X _ { n } \}$

For each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & P \left(X _ {0} = a _ {0}, X _ {1} = a _ {1}, \dots , X _ {n} = a _ {n}\right) \\ = & \left(\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {n} P \left(X _ {j} = a _ {j} \mid X _ {j - 1} = a _ {j - 1}, \dots , X _ {0} = a _ {0}\right)\right) P \left(X _ {0} = a _ {0}\right) \\ = & \left(\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {a _ {j - 1} a _ {j}}\right) \mu_ {a _ {0}}. \end{array}\tag{1.2}
$$

Thus, the joint distribution for any finite n is determined by $\mu$ and $_ { r }$ . In particular, 

$$
P \big (X _ {n} = a _ {n} \mid X _ {0} = a _ {0} \big) = \sum \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {n} p _ {a _ {j - 1} a _ {j}} = (\boldsymbol {P} ^ {n}) _ {a _ {0} a _ {n}},\tag{1.3}
$$

where the sum in the middle term runs over all $a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , \dotsc , a _ { j - 1 }$ and $\pmb { P } ^ { n }$ is the nth power of P. So the behavior of the distribution of $X _ { n }$ can be studied via that of $\pmb { P } ^ { n }$ for large n. But this analytic approach is not as comprehensive as the probabilistic one, via the concept of recurrence, which will be described next. 

## 14.1.4 Limit theory

Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ be a Markov chain with state space $\mathbb { S } = \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , K \} , K \leq$ $\infty .$ , and transition probability matrix $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { P } = \left( \left( p _ { i j } \right) \right) _ { K \times K } . } \end{array}$ 

Definition 14.1.2: (Hitting times). For any set $A \subset \mathbb { S }$ , the hitting time $T _ { A }$ is defined as 

$$
T _ {A} = \inf \{n: X _ {n} \in A, n \geq 1 \}
$$

i.e., it is the first time after 0 that the chain enters A. The random variable $T _ { A }$ is also called the first passage time for A or the first entrance time for A. Note that $T _ { A }$ is a stopping time (cf. Chapter 13) w.r.t. the filtration $\{ { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \equiv \sigma \langle \{ X _ { j } : 0 \leq j \leq n \} \rangle _ { n \geq 0 }$ 

By convention, inf $\varnothing = \infty . \operatorname { I f } A = \{ i \}$ , then write $T _ { \{ i \} } = T _ { i }$ for notational simplicity. 

A concept of fundamental importance is recurrence of a state. 

Definition 14.1.3: (Recurrence). A state i is recurrent or transient according as 

$$
P _ {i} [ T _ {i} <   \infty ] = 1 \quad \text { or } \quad <   1,
$$

where $P _ { i }$ denotes the probability distribution of $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ with $X _ { 0 } = i$ with probability 1. Thus i is recurrent if 

$$
f _ {i i} \equiv P \big (X _ {n} = i \quad \text { for   some } \quad 1 \leq n <   \infty \mid X _ {0} = i \big) = 1.\tag{1.4}
$$

Definition 14.1.4: (Null and positive recurrence). A recurrent state i is called null recurrent if $E _ { i } ( T _ { i } ) = \infty$ and positive recurrent if $E _ { i } ( T _ { i } ) < \infty$ 2 where $E _ { i }$ refers to expectation w.r.t. the probability distribution $P _ { i }$ 

Example 14.1.6: (Frog in the well). Let $\mathbb { S } = \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots \}$ and $P = \left( \left( p _ { i j } \right) \right)$ be given by 

$$
p _ {i, i + 1} = \alpha_ {i} \quad \text { and } \quad p _ {i, 1} = 1 - \alpha_ {i} \quad \text { for   all } \quad i \geq 1, 0 <   \alpha_ {i} <   1.
$$

Then 

$$
P _ {1} [ T _ {1} > r ] = \alpha_ {1} \alpha_ {2} \dots \alpha_ {r}.
$$

So $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { 1 } [ T _ { 1 } < \infty ] = 1 \mathrm { i f f } \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { r } \alpha _ { i }  0 \mathrm { a s } r  \infty \mathrm { i f f } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } ( 1 - \alpha _ { i } ) = \infty } \end{array}$ . Further 1 is positive recurrent if $\bar { \sum _ { r = 1 } ^ { \infty } \Big ( } \prod _ { 1 } ^ { r } \alpha _ { i } \Big ) < \infty$ . Thus, if $\begin{array} { r } { \alpha _ { i } = ( 1 - \frac { 1 } { 2 i ^ { 2 } } ) } \end{array}$ , then 1 is transient; but if $\alpha _ { i } \equiv \alpha , 0 < \alpha < 1$ -for all i, then 1 is positive recurrent. If $\begin{array} { r } { \alpha _ { i } = 1 - \frac { 1 } { c i } , c > 1 } \end{array}$ , then 1 is null recurrent (Problem 14.2). 

Example 14.1.7: (Simple random walk). Let $\mathbb { S } = \mathbb { Z }$ , the set of all integers, $p _ { i , i + 1 } = p , p _ { i , i - 1 } = q , 0 < p = 1 - q < 1$ . Then it can be shown by using the SLLN that for $p \neq { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } , 0$ is transient. But it is harder to show that for $\textstyle p = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } , 0$ is null recurrent (see Corollary 14.1.5 below). 

The next result says that after each return to $i ,$ the Markov chain starts afresh. 

Proposition 14.1.1: (The strong Markov property). For any $\textit { i } \in \mathrm { ~ \mathbb { S } ~ }$ and any initial distribution $\mu$ of $X _ { 0 }$ and any $k < \infty , a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { k }$ in S, $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { \mu } ( X _ { T _ { i } + j } = a _ { j } , \ j = 1 , 2 , \dots , k , \ T _ { i } < \infty ) = P _ { \mu } ( T _ { i } < \infty ) P _ { i } ( X _ { j } = a _ { j } , \ j = 1 , 2 , \dots , k , \ T _ { i } < \infty ) . } \end{array}$ $1 , 2 , \ldots , k )$ 

Proof: For any $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & P _ {\mu} (X _ {T _ {i} + j} = a _ {j}, 1 \leq j \leq k, T _ {i} = n) \\ = & P _ {\mu} (X _ {n + j} = a _ {j}, 1 \leq j \leq k, X _ {n} = i, X _ {r} \neq i, 1 \leq r \leq n - 1) \\ = & P _ {\mu} (X _ {n + j} = a _ {j}, 1 \leq j \leq k \mid X _ {n} = i, X _ {r} \neq i, 1 \leq r \leq n - 1) \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & \cdot P _ {\mu} (X _ {n} = i, X _ {r} \neq i, 1 \leq r \leq n - 1) \\ = & P _ {i} (X _ {j} = a _ {j}, 1 \leq j \leq k) P _ {\mu} (X _ {n} = i, X _ {r} \neq i, 1 \leq r \leq n - 1) \\ = & P _ {i} (X _ {j} = a _ {j}, 1 \leq j \leq k) P _ {\mu} (T _ {i} = n). \end{array}
$$

Adding both sides over n yields the result. 

The strong Markov property leads to the important useful technique of breaking up the time evolution of a Markov chain into iid cycles. This combined with the law of large numbers yield the basic convergence results. 

Definition 14.1.5: (IID cycles). Let i be a state. Let $T _ { i } ^ { ( 0 ) } = 0$ and 

$$
T _ {i} ^ {(k + 1)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \inf \{n: n > T _ {i} ^ {(k)}, X _ {n} = i \}, & \text {if} \quad T _ {i} ^ {(k)} <   \infty , \\ \infty , & \text {if} \quad T _ {i} ^ {(k)} = \infty , \end{array} \right.\tag{1.5}
$$

i.e., for $k = 0 , 1 , 2 , . . . , T _ { i } ^ { ( k ) }$ is the successive return times to state i. 

Proposition 14.1.2: Let i be a recurrent state. Then $P _ { i } \big ( T _ { i } ^ { ( k ) } < \infty \big ) = 1$ for all $k \geq 1$ 

Proof: By definition of recurrence, the claim is true for $k = 1$ . If it is true for $k > 1$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P _ {i} \Big (T _ {i} ^ {(k + 1)} <   \infty \Big) \\ = \sum_ {j = k} ^ {\infty} P \Big (T _ {i} ^ {(k + 1)} <   \infty , T _ {i} ^ {(k)} = j \Big) \\ = \sum_ {j = k} ^ {\infty} P _ {i} \Big (T _ {i} ^ {(1)} <   \infty \Big) P _ {i} \Big (T _ {i} ^ {(k)} = j \Big) \quad (\text { by   Markov   property }) \\ = P _ {i} \Big (T _ {i} ^ {(1)} <   \infty \Big) P _ {i} \Big (T _ {i} ^ {(k)} <   \infty \Big) = 1. \end{array}
$$

Let $\eta _ { r } = \{ X _ { j } , T _ { i } ^ { ( r ) } \leq j \leq T _ { i } ^ { ( r + 1 ) } - 1 ; T _ { i } ^ { ( r + 1 ) } - T _ { i } ^ { ( r ) } \}$ for $r = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots$ The $\eta _ { r } \mathrm { ^ { 3 } s }$ are called cycles or excursions. 

Theorem 14.1.3: Let i be a recurrent state. Under $P _ { i }$ , the sequence $\{ \eta _ { r } \} _ { r = 0 } ^ { \infty }$ are iid as random vectors with a random number of components. More precisely, for any $k \in \mathbb N$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P _ {i} \left(\eta_ {r} = \left(x _ {r 0}, x _ {r 1}, \dots , x _ {r j _ {r}}\right), T _ {i} ^ {(r + 1)} - T _ {i} ^ {(r)} = j _ {r}, r = 0, 1, \dots , k\right) \\ = \prod_ {r = 0} ^ {k} P _ {i} \left(\eta_ {1} = \left(x _ {r 0}, x _ {r 1}, \dots , x _ {r j _ {r}}\right), T _ {i} ^ {(1)} = j _ {r}\right) \end{array} \tag {7}\tag{1.6}
$$

for any $\{ x _ { r 0 } , x _ { r 1 } , \ldots , x _ { r j _ { r } } , j _ { r } \} , r = 0 , 1 , \ldots , k .$ 

Proof: Use the strong Markov property repeatedly (Problem 14.7). 

Proposition 14.1.4: For any state i, let $\begin{array} { r } { N _ { i } \equiv \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } I _ { \{ i \} } ( X _ { n } ) } \end{array}$ be the total number of visits to i. Then, 

(i) i recurrent $\Rightarrow P ( N _ { i } = \infty \mid X _ { 0 } = i ) = 1$ 

(ii) i transien $t \Rightarrow P ( N _ { i } = j \mid X _ { 0 } = i ) = f _ { i i } ^ { j } ( 1 - f _ { i i } )$ for $j = 0 , 1 , 2 , . . .$ where $f _ { i i } = P ( T _ { i } < \infty \mid X _ { 0 } = i )$ is the probability of returning to i starting from $i , \ i . e .$ , under $P _ { i } , \ N _ { i }$ has a geometric distribution with parameter $\left( 1 - f _ { i i } \right)$ 

Proof: Follows from the strong Markov property (Proposition 14.1.1). 

Corollary 14.1.5: A state i is recurrent $i f f$ 

$$
E _ {i} N _ {i} \equiv E (N _ {i} \mid X _ {0} = i) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} p _ {i i} ^ {(n)} = \infty .\tag{1.7}
$$

Proof: If i is recurrent then $P _ { i } ( N _ { i } = \infty ) = 1$ and so $E _ { i } N _ { i } = \infty$ 

If i is transient then $\begin{array} { r } { E _ { i } N _ { i } = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty } j f _ { i i } ^ { j } ( 1 - f _ { i i } ) = \frac { f _ { i i } } { 1 - f _ { i i } } < \infty } \end{array}$ . Also by the monotone convergence theorem, 

$$
E (N _ {i} \mid X _ {0} = i) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E (\delta_ {X _ {n} i} \mid X _ {0} = i) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} p _ {i i} ^ {(n)}.
$$

## An Application

For the simple symmetric random walk (SSRW) in Z, 0 is recurrent. Indeed, 

$$
p _ {0 0} ^ {(n)} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0 & \text { if } \quad n \text { is   odd } \\ \binom {2 k} {k} \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) ^ {2 k} & \text { if } \quad n = 2 k. \end{array} \right.\tag{1.8}
$$

By Stirling’s formula, 

$$
\binom {2 k} {k} = \frac {(2 k) !}{k ! k !} \sim \frac {e ^ {- 2 k} (2 k) ^ {2 k + \frac {1}{2}} \sqrt {2 \pi}}{(e ^ {- k} k ^ {k + \frac {1}{2}} \sqrt {2 \pi}) ^ {2}} \sim \frac {4 ^ {k}}{\sqrt {k}} \frac {1}{\sqrt {\pi}}
$$

and hence 

$$
p _ {0 0} ^ {(2 k)} \sim \frac {1}{\sqrt {\pi}} \frac {1}{\sqrt {k}}.
$$

Thus $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } p _ { 0 0 } ^ { ( 2 k ) } = \infty } \end{array}$ , implying that 0 is recurrent. 

By a similar argument, it can be shown that the simple symmetric random walk in $Z ^ { ( 2 ) }$ , the integer lattice in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ , the origin is recurrent, but in $Z ^ { ( d ) }$ for $d \geq 3$ , the origin is transient (Problem 14.3). 

Corollary 14.1.6: If the state space S is finite, then at least one state must be recurrent. 

Proof: Let $\mathbb { S } \equiv \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , K \} , K < \infty$ . Since $\begin{array} { r } { n = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { K } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \delta _ { X _ { j } i } } \end{array}$ , there exists an $i _ { 0 }$ such that as $\begin{array} { r } { n  \infty , \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } \delta _ { X _ { j } i _ { 0 } }  } \end{array}$ with positive probability. This implies that $i _ { 0 }$ must be recurrent. ✷ 

Definition 14.1.6: (Communication). A state i leads to j (write $i  j )$ if for some $n \ge 1 , p _ { i j } ^ { ( n ) } > 0$ . A pair of states $i , j$ are said to communicate if $i  j$ and $j  i , \mathrm { i . e . }$ , if there exist $n \geq 1 , m \geq 1$ such that $p _ { i j } ^ { ( n ) } > 0$ $p _ { j i } ^ { ( m ) } > 0$ 

Definition 14.1.7: (Irreducibility). A Markov chain with state space $\mathbb { S } \equiv \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , K \} , K \leq \infty$ and transition probability matrix $P \equiv ( ( p _ { i j } ) )$ is irreducible if for each $i , j$ in S, i and j communicate. 

Definition 14.1.8: A state i is absorbing if $p _ { i i } = 1$ 

It is easy to show that if i is absorbing and $j  i$ , then j is transient (Problem 14.4). 

Proposition 14.1.7: (Solidarity property). Let i be recurrent and $i  j$ Then $f _ { j i } = 1$ and j is recurrent, where $f _ { j i } \equiv P ( T _ { i } < \infty \mid X _ { 0 } = j )$ 

Proof: By the (strong) Markov property, $1 - f _ { i i } = P ( T _ { i } = \infty \mid X _ { 0 } = i ) \geq$ $P ( T _ { j } < \infty , T _ { i } = \infty \mid X _ { 0 } = i ) = P ( T _ { i } = \infty \mid X _ { 0 } = j ) P ( T _ { j } < T _ { i } \mid X _ { 0 } = i )$ (intuitively speaking, one possibility of not returning to i (starting from i) is to visit $j$ and then not returning $\mathrm { t o } i ) = ( 1 - f _ { j i } ) f _ { i j } ^ { * }$ , where $f _ { i j } ^ { * } = P \mathrm { ( v i s i t i n g }$ j before visiting $i \mid X _ { 0 } = i )$ . Now i recurrent and $i \stackrel { . } {  } j$ yield $\mathsf { i } - f _ { i i } = 0$ and $f _ { i j } ^ { * } > 0$ (Problem 14.4) and so $1 - f _ { j i } = 0 , \mathrm { i . e . , } f _ { j i } = 1$ . Thus, starting from j, the chain visits $i \ \mathrm { w . p . \ 1 }$ . From i, it keeps returning to i infinitely often. In each of these excursions, the probability $f _ { i j } ^ { * }$ of visiting $j$ is positive and since there are infinite number of such excursions and they are iid, the chain does visit $j$ in one of these excursions w.p. 1. That is $j$ is recurrent. 

Also an alternate proof using the Corollary 14.1.5 is possible (Problem 14.5). 

Proposition 14.1.8: In a finite state space irreducible Markov chain all states are recurrent. 

Proof: By Corollary 14.1.6, there is at least one state $i _ { 0 }$ that is recurrent. By irreducibility and solidarity, this implies all states are recurrent. 

Remark 14.1.2: A stronger result holds, namely, that for a finite state space irreducible Markov chain, all states are positive recurrent (Problem 14.6). 

Theorem 14.1.9: (A law of large numbers). Let i be positive recurrent. Let 

$$
N _ {n} (j) = \# \{k: 0 \leq k \leq n, X _ {k} = j \}, j \in \mathbb {S}\tag{1.9}
$$

be the number of visits to $j$ during $\{ 0 , 1 , \ldots , n \}$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { \left\{ L _ { n } ( j ) \equiv \frac { N _ { n } ( j ) } { n + 1 } \right\} } \end{array}$ be the empirical distribution at time n. Let $X _ { 0 } = i$  , with probability 1. Then 

$$
L _ {n} (j) \rightarrow \frac {V _ {i j}}{E _ {i} (T _ {i})}, w. p. 1\tag{1.10}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { V _ { i j } = E _ { i } \big ( \sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { { T _ { i } } - 1 } \delta _ { X _ { k } , j } \big ) } \end{array}$ is the mean number of visits to $j$ during $\{ 0 , 1 , \ldots , T _ { i } - 1 \}$  -starting from i. In particular, $\begin{array} { r } { L _ { n } ( i )  \frac { 1 } { E _ { i } T _ { i } } } \end{array}$ , w.p. 1. 

Proof: For each n, let $k \equiv k ( n )$ be such that ${ T _ { i } ^ { ( k ) } \leq n < T _ { i } ^ { ( k + 1 ) } }$ . Then, 

$$
N _ {T _ {i} ^ {(k)}} (j) \leq N _ {n} (j) \leq N _ {T _ {i} ^ {(k + 1)}} (j),
$$

i.e., 

$$
\sum_ {r = 0} ^ {k} \xi_ {r} \leq N _ {n} (j) \leq \sum_ {r = 0} ^ {k + 1} \xi_ {r},
$$

where $\xi _ { r } = \# \{ l : T _ { i } ^ { ( r ) } \leq l < T _ { i } ^ { ( r + 1 ) } , X _ { l } = j \}$ is the number of visits to $j$ during the rth excursion. Since $V _ { i j } \equiv E _ { i } \xi _ { 1 } \ : \le \ : E _ { i } T _ { i } < \infty$ , by the SLLN, with probability 1, 

$$
\frac {1}{k (n)} \sum_ {r = 0} ^ {k (n)} \xi_ {r} \rightarrow E _ {i} (\xi_ {1}) = V _ {i j}
$$

and $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { k } T _ { i } ^ { ( k ) }  E _ { i } ( T _ { i } ) } \end{array}$ . Note that since n is between $T _ { i } ^ { ( k ( n ) ) }$ and $T _ { i } ^ { ( k ( n ) + 1 ) }$ ， so $\frac { \ddot { n } } { k ( n ) }  E _ { i } T _ { i }$ . Since 

$$
\frac {k}{n} \frac {1}{k} \sum_ {r = 0} ^ {k} \xi_ {r} \leq \frac {N _ {n} (j)}{n} \leq \frac {k + 1}{n} \frac {1}{k + 1} \sum_ {r = 0} ^ {k + 1} \xi_ {r},
$$

it follows that $\begin{array} { r } { L _ { n } ( j ) = \frac { n } { n + 1 } \frac { N _ { n } ( j ) } { n } \to \frac { E _ { i } ( \xi _ { 1 } ) } { E _ { i } ( T _ { i } ) } } \end{array}$ 

Note that the above proof works for any initial distribution $\mu$ such that $P _ { \mu } ( T _ { i } < \infty ) = 1$ and further, the limit of $L _ { n } ( j )$ is independent of any such $\mu .$ . Thus, if $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ is irreducible and one state i is positive recurrent, then for any initial distribution $\mu , P _ { \mu } ( T _ { i } < \infty ) = 1$ 

Note finally that the proof in Theorem 14.1.9 can be adapted to yield a criterion for transience, null recurrence, and positive recurrence of a state. Thus, the following holds. 

Corollary 14.1.10: Fix a state i. Then (i) $i$ is transient if $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } N _ { n } ( i )$ exists and is finite w.p. 1 for any initial distribution $i f f$ 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} E _ {i} N _ {n} (i) = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {\infty} p _ {i i} ^ {(k)} <   \infty .
$$

(ii) i is null recurrent $i f f \sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { \infty } p _ { i i } ^ { ( k ) } = \infty$ and 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} E _ {i} L _ {n} (i) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i i} ^ {(k)} = 0.
$$

(iii) i is positive recurrent $i f f$ 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} E _ {i} L _ {n} (i) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i i} ^ {(k)} > 0.
$$

(iv) Let $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ be irreducible and let one state i be positive recurrent. Then, for any j and any initial distribution $\mu _ { : }$ 

$$
L _ {n} (j) \to \frac {1}{E _ {j} T _ {j}} \in (0, \infty) w. p. 1.
$$

Thus, for the symmetric simple random walk on the integers 

$$
p _ {0 0} ^ {(2 k)} \sim \frac {c}{\sqrt {k}} \mathrm{as} k \rightarrow \infty , 0 <   c <   \infty
$$

and hence 

$$
\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} p _ {0 0} ^ {(n)} = \infty \quad a n d \quad \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {0 0} ^ {(k)} \to 0.
$$

Thus 0 is null recurrent. 

It is not dificult to show that if $j$ leads to $i ,$ i.e., if $f _ { j i } \equiv P _ { j } ( T _ { i } < \infty )$ is positive then the number $\xi _ { 1 }$ of visits to $j$ between consecutive visits to i has all moments (Problem 14.9). 

Using the SLLN, Theorem 14.1.9 can be extended as follows to cover both null and positive recurrent cases. 

Theorem 14.1.11: Let i be a recurrent state. Then, for any $j$ and any initial distribution $\mu$ such that $P _ { \mu } ( T _ { i } < \infty ) = 1$ ， 

$$
L _ {n} (j) \equiv \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} \delta_ {X _ {k} j} \rightarrow \pi_ {i j} \equiv \frac {V _ {i j}}{E _ {i} T _ {i}}, \quad w. p. 1\tag{1.11}
$$

as $n \to \infty$ where $V _ { i j } < \infty . \ ( I f E _ { i } T _ { i } = \infty$ , then $\pi _ { i j } = 0 ~ f o r ~ a l l ~ j . )$ 

Corollary 14.1.12: Let (S, P) be irreducible and let one state be recurrent. Then, for any $j$ and any initial distribution, 

$$
L _ {n} (j) \to c _ {j} \quad a s \quad n \to \infty , \quad w. p. 1,\tag{1.12}
$$

where $c _ { j } = 1 / E _ { j } T _ { j } i f E _ { j } T _ { j } < \infty$ and $c _ { j } = 0$ otherwise. 

## The Basic Ergodic Theorem

Taking expectation in Theorem 14.1.11 and using the bounded convergence theorem leads to 

Corollary 14.1.13: Let i be recurrent. Then, for any initial distribution $\mu$ with $P _ { \mu } ( T _ { i } < \infty ) = 1$ ， 

$$
E _ {\mu} (L _ {n} (j)) = \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} P _ {\mu} (X _ {k} = j) \rightarrow \frac {V _ {i j}}{E _ {i} (T _ {i})} := \pi_ {i j} \quad a s \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\tag{1.13}
$$

Theorem 14.1.14: Let i be positive recurrent. Let $\pi _ { j } : = \pi _ { i j }$ for $j \in$ S. Then $\{ \pi _ { j } \} _ { j \in \mathbb { S } }$ is a stationary distribution for P, i.e., $\textstyle \sum _ { j } \pi _ { j } = 1$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { l \in \mathbb { S } } \pi _ { l } p _ { l j } = \pi _ { j } } \end{array}$ , for all $j$ . 

Proof: 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} & = & \frac {1}{n + 1} \delta_ {i j} + \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} \\ & = & \frac {1}{n + 1} \delta_ {i j} + \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {l} p _ {i l} ^ {(k - 1)} p _ {l j} \\ & = & \frac {1}{(n + 1)} \delta_ {i j} + \sum_ {l} \left(\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i l} ^ {(k - 1)}\right) p _ {l j}. \end{array}
$$

Taking limit as n and using Fatou’s lemma yields 

$$
\pi_ {j} \geq \sum_ {l} \pi_ {l} p _ {l j}.\tag{1.14}
$$

If strict inequality were to hold for some $j _ { 0 }$ , then adding over $j$ would yield 

$$
\sum_ {j} \pi_ {j} > \sum_ {j} \sum_ {l} \pi_ {l} p _ {l j} = \sum_ {l} \pi_ {l} \left(\sum_ {j} p _ {l j}\right) = \sum_ {l} \pi_ {l}.
$$

Since $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j \in \mathbb { S } } V _ { i j } = E _ { i } T _ { i } , \sum _ { j } \pi _ { j } = 1 } \end{array}$ , so there cannot be a strict inequality in (1.14) for any $j .$ . ✷ 

Therefore, the following has been established. 

Theorem 14.1.15: Let i be a positive recurrent state. Let 

$$
\pi_ {j} := \frac {E _ {i} (\sum_ {k = 0} ^ {T _ {i} - 1} \delta_ {X _ {k} , j})}{E _ {i} (T _ {i})}.
$$

Then 

(i) $\{ \pi _ { j } \} _ { j \in \mathbb { S } }$ is a stationary distribution. 

(ii) For any j and any initial distribution µ with $P _ { \mu } ( T _ { i } < \infty ) = 1$ ， 

$$
(a) L _ {n} (j) \equiv \frac {1}{n + 1} \# \{k: X _ {k} = j, 0 \leq j \leq n \} \rightarrow \pi_ {j} w. p. 1 (P _ {\mu})
$$

$$
(b) \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} P _ {\mu} (X _ {k} = j) \rightarrow \pi_ {j}.
$$

In particular, $i f j = i$ , we have 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i i} ^ {(k)} \rightarrow \pi_ {i} = \frac {1}{E _ {i} (T _ {i})}.\tag{1.15}
$$

Now let i be a positive recurrent state and j be such that $i  j$ . Then $V _ { i j } > 0$ and by the solidarity property, $f _ { j i } = 1$ and $j$ is recurrent. Now taking $\mu = \delta _ { j }$ in (ii) above and using Corollary 14.1.13, leads to the conclusions that 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {j j} ^ {(k)} \rightarrow \pi_ {j} > 0\tag{1.16}
$$

and 

$$
\pi_ {j} = \frac {1}{E _ {j} T _ {j}}.\tag{1.17}
$$

Thus, j is positive recurrent. 

Now Theorem 14.1.15 leads to the basic ergodic theorem for Markov chains. 

Theorem 14.1.16: Let $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ be irreducible and let one state be positive recurrent. Then 

(i) all states are positive recurrent, 

(ii) $\pi \equiv \{ \pi _ { j } \equiv ( E _ { j } T _ { j } ) ^ { - 1 } : j \in \mathbb { S } \}$ is a stationary distribution for $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ 

(iii) for any initial distribution µ and any $j \in \mathbb S$ 

(a) ${ \frac { 1 } { n + 1 } } \sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { n } P _ { \mu } ( X _ { k } = j ) \to \pi _ { j } , \ i . e . , \pi$ is the unique limiting distribution (in the average sense) and hence the unique stationary distribution, 

$$
(b) L _ {n} (j) \equiv \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} \delta_ {X _ {k} j} \rightarrow \pi_ {j} w. p. 1 (P _ {\mu}).
$$

There is a converse to the above result. To develop this, note first that if $j$ is a transient state, then the total number $N _ { j }$ of visits to $j$ is finite w.p. 1 (for any initial distribution $\mu )$ and hence $L _ { n } ( j ) \to 0 \ \mathrm { w . p }$ . 1 and taking expectations, for any i 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} \rightarrow 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \rightarrow \infty .
$$

Now, suppose that $\pi \equiv \{ \pi _ { j } : j \in \mathbb { S } \}$ is a stationary distribution for $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ Then, for all $\begin{array} { r } { j , \pi _ { j } = \sum _ { i \in \mathbb { S } } \pi _ { i } p _ { i j } } \end{array}$ and hence 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \pi_ {j} & = & \sum_ {i \in \mathbb {S}, r \in \mathbb {S}} \sum_ {\pi_ {r} p _ {r i} p _ {i j}} \\ & = & \sum_ {r \in \mathbb {S}} \pi_ {r} p _ {r j} ^ {(2)} \end{array}
$$

and by induction, 

$$
\pi_ {j} = \sum_ {i \in \mathbb {S}} \pi_ {i} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} \quad \text { for   all } \quad k \geq 0
$$

implying 

$$
\pi_ {j} = \sum_ {i \in \mathbb {S}} \pi_ {i} \bigg (\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} \bigg).
$$

Now if $j$ is transient then for any i 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} \rightarrow 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \rightarrow \infty
$$

and so by the bounded convergence theorem 

$$
\pi_ {j} = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {i \in \mathbb {S}} \pi_ {i} \bigg (\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} \bigg) = \sum_ {i \in \mathbb {S}} \pi_ {i} \cdot 0 = 0.
$$

Thus, $\pi _ { j } > 0$ implies $j$ is recurrent. For $j$ recurrent, it follows from arguments similar to those used to establish Theorem 14.1.15 that 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} \rightarrow f _ {i j} \frac {1}{E _ {j} T _ {j}}.
$$

Thus, $\begin{array} { r } { \pi _ { j } ~ = ~ \left( \sum _ { i \in \mathbb { S } } \pi _ { i } f _ { i j } \right) \frac { 1 } { E _ { j } T _ { j } } } \end{array}$ . But $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i \in \mathbb { S } } \pi _ { i } f _ { i j } \ge \pi _ { j } f _ { j j } = \pi _ { j } > 0 . } \end{array}$ . So $E _ { j } T _ { j } < \infty , \mathrm { i . e . } , j$ is positive recurrent. Summarizing the above discussion leads to 

Proposition 14.1.17: Let $\pi \equiv \{ \pi _ { j } : j \in \mathbb { S } \}$ be a stationary distribution for (S, P). Then, $\pi _ { j } > 0$ implies that $j$ is positive recurrent. 

It is now possible to state a converse to Theorem 14.1.16. 

Theorem 14.1.18: Let $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ be irreducible and admit a stationary distribution $\pi \equiv \{ \pi _ { j } : j \in \mathbb { S } \}$ . Then, 

(i) all states are positive recurrent, 

(ii) $\begin{array} { r } { \pi \equiv \{ \pi _ { j } : \pi _ { j } = \frac { 1 } { E _ { j } T _ { j } } , j \in \mathbb { S } \} } \end{array}$ is the unique stationary distribution, 

(iii) for any initial distribution $\mu$ and for all $j \in \mathbb S$ 2 

$$
(a) \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} P _ {\mu} (X _ {k} = j) \rightarrow \pi_ {j},
$$

$$
(b) \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} \delta_ {X _ {k} j} \rightarrow \pi_ {j} w. p. 1 (P _ {\mu}).
$$

In summary, for an irreducible Markov chain $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ with a countable state space, a stationary distribution $\pi$ exists if all states are positive recurrent. In which case, $\pi$ is unique and for any initial distribution $\mu ,$ , the distribution at time $n$ converges to $\pi$ in the Cesaro sense (i.e., average) and the (LLN) law of large numbers holds. For the finite state space case, irreducibility sufices (Problem 14.6). 

If $h : \mathbb { S }  \mathbb { R }$ is a function such that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j \in \mathbb { S } } | h ( j ) | \pi _ { j } < \infty } \end{array}$ , then the LLN can be strengthened to 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} h (X _ {k}) \rightarrow \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} h (j) \pi_ {j} \text {   w.p.   } 1 (P _ {\mu})
$$

for any $\mu$ (Problem 14.10). In particular, if A is any subset of $\mathbb { S } ,$ then 

$$
L _ {n} (A) \equiv \frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} I _ {A} (X _ {k}) \rightarrow \pi (A) \equiv \sum_ {j \in A} \pi_ {j}
$$

w.p. 1 $( P _ { \mu } )$ for any $\mu .$ 

An important question that remains is whether the convergence of $P _ { \mu } ( X _ { n } \mid = j )$ to $\pi _ { j }$ can be strengthened from the average sense to full, i.e., from the convergence to $\pi _ { j }$ of $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { ( n + 1 ) } \sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { n } P _ { \mu } ( X _ { k } = j ) } \end{array}$ to the convergence to $\pi _ { j }$ of $P _ { \mu } ( X _ { n } = j )$ as $n \to \infty$ . For this, the additional hypothesis needed is aperiodicity. 

Definition 14.1.9: For any state i, the period $d _ { i }$ of the state i is the 

$$
g. c. d. \bigl \{n: n \geq 1, p _ {i i} ^ {(n)} > 0 \bigr \}.
$$

Further, i is called aperiodic if $d _ { i } = 1$ 

Example 14.1.8: Let $\mathbb { S } = \{ 0 , 1 , 2 \}$ and 

$$
P = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac {1}{2} & 0 & \frac {1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \right).
$$

Then $d _ { i } = 2$ for all i. 

Note that in this example, since (S, P) is finite and irreducible, it has a unique stationary distribution, given by $\pi = ( { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 4 } } } , { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } , { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 4 } } } )$ and 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {0 0} ^ {(k)} \rightarrow \frac {1}{4} \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \rightarrow \infty
$$

but $p _ { 0 0 } ^ { ( 2 n + 1 ) } = 0$ for each n and $p _ { 0 0 } ^ { ( 2 n ) } \to \frac { 1 } { 4 }$ as $n  \infty$ . This suggests that aperiodicity will be needed. It turns out that if $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ is irreducible, the period $d _ { i }$ is the same for all i (Problem 14.5). 

Theorem 14.1.19: Let (S, P ) be irreducible, positive recurrent and aperiodic $( i . e . , d _ { i } = 1$ for all i). Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be $a \ ( \mathbb { S } , P )$ Markov chain. Then, for any initial distribution µ, $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } P _ { \mu } ( X _ { n } = i ) \equiv \pi _ { i } } \end{array}$ exists for all $i ,$ where $\pi \equiv \{ \pi _ { j } : j \in \mathbb { S } \}$ is the unique stationary distribution. 

There are many proofs known for this, and two of them are outlined below. The first uses the discrete renewal theorem and the second uses a coupling argument. 

Proof 1: (via the discrete renewal theorem). Fix a state i. Recall that for $n \geq 1 , p _ { i i } ^ { ( n ) } = P ( X _ { n } = i \mid X _ { 0 } = i ) , n \geq 0$ and $f _ { i i } ^ { ( n ) } = P ( T _ { i } = n \mid X _ { 0 } = i )$ 2 $n \geq 1$ . Using the Markov property, for $n \geq 1$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} p _ {i i} ^ {(n)} = P (X _ {n} = i \mid X _ {0} = i) & = & \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} P (X _ {n} = i, T _ {i} = k \mid X _ {0} = i) \\ & = & \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} P (T _ {i} = k \mid X _ {0} = i) P (X _ {n} = i \mid X _ {k} = i) \\ & = & \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} f _ {i i} ^ {(k)} p _ {i i} ^ {(n - k)}. \end{array}
$$

Let $a _ { n } \equiv p _ { i i } ^ { ( n ) } , n \ge 0 , p _ { n } \equiv f _ { i i } ^ { ( n ) } , n \ge 1$ . Then $\{ p _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ is a probability distribution and $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ satisfies the discrete renewal equation 

$$
a _ {n} = b _ {n} + \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} a _ {n - k} p _ {k}, n \geq 0
$$

where $b _ { n } = \delta _ { n 0 }$ and $p _ { 0 } = 0$ . It can be shown that $d _ { i } = 1$ if 

$$
g. c. d. \left\{k: k \geq 1, p _ {k} > 0 \right\} = 1.
$$

Further, $\begin{array} { r } { E _ { i } T _ { i } = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } k p _ { k } < \infty } \end{array}$ , by the assumption of positive recurrence. Now it follows from the discrete renewal theorem (see Section 8.5) that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} a _ {n} \text {exists and equals} \frac {\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} b _ {j}}{\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} k p _ {k}} = \frac {1}{E _ {i} T _ {i}} = \pi_ {i}.
$$

Proof 2: (Using coupling arguments). Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ and $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be independent $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ Markov chains such that $Y _ { 0 }$ has distribution π and $X _ { 0 }$ has distribution $\mu .$ Then $\{ Z _ { n } = ( X _ { n } , Y _ { n } ) \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a Markov chain with state space $\mathbb { S } \times \mathbb { S }$ and transition probability $P \times P \equiv \left( ( p _ { ( i , j ) , ( k , \ell ) } = p _ { i k } p _ { j \ell } ) \right)$ Further, it can be shown that (see Hoel, Port and Stone (1972)) 

(a) $\{ \pi _ { i , j } \equiv \pi _ { i } \pi _ { j } : ( i , j ) \in \mathbb { S } \times \mathbb { S } \}$ is a stationary distribution for $\{ Z _ { n } \}$ ， 

(b) since $( \mathbb { S } , P )$ is irreducible and aperiodic, the pair $( \mathbb { S } \times \mathbb { S } , P \times P )$ is irreducible. 

Since $( \mathbb { S } \times \mathbb { S } , P \times P )$ is irreducible and admits a stationary distribution, it is necessarily recurrent and so from any initial distribution the first passage time $T _ { D }$ for the diagonal $D \equiv \{ ( i , i ) : i \in \mathbb { S } \}$ is finite with probability one. Thus, $T _ { c } \equiv \operatorname* { m i n } \{ n : n \geq 1 , X _ { n } = Y _ { n } \}$ is finite w.p. 1. The random variable $T _ { c }$ is called the coupling time. Let 

$$
\tilde {X} _ {n} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} X _ {n} & , n \leq T _ {c} \\ Y _ {n} & , n > T _ {c}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then, it can be verified that $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ and $\{ { \tilde { X } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ are identically distributed Markov chains. Thus 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P (X _ {n} = j) & = & P (\tilde {X} _ {n} = j) \\ & = & P (\tilde {X} _ {n} = j, T _ {c} <   n) + P (\tilde {X} _ {n} = j, T _ {c} \geq n) \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
P (Y _ {n} = j) = P (Y _ {n} = j, T _ {c} <   n) + P (Y _ {n} = j, T _ {c} \geq n)
$$

implying that 

$$
\left| P (X _ {n} = j) - P (Y _ {n} = j) \right| \leq 2 P (T _ {c} \geq n).
$$

Since $P ( T _ { c } \geq n )  0$ as $n \to \infty$ and by the stationarity of π, $P ( Y _ { n } = j ) =$ $\pi _ { j }$ for all n and $j$ it follows that for any $j$ 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} P (X _ {n} = j) \quad \text { exists   and } \quad = \pi_ {j}.
$$

In order to obtain results on rates of convergence for $| P ( X _ { n } = j ) - \pi _ { j } |$ 2 one needs more assumptions on the distribution of return time $T _ { i }$ or the coupling time $T _ { c }$ . For results on this, the books of Hoel et al. (1972), Meyn and Tweedie (1993), and Lindvall (1992) are good sources. It can be shown that in the irreducible case if for some i, $P _ { i } ( T _ { i } > n ) = O ( \lambda _ { 1 } ^ { n } )$ for some $0 < \lambda _ { 1 } < 1$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j \in \mathbb { S } } | P _ { i } ( X _ { n } = j ) - \pi _ { j } | = O ( \lambda _ { 2 } ^ { n } ) } \end{array}$ for some $\lambda _ { 1 } < \lambda _ { 2 } < 1$ In particular, this geometric convergence holds for the finite state space irreducible case. 

The main results of this section are summarized below. 

Theorem 14.1.20: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be a Markov chain with a countable state space $\mathbb { S } = \{ 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots , K \} , K \leq \infty$ and transition probability matrix $P \equiv \left( ( p _ { i j } ) \right)$ . Let (S, P) be irreducible. Then, 

(a) All states are recurrent if for some i in S, 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} p _ {i i} ^ {(n)} = \infty .
$$

(b) All states are positive recurrent $i f f$ for some i in $\mathbb { S } _ { : }$ , 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i i} ^ {(k)} \quad e x i s t s a n d i s s t r i c t l y p o s i t i v e.
$$

(c) There exists a stationary probability distribution π if there exists a positive recurrent state. 

(d) If there exists a stationary distribution $\pi \equiv \{ \pi _ { j } : j \in \mathbb { S } \}$ , then 

(i) it is unique, all states are positive recurrent and for all $j \in \mathbb S$ 2 $\pi _ { j } = ( E _ { j } T _ { j } ) ^ { - 1 }$ 2 

(ii) for all $i , j \in \mathbb { S }$ 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {(k)} \rightarrow \pi_ {j} \quad a s \quad n \rightarrow \infty ,
$$

(iii) for any initial distribution and any $j \in \mathbb S$ 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} \delta_ {X _ {k} j} \rightarrow \pi_ {j} w. p. 1,
$$

(iv) $\begin{array} { r } { i f \sum _ { j \in \mathbb { S } } | h ( j ) | \pi _ { j } < \infty } \end{array}$ , then 

$$
\frac {1}{n + 1} \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} h (X _ {k}) \rightarrow \sum_ {j \in \mathbb {S}} h (j) \pi_ {j} \quad w. p. 1,
$$

(v) $i f ,$ in addition, $d _ { i } = 1$ for some $i \in \mathbb { S }$ , then $d _ { j } = 1$ for all $j \in \mathbb S$ and for all $i , j$ 

$$
p _ {i j} ^ {(n)} \to \pi_ {j} \quad a s \quad n \to \infty .
$$

## 14.2 Markov chains on a general state space

## 14.2.1 Basic definitions

Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be a sequence of random variables with values in some space S that is not necessarily finite or countable. The Markov property says that conditioned on $X _ { n } , X _ { n - 1 } , \ldots , X _ { 0 }$ , the distribution of $X _ { n + 1 }$ depends only on $X _ { n }$ and not on the past, i.e., $X _ { j } : j \leq n - 1$ . When S is not countable, to make this notion of Markov property precise, one needs the following set up. 

Let (S, ) be a measurable space. Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ be a probability space and $\{ X _ { n } ( \omega ) \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be a sequence of maps from Ω to $\mathbb { S }$ such that for each $n , X _ { n }$ is $( \mathcal { F } , \mathbb { S } )$ measurable. Let $\mathcal { F } _ { n } \equiv \sigma \langle \{ X _ { j } : 0 \leq j \leq n \} \rangle$ be the sub-σ-algebra of $\mathcal { F }$ generated by $\{ X _ { j } : 0 \leq j \leq n \}$ . In what follows, for any sub-σ-algebra $\mathcal { V }$ of $\mathcal { F }$ , let $P ( \cdot \mid \mathcal { V } )$ denote the conditional probability given, as defined in Chapter 12. 

Definition 14.2.1: The sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a Markov chain if for all $A \in S$ 2 

$$
P \big ((X _ {n + 1} \in A) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n} \big) = P \big ((X _ {n + 1} \in A) \mid \sigma \langle X _ {n} \rangle \big) \quad \text { w   .   p   . } 1, \text { for   all } n \geq 0,\tag{2.1}
$$

for any initial distribution of $X _ { 0 }$ , where $\sigma \langle X _ { n } \rangle$ is the sub-σ-algebra of $\mathcal { F }$ generated by $X _ { n }$ 

It is easy to verify that (2.1) holds for all $A \in S$ if for any bounded measurable h from (S, ) to R, (R) , 

$$
E \big (h (X _ {n + 1}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n} \big) = E \big (h (X _ {n + 1}) \mid \sigma \langle X _ {n} \rangle \big) \quad \text { w   .   p   . } 1 \text { f   o   r   a   l   l } n \geq 0\tag{2.2}
$$

for any initial distribution of $X _ { 0 }$ 

Another equivalent formulation that makes the Markov property symmetric with respect to time is the following that says that given the present, the past and future are independent. 

Proposition 14.2.1: A sequence of random variables $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ satisfies (2.1) if for any $\{ A _ { j } \} _ { 0 } ^ { n + k } \subset { \mathcal { S } }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \big (X _ {j} \in A _ {j}, j = 0, 1, 2, \ldots , n - 1, n + 1, \ldots , n + k \mid \sigma \langle X _ {n} \rangle \big) \\ & = P \big (X _ {j} \in A _ {j}, j = 0, 1, 2, \ldots , n - 1 \mid \sigma \langle X _ {n} \rangle \big) \times \\ & \qquad P \big (X _ {j} \in A _ {j}, j = n + 1, \ldots , n + k \mid \sigma \langle X _ {n} \rangle \big) \end{array}
$$

w.p. 1. 

The proof is somewhat involved but not dificult. The countable state space case is easier (Problem 14.1). 

An important tool for studying Markov chains is the notion of a transition probability function. 

Definition 14.2.2: A function $P : \mathbb { S } \times \mathcal { S }  [ 0 , 1 ]$ is called a transition probability function on S if 

(i) for all x in $\mathbb { S } , P ( x , \cdot )$ is a probability measure on (S, ), 

(ii) for all $A \in { \mathcal { S } } , P ( \cdot , A )$ is an -measurable function from $( \mathbb { S } , S ) \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ 

Under some general conditions guaranteeing the existence of regular conditional probabilities, the right side of (2.1) can be expressed as $P _ { n } ( X _ { n } , A )$ 2 where $P _ { n } ( \cdot , \cdot )$ is a transition probability function on S. In such a case, yet another formulation of Markov property is in terms of the joint distributions of $\{ X _ { 0 } , X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } \}$ for any finite n. 

Proposition 14.2.2: A sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ satisfies $( 2 . 1 )$ if for any $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and $A _ { 0 } , A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { n } \in { \mathcal { S } }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P (X _ {j} \in A _ {j}, j = 0, 1, 2, \ldots , n) \\ = \int_ {A _ {0}} \int_ {A _ {n - 2}} \int_ {A _ {n - 1}} P _ {n - 1} (x _ {n - 1}, A _ {n}) P _ {n - 2} (x _ {n - 2}, d x _ {n - 1}) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \dots P _ {1} (x _ {0}, d x _ {1}) \mu_ {0} (d x _ {0}), \end{array}
$$

where $\mu _ { 0 } ( A ) = P ( x _ { 0 } \in A ) , A \in { \mathcal { S } }$ 

The proof is by induction and left as an exercise (Problem 14.16). In what follows, it will be assumed that such transition functions exist. 

Definition 14.2.3: A sequence of S-valued random variables $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is called a Markov chain with transition function $P ( \cdot , \cdot )$ if (2.1) holds and the right side equals $P ( X _ { n } , A )$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

## 14.2.2 Examples

Example 14.2.1: (IID sequence). Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be iid S-valued random variables with distribution $\mu$ . Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a Markov chain with transition function $P ( x , A ) \equiv \mu ( A )$ and initial distribution $\mu .$ 

Example 14.2.2: $( ( A d d i t i v e )$ random walk in $\mathbb { R } ^ { k } )$ . Let $\{ \eta _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ be iid $\mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ -valued random variables with distribution ν. Let $X _ { 0 }$ be an $\mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ -valued random variable independent of $\{ \eta _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ and with distribution $\mu .$ . Let 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = X _ {n} + \eta_ {n + 1}
$$

$$
= X _ {0} + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n + 1} \eta_ {j}, n \geq 0.
$$

Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a $\mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ -valued Markov chain with transition function $P ( x , A ) \equiv \nu ( \bar { A } - x )$ and initial distribution $\mu .$ 

Example 14.2.3: (Multiplicative random walk on $\mathbb { R } ^ { + } )$ ). Let $\{ \eta _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be iid nonnegative random variables with distribution $\nu$ and $X _ { 0 }$ be a nonnegative random variable with distribution $\mu$ and independent of $\{ \eta _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ . Let $X _ { n + 1 } = X _ { n } \eta _ { n + 1 } , n \geq 0$ . Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a Markov chain with state space $\mathbb { R } ^ { + }$ and transition function 

$$
P (x, A) = \nu (x ^ {- 1} A) \text {if} x > 0 \text {and} I _ {A} (0) \text {if} x = 0
$$

and initial distribution $\mu .$ 

This is a model for the value of a stock portfolio subject to random growth rates. Clearly, the above iteration scheme leads to $\begin{array} { r } { X _ { n } = X _ { 0 } \cdot \prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \eta _ { i } } \end{array}$ which when normalized appropriately leads to what is known as the geometric Brownian notion model in financial mathematics literature. 

Example 14.2.4: $( A R ( { \cal 1 } )$ time series). Let $\rho \in \mathbb R$ and $\nu$ be a probability measure on $( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) )$ . Let $\{ \eta _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ be iid with distribution $\nu$ and $X _ { 0 }$ be a random variable independent of $\{ \eta _ { j } \} _ { j \ge 1 }$ and with distribution $\mu$ . Let 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = \rho X _ {n} + \eta_ {n + 1}, n \geq 0.
$$

Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a R-valued Markov chain with transition function $P ( x , A ) \equiv \nu ( A - \rho x )$ and initial distribution $\mu .$ 

Example 14.2.5: (Random $A R ( { \boldsymbol { 1 } } )$ vector time series). Let $\{ ( A _ { i } , b _ { i } ) \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ be iid such that $A _ { i }$ is a k $\times \ k$ matrix and $b _ { i }$ is a $k \times 1$ vector. Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\left( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , B ( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } ) \right)$ . Let $X _ { 0 }$ be $\mathbf { a } \ \mathbb { R } ^ { k } .$ -valued random variable independent of $( A _ { i } , b _ { i } ) _ { i \geq 1 }$ and with distribution $\mu$ . Let 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = A _ {n + 1} X _ {n} + b _ {n + 1}, n \geq 0.
$$

Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a $\mathbb { R } ^ { k } .$ -valued Markov chain with transition function $P ( x , B ) \equiv P ( \overline { { A } } _ { 1 } x + b _ { 1 } \in B )$ and initial distribution $\mu$ 

Example 14.2.6: (Waiting time chain). Let $\{ \eta _ { i } \} _ { i \ge 1 }$ be iid real valued random variable with distribution $\nu$ and $X _ { 0 }$ be independent of $\{ \eta _ { i } \} _ { i \ge 1 }$ with distribution $\mu .$ . Let 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = \max \left\{X _ {n} + \eta_ {n + 1}, 0 \right\}.
$$

Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a nonnegative valued Markov chain with transition function $P ( x , A ) { \overset { - } { \equiv } } P { \big ( } \operatorname* { m a x } \{ x + \eta _ { 1 } , 0 \} \in A { \big ) }$ and initial distribution $\mu .$ In the queuing theory context, if $\eta _ { n }$ represents the diference between the nth interarrival time and service time, then $X _ { n }$ represents the waiting time at the nth arrival. 

All the above are special cases of the following: 

Example 14.2.7: (Iterated function system $( I F S ) )$ . Let $( \mathbb { S } , S )$ be a measurable space. Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ be a probability space. Let $\{ f _ { i } ( x , \omega ) \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ be such that for each i, $, \ f _ { i } : \mathbb { S } \times \Omega \to \mathbb { S } { \mathrm { ~ i s ~ } } ( { \mathcal { S } } \times { \mathcal { F } } , { \mathcal { S } } )$ -measurable and the stochastic processes $\{ f _ { i } ( \cdot , \omega ) \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ are iid. Let $X _ { 0 }$ be a S-valued random variable on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ with distribution $\mu$ and independent of $\{ f _ { i } ( \cdot , \cdot ) \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ Let 

$$
X _ {n + 1} (\omega) = f _ {n + 1} (X _ {n} (\omega), \omega), n \geq 0.
$$

Then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is an S-valued Markov chain with transition function $P ( x , A ) \equiv P ( \overline { { f } } _ { 1 } ( x , \omega ) \in A )$ and initial distribution $\mu .$ 

It turns out that when S is a Polish space with $s$ as the Borel $\sigma -$ algebra and $P ( \cdot , \cdot )$ is a transition function on S, any S-valued Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ with transition function $P ( \cdot , \cdot )$ can be generated by an IFS as in Example 14.2.7. For a proof, see Kifer (1988) and Athreya and Stenflo (2003). When $\{ f _ { i } \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ are iid such that $f _ { 1 }$ has only finite many choices $\{ h _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { k }$ , where each $h _ { j }$ is an afine contraction on $\mathbb { R } ^ { p }$ , then the Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \}$ converges in distribution to some $\pi ( \cdot )$ . Further, the limit point set of $\{ X _ { n } \}$ coincides w.p. 1 with the support M of the limit distribution $\pi ( \cdot )$ . This has been exploited by Barnsley and others to solve the inverse problem: given a compact set M in $\mathbb { R } ^ { p }$ , find an IFS $\{ h _ { j } \} _ { j = 1 } ^ { k }$ , of afine contractions so that by generating the Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \}$ , one can get an approximate picture of M. This is called data compression or image generation by Markov chain Monte Carlo. See Barnsley (1992) for details on this. More generally, when $\{ f _ { i } \}$ are Lipschitz maps, the following holds. 

Theorem 14.2.3: Let $\{ f _ { i } ( \cdot , \cdot ) \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ be iid Lipschitz maps on S. Assume 

(i) $E | \log s ( f _ { 1 } ) | < \infty$ and E log $\begin{array} { r l r } { s ( f _ { 1 } ) } & { { } < } & { 0 } \end{array}$ , where $\begin{array} { r l } { s ( f _ { 1 } ) } & { { } = } \end{array}$ $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { x \neq y } \frac { d \big ( f _ { 1 } ( x , \omega ) , f _ { 1 } ( y , \omega ) \big ) } { d ( x , y ) }$ and $d ( \cdot , \cdot )$ is the metric on $\mathbb { S }$ , and 

(ii) for some $x _ { 0 } , E \big ( \log d ( f _ { 1 } ( x _ { 0 } , \omega ) , x _ { 0 } ) \big ) ^ { + } < \infty$ 

Then, 

(i) $\hat { X } _ { n } ( x , \omega ) \equiv f _ { 1 } \big ( f _ { 2 } ( . . . f _ { n - 1 } ( f _ { n } ( x , \omega ) , \omega ) ) \ldots )$ converges w.p. 1 to a random variable $\hat { X } ( \omega )$ that is independent of x, 

(ii) for all x, $X _ { n } ( x , \omega ) \equiv f _ { n } \big ( f _ { n - 1 } \ldots ( f _ { 1 } ( x , \omega ) , \omega ) \ldots )$ converges in distribution to $\hat { X } ( \omega )$ 

That (ii) is a consequence of (i) is clear since for each $n , x , X _ { n } ( x , \omega )$ and $\hat { X } _ { n } ( x , \omega )$ are identically distributed. 

The proof of (i) involves showing that $\{ \hat { X } _ { n } \}$ is a Cauchy sequence in S w.p. 1 (Problem 14.17). 

## 14.2.3 Chapman-Kolmogorov equations

Let $P ( \cdot , \cdot )$ be a transition function on (S, ). For each $n \geq 0$ , define a sequence of functions $\{ P ^ { ( n ) } ( \cdot , \cdot ) \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ by the iteration scheme 

$$
P ^ {(n + 1)} (x, A) = \int_ {\mathbb {S}} P ^ {(n)} (y, A) P (x, d y), n \geq 0,\tag{2.3}
$$

where $P ^ { ( 0 ) } ( x , A ) \equiv I _ { A } ( x )$ . It can be verified by induction that for each $n ,$ $P ^ { ( n ) } ( \cdot , \cdot )$ is a transition probability function. 

Definition 14.2.4: $P ^ { ( n ) } ( \cdot , \cdot )$ defined by (2.3) is called the n-step transition function generated by $P ( \cdot , \cdot )$ 

It is easy to show by induction that if $X _ { 0 } = x { \mathrm { ~ w . p . ~ 1 ~ } }$ , then 

$$
P (X _ {n} \in A) = P ^ {(n)} (x, A) \quad \text { for   all } \quad n \geq 0\tag{2.4}
$$

(Problem 14.18). This leads to the Chapman-Kolmogorov equations. 

Proposition 14.2.4: Let $P ( \cdot , \cdot )$ be a transition probability function on (S, ) and let $P ^ { ( n ) } ( \cdot , \cdot )$ be defined by (2.3). Then for any n, $m \geq 0$ 

$$
P ^ {(n + m)} (x, A) = \int P ^ {(n)} (y, A) P ^ {(m)} (x, d y).\tag{2.5}
$$

Proof: The analytic verification is straightforward by induction. One can verify this probabilistically using the Markov property. Indeed, from (2.4) the left side of (2.5) is 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P _ {x} (X _ {n + m} \in A) & = & E _ {x} \big (P (X _ {n + m} \in A \mid \mathcal {F} _ {m}) \big) \\ & = & E _ {x} \big (P ^ {(n)} (X _ {m}, A) \big) \quad \text {(by Markov property)} \\ & = & \text {right - hand side of (2.5),} \end{array}
$$

where $E _ { x } , P _ { x }$ denote expectation and probability distribution of $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ when $X _ { 0 } = x ~ \mathrm { w . p }$ . 1. ✷ 

From the above, one sees that the study of the limit behavior of the distribution of $X _ { n }$ as $n \to \infty$ can be reduced analytically to the study of the n-step transition probabilities. This in turn can be done in terms of the operator P on the Banach space $B ( \mathbb { S } , \mathbb { R } )$ of bounded measurable real valued functions from S to R (with sup norm), defined by 

$$
(\boldsymbol {P} h) (x) \equiv E _ {x} h (X _ {1}) \equiv \int h (y) P (x, d y).\tag{2.6}
$$

It is easy to verify that P is a positive bounded linear operator on $B ( \mathbb { S } , \mathbb { R } )$ of norm one. The Chapman-Kolmogorov equation (2.4) is equivalent to saying that $E _ { x } h ( X _ { n } ) = ( P ^ { n } h ) ( x )$ . Thus, analytically the study of the limit distribution of $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ can be reduced to that of the sequence $\{ P ^ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ of the operator P . However, probabilistic approaches via the notion of Harris irreducibility and recurrence when applicable and via the notion of Feller continuity when S is a Polish space are more fruitful and will be developed below. 

## 14.2.4 Harris irreducibility, recurrence, and minorization

## 14.2.4.1 Definition of irreducibility

Recall that a Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ with a discrete state space S and transition probability matrix $P \equiv ( ( p _ { i j } ) )$ is irreducible if for every $i , j$ in S, i leads to j, i.e., 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P (X _ {n} = j \quad \text { for   some } \quad n \geq 1 \mid X _ {0} = i) \\ \equiv P _ {i} (T _ {j} <   \infty) \equiv f _ {i j} > 0, \end{array}
$$

where $T _ { j } = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ n : n \geq 1 , X _ { n } = j \}$ is the time of first visit to $j .$ 

To generalize this to the case of general state spaces, one starts with the notion of first entrance time or hitting time (also called the first passage time). 

Definition 14.2.5: For any $A \in S$ , the first entrance time to A is defined as 

$$
T _ {A} \equiv \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \min \{n: n \geq 1, X _ {n} \in A \} \\ \infty \quad \text { if } \quad X _ {n} \not \in A \quad \text { for   any } \quad n \geq 1. \end{array} \right.
$$

Since the event $\{ T _ { A } = 1 \} = \{ X _ { 1 } \in A \}$ and for $k \ge 2 , \{ T _ { A } = k \} = \{ X _ { 1 } \notin$ $A , X _ { 2 } \not \in A , \ldots , X _ { k - 1 } \not \in A , X _ { k } \in A \}$ is an element of $\mathcal { F } _ { k } = \sigma \langle \{ X _ { j } : j \leq k \} \rangle$ $T _ { A }$ is a stopping time w.r.t. the filtration $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ (cf. Chapter 13). 

Definition 14.2.6: Let φ be a nonzero σ-finite measure on (S, ). The Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ (or equivalently, its transition function $P ( \cdot , \cdot ) )$ is said to be φ-irreducible (or irreducible in the sense of Harris with reference measure φ) if for any A in , 

$$
\phi (A) > 0 \Rightarrow L (x, A) \equiv P _ {x} (T _ {A} <   \infty) > 0\tag{2.7}
$$

for all x in S. This says that if a set A in  is considered important by the measure $\phi \ ( \mathrm { i . e . , } \ \phi ( A ) > 0 )$ , then so does the chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ starting from any $x$ in S. If $\begin{array} { r } { G ( x , A ) \equiv \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } P ^ { n } ( x , A ) } \end{array}$ is the Greens function associated with $P _ { \mathrm { : } }$ then (2.7) is equivalent to 

$$
\phi (A) > 0 \Rightarrow G (x, A) > 0 \quad \text { for   all } \quad x \in \mathbb {S},\tag{2.8}
$$

i.e., $\phi ( \cdot )$ is dominated by $G ( x , \cdot )$ for all x in $\mathbb { S } .$ . 

## 14.2.4.2 Examples

Example 14.2.7: If S is countable and $\phi$ is the counting measure on $\mathbb { S } .$ then the irreducibili $\mathrm { t y }$ of a Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ with state space $\mathbb { S }$ is the same as φ-irreducibility. 

Example 14.2.8: If $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ are iid with distribution $\nu ,$ then it is $\nu -$ irreducible. 

Example 14.2.9: It can be verified that the random walk with jump distribution $\nu$ (Example 14.2.2) is φ-irreducible with the Lebesgue measure as $\phi$ if $\nu$ has a nonzero absolutely continuous component with a positive density on some open interval (Problem 14.19 (a)). 

Example 14.2.10: The $\operatorname { A R } ( 1 )$ with $\eta _ { 1 }$ having a nontrivial absolutely continuous component can be shown to be φ-irreducible for some $\phi .$ On the other hand the AR(1) chain 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = \frac {X _ {n}}{2} + \frac {1}{2} \eta_ {n}, n \geq 0,
$$

where $\{ \eta _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ are iid Bernoulli $\left( { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \right)$ random variables, is not φ-irreducible for any $\phi .$ . In general, if $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is a Markov chain that has a discrete distribution for each $n$ and has a limit distribution that is nonatomic, then $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ cannot be φ-irreducible for any $\phi$ (Problem 14.19 (b)). 

The waiting time chain (Example 14.2.6) is irreducible w.r.t. $\phi \equiv \delta _ { 0 }$ , the delta measure at 0 if $P ( \eta _ { 1 } < 0 ) > 0$ (Problem 14.20). 

It can be shown that if $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is φ-irreducible for some σ-finite $\phi .$ , then there exists a probability measure ψ such that $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is ψ-irreducible and it is maximal in the sense that if $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is $\tilde { \phi } -$ irreducible for some $\tilde { \phi } ,$ , then $\tilde { \phi }$ is dominated by $\psi$ . See Nummelin (1984). 

## 14.2.4.3 Harris recurrence

A Markov chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ that is Harris irreducible with reference measure $\phi$ is said to be Harris recurrent if 

$$
A \in \mathcal {S}, \phi (A) > 0 \Rightarrow P _ {x} (T _ {A} <   \infty) = 1 \quad \text { for   all } \quad x \quad \text { in } \quad \mathbb {S}.\tag{2.9}
$$

Recall that irreducibility requires only that $P _ { x } ( T _ { A } < \infty )$ be $> 0$ 

When S is countable and $\phi$ is the counting measure, this reduces to the usual notion of irreducibility and recurrence. If S is not countable but has a singleton $\Delta$ such that $P _ { x } ( T _ { \Delta } < \infty ) = 1$ for all $x$ in $\mathbb { S } _ { i }$ , then the chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ is Harris recurrent with respect to the measure $\begin{array} { r } { \phi ( \cdot ) \equiv \delta _ { \Delta } ( \cdot ) } \end{array}$ , the delta measure at $\Delta$ . The waiting time chain (Example 14.2.6) has such a $\Delta$ in 0 if $E \eta _ { 1 } < 0$ (Problem 14.20). If such a recurrent singleton $\Delta$ exists, then the sample paths of $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ can be broken into iid excursions by looking at the chain between consecutive returns to $\Delta$ . This in turn will allow a complete extension of the basic limit theory from the countable case to this special case. In general, such a singleton may not exist. For example, for the $\operatorname { A R } ( 1 )$ sequence with $\{ \eta _ { i } \} _ { i \ge 1 }$ having a continuous distribution, $P _ { x } ( X _ { n } = x$ for some $n \ \geq \ 1 ) \ = \ 0$ for all x. However, it turns out that for Harris recurrent chains, such a singleton can be constructed via the regeneration theorem below established independently by Athreya and Ney (1978) and Nummelin (1978). 

## 14.2.5 The minorization theorem

A remarkable result of the subject is that when is countably generated, a Harris recurrent chain can be embedded in a chain that has a recurrent singleton. This is achieved via the minorization theorem and the fundamental regeneration theorem below. 

Theorem 14.2.5: (The minorization theorem). Let (S, ) be such that $s$ is countably generated. Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be a Markov chain with state space (S, ) and transition function $P ( \cdot , \cdot )$ such that it is Harris irreducible with reference measure $\phi ( \cdot )$ . Then the following minorization hypothesis holds. 

(i) (Hypothesis M). For every $B _ { 0 } \in { \cal S }$ such that $\phi ( B _ { 0 } ) > 0$ , there exists a set $A _ { 0 } ~ \subset ~ B _ { 0 }$ , an integer $n _ { 0 } \geq 1$ , a constant $0 \textless \alpha \textless 1$ , and a probability measure ν on $( \mathbb { S } , S )$ such that $\phi ( A _ { 0 } ) > 0$ and for all x in $A _ { 0 }$ 2 

$$
P ^ {n _ {0}} (x, A) \geq \alpha \nu (A) \quad f o r a l l \quad A \in \mathcal {S}.
$$

(ii) (The C-set lemma). For any set $B _ { 0 } \in { \cal S }$ such that $\phi ( B _ { 0 } ) > 0$ , there exists a set $A _ { 0 } \subset B _ { 0 }$ , an $n _ { 0 } \geq 1$ , a constant $0 < \alpha ^ { \prime } < 1$ such that for x, y in $A _ { 0 }$ ， 

$$
p ^ {n _ {0}} (x, y) \geq \alpha^ {\prime},
$$

where $p ^ { n _ { 0 } } ( x , \cdot )$ is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the absolutely continuous component of 

$$
P ^ {n _ {0}} (x, \cdot) \quad w. r. t. \quad \phi (\cdot).
$$

The proof of the C-set lemma is a nice application of the martingale convergence theorem (see Orey (1971)). The proof of Theorem 14.2.5 (i) using the C-set lemma is easy and is left as an exercise (Problem 14.21). 

## 14.2.6 The fundamental regeneration theorem

Theorem 14.2.6: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be a Markov chain with state space $( \mathbb { S } , S )$ and transition function $P ( \cdot , \cdot )$ . Suppose there exists a set $A _ { 0 } \in { \mathcal { S } }$ , a constant $0 < \alpha < 1$ , a probability measure $\nu ( \cdot )$ on $( \mathbb { S } , S )$ such that for all x in $A _ { 0 }$ 

$$
P (x, A) \geq \alpha \nu (A) \quad f o r a l l \quad A \in \mathcal {S}.\tag{2.10}
$$

Suppose, in addition, that for all x in $s$ , 

$$
P _ {x} (T _ {A _ {0}} <   \infty) = 1.\tag{2.11}
$$

Then, for any initial distribution $\mu ,$ there exists a sequence of random times $\{ T _ { i } \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ such that under $P _ { \mu }$ , the sequence of excursions $\eta _ { j } \equiv \{ X _ { T _ { j } + r } , 0 \le$ $r < T _ { j + 1 } - T _ { j } , T _ { j + 1 } - T _ { j } \} , j = 1 , 2 , . .$ . are iid with $X _ { T _ { j } } \sim \nu ( \cdot )$ 

Proof: For x in $A _ { 0 }$ , let 

$$
Q (x, \cdot) = \frac {P (x , \cdot) - \alpha \nu (\cdot)}{(1 - \alpha)}.\tag{2.12}
$$

Then, (2.10) implies that for x in $A _ { 0 } , Q ( x , \cdot )$ is a probability measure on $( \mathbb { S } , S )$ . For each x in $A _ { 0 }$ and $n \geq 0$ , let $\eta _ { n + 1 } , \delta _ { n + 1 }$ and $Y _ { n + 1 , x }$ be independent random variables such that $P ( \eta _ { n + 1 } \in \cdot ) = \nu ( \cdot ) , \delta _ { n + 1 }$ is Bernoulli $( \alpha )$ , and $P ( Y _ { n + 1 , x } \in \cdot ) = Q ( x , \cdot )$ . Then given $X _ { n } = x$ in $A _ { 0 } , X _ { n + 1 }$ can be chosen to be 

$$
X _ {n + 1} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \eta_ {n + 1} & \text {if} \quad \delta_ {n + 1} = 1 \\ Y _ {n + 1, x} & \text {if} \quad \delta_ {n + 1} = 0 \end{array} \right.\tag{2.13}
$$

to ensure that $X _ { n + 1 }$ has distribution $P ( x , \cdot )$ . Indeed, for x in $A _ { 0 }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P (\eta_ {n + 1} \in \cdot , \delta_ {n + 1} = 1) + P (Y _ {n + 1, x} \in \cdot , \delta_ {n + 1} = 0) \\ = \nu (\cdot) \alpha + (1 - \alpha) Q (x, \cdot) = P (x, \cdot). \end{array}
$$

Thus, each time the chain enters $A _ { 0 }$ , there is a probability α that the position next time will have distribution $\nu ( \cdot )$ , independent of $x \in A _ { 0 }$ as well as of all past history, i.e., that of starting afresh with distribution $\nu ( \cdot )$ Now if (2.11) also holds, then for any x in $\mathbb { S } ,$ , by Markov property, the chain enters $A _ { 0 }$ infinitely often w.p. 1 $( P _ { x } )$ 

Let $\tau _ { 1 } < \tau _ { 2 } < \tau _ { 3 } < \cdots$ denote the times of successive visits to $A _ { 0 }$ . Since $X _ { \tau _ { i } } ~ \in ~ A _ { 0 }$ , by the above construction (cf. (2.13)), there is a probability $\alpha > 0$ that $X _ { \tau _ { i } + 1 }$ will be distributed as $\nu ( \cdot )$ , completely independent of $X _ { j }$ for $j \le \tau _ { i }$ and $\tau _ { i }$ . By comparison with coin tossing, this implies that for any x, w.p. 1 (P<sub>x</sub>), there is a finite index $i _ { 0 }$ such that $\delta _ { \tau _ { i _ { 0 } } + 1 } = 1$ and hence $X _ { \tau _ { i _ { 0 } } + 1 }$ will be distributed as $\nu ( \cdot )$ , independent of all history of the chain $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ including that of the $\delta _ { \tau _ { i } + 1 }$ and $Y _ { \tau _ { i } + 1 } , i \le i _ { 0 }$ up to the time $\tau _ { i _ { 0 } }$ . That is, at $\tau _ { i _ { 0 } + 1 }$ the chain starts afresh with distribution $\nu ( \cdot )$ . Thus, it follows that for any initial distribution $\mu ,$ there is a random time $T$ such that $X _ { T }$ is distributed as $\nu ( \cdot )$ and is independent of all history up to $T - 1$ More precisely, for any $\mu , P _ { \mu } ( T < \infty ) = 1$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P _ {\mu} \left(X _ {j} \in A _ {j}, j = 0, 1, 2, \ldots , n + k, T = n + 1\right) \\ & = P _ {\mu} \left(X _ {j} \in A _ {j}, j = 0, 1, 2, \ldots , n, T = n + 1\right) \times \\ & \qquad P _ {\nu} \left(X _ {0} \in A _ {n + 1}, X _ {1} \in A _ {n + 2}, \ldots , X _ {k - 1} \in A _ {n + k}\right). \end{array}
$$

Since this is true for any $\mu ,$ it is true for $\mu = \nu$ and hence the theorem follows. ✷ 

A consequence of the above theorem is following. 

Theorem 14.2.7: Suppose in Theorem $\it { 1 4 . 2 . 6 } ,$ instead of (2.10) and $\it { ( 2 . 1 1 ) }$ , the following holds. 

There exists an $n _ { 0 } \geq 1$ such that for all x in $A _ { 0 }$ , A in ${ \mathbf { } } S ,$ , 

$$
P ^ {n _ {0}} (x, A) \geq \alpha \nu (A)\tag{2.14}
$$

and for all x in $A _ { 0 }$ 

$$
P _ {x} (X _ {n n _ {0}} \in A _ {0} \quad f o r s o m e \quad n \geq 1) = 1\tag{2.15}
$$

and 

$$
P _ {x} (T _ {A _ {0}} <   \infty) = 1 \quad f o r a l l x i n \mathbb {S}.\tag{2.16}
$$

Let $Y _ { n } \equiv X _ { n n _ { 0 } } , n \ge 0$ (where $n n _ { 0 }$ stands for the product of n and $n _ { 0 } )$ Then, for any initial distribution $\mu _ { : }$ , there exist random times $\{ T _ { i } \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ such that under $P _ { \mu }$ , the sequence $\eta _ { j } \equiv \{ Y _ { j } : T _ { j + r } , 0 \leq r < T _ { j + 1 } - T _ { j } , T _ { j + 1 } - T _ { j } \}$ for $j = 1 , 2 , \dots$ are iid with $Y _ { T _ { j } } \sim \nu ( \cdot )$
