## Limit Theorems for Dependent Processes

## 16.1 A central limit theorem for martingales

Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of random variables on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ , and let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration, i.e., a sequence of σ-algebras on Ω such that ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \subset { \mathcal { F } } _ { n + 1 } \subset { \mathcal { F } }$ for all $n \geq 1$ . From Chapter 13, recall that $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is called a martingale if $X _ { n }$ is ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ -measurable for each $n \geq 1$ and $E ( X _ { n + 1 } \mid$ ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n } ) = X _ { n }$ for each $n \geq 1$ 

Given a martingale $\{ X _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ , define 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} Y _ {1} & = & X _ {1} - E X _ {1}, \\ Y _ {n} & = & X _ {n} - X _ {n - 1}, n \geq 1. \end{array}
$$

Note that each $Y _ { n }$ is ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ -measurable and 

$$
E (Y _ {n} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n - 1}) = 0 \quad \text { for   all } \quad n \geq 1,\tag{1.1}
$$

where $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 } = \{ \Omega , \emptyset \}$ 

Definition 16.1.1: Let $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a collection of random variables on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ and let $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ be a filtration. Then, $\{ Y _ { n } , { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is called a martingale diference array (mda) if $Y _ { n }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { n ^ { - } }$ measurable for each $n \geq 1$ and (1.1) holds. 

For example, if $\{ Y _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 }$ is a sequence of zero mean independent random variables, then $\{ Y _ { n } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a mda w.r.t. the natural filtration ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n } =$ $\sigma \langle Y _ { 1 } , \ldots , Y _ { n } \rangle , n \geq 1$ . Other examples of mda’s can be constructed from the examples given in Chapter 13. The main result of this section shows that for square-integrable mda’s satisfying a Lindeberg-type condition, the CLT holds. For more on limit theorems for mdas, see Hall and Heyde (1980). 

Theorem 16.1.1: For each $n \geq 1$ , let $\{ Y _ { n i } , \mathcal { F } _ { n i } \} _ { i \geq 1 }$ be a mda on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ with $E Y _ { n i } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ for all $i \geq 1$ and let $\tau _ { n }$ be a finite stopping time w.r.t. $\{ \mathcal { F } _ { n i } \} _ { i \ge 1 }$ . Suppose that for some constant $\sigma ^ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\tau_ {n}} E \Big (Y _ {n i} ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, i - 1} \Big) \longrightarrow_ {p} \sigma^ {2} \quad a s \quad n \to \infty\tag{1.2}
$$

and that for each $\epsilon > 0$ 2 

$$
\Delta_ {n} (\epsilon) \equiv \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\tau_ {n}} E \Big (Y _ {n i} ^ {2} I (| Y _ {n i} | > \epsilon) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, i - 1} \Big) \longrightarrow_ {p} 0 \quad a s \quad n \to \infty .\tag{1.3}
$$

Then, 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\tau_ {n}} Y _ {n i} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma^ {2}).\tag{1.4}
$$

Proof: First the theorem will be proved under the additional condition that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \tau_ {n} & = & m _ {n} \text {   for   all   } n \geq 1 \text {   for   some   nonrandom   sequence   of } \\ & & \text { positive   integers   } \{m _ {n} \} _ {n \geq 1} \end{array}\tag{1.5}
$$

and that for some $c \in ( 0 , \infty )$ ), 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {n}} E \left(Y _ {n i} ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, i - 1}\right) \leq c \quad \text { w   .   p   . } 1.\tag{1.6}
$$

Let $\sigma _ { n i } ^ { 2 } = E { \left( Y _ { n i } ^ { 2 } \mid \mathcal { F } _ { n , i - 1 } \right) } , i \geq 1 , n \geq 1$ . Also, write m for $m _ { n }$ to ease the notation. Since $\sigma _ { n i } ^ { 2 }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { n , i - 1 } \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e }$ , for any $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| E \exp \left(\iota t \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} Y _ {n j}\right) - \exp \left(- \sigma^ {2} t ^ {2} / 2\right) \right| \\ \leq \left| E \exp \left(\iota t \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} Y _ {n j}\right) - E \exp \left(\iota t \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m - 1} Y _ {n j}\right) \exp \left(- t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n m} ^ {2} / 2\right) \right| \\ + \dots + \left| E \exp \left(\iota t Y _ {n 1}\right) \exp \left(- \sum_ {j = 2} ^ {m} t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} / 2\right) \right. \\ \left. - \left[ \exp \left(- \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} / 2\right) \right] \right| \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & + \left| E \exp \left(- \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} / 2\right) - \exp (- t ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} / 2) \right| \\ \leq & \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} E \Big | E \Big \{\exp (\iota t Y _ {n k}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \Big \} - \exp (- t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} / 2) \Big | \\ & + \left| E \exp \left(- \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n j} ^ {2} / 2\right) - \exp (- t ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} / 2) \right| \\ \equiv & I _ {1 n} + I _ {2 n}, \quad \text {say.} \end{array}\tag{1.7}
$$

By (1.2), (1.5), and the BCT, 

$$
I _ {2 n} \rightarrow 0 \quad \text { as } \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\tag{1.8}
$$

To estimate $I _ { 1 n }$ , note that for any $1 \leq k \leq n$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} E \Big \{\exp (\iota t Y _ {n k}) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \Big \} \\ = & 1 + \iota t E \big (Y _ {n k} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \big) + \frac {(\iota t) ^ {2}}{2}   E \big (Y _ {n k} ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \big) + \theta_ {n k} (t) \\ = & 1 - \frac {t ^ {2}}{2}   \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} + \theta_ {n k} (t) \end{array}\tag{1.9}
$$

and 

$$
\exp \left(- t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} / 2\right) = 1 - \frac {t ^ {2}}{2} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} + \gamma_ {n k}, \quad \mathrm{say}.\tag{1.10}
$$

It is easy to verify that 

$$
| \theta_ {n k} | \leq E \bigg [ \min \left\{(t Y _ {n k}) ^ {2}, \frac {| t Y _ {n k} | ^ {3}}{6} \right\} \bigg | \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \bigg ]
$$

and 

$$
\left| \gamma_ {n k} \right| \leq \left(t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2}\right) ^ {2} \exp \left(t ^ {2} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} / 2\right) / 8.
$$

Hence, by (1.3), (1.6), (1.9), and (1.10), for any  in (0,1), 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} I _ {1 n} & \leq & \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} E \Big \{| \theta_ {n k} | + | \gamma_ {n k} | \Big \} \\ & \leq & t ^ {2} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} E \Big | E \Big \{Y _ {n k} ^ {2} I (| Y _ {n k} | > \epsilon) \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \Big \} \Big | \\ & & + | t | ^ {3} \epsilon \cdot \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} E \Big | E \big (Y _ {n k} ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \big) \Big | + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} E \Big \{t ^ {4} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {4} \exp (t ^ {2} c / 2) \Big \} \\ & \leq & t ^ {2} E   \Delta_ {n} (\epsilon) + | t | ^ {3} \cdot \epsilon \cdot E \bigg [ \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} \bigg ] \\ & & + t ^ {4}   \exp (t ^ {2} c / 2)   E \bigg [ \bigg (\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} \bigg) \Big \{\max _ {l \leq k \leq m} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} \Big \} \bigg ]. \end{array}
$$

Note that for any $\epsilon > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E \max _ {1 \leq k \leq m} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} & \leq & \epsilon^ {2} + E \Big [ \max _ {1 \leq k \leq m} E \Big \{Y _ {n k} ^ {2} I \big (| Y _ {n k} | > \epsilon \big) \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \Big \} \Big ] \\ & \leq & \epsilon^ {2} + E \Delta_ {n} (\epsilon). \end{array}
$$

Hence, by (1.3), (1.6), and the BCT, for any $\epsilon \in ( 0 , 1 )$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} I _ {1 n} & \leq & \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} \Big [ t ^ {2} E \Delta_ {n} (\epsilon) + | t | ^ {3} \epsilon \cdot c \\ & & + t ^ {4} c e ^ {t ^ {2} c / 2} \Big \{\epsilon^ {2} + E \Delta_ {n} (\epsilon) \Big \} \Big ] \\ & \leq & c _ {1} (t)   \epsilon \end{array}
$$

for some $c _ { 1 } ( t ) \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , not depending on . Thus implies that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} I _ {1 n} = 0.\tag{1.11}
$$

Clearly (1.7), (1.8), and (1.11) yield (1.4), whenever (1.5) and (1.6) are true. 

Next, suppose that condition (1.6) is not assumed a priori but (1.5) holds true. Fix $c > \sigma ^ { 2 }$ and define the sets $\begin{array} { r } { B _ { n k } = \{ \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \sigma _ { n i } ^ { 2 } \leq c \} } \end{array}$ , and the variables $\check { Y } _ { n k } = Y _ { n k } I _ { B _ { n k } } , k \geq 1 , n \geq 1$ . Note that $B _ { n k } \in \mathcal { F } _ { n , k - 1 }$ and hence, 

$$
E \big (\check {Y} _ {n k} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \big) = I _ {B _ {n k}} E \big (Y _ {n k} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \big) = 0,
$$

and 

$$
\check {\sigma} _ {n k} ^ {2} \equiv E \big (\check {Y} _ {n k} ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n, k - 1} \big) = I _ {B _ {n k}} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2},\tag{1.12}
$$

for all $k \geq 1$ . In particular, $\left\{ { \check { Y } } _ { n k } , \mathcal { F } _ { n , k } \right\}$ is a mda. Since $B _ { n , k - 1 } \supset B _ { n k }$ for all k, by the definitions of the sets $B _ { n k } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { { s } }$ , it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \check {\sigma} _ {n k} ^ {2} & = & \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} I _ {B _ {n k}} \\ & = & \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} I _ {B _ {n m}} + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m - 1} \sigma_ {n k} ^ {2} \big (I _ {B _ {n, m - 1}} - I _ {B _ {n m}} \big) \\ & & + \dots + \sigma_ {n 1} ^ {2} \big (I _ {B _ {n 1}} - I _ {B _ {n 2}} \big) \\ & \leq & c I _ {B _ {n m}} + c \big (I _ {B _ {n, m - 1}} - I _ {B _ {n m}} \big) + \dots + \big (c I _ {B _ {n 1}} - I _ {B _ {n 2}} \big) \\ & \leq & c. \end{array}\tag{1.13}
$$

Thus, the mda $\left\{ \check { Y } _ { n k } , \mathcal { F } _ { n k } \right\} _ { k \geq 1 }$ satisfies (1.6). Next note that by (1.2) and (1.5), 

$$
P \big (B _ {n m} ^ {c} \big) \to 0 \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty .\tag{1.14}
$$

Also, by (1.12), $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { m } \check { \sigma } _ { n k } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { m } \sigma _ { n k } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ on $B _ { n m }$ . Hence, it follows that 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \check {\sigma} _ {n k} ^ {2} \longrightarrow_ {p} \sigma^ {2},
$$

i.e., the mda $\big \{ \check { Y } _ { n k } , \mathcal { F } _ { n k } \big \}$ satisfies (1.2). Further, the inequality ${ ^ { \circ } | \check { Y } _ { n k } | } \le$ $| Y _ { n k } | ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$  and the fact that the function $h ( x ) = x ^ { 2 } I ( | x | > \epsilon )$ $x > 0$ is nonde-)， creasing jointly imply that (1.3) holds for $\big \{ \breve { Y } _ { n k } , \mathop { \mathcal { F } _ { n k } } \big \}$ . Hence, by the case already proved, 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \check {Y} _ {n k} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma^ {2}).\tag{1.15}
$$

But $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { m } \check { Y } _ { n k } = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { m } Y _ { n k } } \end{array}$ on $B _ { n m }$ . Hence, by (1.14), 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} Y _ {n k} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma^ {2}),\tag{1.16}
$$

and therefore, the CLT holds without the restriction in (1.6). 

Next consider relaxing the restrictions in (1.5) (and (1.6)). Since $P ( \tau _ { n } <$ $\infty ) = 1$ , there exist positive integers $m _ { n }$ such (Problem 16.2) that 

$$
P \big (\tau_ {n} > m _ {n} \big) \to 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \to \infty .\tag{1.17}
$$

Next define 

$$
\tilde {Y} _ {n k} = Y _ {n k} I (\tau_ {n} \geq k), k \geq 1, n \geq 1.\tag{1.18}
$$

It is easy to check (Problem 16.3) that $\{ \tilde { Y } _ { n k } , \mathcal { F } _ { n k } \}$ is a mda, and that $\{ \tilde { Y } _ { n k } , \mathcal { F } _ { n k } \}$ satisfies (1.2) and (1.3) with $\tau _ { n }$ replaced by $m _ { n }$ (Problem 16.4). Hence, by the previous case already proved, 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m _ {n}} \tilde {Y} _ {n k} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma^ {2}).
$$

Next note that (cf. (4.1), Proclem 16.4), 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\tau_ {n}} Y _ {n k} - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m _ {n}} \tilde {Y} _ {n k} \longrightarrow_ {p} 0 \quad \text {as} \quad n \to \infty .\tag{1.19}
$$

Hence, (1.4) holds and the proof of the theorem is complete. 

## 16.2 Mixing sequences

This section deals with a class of dependent processes, called the mixing processes, where the degree of dependence decreases as the distance (in time) between two given sets of random variables goes to infinity. The ‘degree of dependence’ is measured by various mixing coeficients, which are defined in Section 16.2.1 below. Some basic properties of the mixing coeficients are presented in Section 16.2.2. Limit theorems for sums of mixing random variables are given in Section 16.2.3. 

## 16.2.1 Mixing coeficients

Definition 16.2.1: Let $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ be a probability space and $\mathcal { G } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { G } _ { 2 }$ be sub-σ-algebras of $\mathcal { F }$ . 

(a) The α-mixing or strong mixing coeficient between $\mathcal { G } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathcal { G } _ { 2 }$ is defined as 

$$
\alpha (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}) \equiv \sup \left\{\left| P (A \cap B) - P (A) P (B) \right|: A \in \mathcal {G} _ {1}, B \in \mathcal {G} _ {2} \right\}.\tag{2.1}
$$

(b) The β-mixing coeficient or the coeficient of absolute regularity between $\mathcal { G } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathcal { G } _ { 2 }$ is defined as 

$$
\beta (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}) \equiv \frac {1}{2} \sup \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\ell} \left| P (A _ {i} \cap B _ {j}) - P (A _ {i}) P (B _ {j}) \right|,\tag{2.2}
$$

where the supremum is taken over all finite partitions $\{ A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { k } \}$ and $\{ B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { \ell } \}$ of Ω by sets $A _ { i } \in { \mathcal G } _ { 1 }$ and $B _ { j } \in \mathcal { G } _ { 2 } , 1 \le i \le k .$ $1 \leq j \leq \ell , \ell , k \in \mathbb { N }$ 

(c) The ρ-mixing coeficient or the coeficient of maximal correlation between $\mathcal { G } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathcal { G } _ { 2 }$ is defined as 

$$
\rho (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}) \equiv \sup \left\{\rho_ {X _ {1}, X _ {2}}: X _ {i} \in L ^ {2} (\Omega , \mathcal {G} _ {i}, P), i = 1, 2 \right\}\tag{2.3}
$$

where $\rho _ { X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } } \equiv \frac { \mathrm { C o v } ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } ) } { \sqrt { \mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) \mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { 2 } ) } }$ is the correlation coeficient of $X _ { 1 }$ and $X _ { 2 }$ . 

It is easy to check (Problem 16.5 (a) and (d)) that all three mixing coeficients take values in the interval [0, 1] and that $\rho ( \mathcal { G } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { G } _ { 2 } ) = \operatorname* { s u p } \left\{ | E X _ { 1 } X _ { 2 } | \right.$ $X _ { i } \in L ^ { 2 } ( \Omega , \mathcal { G } _ { i } , P ) E X _ { i } = 0 , E X _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } = 1 , i = 1 , 2 \}$ . When the σ-algebras $\mathcal { G } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathcal { G } _ { 2 }$ are independent, these coeficients equal zero, and vice versa. Thus, nonzero values of the mixing coeficients give various measures of the degree of dependence between $\mathcal { G } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathcal { G } _ { 2 }$ . It is easy to check (Problem 16.5 (c)) that 

$$
\alpha (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}) \leq \beta (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}) \quad \text { and } \quad \alpha (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}) \leq \rho (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}).\tag{2.4}
$$

However, no ordering between the $\beta ( \mathcal { G } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { G } _ { 2 } )$ and $\rho ( \mathcal { G } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { G } _ { 2 } )$ exists, in general (Problem 16.6). There are two other mixing coeficients that are also often used in the literature. These are given by the φ-mixing coeficient 

$$
\phi (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}) \equiv \sup \left\{\left| P (A) - P (A \mid B) \right|: B \in \mathcal {G} _ {1}, P (B) > 0, A \in \mathcal {G} _ {2} \right\},\tag{2.5}
$$

and the Ψ-mixing coeficient 

$$
\Psi (\mathcal {G} _ {1}, \mathcal {G} _ {2}) \equiv \sup _ {A \in \mathcal {G} _ {1} ^ {*}, B \in \mathcal {G} _ {2} ^ {*}} \frac {| P (A \cap B) - P (A) P (B) |}{P (A) P (B)},\tag{2.6}
$$

where $P ( A \mid B ) = P ( A \cap B ) / P ( B )$ for $P ( B ) > 0$ , and where $\mathcal { G } _ { i } ^ { * } = \{ A : A \in$ $\mathcal { G } _ { i } , P ( A ) > 0 \} , i = 1 , 2$ . It is easy to check that $\Psi ( { \mathcal { G } } _ { 1 } , { \mathcal { G } } _ { 2 } ) \geq \phi ( { \mathcal { G } } _ { 1 } , { \mathcal { G } } _ { 2 } ) \geq$ $\beta ( \mathcal { G } _ { 1 } , \mathcal { G } _ { 2 } )$ 

Definition 16.2.2: Let $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ be a (doubly-infinite) sequence of random variables on a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ . Then, the strong- or α-mixing coeficient of $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ , denoted by $\alpha _ { X } ( \cdot )$ , is defined by 

$$
\alpha_ {X} (n) \equiv \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {Z}} \alpha \left(\sigma \langle \left\{X _ {j}: j \leq i, j \in \mathbb {Z} \right\} \rangle , \sigma \langle \left\{X _ {j}: j \geq i + n, j \in \mathbb {Z} \right\} \rangle\right), n \geq 1,\tag{2.7}
$$

where the $\alpha ( \cdot , \cdot )$ on the right side of (2.7) is as defined in (2.1). The process $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is called strongly mixing or α-mixing if 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \alpha_ {X} (n) = 0.\tag{2.8}
$$

The other mixing coeficients of $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } } ~ ( \mathrm { e . g . } , \beta _ { X } ( \cdot ) , \rho _ { X } ( \cdot )$ , etc.) are defined similarly. 

For a one-sided sequence $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \ge 1 }$ , the α-mixing coeficient $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \ge 1 }$ is defined by replacing $\mathbb { Z }$ on the right side of (2.7) by N on all three occurrences. A similar modification is needed for the other mixing coeficients. When there is no chance of confusion, the coeficients $\alpha _ { X } ( \cdot ) , \beta _ { X } ( \cdot ) , \ldots , \mathrm { e t c } .$ 2 will be written as $\alpha ( \cdot ) , \beta ( \cdot ) , \ldots$ , etc., to ease the notation. 

Another important notion of ‘weak’ dependence is given by the following: 

Definition 16.2.3: Let $m \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ be an integer and $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ be a collection of random variables on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ . Then, $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is called m-dependent if for every $k \in \mathbb { Z } , \{ X _ { i } : i \leq k , i \in \mathbb { Z } \}$ and $\{ X _ { i } : i > k + m , i \in \mathbb { Z } \}$ are independent. 

Example 16.2.1: If $\{ \epsilon _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is a collection of independent random variables and $X _ { i } = ( \epsilon _ { i } + \epsilon _ { i + 1 } ) , i \in \mathbb { Z }$ , then $\{ \epsilon _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is 0-dependent and $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is 1-dependent. It is easy to see that if $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is m-dependent for some $m \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ , then $\alpha _ { X } ^ { * } ( n ) = 0$ for all $n > m$ , where $\alpha _ { X } ^ { \ast } \in \left\{ \alpha _ { X } , \beta _ { X } , \rho _ { X } , \phi _ { X } , \Psi _ { X } \right\}$ Therefore, m-dependence of $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ implies that the process $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is $\alpha _ { X } ^ { * } { \mathrm { - m i x i n g } }$ . In this sense, the condition of m-dependence is the strongest and the condition of α-mixing is the weakest among all weak dependence conditions introduced here. 

Example 16.2.2: Let $\{ \epsilon _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ be a collection of iid random variables with $E \epsilon _ { 1 } = 0 , E \epsilon _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ and let 

$$
X _ {n} = \sum_ {i \in \mathbb {Z}} a _ {i} \epsilon_ {n - i}, n \in \mathbb {Z}\tag{2.9}
$$

where $a _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ and $a _ { i } = 0 \big ( \exp ( - c _ { i } ) \big )$ as $i \to \infty , c \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . If $\epsilon _ { 1 }$ has an  -integrable characteristic function, then $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is strongly mixing (Chanda (1974), Gorodetskii (1977), Withers (1981), Athreya and Pantula (1986)). 

Example 16.2.3: Let $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ be a zero mean stationary Gaussian process. Suppose that $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ has spectral density $f : ( - \pi , \pi ) \to [ 0 , \infty )$ , i.e., 

$$
E X _ {0} X _ {k} = \int_ {- \pi} ^ {\pi} e ^ {\iota k x} f (x) d x, k \in \mathbb {Z}.\tag{2.10}
$$

Then, $\alpha _ { X } ( n ) \leq \rho _ { X } ( n ) \leq 2 \pi \alpha ( n ) , n \geq 1$ and, therefore, $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is α-mixing if it is ρ-mixing (Ibragimov and Rozanov (1978), Chapter 4). Further, $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is α-mixing if the spectral density f admits the representation 

$$
f (t) = \left| p (e ^ {\iota t}) \right| ^ {2} \exp \big (u (e ^ {\iota t}) + \tilde {v} (e ^ {\iota t}) \big),\tag{2.11}
$$

where $p ( \cdot )$ is a polynomial, u and v are continuous real-valued functions on the unit circle in the complex plane, and $\tilde { v }$ is the conjugate function of $u .$ It is also known that if the Gaussian process $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is φ-mixing, then it is necessarily m-dependent for some $m \in \mathbb { Z } _ { + }$ . Thus, for Gaussian processes, the condition of α-mixing is as strong as ρ-mixing and the conditions of $\phi -$ mixing and Ψ-mixing are equivalent to m-dependence. See Ibragimov and Rozanov (1978) for more details. 

## 16.2.2 Coupling and covariance inequalities

The mixing coeficients can be seen as measures of deviations from independence. The idea of coupling is to construct independent copies of a given pair of random vectors on a suitable probability space such that the Euclidean distance between these copies admits a bound in terms of the mixing coeficient between the (σ-algebras generated by the) random vectors. Thus, coupling gives a geometric interpretation of the mixing coeficients. The first result is for $\beta { \mathrm { - m i x i n g } }$ random vectors. 

Theorem 16.2.1: (Berbee’s theorem). Let $( X , Y )$ be a random vector on a probability space $( \Omega _ { 0 } , \mathcal { F } _ { 0 } , P _ { 0 } )$ such that X takes values in $\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $Y$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { s } , d , s \in \mathbb { N }$ . Then, there exist an enlarged probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ and a s-dimensional random vector $Y ^ { * }$ such that 

(i) $( X , Y , Y ^ { * } )$ are defined on $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ 

(ii) $Y ^ { * }$ is independent of X under $P$ and $( X , Y )$ have the same distribution under P and $P _ { 0 }$ 

(iii) $P ( Y \neq Y ^ { * } ) = \beta ( \sigma \langle X \rangle , \sigma \langle Y \rangle )$ 

Proof: See Corollary 4.2.5 of Berbee (1979). 

A weaker version of the above result is available for α-mixing random variables, where the diference between $Y$ and its independent copy admits a bound in terms of the α-mixing coeficient. 

Theorem 16.2.2: (Bradley’s theorem). In Theorem 16.2.1, assume $s =$ 1 and $0 < E | Y | ^ { \gamma } < \infty$ for some $0 < \gamma < \infty$ . Then, for all $0 ~ < ~ y ~ \leq$ $( E | Y | ^ { \gamma } ) ^ { 1 / \gamma }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P \big (| Y - Y ^ {*} | \geq y \big) & \leq & 1 8 \Big [ \alpha \big (\sigma \langle X \rangle , \sigma \langle Y \rangle \big) \Big ] ^ {2 \gamma / 1 + 2 \gamma} \\ & & (E | Y | ^ {\gamma}) ^ {1 / 1 + 2 \gamma}   y ^ {- \gamma / (1 + 2 \gamma)}. \end{array}\tag{2.12}
$$

Proof: See Theorem 3 of Bradley (1983). 

Next, some bounds on the covariance between mixing random variables are established. These will be useful for deriving limit theorems for sums of mixing random variables. For a random variable X, define the function 

$$
Q _ {X} (u) = \inf \left\{t: P (| X | > t) \leq u \right\}, \quad u \in (0, 1).\tag{2.13}
$$

Thus, $Q _ { X } ( u )$ is the quantile function of $| X |$ at $( 1 - u )$ 

Theorem 16.2.3: (Rio’s inequality). Let X and Y be two random variables with $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } Q _ { X } ( u ) Q _ { Y } ( u ) d u < \infty } \end{array}$ . Then, 

$$
\left| C o v (X, Y) \right| \leq 2 \int_ {0} ^ {2 \alpha} Q _ {X} (u) Q _ {Y} (u) d u\tag{2.14}
$$

where $\alpha = \alpha \bigl ( \sigma \langle X \rangle , \sigma \langle Y \rangle \bigr )$ 

Proof: By Tonelli’s theorem, 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} E X ^ {+} Y ^ {+} & = & E \bigg [ \bigg (\int_ {0} ^ {X ^ {+}} d u \bigg) \bigg (\int_ {0} ^ {Y ^ {+}} d u \bigg) \bigg ] \\ & = & E \bigg (\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} I (X ^ {+} > u) I (Y ^ {+} > v) d u d v \bigg) \\ & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P (X > u, Y > v) d u d v \end{array}
$$

and similarly, $\begin{array} { r } { E X ^ { + } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } P ( X > u ) d u } \end{array}$ . Hence, by (2.1), it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \operatorname{Cov} (X ^ {+}, Y ^ {+}) \right| \\ = \left| \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} [ P (X > u, Y > v) - P (X > u) P (Y > v) ] d u d v \right| \\ \leq \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \min \{\alpha , P (X > u), P (Y > v) \} d u d v. \end{array}\tag{2.15}
$$

Next note that for any real numbers a, b, c, d 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} (\alpha \wedge a \wedge c) + (\alpha \wedge a \wedge d) + (\alpha \wedge b \wedge c) + (\alpha \wedge b \wedge d) \\ \leq & [ 2 (\alpha \wedge a) ] \wedge (c + d) + [ 2 (\alpha \wedge b) ] \wedge (c + d) \\ \leq & 2 [ 2 \alpha \wedge (a + b) \wedge (c + d) ]. \end{array}\tag{2.16}
$$

Now using (2.15), (2.16), and the identity $\operatorname { C o v } ( X , Y ) = \operatorname { C o v } ( X ^ { + } , Y ^ { + } ) +$ $\operatorname { C o v } ( X ^ { - } , Y ^ { - } ) - \operatorname { C o v } ( X ^ { + } , Y ^ { - } ) - \operatorname { C o v } ( X ^ { - } , Y ^ { + } )$ , one gets 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \big | \operatorname{Cov} (X, Y) \big | \\ \leq 2 \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \min \big \{2 \alpha , P (| X | > u), P (| Y | > v) \big \} d u d v. \end{array}\tag{2.17}
$$

Hence, it is enough to show that the right sides of (2.14) and (2.17) agree. To that end, let U be a Uniform (0,1) random variable and define $( W _ { 1 } , W _ { 2 } ) =$ $( 0 , 0 ) I ( U \ge 2 \alpha ) + \big ( Q _ { X } ( U ) , Q _ { Y } ( U ) \big ) I ( U < 2 \alpha )$ . Then 

$$
E W _ {1} W _ {2} = \int_ {0} ^ {2 \alpha} Q _ {X} (u) Q _ {Y} (u) d u.\tag{2.18}
$$

On the other hand, noting that $Q _ { X } ( a ) > t \mathrm { i f f } P ( | X | > t ) > a$ , one has 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} E W _ {1} W _ {2} & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \big (W _ {1} > u, W _ {2} > v \big) d u d v \\ & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \big (U <   2 \alpha , Q _ {X} (U) > u, Q _ {Y} (U) > v \big) d u d v \\ & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \min \big \{2 \alpha , P (| X | > u), P (| Y | > v) \big \} d u d v. \end{array}
$$

Hence, the theorem follows from (2.17), (2.18), and the above identity. ✷ 

Corollary 16.2.4: Let X and Y be two random variables with $\alpha ( \sigma \langle X \rangle , \sigma \langle Y \rangle ) = \alpha \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ 

(i) (Davydov’s inequality). Suppose that $E | X | ^ { p } < \infty , E | Y | ^ { q } < \infty$ for some $p , q \in ( 1 , \infty )$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { p } + \frac { 1 } { q } < 1 } \end{array}$ . Then, $E | X Y | < \infty$ and 

$$
\big | C o v (X, Y) \big | \leq 2 r (2 \alpha) ^ {1 / r} \big (E | X | ^ {p} \big) ^ {1 / p} \big (E | Y | ^ {q} \big) ^ {1 / q},\tag{2.19}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { r } = 1 - \left( \frac { 1 } { p } + \frac { 1 } { q } \right) } \end{array}$ 

(ii) If $P \big ( | X | \leq c _ { 1 } \big ) = 1 = P ( | Y | \leq c _ { 2 } \big )$ for some constants $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ then 

$$
\left| C o v (X, Y) \right| \leq 4 c _ {1} c _ {2} \alpha .\tag{2.20}
$$

Proof: Let $a = ( E | X | ^ { p } ) ^ { 1 / p }$ and $b = ( E | Y | ^ { q } ) ^ { 1 / q }$ . W.l.o.g., suppose that $a , b \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Then, by Markov’s inequality, for any $0 < u < 1$ 2 

$$
P \big (| X | > a u ^ {- 1 / p} \big) \leq E | X | ^ {p} / (a u ^ {- 1 / p}) ^ {p} = u
$$

and hence, $Q _ { X } ( u ) \leq a u ^ { - 1 / p }$ . Similarly, $Q _ { Y } ( u ) \leq b u ^ { - 1 / q } , 0 < u < 1$ . Hence, by Theorem 16.2.3, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \big | \mathrm{Cov} (X, Y) \big | & \leq & 2 \int_ {0} ^ {2 \alpha} a b   u ^ {- 1 / p - 1 / q} d u \\ & = & 2 a b (2 \alpha) ^ {1 - 1 / p - 1 / q} \Big / \Big (1 - \frac {1}{p} - \frac {1}{q} \Big). \end{array}
$$

which is equivalent to (2.19). 

The proof of (2.20) is a direct consequence of Rio’s inequality and the bounds $Q _ { X } ( u ) \leq c _ { 1 }$ and $Q _ { Y } ( u ) \leq c _ { 2 }$ for all $0 < u < 1$ ✷ 

## 16.3 Central limit theorems for mixing sequences

In this section, CLTs for sequences of random variables satisfying diferent mixing conditions are proved. 

Proposition 16.3.1: Let $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ be a collection of random variables with strong mixing coeficient $\alpha ( \cdot )$ 

(i) Suppose that $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \alpha ( n ) < \infty$ and for some $c \in ( 0 , \infty ) , P ( | X _ { i } | \leq$ $c ) = 1$ for all i. Then, 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} C o v (X _ {1}, X _ {n + 1}) \text { converges   absolutely. }\tag{3.1}
$$

(ii) Suppose that $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \alpha ( n ) ^ { \delta / 2 + \delta } < \infty$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } } E | X _ { i } | ^ { 2 + \delta } < \infty } \end{array}$ for some $\delta \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Then, (3.1) holds. 

## Proof: A direct consequence of Corollary 16.2.4.

Next suppose that the collection of random variables $\{ X _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { Z } }$ is stationary and that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) + \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \left| \operatorname { C o v } ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 1 + n } ) \right| < \infty } \end{array}$ . Then by the DCT, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} n \mathrm{Var} (\bar {X} _ {n}) & = & n ^ {- 1} \mathrm{Var} \bigg (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} \bigg) \\ & = & n ^ {- 1} \bigg [ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathrm{Var} (X _ {i}) + 2 \sum_ {1 \leq i <   j \leq n} \mathrm{Cov} (X _ {i}, X _ {j}) \bigg ] \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} & = & n ^ {- 1} \bigg [ n \operatorname{Var} (X _ {1}) + 2 \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n - 1} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n - i} \operatorname{Cov} (X _ {i}, X _ {i + k}) \bigg ] \\ & = & n ^ {- 1} \bigg [ n \operatorname{Var} (X _ {1}) + 2 \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n - 1} (n - k) \operatorname{Cov} (X _ {1}, X _ {1 + k}) \bigg ] \\ \longrightarrow \sigma_ {\infty} ^ {2} & \equiv & \operatorname{Var} (X _ {1}) + 2 \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \operatorname{Cov} (X _ {1}, X _ {1 + k}) \quad \text {as} \quad n \to \infty . \end{array}\tag{3.2}
$$

In particular, under the conditions of part (i) or part (ii) of Proposition 16.3.1, 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \operatorname{Var} (\sqrt {n}   \bar {X} _ {n}) \quad \text { exists   and   equals } \quad \sigma_ {\infty} ^ {2}.
$$

In general, it is not guaranteed that $\sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } > 0$ . Indeed, it is not dificult to construct an example of a stationary strong mixing sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ such that $\sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } = 0$ (Problem 16.8). However, in addition to the conditions of Proposition 16.3.1, if it is assumed that $\sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } > 0$ , then a CLT for $\sqrt { n } ( \bar { X } _ { n } -$ $E X _ { 1 } )$ holds in the stationary case; see Corollary 16.3.3 and 16.3.6 below. 

A classical method of proving the CLT (and other limit theorems) for mixing random variables is based on the idea of blocking, introduced by S. N. Bernstein. Intuitively, the ‘blocking’ approach can be described as follows: Suppose, $\mu = E X _ { 1 } = 0$ . First, write the sum $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i }$ in terms of alternating sums of ‘big blocks’ $B _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ (of length ${ \mathrm { } } ^ { \cdot } p { \mathrm { } } ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { ~ s a y } } )$ and ‘little blocks’ $L _ { i } { ' } \mathrm { s }$ (of length $^ { \circ } q ^ { \prime }$ say) as 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} & = & \left(X _ {1} + \dots + X _ {p}\right) + \left(X _ {p + 1} + \dots + X _ {p + q}\right) \\ & & + \left(X _ {p + q + 1} + \dots + X _ {2 p + q}\right) + \dots \\ & = & B _ {1} + L _ {1} + B _ {2} + L _ {2} + \dots + (B _ {K} + L _ {K}) + R _ {n}, \end{array}
$$

where the last term $R _ { n }$ is the excess (if any) over the last complete pair of big- and little-blocks $\left( { { B } _ { K } } , { { L } _ { K } } \right)$ . Next, group together the $B _ { i } { } ^ { \mathrm { : } }$ s and $L _ { i } { ' } \mathrm { s }$ to write 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K} B _ {j} + \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K} L _ {j} + R _ {n} / \sqrt {n}.\tag{3.3}
$$

If $q \ll p \ll n$ , then, the number of $X _ { i }$ ’s in $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { K } L _ { j }$ and in $R _ { n }$ are of smaller order than n, the total number of $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ . Using this, one can show that the contribution of the last two terms in (3.3) to the limit is negligible, i.e., 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K} L _ {j} + R _ {n}\right) \longrightarrow_ {p} 0.
$$

To handle the first term, $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { n } } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { K } B _ { i } } \end{array}$ , note that the $B _ { j } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ are functions of disjoint collections of $X _ { j } \mathrm { ' s }$ that are separated by a distance of $q$ or more. 

By letting $q \to \infty$ suitably and using the mixing condition, one can replace the $B _ { j } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ by their independent copies, and appeal to the Lindeberg CLT for sums of independent random variables to conclude that 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K} B _ {j} \longrightarrow^ {d} N \left(0, \sigma_ {\infty} ^ {2}\right).
$$

Although the blocking approach is described here for stationary random variables, with minor modifications, it is applicable to certain nonstationary sequences as shown below. 

Theorem 16.3.2: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of random variables (not necessarily stationary) with strong mixing coeficient $\alpha ( \cdot )$ . Suppose that there exist constants $\sigma _ { 0 } ^ { 2 } , c \in ( 0 , \infty )$ such that 

$$
P (| X _ {i} | \leq c) = 1 \quad f o r a l l \quad i \in \mathbb {N},\tag{3.4}
$$

$$
\gamma_ {n} \equiv \sup _ {j \geq 1} \left| n ^ {- 1}   V a r \bigg (\sum_ {i = j} ^ {j + n - 1} X _ {i} \bigg) - \sigma_ {0} ^ {2} \right|\rightarrow 0 \quad a s \quad n \rightarrow \infty ,\tag{3.5}
$$

and that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \alpha (n) <   \infty .\tag{3.6}
$$

Then, 

$$
\sqrt {n} \big (\bar {X} _ {n} - \bar {\mu} _ {n} \big) \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {0} ^ {2}) a s n \to \infty\tag{3.7}
$$

where $\bar { \mu } _ { n } = E \bar { X } _ { n }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { X } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } , n \geq 1 } \end{array}$ 

An important special case of Theorem 16.3.2 is the following: 

Corollary 16.3.3: If $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a sequence of stationary bounded random variables with $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \alpha ( n ) < { \overline { { \infty } } }$ , and if $\sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 }$ of (3.2) is positive, then, with $\mu = E X _ { 1 }$ 

$$
\sqrt {n} \big (\bar {X} _ {n} - \mu \big) \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {\infty} ^ {2}) a s n \to \infty .\tag{3.8}
$$

Proof: For stationary random variables, (3.5) holds with $\sigma _ { 0 } ^ { 2 } = \sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 }$ (cf. (3.2)). Hence, the Corollary follows from Theorem 16.3.2. ✷ 

For proving the theorem, the following auxiliary result will be used. 

Lemma 16.3.4: Suppose that the conditions of Theorem 16.3.2 hold. Then, 

$$
\sup _ {m \geq 1} E \bigg [ \sum_ {i = m} ^ {m + n - 1} (X _ {i} - E X _ {i}) \bigg ] ^ {4} = o (n ^ {3}) \quad a s \quad n \to \infty .
$$

Proof: W.l.o.g., let $E X _ { i } = 0$ for all i. Note that for any $m \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \bigg (\sum_ {j = m} ^ {n + m - 1} X _ {j} \bigg) ^ {4} \\ \quad = \sum_ {j} E X _ {j} ^ {4} + 6 \sum_ {i <   j} E X _ {i} ^ {2} X _ {j} ^ {2} + 4 \sum_ {i \neq j} E X _ {i} ^ {3} X _ {j} \\ \quad \quad + 6 \sum_ {i \neq j \neq k} E X _ {i} ^ {2} X _ {j} X _ {k} + \sum_ {i \neq j \neq k \neq \ell} E X _ {i} X _ {j} X _ {k} X _ {\ell} \\ \quad \equiv I _ {1 n} + \dots + I _ {5 n}, \text {say,} \end{array}\tag{3.9}
$$

where the indices $i , j , k , \ell$ in the above sums lie between m and $m + n - 1$ By (3.4), 

$$
\left| I _ {1 n} \right| + \left| I _ {2 n} \right| + \left| I _ {3 n} \right| \leq n \cdot c ^ {4} + 7 n (n - 1) c ^ {4} \leq 7 n ^ {2} c ^ {4}.\tag{3.10}
$$

* * * * * *By Corollary 16.2.4 (ii), noting that $E X _ { i } = 0$ for all i, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \left| I _ {4 n} \right| & \leq & 1 2 \sum_ {i <   j <   k} \left\{\left| E X _ {i} ^ {2} X _ {j} X _ {k} \right| + \left| E X _ {i} X _ {j} ^ {2} X _ {k} \right| + \left| E X _ {i} X _ {j} X _ {k} ^ {2} \right| \right\} \\ & \leq & 1 2 \sum_ {i <   j <   k} \left\{4 c ^ {4} \alpha (j - k) + 4 c ^ {4} \alpha (j - k) + 4 c ^ {4} \alpha (j - i) \right\} \\ & \leq & 1 4 4 c ^ {4} n ^ {2} \bigg [ \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {n - 1} \alpha (r) \bigg ]. \end{array}\tag{3.11}
$$

Similarly, 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l} \left| I _ {5 n} \right| & \leq & (4!) \sum_ {i <   j <   k <   \ell} \left| E X _ {i} X _ {j} X _ {k} X _ {\ell} \right| \\ & \leq & 2 4 \sum_ {i <   j <   k <   \ell} 4 c ^ {4} \big [ \alpha (j - i) \wedge \alpha (\ell - k) \big ] \\ & = & 9 6 c ^ {4} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n - 3} \sum_ {j = i + 1} ^ {n - 2} \sum_ {k = j + 1} ^ {n - 1} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {n - k} \big [ \alpha (j - i) \wedge \alpha (r) \big ] \\ & = & 9 6 c ^ {4} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n - 3} \sum_ {s = 1} ^ {n - 2 - i} \sum_ {k = i + s + 1} ^ {n - 1} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {n - k} \big [ \alpha (s) \wedge \alpha (r) \big ] \\ & \leq & 9 6 c ^ {4} n ^ {2} \sum_ {s = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {n} \big [ \alpha (s) \wedge \alpha (r) \big ] \\ & = & 9 6 c ^ {4} n ^ {2} \Big [ \sum_ {s = 1} ^ {n} \alpha (s) + 2 \sum_ {s = 1} ^ {n - 1} \sum_ {r = s + 1} ^ {n} \alpha (r) \Big ] \\ & \leq & 1 9 2 c ^ {4} n ^ {2} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {n} r \alpha (r) \end{array}
$$

$$
\leq 1 9 2 c ^ {4} n ^ {2} \left[ n ^ {1 / 2} \sum_ {r = 1} ^ {\infty} \alpha (r) + n \sum_ {r \geq \sqrt {n}} \alpha (r) \right].\tag{3.12}
$$

Since $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { r > { \sqrt { n } } } \alpha ( r ) = o ( 1 ) } \end{array}$ and the bounds in (3.9)–(3.12) do not depend on m, Lemma 16.3.4 follows. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 16.3.2: W.l.o.g., let $E X _ { j } = 0$ for all $j .$ . Let $p \equiv p _ { n }$ $q \equiv q _ { n } = \lfloor n ^ { 1 / 2 } \rfloor , n \geq 1$ be integers satisfying

when a choice of $\left\{ p _ { n } \right\}$ will be specified later. Let $r = p + q$ and $K = \lfloor n / r \rfloor$ As outlined earlier, for $i = 1 , \ldots , K$ , let

and let

$$
\sqrt {n} \bar {X} _ {n} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} B _ {i} + \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} L _ {i} + \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} R _ {n}.\tag{3.14}

Next note that the variables $L _ { i }$ and $L _ { i + k }$ depend on two disjoint sets of $X _ { j }$ ’s that are separated by a distance of $\left[ ( i + k { - } 1 ) r + p - i r \right] = ( k { - } 1 ) r + p >$ $k p$ . Hence, by (3.5), Corollary 16.2.4 (ii) and the monotonicity of $\alpha ( \cdot )$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} E \bigg (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} L _ {i} / \sqrt {n} \bigg) ^ {2} \\ \leq & n ^ {- 1} \bigg [ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} E L _ {i} ^ {2} + 2 \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K - 1} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K - i} \big | E L _ {i} L _ {i + k} \big | \bigg ] \\ \leq & n ^ {- 1} \bigg [ K q \big (\sigma_ {0} ^ {2} + \gamma_ {q} \big) + 2 K \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K - 1} 4 q ^ {2} c ^ {2} \alpha (k p) \bigg ] \\ \leq & n ^ {- 1} K q \bigg [ \big (\sigma_ {0} ^ {2} + \gamma_ {q} \big) + 8 q c ^ {2} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K - 1} \Big \{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {p} \alpha (k p - j) \Big \} \Big / p \bigg ] \\ = & O \bigg (n ^ {- 1} K q + n ^ {- 1} K q ^ {2} p ^ {- 1} \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {\infty} \alpha (j) \bigg) \\ = & O \Big (\frac {q}{p} + \Big (\frac {q}{p} \Big) ^ {2} \Big) \to 0 \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty , \end{array}\tag{3.16}
$$

as $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { n } { K p }  1 } \end{array}$ as $n \to \infty$ 

Next consider the term $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { n } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { K } B _ { i } } \end{array}$ . Note that $\alpha \big ( \sigma \langle B _ { j } \rangle , \sigma \langle \{ B _ { i } : i \ \ge$ $j + 1 \} \rangle \bigr ) \leq \alpha ( q )$ for all $1 \leq j < K$ . By applying Corollary 16.2.4 (ii) to the -real and imaginary parts, one gets for any $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\left| E \exp \left(\iota t \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K} B _ {j} / \sqrt {n}\right) - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {K} E \exp \left(\iota t B _ {j} / \sqrt {n}\right) \right|\\\leq \quad \left| E \exp \left(\iota t \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {K} B _ {j} / \sqrt {n}\right) - E \exp \left(\iota t B _ {1} / \sqrt {n}\right) E \exp \left(\iota t \sum_ {j = 2} ^ {K} B _ {j} / \sqrt {n}\right) \right|\\+ \dots + \left| \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {K - 2} E \exp \left(\iota t B _ {j} / \sqrt {n}\right) \left\{E \exp \left(\iota t (B _ {K - 1} + B _ {K}) / \sqrt {n}\right) \right\} - \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {K} E \exp \left(\iota t B _ {j} / \sqrt {n}\right) \right|\\\leq 1 6   \alpha (q) \cdot K\\= O \Big (q \alpha (q)   {\frac {n}{p q}} \Big) \rightarrow 0    \text { as }    n \rightarrow \infty .\end{array}\tag {3.17}
$$

The last step follows by noting that $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \alpha ( n ) < \infty \Rightarrow n \alpha ( n ) \to 0$ as $n $ . Let $\tilde { B } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \tilde { B } _ { K }$ be independent random variables such that $\tilde { B } _ { i } = ^ { d } ~ B _ { i }$ 2 $1 \leq i \leq K$ . Note that by (3.5), 

$$
\left| \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} E \tilde {B} _ {i} ^ {2} - \sigma_ {0} ^ {2} \right|
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l}\leq&\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} \left| E B _ {i} ^ {2} - p \sigma_ {0} ^ {2} \right| + \left| n ^ {- 1} K p - 1 \right| \sigma_ {0} ^ {2}\\\leq&\frac {K p}{n} \gamma_ {p} + n ^ {- 1} | K p - n | \sigma_ {0} ^ {2} \rightarrow 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\end{array}\tag{3.18}

Next, for $k \in \mathbb N$ , let $\begin{array} { r } { \Gamma _ { 1 } ( k ) = \operatorname* { s u p } \big \{ E \big ( \sum _ { i = m } ^ { m + k - 1 } X _ { i } \big ) ^ { 4 } k ^ { - 3 } : m \geq 1 \big \} } \end{array}$ and $\Gamma _ { 1 } ^ { * } ( k ) = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ \Gamma _ { 1 } ( j ) : j \geq k \}$   . $$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} E \big (\tilde {B} _ {i} / \sqrt {n} \big) ^ {4} & = & n ^ {- 2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} E B _ {i} ^ {4} \\ & \leq & n ^ {- 2} K p ^ {3} \Gamma_ {1} ^ {*} (p) \to 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \to \infty . \end{array}\tag{3.19}
$$

Using (3.18) and (3.19), it is easy to check that the triangular array of independent random variables $\left\{ \tilde { B } _ { 1 } / \sqrt { n } , \ldots , \tilde { B } _ { K } / \sqrt { n } \right\} _ { n \ge 1 }$ satisfies the Lyapounov’s condition and hence,

\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} \tilde {B} _ {i} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {0} ^ {2}) \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty .

By (3.17), this implies that 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {K} B _ {i} \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {0} ^ {2}).\tag{3.20}
$$

Theorem 16.3.2 now follows from (3.14), (3.15), (3.16), and (3.20). 

For unbounded strongly mixing random variables, a CLT can be proved under moment and mixing conditions similar to Proposition 16.3.1 (ii). The key idea here is to use Theorem 16.3.2 for the sum of a truncated part of the unbounded random variables and then show that the sum over the remaining part is negligible in the limit. 

Theorem 16.3.5: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of random variables (not necessarily stationary) such that for some $\delta ~ \in ~ ( 0 , \infty ) , \ \zeta _ { \delta } ~ \equiv$ $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n \geq 1 } \left( E | X _ { n } | ^ { 2 + \delta } \right) ^ { 1 / 2 + \delta } < \infty } \end{array}$ and 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \alpha (n) ^ {\delta / 2 + \delta} <   \infty .\tag{3.21}
$$

Suppose that there exist $M _ { 0 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ and a function $\tau ( \cdot ) : ( M _ { 0 } , \infty ) $ $( 0 , \infty )$ such that for all $M > M _ { 0 }$ 2 

$$

This completes the proof of Theorem 16.3.5.

In the case that the sequence $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is stationary, further refinements of Corollaries 16.3.3 and 16.3.6 are possible. The following result, due to Doukhan, Massart and Rio (1994) uses a diferent method of proof to establish the CLT under stationarity. To describe it, for any nonincreasing sequence of positive real numbers $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ , define the function $a ( t )$ and its inverse $a ^ { - 1 } ( t )$ , respectively, by 

$$
a (t) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} a _ {n} I (n - 1 <   t \leq n), t > 0,
$$

and 

$$
a ^ {- 1} (u) = \inf \{t: a (t) \leq u \}, u \in (0, \infty).
$$

Theorem 16.3.7: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of stationary random variables with $E X _ { 1 } = \mu \in \mathbb { R } , E X _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ and strong mixing coeficient $\alpha ( \cdot )$ Suppose that 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} \alpha^ {- 1} (u) Q _ {X _ {1}} (u) ^ {2} d u <   \infty ,\tag{3.29}
$$

where $Q _ { X _ { 1 } } ( u ) = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t : P ( | X _ { 1 } | > t ) \leq u \} , 0 < u < 1$ is as in (2.13). Then, $0 \leq \sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } < \infty . \ I f \sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } > 0 \quad$ , then 

$$
\sqrt {n} (\bar {X} _ {n} - \mu) \longrightarrow^ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {\infty} ^ {2}).
$$

Proof: See Doukhan et al. (1994). 

Note that if $P ( | X _ { 1 } | \leq c ) = 1$ for some $c \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , then $Q _ { X _ { 1 } } ( u ) \leq c$ for all $u \in ( 0 , 1 )$ and (3.29) holds if $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } \alpha ^ { - 1 } ( u ) d u < \infty$ if $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \alpha ( n ) < \infty$ . Thus,  Theorem 16.3.7 yields Corollary 16.3.3 as a special case. Similarly, it can be shown that if $E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 2 + \delta } < \infty$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \alpha ( { \hat { n ) } } ^ { \delta / 2 + \delta } < \infty$ , then (3.29) holds and, therefore, Theorem 16.3.7 also yields Corollary 16.3.6 as a special case. For another example, suppose $\alpha ( n ) = O { \big ( } \exp ( - c n ) { \big ) }$ as $n  \infty$ for some $c \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Then, (3.29) holds if 

$$
E X _ {1} ^ {2} \log \left(1 + | X _ {1} |\right) <   \infty .\tag{3.30}
$$

In this case, the logarithmic factor in (3.30) cannot be dropped. More precisely, it is known that finiteness of the second moment alone (with arbitrarily fast rate of decay of the strong mixing coeficient) is not enough to guarantee the CLT (Herrndorf (1983)) for strong mixing random variables. 

For the ρ-mixing random variables, the following result is known. A process $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is called second order stationary if 

$$
E X _ {n} ^ {2} <   \infty , E X _ {n} = E X _ {1} \mathrm{and} E X _ {n} X _ {n + k} = E X _ {1} X _ {1 + k}\tag{3.31}
$$

for all $n \geq 1 , k \geq 0$ 

Theorem 16.3.8: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of $\rho { - } m i x i n g ;$ second order stationary random variables with $E X _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ and $E X _ { 1 } = \mu$ . Suppose that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho (2 ^ {n}) <   \infty .\tag{3.32}
$$

$$
V a r \bigl (\sqrt {n}   \bar {X} _ {n} \bigr) \to \sigma_ {\infty} ^ {2}.
$$

$I f \sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , then $\sqrt { n } \big ( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu \big ) \longrightarrow ^ { d } N ( 0 , \sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } )$ 

Proof: See Peligrad (1982). 

Thus, unlike the strong mixing case, in the ρ-mixing case the CLT holds under finiteness of the second moment, provided (3.32) holds and $\sigma _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } > 0$

## 17.1 The bootstrap method for independent variables

## 17.1.1 A description of the bootstrap method

The bootstrap method, introduced in statistics by Efron (1979), is a powerful tool for solving many statistical inference problems. Let $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ be iid random variables with common cdf $F .$ . Let $\theta = \theta ( F )$ be a parameter and $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ be an estimator of $\theta$ based on observations $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ , i.e., ${ \widehat { \theta } } _ { n } = t _ { n } ( X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } )$ for some measurable function $t _ { n } ( \cdot )$ of the random variables $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ . The parameter $\theta$ is called a ‘level $\Gamma ^ { \prime }$ parameter and the parameters related to the distribution of $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ are called ‘level $2 ^ { \prime }$ parameters (cf. Lahiri (2003)). For example, ${ \mathrm { V a r } } ( { \hat { \theta } } _ { n } )$ or a median of (the distribution of) $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ are ‘level $2 ^ { \cdot }$ parameters. The bootstrap is a general method for estimating such ‘level $2 ^ { \bullet }$ parameters. 

To describe the bootstrap method, let 

$$
R _ {n} = r _ {n} (X _ {1}, \ldots , X _ {n}; F)\tag{1.1a}
$$

be a random variable that is a known function of $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ and $F$ . An example of $R _ { n }$ is given by 

$$
\tilde {R} _ {n} = \sqrt {n} (\bar {X} _ {n} - \mu) / \sigma ,\tag{1.1b}
$$

the normalized sample mean, where ${ \bar { X } } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i }$ is the sample mean, $\mu = E X _ { 1 }$ <sub>1</sub> and $\sigma ^ { 2 } = \operatorname { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } )$ . The objective here is to approximate (estimate) the unknown distribution of $R _ { n }$ and its functionals. Let ${ \hat { F } } _ { n }$ be an estimator of $F$ based on $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ . For example, one may take ${ \hat { F } } _ { n }$ to be the empirical distribution function (edf) of $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ , given by 

$$
F _ {n} (x) = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} I (X _ {i} \leq x), x \in \mathbb {R}.\tag{1.1c}
$$

Next, given $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ , generate conditionally iid random variables $X _ { 1 } ^ { * } , \ldots , X _ { m } ^ { * }$ with common distribution ${ \hat { F } } _ { n }$ , where m denotes the bootstrap sample size. Define the bootstrap version R∗ $R _ { m , n } ^ { * }$ of $R _ { n }$ by replacing the $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathfrak { s }$ s with $X _ { i } ^ { * } { \mathrm { , ~ } } F$ with ${ \hat { F } } _ { n }$ , and n with m in the definition of $R _ { n }$ . Then, 

$$
R _ {m, n} ^ {*} = r _ {m} \big (X _ {1} ^ {*}, \ldots , X _ {m} ^ {*}; \hat {F} _ {n} \big).\tag{1.2}
$$

Let $G _ { n }$ denote the distribution of $R _ { n }$ . The bootstrap estimator of $G _ { n }$ is given by the conditional distribution $\hat { G } _ { m , n } ~ ( \mathrm { s a y } )$ of $R _ { m , n } ^ { * }$ given $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } .$ Further, the bootstrap estimator of a functional $\phi _ { n } = { \dot { \phi } } ( G _ { n } )$ is given by 

$$
\hat {\phi} _ {m, n} \equiv \phi (\hat {G} _ {m, n}).
$$

For example, the bootstrap estimator of the kth moment $E ( R _ { n } ) ^ { k }$ of $R _ { n }$ is given by $E _ { * } ( R _ { n } ^ { * } ) ^ { k } , k \in \mathbb { N }$ , where $E _ { * }$ denotes the conditional expectation given $\{ X _ { n } , n \geq 1 \}$ . This follows from the above ‘plug-in’ method applied to the functional $\begin{array} { r } { \phi ( G ) \equiv \int x ^ { k } d G ( x ) } \end{array}$ , as $\begin{array} { r } { E ( R _ { n } ) ^ { k } = \int x ^ { k } d G _ { n } ( x ) = \phi ( G _ { n } ) } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { E _ { * } ( R _ { m , n } ^ { * } ) ^ { k } = \int \ d x ^ { k } d \hat { G } _ { m , n } ( x ) = \phi ( \hat { G } _ { m , n } ) } \end{array}$ . Similarly, the bootstrap es-timator of the α-quantile $( 0 < \alpha < 1 )$ of $R _ { n }$ is given by the α-quantile of (the conditional distribution of) $R _ { m , n } ^ { * }$ . In general, closed form expressions for bootstrap estimators are not available. One may use Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate them numerically. See Hall (1992) for more details. 

Note that $\hat { G } _ { m , n }$ and hence, the bootstrap estimators $\hat { \phi } _ { m , n } = \phi ( \hat { G } _ { m , n } )$ depend on the choice of the initial estimator $\hat { F } _ { n }$ of $F$ . The most common choice of $\hat { F } _ { n }$ is given by $F _ { n }$ of (1.1), in which case the bootstrap variables $X _ { 1 } ^ { * } , \ldots , X _ { m } ^ { * }$ can be equivalently generated by simple random sampling with replacement from $\{ X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } \}$ . The following example illustrates the construction of the bootstrap version for $R _ { n } = \tilde { R } _ { n }$ as in (1.1b). 

Example 17.1.1: For the normalized sample mean ${ \tilde { R } } _ { n } = \sqrt { n } ( { \bar { X } } _ { n } - \mu ) / \sigma$ 2 its bootstrap version based on a resample of size m from ${ \hat { F } } _ { n }$ is given by 

$$
\tilde {R} _ {m, n} ^ {*} = \sqrt {n} \big (\bar {X} _ {m} ^ {*} - \hat {\mu} _ {n} \big) / \hat {\sigma} _ {n},\tag{1.3}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { X } _ { m } ^ { * } ~ = ~ \bar { X } _ { m , n } ^ { * } ~ = ~ m ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } ^ { * } } \end{array}$ is the bootstrap sample mean, $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { \mu } _ { n } = \int { x } d \hat { F } _ { n } ( x ) } \end{array}$ is the (conditional) mean of $X _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ under ${ \hat { F } } _ { n }$ and $\hat { \sigma } _ { n } ^ { 2 }$ is the conditional variance of $X _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ under $\hat { F } _ { n }$ . For ${ \hat { F } } _ { n } = F _ { n }$ , it is easy to check that $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { \mu } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } = \bar { X } _ { n } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( X _ { i } - \bar { X } _ { n } ) ^ { 2 } \equiv s _ { n } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , the sample variance of $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ . Thus, the ‘ordinary’ bootstrap version of ${ \tilde { R } } _ { n }$ (with ${ \hat { F } } _ { n } = F _ { n } )$ is given by 

$$
\tilde {R} _ {m, n} ^ {*} = \sqrt {n} \big (\bar {X} _ {m} ^ {*} - \bar {X} _ {n} \big) / s _ {n}.\tag{1.4}
$$

Some questions that arise naturally in this context are: Does the bootstrap distribution of $\tilde { R } _ { m , n } ^ { * }$ give a valid approximation to the distribution of $\tilde { R } _ { n } \tilde { \it { : } }$ How good is the approximation generated by the bootstrap? How does the quality of approximation depend on the resample size or on the underlying cdf $F ?$ Some of these issues are addressed next. Write $P _ { * }$ to denote the conditional probability given $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \dots$ . and ${ \mathrm { s u p } } _ { x }$ to denote supremum over $x \in \mathbb { R }$ 

## 17.1.2 Validity of the bootstrap: Sample mean

Theorem 17.1.1: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables with $E X _ { 1 } = \mu$ and Var $\left( X _ { 1 } \right) = \sigma ^ { 2 } \in \left( 0 , \infty \right)$ . Let $\tilde { R } _ { n } = \sqrt { n } ( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu ) / \sigma$ and let ${ \tilde { R } } _ { n , n } ^ { * }$ be its ‘ordinary’ bootstrap version given by $( 1 . 4 )$ with $m = n$ . Then 

$$
\Delta_ {n} \equiv \sup _ {x} \left| P (\tilde {R} _ {n} \leq x) - P _ {*} (\tilde {R} _ {n, n} ^ {*} \leq x) \right|\rightarrow 0 \quad a s \quad n \rightarrow \infty , \quad a. s.\tag{1.5}
$$

Proof: $\mathrm { W . l . o . g . }$ , suppose that $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1$ . By the CLT, $\tilde { R } _ { n } \equiv$ $\sqrt { n } \bar { X } _ { n } \longrightarrow ^ { d } N ( 0 , 1 )$ . Hence, it is enough to show that as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
\Delta_ {1 n} \equiv \sup _ {x} \left| P _ {*} \big (\sqrt {n} (\bar {X} _ {n} ^ {*} - \bar {X} _ {n}) \leq s _ {n} x \big) - \Phi (x) \right| = o (1) \quad \mathrm{a.s.},
$$

where $\Phi ( \cdot )$ denotes the cdf of the $N ( 0 , 1 )$ distribution. By the Berry-Esseen theorem, 

$$
\Delta_ {1 n} \leq (2. 7 5) \frac {E _ {*} | X _ {1} ^ {*} - \bar {X} _ {n} | ^ {3}}{\sqrt {n} s _ {n} ^ {3}} \leq \frac {2 ^ {3} \cdot (2 . 7 5)}{\sqrt {n}} \frac {E _ {*} | X _ {1} ^ {*} | ^ {3}}{s _ {n} ^ {3}}.
$$

By the SLLN, $s _ { n } ^ { 2 } \to \sigma ^ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ and by the Marcinkiewz-Zygmund SLLN 

$$
\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} E _ {*} | X _ {1} ^ {*} | ^ {3} = \frac {1}{n ^ {3 / 2}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} | X _ {i} | ^ {3} \rightarrow 0 \quad \mathrm{as} \quad n \rightarrow \infty \quad \mathrm{a.s.}
$$

Hence, $\Delta _ { 1 n } = o ( 1 )$ as $n  \infty ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . and the theorem is proved. 

One can also give a more direct proof of Theorem 17.1.1 using the Lindeberg-Feller CLT (Problem 17.1). 

Theorem 17.1.1 shows that the bootstrap approximation to the distribution of the normalized sample mean is valid under the same conditions that guarantee the CLT. Under additional moment conditions, a more precise bound on the order of $\Delta _ { n }$ can be given. If $E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 3 } < \infty$ , then by the SLLN, $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } | X _ { j } | ^ { 3 } \to E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 3 } } \end{array}$ as $n  \infty$ , a.s. and hence, the last step in the proof of Theorem 17.1.1, it follows that $\Delta _ { n } = O ( n ^ { - 1 / 2 } )$ a.s. Thus, in this case, the rate of bootstrap approximation to the distribution of ${ \tilde { R } } _ { n }$ is as good as that of the normal approximation to the distribution of ${ \ddot { R } } _ { n }$ . An important result of Singh (1981) shows that the error rate of bootstrap approximation is indeed smaller, provided the distribution of $X _ { 1 }$ is nonlattice (cf. Chapter 11), i.e., 

$$
| E \exp (\iota t X _ {1}) | \neq 1 \quad \text { for   all } \quad t \in \mathbb {R} \setminus \{0 \}.
$$

A precise statement of this result is given in Theorem 17.1.2 below. 

## 17.1.3 Second order correctness of the bootstrap

Theorem 17.1.2: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid nonlattice random variables with $E | X _ { 1 } | ^ { 3 } < \infty$ . Also, let $\tilde { R } _ { n } , \tilde { R } _ { n , n } ^ { * }$ , and $\Delta _ { n }$ be as in Theorem 17.1.1. Then, 

$$
\Delta_ {n} = o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \quad a s \quad n \to \infty , \quad a. s.\tag{1.6}
$$

Proof: Only an outline of the proof will be given here. By Theorem 11.4.4 on Edgeworth expansions, it follows that 

$$
\sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} \left| P (\tilde {R} _ {n} \leq x) - \left[ \Phi (x) - \frac {\mu_ {3}}{6 \sqrt {n} \sigma^ {3}} (x ^ {2} - 1) \phi (x) \right] \right| = o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty ,\tag{1.7}
$$

where $\mu _ { 3 } = E ( X _ { 1 } - \mu ) ^ { 3 } $ and $\phi ( x ) = ( 2 \pi ) ^ { - 1 / 2 } \exp ( - x ^ { 2 } / 2 )$ $x \in \mathbb { R }$ . It can be shown that the conditional distribution of ${ \tilde { R } } _ { n , n } ^ { * }$ given $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ , also admits a similar expansion that is valid almost surely: 

$$
\sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} \left| P _ {*} (\tilde {R} _ {n} \leq x) - \left[ \Phi (x) - \frac {\hat {\mu} _ {3 , n}}{6 \sqrt {n} \hat {\sigma} _ {n} ^ {3}} (x ^ {2} - 1) \phi (x) \right] \right|
$$

$$
= o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty , \quad \text { a.s. },\tag{1.8}
$$

where $\hat { \mu } _ { 3 , n } = E _ { * } ( X _ { 1 } ^ { * } - \bar { X } _ { n } ) ^ { 3 }$ . By the SLLN, as $n \to \infty , { \hat { \mu } } _ { 3 , n } \to \mu _ { 3 }$ a.s. and $\hat { \sigma } _ { n } ^ { 2 } \to \bar { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ a.s. Hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \Delta_ {n} & \leq & \left| \frac {\hat {\mu} _ {3 , n}}{\hat {\sigma} _ {n} ^ {3}} - \frac {\mu_ {3}}{\sigma^ {3}} \right| \left\{\sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} | x ^ {2} - 1 | \phi (x) \right\} \frac {1}{6 \sqrt {n}} + o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \quad \text {a.s.} \\ & = & o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \quad \text {a.s.} \end{array}
$$

Under the conditions of Theorem 17.1.2, the bootstrap approximation to the distribution of ${ \tilde { R } } _ { n }$ outperforms the classical normal approximation, since the latter has an error of order $O ( n ^ { - 1 / 2 } )$ . In the literature, this property is referred to as the second order correctness (s.o.c.) of the bootstrap. It can be shown that under additional conditions, the order of $\Delta _ { n }$ is $O \big ( n ^ { - 1 } \sqrt { \log \log n } \big )$ a.s., and therefore the bootstrap gives an accurate  -approximation even for small sample sizes where the asymptotic normal approximation is inadequate. For iid random variables with a smooth cdf F, s.o.c. of the bootstrap has been established in more complex problems, such as in the case of the studentized sample mean $T _ { n } \equiv \sqrt { n } ( \bar { X } _ { n } - \mu ) / s _ { n }$ For a detailed description of the second and higher order properties of the bootstrap for independent random variables, see Hall (1992). 

## 17.1.4 Bootstrap for lattice distributions

Next consider the case where the underlying cdf $F$ does not satisfy the nonlatticeness condition of Theorem 17.1.2. Then, 

$$
\left| E \exp (\iota t X _ {1}) \right| = 1 \quad \text { for   some } \quad t \neq 0
$$

and it can be shown (cf. Chapter 10) that $X _ { 1 }$ takes all its values in a lattice of the form $\{ a + j h : j \in \mathbb { Z } \} , a \in \mathbb { R } , h > 0$ . The smallest $h > 0$ satisfying 

$$
P \big (X _ {1} \in \{a + j h: j \in \mathbb {Z} \} \big) = 1
$$

is called the (maximal) span of $F .$ . For the normalized sample mean of lattice random variables, s.o.c. of the bootstrap fails under standard metrics, such as the sup-norm metric and the Levy metric. Recall that for any two distribution functions $F$ and G on R, 

$$
d _ {L} (F, G) = \inf \left\{\epsilon > 0: F (x - \epsilon) - \epsilon <   G (x) <   F (x + \epsilon) + \epsilon \quad \text { for   all } \quad x \in \mathbb {R} \right\}\tag{1.9}
$$

defines the Levy metric on the set of probability distribution on R. 

Theorem 17.1.3: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid lattice random variables with span $h \in ( 0 , \infty )$ and let ${ \tilde { R } } _ { n } , \ { \tilde { R } } _ { n , n } ^ { * }$ , and $\Delta _ { n }$ be as in Theorem 17.1.1. If $E ( X _ { 1 } ^ { 4 } ) < \infty$ , then 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} \sqrt {n} \Delta_ {n} = \frac {h}{\sqrt {2 \pi \sigma^ {2}}} a. s.\tag{1.10}
$$

and 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} \sqrt {n} d _ {L} (G _ {n}, \hat {G} _ {n}) = \frac {h}{\sigma (1 + \sqrt {2 \pi})} \quad a. s.\tag{1.11}
$$

$$
w h e r e G _ {n} (x) = P (\tilde {R} _ {n} \leq x) a n d \hat {G} _ {n} (x) = P _ {*} (\tilde {R} _ {n, n} ^ {*} \leq x), x \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

Thus, the above theorem shows that for lattice random variables, the bootstrap approximation to the distribution of $R _ { n }$ may not be better than the normal approximation in the supremum and the Levy metric. In Theorem 17.1.3, relation (1.10) is due to Singh (1981) and (1.11) is due to Lahiri (1994). 

Proof: Here again, an outline of the proof is given. By Theorem 11.4.5, 

$$
\sup _ {x} \left| P (R _ {n} \leq x) - \xi_ {n} (x) \right| = o (n ^ {- 1 / 2})\tag{1.12}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \xi _ { n } ( x ) = \Phi ( x ) + \frac { \mu _ { 3 } } { 6 \sigma ^ { 3 } \sqrt { n } } ( 1 - x ^ { 2 } ) \phi ( x ) + \frac { h } { \sigma \sqrt { n } } Q ( [ \sqrt { n } x \sigma - n x _ { 0 } ] / h ) \phi ( x ) } \end{array}$ 2 $x \in \mathbb { R } , Q ( x ) = { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } - x + \lfloor x \rfloor$ , and $x _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R }$ is such that $P ( X _ { 1 } = x _ { 0 } + \mu ) > 0$ Also, by Theorem 1 of Singh (1981), 

$$
\sup _ {x} \left| P _ {*} (R _ {n, n} ^ {*} \leq x) - \hat {\xi} _ {n} (x) \right| = o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \quad \text { as } \quad n \to \infty , \quad \text { a.s. },\tag{1.13}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { \xi } _ { n } ( x ) = \Phi ( x ) + \frac { \hat { \mu } _ { 3 , n } } { 6 s _ { - } ^ { 3 } \sqrt { n } } ( 1 - x ^ { 2 } ) \phi ( x ) + \frac { h } { \sigma \sqrt { n } } Q ( \sqrt { n } x s _ { n } / h ) , x \in \mathbb { R } } \end{array}$ and $\hat { \mu } _ { 3 , n } = E _ { * } ( X _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } - \bar { X } _ { n } ) ^ { 3 }$ . Hence, by (1.12) and (1.13), 

$$
\frac {\sigma \sqrt {n}}{h} \cdot \Delta_ {n} = \sup _ {x \in \mathbb {R}} \left| Q ([ \sqrt {n} x \sigma - n x _ {0} ] / h) - Q (\sqrt {n} x s _ {n} / h) \right| \phi (x) + o (1)\tag{a.s.}
$$

Since $Q ( x ) \in [ - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } , { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ]$ for all x and $\begin{array} { r } { \phi ( 0 ) = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 \pi } } } \end{array}$ , it is clear that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {\sigma \sqrt {n}}{h} \Delta_ {n} \leq \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi}} \quad \text { a.s. }\tag{1.14}
$$

To get the lower bound, suppose that for almost all realizations of $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ and for any given , $\delta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , there is a sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \in$ (0, ) such that 

$$
\sqrt {n}   x _ {n} s _ {n} / h \in \mathbb {Z} \text { and } \langle [ \sqrt {n}   x _ {n} \sigma - n x _ {0} ] / h \rangle \in (1 - \delta , 1) \quad \text { i.o. },\tag{1.15}
$$

where $\langle y \rangle$ denotes the fractional part of y, i.e., $\langle y \rangle = y - \lfloor y \rfloor , y \in \mathbb { R }$ . Then, for each n satisfying (1.15), 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \frac {\sigma \sqrt {n}}{h} \Delta_ {n} & \geq & \Big | Q ([ \sqrt {n}   x _ {n} \sigma - n x _ {0} ] / h) - \frac {1}{2} \Big | \phi (x _ {n}) + o (1) \\ & \geq & \inf _ {y \in (1 - \delta , 1)} \Big | Q (y) - \frac {1}{2} \Big | \cdot \inf _ {x \in (0, \epsilon)} \phi (x) + o (1). \end{array}\tag{1.16}

Since $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { y \to 1 - } Q ( y ) = - \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ , (1.14) and (1.16) together yield (1.10). The existence of the sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ satisfying (1.15) can be established by using the LIL. For an outline of the main arguments, see Problem 17.4. 

Next consider (1.11). Let $c _ { n } = \| G _ { n } - \hat { G } _ { n } \| _ { \infty } + n ^ { - 1 / 2 }$ . Since $d _ { L } ( G _ { n } , \hat { G } _ { n } ) \leq$ $\| G _ { n } - \hat { G } _ { n } \| , \ d _ { L } ( G _ { n } , \hat { G } _ { n } ) = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ 0 < \epsilon < c _ { n } : G _ { n } ( x - \epsilon ) - \epsilon < \hat { G } _ { n } ( x ) < \hat { G } _ { n } ( x - \epsilon ) \} .$ $\hat { G } _ { n } ( x + \epsilon ) + \epsilon$ for all $x \in \mathbb { R } \}$ . Using (1.12) and (1.13), it can be shown that for $0 < \epsilon < c _ { n }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\hat {G} _ {n} (x) <   G _ {n} (x + \epsilon) + \epsilon \quad \text {for all} \quad x \in \mathbb {R}} \\ {\Leftrightarrow} & {\big (Q (x) - Q (x \tau_ {n} + (\sqrt {n}   \epsilon \sigma - n x _ {0}) / h) \big) \phi (h x / s _ {n} \sqrt {n})} \\ & {<   h ^ {- 1} \epsilon \sigma \sqrt {n} (1 + \phi (h x / s _ {n} \sqrt {n})) + o (1) \quad \text {for all} \quad x \in \mathbb {R},} \end{array}\tag{1.17}
$$

where $\tau _ { n } = \sigma / s _ { n }$ and the $o ( 1 )$ term is uniform over $x \in \mathbb { R }$ . Similarly, for $0 < \epsilon < c _ { n }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} & G _ {n} (x - \epsilon) - \epsilon <   \hat {G} _ {n} (x) \quad \text { for   all } \quad x \in \mathbb {R} \\ \Leftrightarrow & \big (Q (x) - Q (x \tau_ {n} - (\sqrt {n}   \epsilon \sigma + n x _ {0}) / h) \big) \phi (h x / s _ {n} \sqrt {n}) \\ & > h ^ {- 1} \epsilon \sigma \sqrt {n} \big (1 + \phi (h x / s _ {n} \sqrt {n}) \big) + o (1) \quad \text { for   all } \quad x \in \mathbb {R}. \end{array}\tag{1.18}

It is easy to check that (1.17) and (1.18) are satisfied if $\epsilon = h \bigl \{ ( 1 +$ $\sqrt { 2 \pi } ) \sigma \sqrt { n } \} ^ { - 1 } + o ( n ^ { - 1 / 2 } )$ . Hence,

$$

for some ${ \tilde { x } } \epsilon \mathbb { R }$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & h ^ {- 1} \epsilon_ {n} \sigma \sqrt {n} \big (1 + \phi (h \tilde {x} / s _ {n} \sqrt {n}) \big) > (1 - \eta) / \sqrt {2 \pi} + o (1) \\ \Rightarrow & h ^ {- 1} \sigma \epsilon_ {n} \sqrt {n} \big (1 + \phi (0) \big) > (1 - \eta) \sqrt {2 \pi} + o (1) \\ \Rightarrow & \epsilon_ {n} > (1 - \eta) h (1 + \sqrt {2 \pi}) ^ {- 1} (\sigma \sqrt {n}) ^ {- 1} + o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \\ \Rightarrow & d _ {L} (G _ {n}, \hat {G} _ {n}) > (1 - \eta) h (1 + \sqrt {2 \pi}) ^ {- 1} (\sigma \sqrt {n}) ^ {- 1} + o (n ^ {- 1 / 2}). \end{array}

## 17.1.5 Bootstrap for heavy tailed random variables

Next consider the case where the $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are heavy tailed, i.e., the $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ have infinite variance. More specifically, let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be iid with common cdf $F$ such that as $x \to \infty$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{c} 1 - F (x) \sim x ^ {- 2} L (x) \\ F (- x) \sim c x ^ {- 2} L (x) \end{array}\tag{1.21}
$$

for some $\alpha \in ( 1 , 2 ) , c \in ( 0 , \infty )$ and for some function $L ( \cdot ) : ( 0 , \infty ) \to ( 0 , \infty )$ that is slowly varying at , i.e., L( ) is bounded on every bounded interval of $( 0 , \infty )$ and 

$$
\lim _ {y \to \infty} L (t y) / L (y) = 1 \quad \text { for   all } \quad t \in (0, \infty).\tag{1.22}
$$

Since $\alpha \in ( 1 , 2 )$ $E | X _ { 1 } | < \infty$ , but $E X _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } = \infty$ . Thus, the $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ have infinite variance but finite mean. In this case, it is known (cf. Chapter 11) that for some sequence $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ of normalizing constants 

$$
T _ {n} \equiv \frac {n (\bar {X} _ {n} - \mu)}{a _ {n}} \longrightarrow^ {d} W _ {\alpha},\tag{1.23}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { X } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i } , \mu = E X _ { 1 } } \end{array}$ and $W _ { \alpha }$ has a stable distribution of order α. The characteristic function of $W _ { \alpha }$ is given by 

$$
\phi_ {\alpha} (t) = \exp \Big (\int h (t, x) d \lambda_ {\alpha} (x) \Big), t \in \mathbb {R},\tag{1.24}
$$

where $h ( t , x ) = \big ( e ^ { \iota t x } - 1 - \iota t \big ) , x , t \in \mathbb { R }$ and where $\lambda _ { \alpha } ( \cdot )$ is a measure on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ satisfying 

$$
\lambda_ {\alpha} ([ x, \infty)) = x ^ {- \alpha} \quad \text { and } \quad \lambda_ {\alpha} ((- \infty , - x ]) = c x ^ {- \alpha}, x > 0.\tag{1.25}
$$

The normalizing constants $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset ( 0 , \infty )$ in (1.23) are determined by the relation 

$$
n P (X _ {1} > a _ {n}) \equiv n a _ {n} ^ {- 2} L (a _ {n}) \rightarrow 1 \quad \text { as } \quad n \rightarrow \infty .\tag{1.26}
$$

To apply the bootstrap, let $X _ { 1 } ^ { * } , \ldots , X _ { m } ^ { * }$ denote a random sample of size m, drawn with replacement form $\{ X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } \}$ . Then, the bootstrap version of $T _ { n }$ is given by 

$$
T _ {m, n} ^ {*} = m (\bar {X} _ {m} ^ {*} - \bar {X} _ {n}) / a _ {m}\tag{1.27}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { X } _ { m } ^ { * } = m ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } X _ { i } ^ { * } } \end{array}$ is the bootstrap sample mean. The main result of this section shows that $\mathcal { L } ( T _ { m , n } ^ { * } \mid X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } )$ , the conditional distribution of $T _ { m , n } ^ { * }$ given $X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ has a random limit for the usual choice of the resample size, $m = n$ and, hence, is an “inconsistent estimator” of $\mathcal { L } ( T _ { n } )$ the distribution of $T _ { n }$ . In contrast, consistency of the bootstrap approximation holds if $m = o ( n )$ , i.e., the resample size is of smaller order than the sample size. To describe the random limit in the $m = n$ case, the notion of a random Poisson measure is needed, which is introduced in the following definition. 

Definition 17.1.1: $M ( \cdot )$ is called a random Poisson measure on $\left( \mathbb { R } , B ( \mathbb { R } ) \right)$ with mean measure $\lambda _ { \alpha } ( \cdot )$ of (1.25), if $\{ M ( A ) : A \in B ( \mathbb { R } ) \}$  -is a collection of random variables defined on some probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ such that for each $w \in \Omega , M ( \cdot ) ( w )$ is a measure on R, (R) , and for any disjoint finite collection of sets $A _ { 1 } , \dots , A _ { m } \in \mathcal { B } ( \mathbb { R } ) , m \in \mathbb { N } , \left\{ M ( A _ { 1 } ) , \dots , M ( A _ { m } ) \right\}$ are independent Poisson random variables and $M ( A _ { i } ) \sim \operatorname { P o i s s o n } \left( \lambda _ { \alpha } ( A _ { i } ) \right)$ $i = 1 , \ldots , m$ 

Theorem 17.1.4: Let $\{ X _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of iid random variables satisfying (1.21) for some $\alpha \in ( 1 , 2 )$ and let $T _ { n } , T _ { m , n } ^ { * }$ be as in (1.23) and (1.27), respectively. 

(i) If m = o(n) as $n \to \infty$ , then 

$$
\sup _ {x} \left| P _ {*} (T _ {m, n} ^ {*} \leq x) - P (T _ {n} \leq x) \right| \longrightarrow_ {p} 0 \quad a s \quad n \to \infty .\tag{1.28}
$$

(ii) Suppose that $m = n$ for all $n \geq 1$ . Then, for any $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 2 

$$
E _ {*} \exp \left(\iota t T _ {n, n} ^ {*}\right) \longrightarrow^ {d} \exp \Big (\int h (t, x) d M (x) \Big),\tag{1.29}
$$

where $M ( \cdot )$ is the random Poisson measure defined above and $h ( t , x ) = ( e ^ { \iota t x } - 1 - \iota t )$ 

Remark 17.1.1: Part (ii) of Theorem 17.1.4 shows that the bootstrap fails to provide a valid approximation to the distribution of the normalized sample mean of heavy tailed random variables when $m = n$ . Failure of the bootstrap in the heavy tail case was first proved by Athreya $( 1 9 8 7 a )$ , who established weak convergence of the finite dimensional vectors $( P _ { * } ( T _ { n , n } ^ { * } \leq$ $x _ { 1 } ) , \ldots , P _ { * } ( \tilde { T } _ { n , n } ^ { * } \ \leq \ x _ { m } ) )$ based on a slightly diferent bootstrap version $\tilde { T } _ { n , n } ^ { * }$ of $T _ { n }$ , where $\tilde { T } _ { n , n } ^ { * } = n ( \bar { X } ^ { * } - \bar { X } _ { n } ) / X _ { ( n ) }$ and $X _ { ( n ) } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ X _ { 1 } , \ldots , X _ { n } \}$ Extensions of these results are given in Athreya (1987b) and Arcones and Gin´e (1989, 1991). A necessary and suficient condition for the validity of the bootstrap for the sample mean with resample size $m = n$ is that $X _ { 1 }$ belongs to the domain of attraction of the normal distribution (Gin´e and Zinn (1989)).
