Appendix A Advanced Calculus: A Review 

This Appendix is a brief review of elementary set theory, real numbers, limits, sequences and series, continuity, diferentiability, Riemann integration, complex numbers, exponential and trigonometric functions, and metric spaces. For proofs and further details, see Rudin (1976) and Royden (1988). 

## A.1 Elementary set theory

This section reviews the following: sets, set operations, product sets (finite and infinite), equivalence relation, axiom of choice, countability, and uncountability. 

Definition A.1.1: A set is a collection of objects. 

It is typically defined as a collection of objects with a common defining property. For example, the collection of even integers can be written as $\mathbb { E } \equiv \{ n : n$ <sup>is</sup> <sup>an</sup> <sup>even</sup> <sup>integer</sup>}<sup>.</sup> <sup>In</sup> <sup>general,</sup> <sup>a</sup> <sup>set</sup> <sup>Ω</sup> <sup>with</sup> <sup>defining</sup> <sup>property</sup> <sup>p</sup> is written as 

$$
\Omega = \{\omega : \omega \text { has   property } p \}.
$$

The individual elements are denoted by the small letters $\omega , a , x , s , t ,$ etc., and the sets by capital letters Ω, A, X, S, T, etc. 

Example A.1.1: The closed interval $[ 0 , 1 ] \equiv \{ x : x$ a real number, $0 \leq$ $x \leq 1 \}$ 

Example A.1.2: The set of positive rationals $\textstyle \equiv { \left\{ x : x = { \frac { m } { n } } \right. }$ , m and n positive integers . 

Example A.1.3: The set of polynomials in x of degree $1 0 \equiv \{ P ( { \boldsymbol { x } } ) ~ :$ $\begin{array} { r } { P ( x ) = \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { 1 0 } a _ { j } x ^ { j } , a _ { j } \mathrm { ~ r e a l } , j = 0 , \dots , 1 0 , a _ { 1 0 } \neq 0 \} } \end{array}$ 

Example A.1.4: The set of all polynomials in $x \equiv \{ P ( x ) : P ( x ) =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { n } a _ { j } x ^ { j }$ , n a nonnegative integer, $a _ { j }$ real, $j = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ 

## A.1.1 Set operations

Definition A.1.2: Let A be a set. A set B is called a subset of A and written as $B \subset A$ if every element of B is also an element of A. Two sets A and B are the same and written as $A = B$ if each is a subset of the other. A subset $A \subset \Omega$ is called empty and denoted by if there exists no $\omega$ in Ω such that $\omega \in A$ 

Using the mathematical notation $\in \mathrm { a n d } \Rightarrow$ , one writes 

$$
B \subset A \quad \text { if } \quad x \in B \Rightarrow x \in A.
$$

Here $\cdot _ { \in } ,$ means “belongs $\mathrm { t o } ^ { \dag }$ and  means “implies.” 

Example A.1.5: Let N be the set of natural numbers, i.e., $\mathbb { N } =$ $\{ 1 , 2 , 3 , \ldots \}$ . Let E be the set of even natural numbers, i.e., $\mathbb { E } = \{ n : n \in \mathbb { N }$ 2 $n = 2 k$ for some $k \in \mathbb { N } \}$ . Then $\mathbb { E } \subset \mathbb { N }$ 

Example A.1.6: Let $A = [ 0 , 1 ]$ and B be the set of x in A such that $\textstyle x ^ { 2 } < { \frac { 1 } { 4 } }$ . Then $B = \{ x : 0 \leq x < { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \} \subset A$ 

Definition A.1.3: (Intersection and union). Let $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 }$ be subsets of a set Ω. Then $A _ { 1 }$ union $A _ { 2 }$ , written as $A _ { 1 } \cup A _ { 2 } , \mathrm { i s }$ the set defined by 

$$
A _ {1} \cup A _ {2} = \{\omega : \omega \in A _ {1} \text {   or   } \omega \in A _ {2} \text {   or   both } \}.
$$

Similarly, $A _ { 1 }$ intersection $A _ { 2 }$ , written as $A _ { 1 } \cap A _ { 2 }$ , is the set defined by 

$$
A _ {1} \cap A _ {2} = \{\omega : \omega \in A _ {1} \text { and } \omega \in A _ {2} \}.
$$

Example A.1.7: Let $\Omega \equiv \mathbb { N } \equiv \{ 1 , 2 , 3 , . . . \}$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} A _ {1} & = & \{\omega : \omega = 3 k \text {   for   some   } k \in \mathbb {N} \} \quad \text { and } \\ A _ {2} & = & \{\omega : \omega \equiv 5 k \text {   for   some   } k \in \mathbb {N} \}. \end{array}
$$

Then $A _ { 1 } \cup A _ { 2 } = \{ \omega : \omega$ is divisible by at least one of the two integers 3 <sup>and</sup> <sup>5</sup>}<sup>,</sup> $A _ { 1 } \cap A _ { 2 } = \{ \omega : \omega$ is divisible by both 3 and 5 . 

Definition A.1.4: Let Ω and I be nonempty sets. Let $\{ A _ { \alpha } : \alpha \in I \}$ be a collection of subsets of Ω. Then I is called the index set. 

The union of $\{ A _ { \alpha } : \alpha \in I \}$ is defined as 

$$
\bigcup_ {\alpha \in I} A _ {\alpha} \equiv \{\omega : \omega \in A _ {\alpha} \text {   for   some   } \alpha \in I \}.
$$

The intersection of $\{ A _ { \alpha } : \alpha \in I \}$ is defined as 

$$
\bigcap_ {\alpha \in I} A _ {\alpha} \equiv \{\omega : \omega \in A _ {\alpha} \text {for every} \alpha \in I \}.
$$

Definition A.1.5: (Complement of a set). Let $A \subset \Omega$ . Then the complement of the set A, written as $A ^ { c } \ ( \mathrm { o r } \ \tilde { A } )$ , is defined by $A ^ { c } \equiv \{ \omega : \omega \notin A \}$ 

Example A.1.8: If $\Omega = \mathbb { N }$ and A is the set of all integers that are divisible by 2, then $A ^ { c }$ is the set of all odd integers, i.e., $A ^ { c } = \{ 1 , 3 , 5 , 7 , \dots \}$ 

Proposition A.1.1: (DeMorgan’s law). For any $\{ A _ { \alpha } : a \in I \}$ of subsets of $\Omega , ( \cup _ { \alpha \in I } A _ { \alpha } ) ^ { c } = \cap _ { \alpha \in I } A _ { \alpha } ^ { c } , ( \cap _ { \alpha \in I } A _ { \alpha } ) ^ { c } = \cup _ { \alpha \in I } A _ { \alpha } ^ { c }$ 

Proof: To show that two sets A and B are the same, it sufices to show that 

$$
\omega \in A \Rightarrow \omega \in B \quad \text { and } \quad \omega \in B \Rightarrow \omega \in A.
$$

Let $\omega \in ( \cup _ { \alpha \in I } A _ { \alpha } ) ^ { c }$ . Then ω $\not \in \cup _ { \alpha \in I } A _ { \alpha }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \Rightarrow & \omega \notin A _ {\alpha} \text {   for   any   } \alpha \in I \\ \Rightarrow & \omega \in A _ {\alpha} ^ {c} \text {   for   each   } \alpha \in I \\ \Rightarrow & \omega \in \bigcap_ {\alpha \in I} A _ {\alpha} ^ {c}. \end{array}
$$

Thus $( \cup _ { \alpha \in I } A _ { \alpha } ) ^ { c } \subset \cap _ { \alpha \in I } A _ { \alpha } ^ { c }$ . The opposite inclusion and the second identity are similarly proved. ✷ 

Definition A.1.6: (Product sets). Let $\Omega _ { 1 }$ and $\Omega _ { 2 }$ be two nonempty sets. Then the product set of $\Omega _ { 1 }$ and $\Omega _ { 2 }$ , denoted by $\Omega \equiv \Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 }$ , consists of all ordered pairs $( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } )$ such that $\omega _ { 1 } \in \Omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } \in \Omega _ { 2 }$ 

Note that if $\Omega _ { 1 } = \Omega _ { 2 }$ and $\omega _ { 1 } \neq \omega _ { 2 }$ , then the pair $( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } )$ is not the same as $( \omega _ { 2 } , \omega _ { 1 } ) , \mathrm { i . e . }$ , the order is important. 

Example A.1.9: $\Omega _ { 1 } = [ 0 , 1 ] , \Omega _ { 2 } = [ 2 , 3 ]$ . Then $\Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } = \{ ( x , y ) : 0 \leq$ $x \leq 1 , \ 2 \leq y \leq 3 \}$ 

Definition A.1.7: (Finite products). If $\Omega _ { i } , i = 1 , 2 \ldots , k$ are nonempty sets, then 

$$
\Omega = \Omega_ {1} \times \Omega_ {2} \times \ldots \times \Omega_ {k}
$$

is the set of all ordered k vectors $\left( \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } , \ldots , \omega _ { k } \right)$ where $\omega _ { i } \in \Omega _ { i } . \mathrm { I f } \Omega _ { i } = \Omega _ { 1 }$ for all $1 \leq i \leq k$ , then $\Omega _ { 1 } \times \Omega _ { 2 } \times . . . \times \Omega _ { k }$ is written as $\Omega _ { 1 } ^ { ( k ) }$ or $\Omega _ { 1 } ^ { k }$ 

Definition A.1.8: (Infinite products). Let $\{ \Omega _ { \alpha } : \alpha \in I \}$ be an infinite collection of nonempty sets. Then $\times _ { \alpha \in I } \Omega _ { \alpha }$ , the product set, is defined as $\{ f : f$ is a function defined on I such that for each α, $f ( \alpha ) \in \Omega _ { \alpha } \}$ . If $\Omega _ { \alpha } = \Omega$ for all $\alpha \in I .$ , then $\times _ { \alpha \in I } \Omega _ { \alpha }$ is also written as $\Omega ^ { I }$ 

It is a basic axiom of set theory, known as the axiom of choice (A.C.), that this space is nonempty. That is, given an arbitrary collection of nonempty sets, it is possible to form a parliament with one representative from each set. 

For a long time it was thought this should follow from the other axioms of set theory. But it is shown in Cohen (1966) that it is an independent axiom. That is, both the A.C. and its negation are consistent with the rest of the axioms of set theory. 

There are several equivalent versions of A.C. These are Zorn’s lemma, Hausdorf’s maximality principle, the ‘Principle of Well Ordering,’ and Tukey’s lemma. For a proof of these equivalences, see Hewitt and Stromberg (1965). 

Definition A.1.9: (Functions, countability and uncountability). A function f is a correspondence between the elements of a set X and another set Y and is written as $f : X \to Y$ . It satisfies the condition that for each x, there is a unique y in Y that corresponds to it and is denoted as 

$$
y = f (x).
$$

The set X is called the domain of f and the set $f ( X )$ , defined as, $f ( X ) \equiv$ $\{ y$ : there exists x in X such that $f ( x ) = y \}$ is called the range of f. It is possible that many $x _ { \mathrm { ~ S ~ } } ^ { \prime }$ may correspond to the same y and also there may exist y in $Y$ for which there is no x such that $f ( x ) = y$ . If f(X) is all of Y, then the map is called onto. If for each y in $f ( X )$ , there is a unique x in X such that $f ( x ) = y$ , then f is called (1–1) or one-to-one. If f is one-to-one and onto, then X and Y are said to have the same cardinality. 

Definition A.1.10: Let $f : X \to Y$ be (1–1) and onto. Then, for each y in Y, there is a unique element x in X such that $f ( x ) = y$ . This x is denoted as $f ^ { - 1 } ( y )$ . Note that in this case, $g ( y ) \equiv f ^ { - 1 } ( y )$ is a (1–1) onto map from Y to X and is called the inverse of f. 

Example A.1.10: Let $X = \mathbb { N } \equiv \{ 1 , 2 , 3 , . . . \}$ . Let $Y = \{ n : n = 2 k , k \in \mathbb { N } \}$ be the set of even integers. Then the map $f ( x ) = 2 x$ is a (1–1) onto map from X to Y. 

Example A.1.11: Let X be N and let P be the set of all prime numbers. Then X and P have the same cardinality. 

Definition A.1.11: A set X is finite if there exists $n \in \mathbb N$ such that X and $Y \equiv \{ 1 , 2 , \dots , n \}$ have the same cardinality, i.e., there exists a (1–1) onto map from Y to X. A set X is countable if X and N have the same cardinality, i.e., there exists a (1–1) onto map from N to X. A set X is uncountable if it is not finite or countable. 

Example A.1.12: The set $\{ 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots , 9 \}$ is finite, the set $\mathbb { N } ^ { k } \ ( k \in \mathbb { N } )$ is countable and $\mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ is uncountable (Problem A.6). 

Definition A.1.12: Let Ω be a nonempty set. Then the power set of Ω, denoted by ${ \mathcal { P } } ( \Omega )$ , is the collection of all subsets of Ω, i.e., 

$$
\mathcal {P} (\Omega) \equiv \{A: A \subset \Omega \}.
$$

Remark A.1.1: (N) is an uncountable set (Problem A.5). 

## A.1.2 The principle of induction

The set N of natural numbers has the well ordering property that every nonempty subset A of N has a smallest element s such that (i) $s \in A$ and (ii) $a \in A \Rightarrow a \geq s$ . This property is one of the basic postulates in the definition of N. The principle of induction is a consequence of the well ordering property. It says the following: 

Let $\{ P ( n ) : n \in \mathbb { N } \}$ be a collection of propositions (or statements). Suppose that 

(i) P(1) is true. 

(ii) For each $n \in \mathbb { N } , P ( n )$ true  P(n + 1) true. 

Then, $P ( n )$ is true for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

See Problem A.9 for some examples. 

## A.1.3 Equivalence relations

Definition A.1.13: 

(a) Let Ω be a nonempty set. Let G be a nonempty subset of $\Omega \times \Omega$ Write $x \sim y \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } ( x , y ) \in G$ and call it a relation defined by G. 

(b) A relation defined by G is an equivalence relation if 

(i) (reflexive) for all x in $\Omega , x \sim x , { \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } } ( x , x ) \in G ;$ 

(ii) (symmetric) $x \sim y \Rightarrow y \sim x , { \mathrm { i . e . , } } \left( x , y \right) \in G \Rightarrow \left( y , x \right) \in G ;$ 

(iii) (transitive) $x \sim y , y \sim z \Rightarrow x \sim z , { \mathrm { i . e . , } } \left( x , y \right) \in G , \left( y , z \right) \in G \Rightarrow$ $( x , z ) \in G .$ 

Example A.1.13: Let $\Omega = \mathbb { Z } .$ , the set of all integers, $G = \{ ( m , n ) : m - n$ is divisible by 3 . Thus, m  n if $( m - n )$ is a multiple of 3. It is easy to verify that this is an equivalence relation. 

Definition A.1.14: (Equivalence classes). Let Ω be a nonempty set. Let G define an equivalence relation on Ω. For each x in Ω, the set $[ x ] \equiv \{ y :$ $x \sim y \}$ is called the equivalence class generated by x. 

Proposition A.1.2: Let be the set of all equivalence classes in Ω generated by an equivalence relation defined by G. Then 

$$
(i) C _ {1}, C _ {2} \in \mathcal {C} \Rightarrow C _ {1} = C _ {2} o r C _ {1} \cap C _ {2} = \emptyset .
$$

(ii) $\bigcup _ { C \in { \mathcal { C } } } C = \Omega .$ 

## Proof:

(i) Suppose $C _ { 1 } \cap C _ { 2 } \neq \emptyset$ . Then there exist $x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 }$ , y such that $C _ { 1 } = [ x _ { 1 } ]$ $C _ { 2 } = [ x _ { 2 } ]$ and $y \in C _ { 1 } \cap C _ { 2 }$ . This implies $x _ { 1 } \sim y , x _ { 2 } \sim y$ . But by symmetry $y \sim x _ { 2 }$ and this implies by transitivity that $x _ { 1 } \sim x _ { 2 } , \mathrm { i . e . }$ $x _ { 2 } \in C _ { 1 }$ implying $C _ { 2 } \subset C _ { 1 }$ . Similarly, $C _ { 1 } \subset C _ { 2 } , { \mathrm { i . e . , } } C _ { 1 } = C _ { 2 }$ 

(ii) For each x in $\Omega , ( x , x ) \in G$ and so [x] is not empty and $x \in [ x ]$ ✷ 

The above proposition says that every equivalence relation on Ω leads to a decomposition of Ω into equivalence classes that are disjoint and whose union is all of Ω. In the example given above, the set Z of all integers can be decomposed to three equivalence classes $\mathcal { C } _ { j } \equiv \{ n : n = 3 m + j$ for some $m \in \mathbb { Z } \} , j = 0 , 1 , 2$ 

## A.2 Real numbers, continuity, diferentiability, and integration

## A.2.1 Real numbers

This section reviews the following: integers, rationals, real numbers; algebraic, order, and completeness axioms; Archimedean property, denseness of rationals. 

There are at least two approaches to defining the real number system. 

Approach 1. Start with the natural numbers N, construct the set Z of all integers $( \mathbb { N } \cup \{ 0 \} \cup ( - \mathbb { N } ) )$ , and next, the set Q of rationals and then the set R of real numbers either as the set of all Cauchy sequences of rationals or as Dedekind cuts. The step going from $\mathbb { Q }$ to R via Cauchy sequences is also available for completing any incomplete metric space (see Section A.4). 

Approach 2. Define the set of real numbers R as a set that satisfies three sets of axioms. The first set is algebraic involving addition and multiplication. The second set is on ordering that, with the first, makes R an ordered field (see Royden (1988) for a definition). The third set is a single axiom known as the completeness axiom. Thus R is defined as a complete ordered field. 

The algebraic axioms say that there are two binary operations known as addition (+) and multiplication ( ) that render R a field. See Royden (1988) for the nine axioms for this set. 

The order axiom says that there is a set $\mathbb { P } \subset \mathbb { R }$ , to be called positive numbers such that 

$$
\text {(i)} x, y \in \mathbb {P} \Rightarrow x \cdot y \in \mathbb {P}, x + y \in \mathbb {P}
$$

(ii) $x \in \mathbb { P } \Rightarrow - x \notin \mathbb { P }$ 

$$
\text {(iii)} x \in \mathbb {R} \Rightarrow x = 0 \text { or } x \in \mathbb {P} \text { or } - x \in \mathbb {P}.
$$

The set Q of rational numbers is an ordered field (i.e., it satisfies the algebraic and order axioms). But Q does not satisfy the completeness axiom (see below). 

Given P, one can define an order on R by defining $x \ < \ y$ (read x less than y) to mean $y - x \in \mathbb { P }$ . Since for all x, y in R, (x  y) is either 0 or $( x - y ) \in \mathbb { P } { \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } } ( y - x ) \in \mathbb { P }$ , it follows that for all x, y in R, either $x = y$ or $x < y \ \mathrm { o r } \ x > y$ . This is called total or linear order. 

Definition A.2.1: (Upper and lower bounds). 

(a) Let $A \subset \mathbb { R }$ . A real number M is an upper bound for A if $a \in A \Rightarrow$ $a \leq M$ and m is a lower bound for A if $a \in A \Rightarrow a \geq m$ 

(b) The supremum of a set A, denoted by sup A or the least upper bound $( l . u . b . )$ of A, is defined by the following conditions: 

(i) x $\langle \in A \Rightarrow x \leq \operatorname* { s u p } A ,$ 

(ii) K < sup A  there exists $x \in A$ such that $K < x$ 

The completeness axiom says that if $A \subset \mathbb { R }$ has an upper bound M in R, then there exists a M<sup>˜</sup> in R such that $\tilde { M } = \operatorname* { s u p } A$ 

That is, every set A that is bounded above in R has a l.u.b. in R. The ordered field of rationals Q does not possess this property. One well-known example is the set 

$$
A = \{r: r \in \mathbb {Q}, r ^ {2} <   2 \}.
$$

Then A is bounded above in $\mathbb { Q }$ but has no l.u.b. in $\mathbb { Q }$ (Problem A.11). 

Next some consequences of the completeness axiom are discussed. 

Proposition A.2.1: (Axiom of Eudoxus and Archimedes (AOE)). For all x in R, there exists a natural number n such that $n > x$ 

Proof: If $x \leq 1$ , take $n = 2 . \operatorname { I f } x > 1$ , let $S _ { x } \equiv \{ k : k \in \mathbb { N } , k \leq x \}$ . Then $S _ { x }$ is not empty and is bounded above. By the completeness axiom, there is a real number y that is the l.u.b. of $S _ { x }$ . Thus $\begin{array} { r } { y - \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ is not an upper bound for $S _ { x }$ and so there exists $k _ { 0 } \in S _ { x }$ such that $y - \textstyle { \frac { \Gamma } { 2 } } < k _ { 0 }$ . This implies that $\begin{array} { r } { ( k _ { 0 } + 1 ) > y - \frac { 1 } { 2 } + 1 = y + \frac { 1 } { 2 } > y } \end{array}$ and so $( k _ { 0 } + 1 ) \ \bar { \not \in } \ S _ { x }$ . By the linear order in R, $( k _ { 0 } + 1 ) \bar { > } x$ and so $( \bar { k } _ { 0 } + 1 )$ is the desired integer. ✷ 

Corollary A.2.2: For any x, $y \in \mathbb { R }$ with $x < y$ , there is $a \textit { r }$ in $\mathbb { Q }$ such that $x < r < y$ 

Proof: Let $z = ( y - x ) ^ { - 1 }$ . Then there is an integer k such that $0 < z < k$ (by AOE.) Again by AOE, there is a positive integer n such that $n > y k .$ Let $S = \{ n : n \in \mathbb { N } , n > y k \}$ . Since $S \neq \emptyset .$ , it has a smallest element (by the well ordering property of N) say, p. Then $\begin{array} { r } { p - 1 < y k < p , \mathrm { i . e . , } \frac { p - 1 } { k } < y < \frac { p } { k } } \end{array}$ Since $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { k } \ < \ \frac { 1 } { z } \ = \ ( y - x ) } \end{array}$ and $\textstyle { \frac { p } { k } } \ > \ y$ , it follows that ${ \frac { p - 1 } { k } } > x$ . Now take $\textstyle r = { \frac { p - 1 } { k } }$ ✷ 

Remark A.2.1: This property is often stated as: The set $\mathbb { Q }$ of rationals is dense in the set R of real numbers. 

Definition A.2.2: The set $\bar { \mathbb { R } }$ of extended real numbers is the set consisting of R and two elements identified as $+ \infty$ (plus infinity) and $- \infty$ (negative infinity) with the following definition of addition (+) and multiplication ( ). For any x in R, $x + \infty = \infty , x - \infty = - \infty , x \cdot \infty = \infty { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } x > 0$ ， $x \cdot \infty \ = \ - \infty { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } x < 0 , 0 \cdot \infty = 0 , \infty + \infty = \infty , - \infty - \infty = - \infty$ $\infty \cdot ( \pm \infty ) = \pm \infty , ( - \infty ) \cdot ( \pm \infty ) = \mp \infty$ . But $\infty - \infty$ is not defined. The order property on R<sup>¯</sup> is defined by extending that on R with the additional condition $x \in \mathbb { R } \Rightarrow - \infty < x < + \infty$ . Finally, if $A \subset \mathbb { R }$ does not have an upper bound in R, then sup A is defined as + and if $A \subset \mathbb { R }$ does not have a lower bound in R, then inf A is defined as . 

## A.2.2 Sequences, series, limits, limsup, liminf

Definition A.2.3: Let $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of real numbers. 

(i) For a real number $a , \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } x _ { n } = a$ if for every $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists a positive integer $N _ { \epsilon }$ such that $n \geq N _ { \epsilon } \Rightarrow | x _ { n } - a | < \epsilon$ 

(ii) lim $x _ { n } = \infty$ if for any K in R, there exists an integer $N _ { K }$ such that n→∞ $n \geq N _ { K } \Rightarrow x _ { n } > K$ 

(iii) $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } x _ { n } = - \infty { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } ( - x _ { n } ) = \infty .$ 

(iv) lim sup n→∞ $x _ { n } \equiv \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } x _ { n } = \operatorname* { i n f } _ { n \geq 1 } ( \operatorname* { s u p } _ { j > n } x _ { j } ) .$ 

(v) $\operatorname* { l i m i n f } _ { n \to \infty } \ x _ { n } \equiv \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } x _ { n } = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n \geq 1 } ( \operatorname* { i n f } _ { j \geq n } x _ { j } ) .$ 

Definition A.2.4: (Cauchy sequences). A sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset \mathbb { R }$ is called a Cauchy sequence if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ , there is $N _ { \varepsilon }$ such that $n , m \geq N _ { \varepsilon } \Rightarrow$ $| x _ { m } - x _ { n } | < \varepsilon$ 

Proposition A.2.3: $I f \{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset \mathbb { R } \ i s$ convergent in $\mathbb { R } \quad ( i . e .$ ， $\quad \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } x _ { n } \ = \ a$ exists in R), then $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } i s$ Cauchy. Conversely, if $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } \subset \mathbb { R }$ is Cauchy, then there exists an $a \in \mathbb { R }$ such that $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } x _ { n } =$ a. 

The proof is based on the use of the l.u.b. axiom (Problem A.14). 

Definition A.2.5: Let $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of real numbers. For $n \geq 1$ $\begin{array} { r } { s _ { n } \equiv \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { j } } \end{array}$ is called the nth partial sum of the series $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } x _ { j }$ . The series $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } x _ { j }$ is said to converge to s in R if $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } s _ { n } = s . \operatorname { I f } \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } s _ { n } = \pm \infty } \end{array}$ then the series $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } x _ { j }$ is said to diverge to $\pm \infty$ 

Note that if $x _ { j } ~ \geq ~ 0$ for all $j$ , then either $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } s _ { n } \ = \ s \in \mathbb { R } } \end{array}$ , or $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } s _ { n } = \infty$ 

Example A.2.1: (Geometric series). Fix $0 < r < 1$ . Let $x _ { n } = r ^ { n } , n \geq 0$ Then $\textstyle s _ { n } = 1 + r + . . . + r ^ { n } = { \frac { 1 - r ^ { n + 1 } } { 1 - r } }$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } r ^ { j }$ converges to $\begin{array} { r } { s = \frac { 1 } { 1 - r } } \end{array}$ 

Example A.2.2: Consider the series $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } { \frac { 1 } { j ^ { p } } } , 0 < p < \infty$ . It can be shown that this converges for $p > 1$ and diverges to for $0 < p \leq 1$ 

Definition A.2.6: The series $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } x _ { j }$ converges absolutely if the series $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } | x _ { j } |$ converges in R. 

There exist series $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } x _ { j }$ that converge but not absolutely. For example, $\textstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } { \frac { ( - 1 ) ^ { j } } { j } }$ . For further material on convergence properties of series, such as tests for convergence, rates of convergence, etc., see Rudin (1976). 

Definition A.2.7: (Power series). Let $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 0 }$ be a sequence of real numbers. For $x \in \mathbb { R }$ , the series $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } a _ { n } x ^ { n }$ is called a power series. If the series $\scriptstyle \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } a _ { n } x ^ { n }$ converges for all x in $B \subset \mathbb { R }$ , the power series $\scriptstyle \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } a _ { n } x ^ { n }$ is said to be convergent on B. 

Proposition A.2.4: Let $\{ a _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 0 }$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $\rho =$ $( \operatorname* { l i m } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n \to \infty } | a _ { n } | ^ { \frac { 1 } { n } } ) ^ { - 1 }$ . Then 

(i) $\begin{array} { r } { \left| x \right| < \rho \Rightarrow \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } \left| a _ { n } x ^ { n } \right| } \end{array}$ converges. 

(ii) $\begin{array} { r } { \left| x \right| > \rho \Rightarrow \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } \left| a _ { n } x ^ { n } \right| } \end{array}$ diverges to $+ \infty$ 

Proof of this is left as an exercise (Problem A.15). 

Definition A.2.8: $\rho \equiv ( \operatorname* { l i m } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n \to \infty } | a _ { n } | ^ { \frac { 1 } { n } } ) ^ { - 1 }$ is called the radius of convergence of the power series $\scriptstyle \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } a _ { n } x ^ { n }$ 

## A.2.3 Continuity and diferentiability

Definition A.2.9: Let $f : A \to \mathbb { R } , A \subset \mathbb { R } .$ . Then 

(a) f is continuous at x<sub>0</sub> in A if for every $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that $x \in A , | x - x _ { 0 } | < \delta$ , implies $| f ( x ) - f ( x _ { 0 } ) | < \epsilon .$ . (Here, δ may depend on  and x<sub>0</sub>.) 

(b) f is continuous on $B \subset A$ if it is continuous at every $x _ { 0 }$ in B. 

(c) f is uniformly continuous on $B \subset A$ if for every $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists a $\delta _ { \epsilon } > 0$ such that sup $\{ | f ( x ) - f ( y ) | : x , y \in B , | x - y | < \delta _ { \epsilon } \} < \epsilon .$ 

Some properties of continuous functions are listed below. 

## Proposition A.2.5:

(i) (Sums, products, and ratios of continuous functions). Let $f , g : A $ $\mathbb { R } , A \subset \mathbb { R }$ . Let f and g be continuous on $B \subset A$ . Then 

(a) f + g, f  g, α  f for any α $\in \mathbb { R }$ are all continuous on B. 

(b) $f ( x ) / g ( x )$ is continuous at x<sub>0</sub> in B, provided $g ( x _ { 0 } ) \neq 0$ 

(ii) (Continuous functions on a closed bounded interval). Let f be continuous on a closed and bounded interval $[ a , b ]$ . Then 

(a) f is bounded, i.e., sup $\{ | f ( x ) | : a \leq x \leq b \} < \infty$ 2 

(b) it achieves its maximum and minimum, i.e., there exist x<sub>0</sub>, y<sub>0</sub> in $[ a , b ]$ such that $f ( x _ { 0 } ) \geq f ( x ) \geq f ( y _ { 0 } )$ for all $\textit { x i n } [ a , b ]$ and f attains all values in $[ f ( y _ { 0 } ) , f ( x _ { 0 } ) ] , i . e .$ , for all $\ell \in [ f ( y _ { 0 } ) , f ( x _ { 0 } ) ]$ 2 there exists $z \in [ a , b ]$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { f ( z ) = \ell } \end{array}$ . Thus, f maps bounded closed intervals onto bounded closed intervals. 

(c) f is uniformly continuous on [a, b].

(iv) (Uniform limits of continuous functions). Let $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ , be a sequence of functions continuous on A to R, $A \subset \mathbb { R }$ . If $\operatorname { s u p } \bar { \{ }  | f _ { n } ( x ) - f ( x ) | ~ ;$ : $x \in A \}  0$ as n for some $f : A \to \mathbb { R } , \ i . e . , \ f _ { n }$ converges to f uniformly on A, then f is continuous on A. 

Remark A.2.2: The function $f ( x ) \equiv x$ is clearly continuous on R. Now by Proposition A.2.5 (i) and (iv), it follows that all polynomials are continuous on R, and hence, so are their uniform limits. Weierstrass’ approximation theorem is a sort of converse to this. That is, every continuous function on a closed and bounded interval is the uniform limit of polynomials. More precisely, one has the following: 

Theorem A.2.6: Let $f : [ a , b ] \to \mathbb { R }$ be continuous. Then for any $\epsilon > 0$ there is a polynomial $\begin{array} { r } { p ( x ) = \sum _ { 0 } ^ { n } a _ { j } x ^ { j } , a _ { j } \in \mathbb { R } , j = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots , n } \end{array}$ such that $\operatorname* { s u p } \{ | f ( x ) - p ( x ) | : x \in [ a , b ] \} < \dot { \epsilon }$ 

It should be noted that a power series $\begin{array} { r } { A ( x ) \equiv \sum _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } a _ { n } x ^ { n } } \end{array}$ is the uniform limits of polynomials on $[ - \lambda , \lambda ]$ for any $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < \lambda < \rho \equiv \big ( \overline { { \operatorname* { l i m } } } _ { n \to \infty } | a _ { n } | ^ { 1 / n } \big ) ^ { - 1 } } \end{array}$ and hence is continuous on $( - \rho , \rho )$ 

Definition A.2.10: Let $f : ( a , b )  \mathbb { R } , ( a , b ) \subset \mathbb { R }$ . The function f is said to be diferentiable at $x _ { 0 } \in ( a , b )$ if 

$$
\lim _ {h \to 0} \frac {f (x _ {0} + h) - f (x _ {0})}{h} \equiv f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) \quad \mathrm{existsin} \quad \mathbb {R}.
$$

A function is diferentiable in $( a , b )$ if it is diferentiable at each x in $( a , b )$ 

Some important consequences of diferentiability are listed below. 

Proposition A.2.7: Let $f , g : ( a , b ) \to \mathbb { R } , ( a , b ) \subset \mathbb { R }$ . Then 

(i) f diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ in $( a , b )$ implies f is continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ . 

(ii) (Mean value theorem). f diferentiable on $( a , b )$ , f continuous on $[ a , b ]$ implies that for some $a < c < b , \ : f ( b ) - f ( a ) = ( b - a ) f ^ { \prime } ( c )$ 

(iii) (Maxima and minima). f diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ and for some $\delta > 0$ $f ( x ) \leq f ( x _ { 0 } )$ for all $x \in ( x _ { 0 } - \delta , x _ { 0 } + \delta )$ implies that $f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = 0$ 

(iv) (Sums, products and ratios). f, g diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ implies that for any α, $\beta$ in R, $( \alpha f + \beta g ) , f - g$ are diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ with 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} (\alpha f + \beta g) ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) & = & \alpha f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) + \beta g ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}), \\ (f g) ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) & = & f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) g (x _ {0}) + f (x _ {0}) g ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}), \end{array}
$$

and if $g ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) \neq 0$ , then f/g is diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ with 

$$
(f / g) ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) = \frac {f ^ {\prime} (x _ {0}) g (x _ {0}) - f (x _ {0}) g ^ {\prime} (x _ {0})}{(g (x _ {0})) ^ {2}}.
$$

(v) (Chain rule). If f is diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ and g is diferentiable at $f ( x _ { 0 } )$ , then $h ( x ) \ \equiv \ g ( f ( x ) )$ is diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ with $h ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) =$ $g ^ { \prime } ( f ( x _ { 0 } ) ) f ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } )$ 

(vi) (Diferentiability of power series). Let $\begin{array} { r } { A ( x ) \equiv \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } { a _ { n } x ^ { n } } } \end{array}$ be a power series with radius of convergence $\rho \equiv ( \overline { { \mathrm { l i m } } } _ { n  \infty } | a _ { n } | ^ { 1 / n } ) ^ { - 1 } > 0$ . Then $A ( \cdot )$ is diferentiable infinitely many times on $( - \rho , \rho )$ and for x in $( - \rho , \rho )$ 2 

$$
\frac {d ^ {k} A (x)}{d x ^ {k}} = \sum_ {n = k} ^ {\infty} n (n - 1) \dots (n - k + 1) x ^ {n - k}, k \geq 1.
$$

Remark A.2.3: It should be noted that the converse to (a) in the above proposition does not hold. For example, the function $f ( x ) = \left| x \right|$ is continuous at $x _ { 0 } = 0$ but is not diferentiable at $x _ { 0 }$ . Indeed, Weierstrass showed that there exists a function $f : [ 0 , 1 ] \to \mathbb { R }$ such that it is continuous on [0, 1] but is not diferentiable at any x in (0, 1). 

Also note that the mean value theorem implies that if $f ^ { \prime } ( \cdot ) \geq 0$ on $( a , b )$ ， then f is nondecreasing on $( a , b )$ 

Definition A.2.11: (Taylor series). Let f be a map from $I \equiv ( a - \eta , a + \eta )$ to R for some $a \in \mathbb { R } , \eta > 0$ . ## A.2.4 Riemann integration

Let $f : [ a , b ] \to \mathbb { R } , [ a , b ] \subset \mathbb { R }$ . Let sup $\{ | f ( x ) | : a \leq x \leq b \} < \infty$ . For any partition $P \equiv \{ a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < x _ { 2 } < x _ { k } = b \}$ , let 

$$
U (P, f) \equiv \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} M _ {i} (P) \Delta_ {i} (P) \text { and }
$$

$$
L (P, f) \equiv \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} m _ {i} (P) \Delta_ {i} (P)
$$

where 

$$
M _ {i} (P) = \sup \{f (x): x _ {i} \leq x \leq x _ {i} \},
$$

$$
m _ {i} (P) = \inf \{f (x): x _ {i - 1} \leq x \leq x _ {i} \},
$$

$$
{\Delta_ {i} (P)} = {(x _ {i} - x _ {i - 1})}
$$

for $i = 1 , 2 , \dots , k .$ 

Definition A.2.12: The upper and lower Riemann integrals of f over [a, b], denoted by ${ \overline { { \int } } } _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x ) d x$ and $\underline { { \int } } _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x ) d x$ , respectively defined as 

$$
\overline {{\int}} _ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x \equiv \inf \{U (P, f): P \text {   a   partition   of   } [ a, b ] \}
$$

$$
\underline {{\int}} _ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x \equiv \sup \{L (P, f): P \text {   a   partition   of   } [ a, b ] \}.
$$

Definition A.2.13: Let $f : [ a , b ] \to \mathbb { R } , [ a , b ] \subset \mathbb { R }$ and let $\operatorname* { s u p } \{ | f ( x ) | : a \leq$ $x \leq b \} < \infty$ . The function f is Riemann integrable on [a, b] if 

$$
\overline {{\int}} _ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x = \underline {{\int}} _ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x
$$

and the common value is denoted as $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x ) d x .$ 

The following are some important results on Riemann integration. 

## Proposition A.2.8:

(i) Let $f : [ a , b ] \to \mathbb { R } , [ a , b ] \subset \mathbb { R }$ be continuous. Then f is Riemann integrable and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x ) d x = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \frac { 1 } { k _ { n } } \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { k _ { n } } f ( x _ { n i } ) \Delta _ { n i } } \end{array}$ where $\{ P _ { n } \equiv$ $\{ x _ { n i } : 1 \leq i \leq k _ { n } \} \}$ is a sequence of partitions of $[ a , b ]$ such that $\Delta _ { n } \equiv \left\{ \operatorname* { m a x } ( x _ { n i } - x _ { n , i - 1 } ) : 1 \leq i \leq k _ { n } \right\} \to 0 \mathrm { ~ } a s \mathrm { ~ } n \to \infty$ 

(ii) If f, g are Riemann integrable on $[ a , b ]$ , then $\alpha f + \beta g , \alpha , \beta \in \mathbb { R }$ and fg are Riemann integrable on $[ a , b ]$ and 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {b} (\alpha f + \beta g) (x) d x = \alpha \int_ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x + \beta \int_ {a} ^ {b} g (x) d x.
$$

(iii) Let f be Riemann integrable on $[ a , b ]$ and $[ b , c ] , - \infty < a < b < c < \infty$ Then f is Riemann integrable on $[ a , c ]$ and 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {c} f (x) d x = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x + \int_ {b} ^ {c} f (x) d x.
$$

(iv) (Fundamental theorem of Riemann integration: Part I). Let f be Riemann integrable on [a, b]. Then it is Riemann integrable on [a, c] for all $a \leq c \leq b$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { F ( x ) } \equiv \int _ { a } ^ { x } f ( u ) d u , a \le x \le b } \end{array}$ . Then 

(a) $F ( \cdot )$ is continuous on $[ a , b ]$ 

(b) $I f f ( \cdot )$ is continuous at $x _ { 0 } \in ( a , b )$ , then $F ( \cdot )$ is diferentiable at x<sub>0</sub> and $F ^ { \prime } ( x _ { 0 } ) = f ( x _ { 0 } )$ 

(v) (Fundamental theorem: Part II). If $F : [ a , b ] \to \mathbb { R }$ is diferentiable on $( a , b ) , f : [ a , b ] \to \mathbb { R }$ is continuous on $[ a , b ]$ and $F ^ { \prime } ( x ) = f ( x )$ for all $a < x < b _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { F ( x ) = F ( a ) + \int _ { a } ^ { c } f ( x ) d x , a \le c \le b } \end{array}$ 

(vi) (Integration by parts). If f and g are continuous and diferentiable on $( a , b )$ with f and $g ^ { \prime }$ continuous on $( a , b )$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {c} ^ {d} f (x) g ^ {\prime} (x) d x + \int_ {c} ^ {d} f ^ {\prime} (x) g (x) d x \\ = f (d) g (d) - f (c) g (c) \quad \text { for   all } \quad a <   c <   d <   b. \end{array}
$$

(vii) (Interchange of limits and integration). Let $f _ { n } , \ f$ be continuous on $[ a , b ]$ to R. Let $f _ { n }$ converge to f uniformly on [a, b]. Then 

$$
F _ {n} (c) \equiv \int_ {a} ^ {c} f _ {n} (x) d x \rightarrow F (c) \equiv \int_ {a} ^ {c} f (x) d x
$$

uniformly on $[ a , b ]$ 

## A.3 Complex numbers, exponential and trigonometric functions

Definition A.3.1: The set C of complex numbers is defined as the set $\mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R }$ of all ordered pairs of real numbers endowed with addition and multiplication as follows: 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} (a _ {1}, b _ {1}) + (a _ {2}, b _ {2}) & = & (a _ {1} + a _ {2}, b _ {1} + b _ {2}) \\ (a _ {1}, b _ {1}) \cdot (a _ {2}, b _ {2}) & = & (a _ {1} a _ {2} - b _ {1} b _ {2}, a _ {1} b _ {2} + a _ {2} b _ {1}). \end{array}\tag{3.1}
$$

It can be verified that C satisfies the field axioms Royden (1988). By defining ι to be the element (0,1), one can write the elements of C in the form $( a , b ) = a + \iota b$ and do addition and multiplication with the rule of replacing $\boldsymbol { \iota } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { b y } - 1$ . Clearly, the set R of real numbers can be identified with the set $\{ ( a , 0 ) : a \in \mathbb { R } \}$ . The set $\{ ( 0 , b ) : b \in \mathbb { R } \}$ is called the set of purely imaginary numbers.

Clearly, $z { \bar { z } } = { \bar { z } } z = | z | ^ { 2 }$ and any $z \neq 0$ can be written as $z ~ = ~ | z | \omega$ where $| \omega | = 1 . \mathrm { ~ A ~ }$ set $A \subset \mathbb { C }$ is bounded if $\operatorname* { s u p } \{ | z | : z \ \in \ A \} \ < \ \infty$ . If $d ( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } ) \equiv | z _ { 1 } - z _ { 2 } |$ , then $( \mathbb { C } , d )$ is a complete separable metric space (see Section $\mathrm { A . 4 } )$ . Clearly, ${ z _ { n } } = ( a _ { n } , b _ { n } )$ converges to $z = ( a , b )$ in this metric if $\mathrm { R e } ( z _ { n } ) = a _ { n } \to \mathrm { R e } ( z ) = a \mathrm { a n d } \mathrm { I m } ( z _ { n } ) = b _ { n } \to \mathrm { I m } ( z ) = b .$ 

Definition A.3.3: The exponential function is a map from C to C defined by 

$$
\exp (z) \equiv \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {z ^ {n}}{n !}\tag{3.3}
$$

where the right side is defined as the limit of the partial sum sequence $\textstyle \{ \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { m } { \frac { z ^ { n } } { n ! } } \} _ { m \geq 0 }$ , which exists since $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } { \frac { | z | ^ { n } } { n ! } } < \infty } \end{array}$ for each $z \in \mathbb { C }$ . In fact,  the convergence of the partial sum sequence is uniform on every bounded subset A of C. This in turn implies that the exponential function is continuous on C. 

Notation: $\exp ( z )$ will also be written as $e ^ { z }$ 

Definition A.3.4: The number $\textstyle e ^ { 1 } \equiv \sum _ { n = 0 } ^ { \infty } { \frac { 1 } { n ! } }$ will be called e. It is not dificult to show that $\begin{array} { r } { e = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } ( 1 + \frac { 1 } { n } ) ^ { \dot { n } } } \end{array}$ . By definition of $e ^ { z } , e ^ { 0 } = 1$ 

Definition A.3.5: The cosine and sine functions from $\mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ are defined by 

$$
\cos t \equiv \mathrm{Re} (e ^ {\iota t}) = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {\infty} (- 1) ^ {k} \frac {t ^ {2 k}}{(2 k) !}
$$

$$
\sin t \equiv \operatorname{Im} (e ^ {\iota t}) = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {\infty} (- 1) ^ {k} \frac {t ^ {2 k + 1}}{(2 k + 1) !}.
$$

Thus, one gets Euler’s formula $e ^ { \iota t } = \cos t + \iota \sin t ,$ for all $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 

The following are some important and useful properties of the exponential and the cosine and sine (also called trigonometric) functions.

Set $\pi = 2 t _ { 0 }$ . Since cos ${ \frac { \pi } { 2 } } \ = \ 0 , \ ( \mathrm { i v } )$ implies sin $\textstyle { \frac { \pi } { 2 } } = 1$ and hence that $e ^ { \iota \frac { \pi } { 2 } } = \iota$ 

(vi) Clearly, $e ^ { \iota { \frac { \pi } { 2 } } } = \iota$ implies that $e ^ { \imath \pi } = - 1$ and $e ^ { \iota 2 \pi } = 1$ and $e ^ { \iota 2 \pi k } = 1$ for all integers k. Since $e ^ { \iota 2 \pi } = 1$ , it follows that $e ^ { z } = e ^ { z + \iota 2 \pi }$ for all $z \in \mathbb { C }$ 2 

It is now possible to prove various results involving π that one learns in calculus from the above definition. For example, that the arc length of the unit circle $\{ z : | z | = 1 \}$ is $2 \pi$ and that $\textstyle \int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } { \frac { 1 } { 1 + x ^ { 2 } } } d x = \pi$ , etc. (Problems A.19 and $\mathrm { A . 2 0 ) }$ 

The following assertions about $e ^ { z }$ can be proved with some more efort. 

Theorem A.3.2: 

(i) $e ^ { z } = 1 \ i f f z = 2 \pi \iota k$ for some integer $k$ . 

(ii) The map $t \to e ^ { \iota t }$ from R is onto the unit circle. 

(iii) For any $\omega \in \mathbb { C } , \omega \neq 0$ there is $a \ z \in \mathbb { C }$ such that $\omega = e ^ { z }$ 

For a proof of this theorem as well as more details on Theorem A.3.1, see Rudin (1987). 

Theorem A.3.3: (Orthogonality of $\{ e ^ { \iota 2 \pi n t } \} _ { n \in \mathbb { Z } } )$ . For any $n \in \mathbb { Z }$ $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } e ^ { \iota 2 \pi n t } d t = 0$ if $n \neq 0$ and 1 if $n = 0$ 

Proof: Since $( e ^ { \iota t } ) ^ { \prime } = \iota e ^ { \iota t }$ 

$$
(e ^ {\iota 2 \pi n t}) ^ {\prime} = \iota 2 \pi n e ^ {\iota 2 \pi n t}, n \in \mathbb {Z}
$$

and so for $n \neq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \int_ {0} ^ {1} e ^ {\iota 2 \pi n t} d t & = & \frac {1}{\iota 2 \pi n} \int_ {0} ^ {1} (e ^ {\iota 2 \pi n t}) ^ {\prime} d t \\ & = & \frac {1}{\iota 2 \pi n} (e ^ {\iota 2 \pi n} - 1) = 0. \end{array}
$$

Corollary A.3.4: The family cos $2 \pi n t : n = 0 , 1 , 2 , . . . \} \cup \{ \sin 2 \pi n t : n =$ $1 , 2 , \ldots \}$ are orthogonal in $L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 1 ]$ (Problem A.22), i.e., for any two f, g in this family, $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } f ( x ) g ( x ) d x = 0 } \end{array}$ for $f \neq g$ 

## A.4 Metric spaces

## A.4.1 Basic definitions

This section reviews the following: metric spaces, Cauchy sequences, completeness, functions, continuity, compactness, convergence of sequences functions, and uniform convergence. 

Definition A.4.1: Let S be a nonempty set. Let $d : \mathbb { S } \times \mathbb { S } \to \mathbb { R } _ { + } = [ 0 , \infty )$ be such that 

(i) $d ( x , y ) = d ( y , x )$ for any x, y in S. 

(ii) $d ( x , z ) \leq d ( x , y ) + d ( y , z )$ for any x, y, z in S. 

(iii) $d ( x , y ) = 0 { \mathrm { ~ i f f ~ } } x = y .$ 

Such a d is called a metric on S and the pair $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ a metric space. Property (ii) is called the triangle inequality. 

Example A.4.1: Let $\mathbb { R } ^ { k } \equiv \left\{ \left( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { k } \right) : x _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } , 1 \leq i \leq k \right\}$ be the k-dimensional Euclidean space. For $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { k } ) , \ y =$ $( y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } , \ldots , y _ { k } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ , let 

$$
d _ {p} (x, y) = \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} | x _ {i} - y _ {i} | ^ {p}\right) ^ {\frac {1}{p}},
$$

and $d _ { \infty } ( x , y ) = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ | x _ { i } - y _ { i } | : 1 \leq i \leq k \}$ 

It can be shown that $d _ { p } ( \cdot , \cdot )$ is a metric on $\mathbb { R }$ for all $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ (Problem A.24). 

Definition A.4.2: A sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ in a metric space $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ converges to an x in S if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ , there is a $N _ { \varepsilon }$ such that $n \geq N _ { \varepsilon } \Rightarrow d ( x _ { n } , x ) < \varepsilon$ and is written as $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } x _ { n } = x$ 

Definition A.4.3: A sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ in a metric space $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ is Cauchy if for all $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists $N _ { \varepsilon }$ such that n, $m \geq N _ { \varepsilon } \Rightarrow d ( x _ { n } , x _ { m } ) < \varepsilon$ 

Definition A.4.4: A metric space $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ is complete if every Cauchy sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converges to some x in S. 

## Example A.4.2:

(a) Let $\mathbb { S } = \mathbb { Q }$ , the set of rationals and $d ( x , y ) \equiv | x - y |$ . Then $( \mathbb { Q } , d )$ is a metric space that is not complete. 

(b) Let $\mathbb { S } = \mathbb { R }$ and $d ( x , y ) = | x - y |$ . Then $( \mathbb { R } , d )$ is complete (cf. Proposition A.2.3). 

(c) Let $\mathbb { S } = \mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ . Then $( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , d _ { p } )$ is complete for every $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , where $d _ { p }$ is as in Example A.4.1. 

Remark A.4.1: (Completion of an incomplete metric space). Let $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ be a metric space. Let $\tilde { \mathbb { S } }$ be the set of all Cauchy sequences in S. Identify each x in S with the Cauchy sequence $\{ x _ { n } = x \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ . Define a function from $\tilde { \mathbb { S } } \times \tilde { \mathbb { S } }$ to $\mathbb { R } _ { + }$ by 

$$
\tilde {d} (\{x _ {n} \} _ {n \geq 1}, \{y _ {n} \} _ {n \geq 1}) = \limsup _ {n \to \infty} d (x _ {n}, y _ {n}).
$$

It is easy to verify that $\tilde { d }$ is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality. Define $s _ { 1 } = \{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $s _ { 2 } = \{ y _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ to be equivalent (write $\left\{ x _ { n } \right\} \sim$ $\left\{ y _ { n } \right\} )$ if $\tilde { d } ( s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } ) = 0$ . Let $\bar { \mathbb S }$ be the set of all equivalence classes in S<sup>˜</sup> and define $\bar { d } ( c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } ) \equiv \tilde { d } ( s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } )$ , where $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 }$ are equivalence classes and $s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 }$ are arbitrary elements of $c _ { 1 }$ and $c _ { 2 }$ , respectively. 

It can now be verified that $( \bar { \mathbb { S } } , \bar { d } )$ is a complete metric space and $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ is embedded in $( \bar { \mathbb { S } } , \bar { d } )$ by identifying each x in S with the equivalence class containing the sequence $\{ x _ { n } = x \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ 

Definition A.4.5: A metric space $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ is separable if there exists a subset $D \subset \mathbb { S }$ that is countable and dense in S, i.e., for each x in S and $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a y in $D$ such that $d ( x , y ) < \varepsilon$ 

Example A.4.3: By the Archimedean property, $\mathbb { Q }$ is dense in R. Similarly $\mathbb { Q } ^ { k }$ , the set of all k vectors with components from Q, is dense in $\mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ 

Definition A.4.6: A metric space (S, d) is called Polish if it is complete and separable. 

Example A.4.4: $( \mathbb { R } ^ { k } , d _ { p } )$ in Example A.4.2 is Polish. 

## A.4.2 Continuous functions

Let $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ and $( \mathbb { T } , \rho )$ be two metric spaces. Let $f : \mathbb { S } \to \mathbb { T }$ be a map from S to T. 

## Definition A.4.7:

(a) f is continuous at p in S if for each $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $d ( x , p ) < \delta \Rightarrow \rho ( f ( x ) , f ( p ) ) < \varepsilon$ . (Here the δ may depend on ε and p.) 

(b) f is continuous on a set $B \subset { \mathbb S } \mathrm { i f }$ it is continuous at every $p \in B$ 

(c) f is uniformly continuous on B if for each $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists $\delta > 0$ such that for each pair $x , y$ in S, $, d ( x , y ) < \delta \Rightarrow \rho ( f ( x ) , f ( y ) ) < \varepsilon .$ 

Definition A.4.8: Let $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ be a metric space. 

(a) A set $O \subset ( { \mathbb S } , d )$ is open if $x \in O \Rightarrow \mathrm { t h e r e }$ exists $\delta > 0$ such that $d ( x , y ) < \delta \Rightarrow y \in O$ . That is, at every point x in O, an open ball $B _ { x } ( \delta ) \equiv \{ y : d ( x , y ) < \delta \}$ of positive radius δ is a subset of O. 

(b) A set $C \subset ( \mathbb { S } , d )$ is closed if $C ^ { c }$ is open. 

Theorem A.4.1: Let $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ and $( \mathbb { T } , \rho )$ be metric spaces. A map $f : \mathbb { S } $ T in continuous on S if for each O open in $\mathbb { T } , f ^ { - 1 } ( O )$ is open in S. 

Proof is left as an exercise (Problem A.28). 

## A.4.3 Compactness

Definition A.4.9: A collection of open sets $\{ O _ { \alpha } : \alpha \in I \}$ is an open cover for a set $B \subset ( \mathbb { S } , d )$ if for each $x \in B$ , there exists $\alpha \in I$ such that $x \in O _ { \alpha }$ 

Example A.4.5: Let $B = ( 0 , 1 )$ . Then the collection $\begin{array} { r } { \small \left\{ \left( \alpha - \frac { \alpha } { 2 } , \alpha + \frac { ( 1 - \alpha ) } { 2 } \right) \right. } \end{array}$ $\alpha \in \mathbb { Q } \cap ( 0 , 1 ) \}$ is an open cover for B. 

Definition A.4.10: Let $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ be a metric space. A set $K \subset \mathbb { S }$ is called compact if given any open cover $\{ O _ { \alpha } : \alpha \in I \}$ for K, there exists a finite subcollection $\{ O _ { \alpha _ { i } } : \alpha _ { i } \in I , i = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n , n < \infty \}$ that is an open cover for K. 

Example A.4.6: The set $B = ( 0 , 1 )$ is not compact as the open cover in the above Example A.3.4 does not admit a finite subcover. 

The next result is the well-known Heine-Borel theorem. 

## Theorem A.4.2:

(i) For any $- \infty < a < b < \infty$ , the closed interval $[ a , b ]$ is compact in R. 

(ii) Any $K \subset \mathbb { R }$ is compact if it is bounded and closed. 

For a proof, see Rudin (1976). From Proposition A.4.1, it is seen that the inverse image of an open set under a continuous function is open but the forward image may not have this property. But the following is true. 

Theorem A.4.3: Let $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ and $( \mathbb { T } , \rho )$ be two metric spaces and let $f : ( \mathbb { S } , d ) \to ( \mathbb { T } , \rho )$ be continuous. Let $K \subset \mathbb { S }$ be compact. Then $f ( K )$ is compact. 

The proof is left as an exercise (Problem A.35). 

## A.4.4 Sequences of functions and uniform convergence

Definition A.4.11: Let $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ and $( \mathbb { T } , \rho )$ be two metric spaces and let $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of functions from $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ to $( \mathbb { T } , \rho )$ . The sequence $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is said to: 

(a) converge pointwise to f on a set $A \subset \mathbb { S } { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } f _ { n } ( x ) = f ( x )$ for each x in A; 

(b) converges uniformly to f on a set $A \subset \mathbb { S } { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } }$ for each $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists $N _ { \varepsilon } > 0$ (depending on ε and A) such that 

$$
n \geq N _ {\varepsilon} \Rightarrow \rho (f _ {n} (x), f (x)) <   \varepsilon \text {   for   all   } x \text {   in   } A.
$$

A consequence of uniform convergence is the preservation of the continuity property. 

Theorem A.4.4: Let $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ and $( \mathbb { T } , \rho )$ be two metric spaces and let $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ be a sequence of functions from $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ to $( \mathbb { T } , \rho )$ . Let for each $n \geq 1$ $f _ { n }$ be continuous on $A \subset \mathbb { S }$ . Let $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converge to f uniformly on A. Then f is continuous on A. 

Proof: The proof is based on the “break up into three parts” idea. By the triangle inequality, 

$$
\rho (f (x), f (y)) \leq \rho (f (x), f _ {n} (x)) + \rho (f _ {n} (x), f _ {n} (y)) + \rho (f _ {n} (y), f (y)).
$$

Fix x in A. By the uniform convergence on A, sup $\{ \rho ( f _ { n } ( u ) , f ( u ) ) : u \in$ $A \}  0$ as $n \to \infty$ . So for each $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists $N _ { \varepsilon } < \infty$ -such that $n \geq$ $N _ { \varepsilon } \Rightarrow \rho \big ( f _ { n } ( u ) , f ( u ) \big ) < \frac { \varepsilon } { 3 }$ for all u in A. Now since $f _ { N _ { \varepsilon } } ( \cdot )$ is continuous on A, there exists a $\delta > 0$ (depending on $N _ { \varepsilon }$ and x), such that $d ( x , y ) < \delta , y \in$ $A \Rightarrow \rho \big ( f _ { N _ { \varepsilon } } ( y ) , f _ { N _ { \varepsilon } } ( x ) \big ) < \frac { \varepsilon } { 3 }$ . Thus, $y \in A , d ( x , y ) < \delta \Rightarrow \rho { \big ( } f ( x ) , f ( y ) { \big ) } <$ $\textstyle { \frac { 2 \varepsilon } { 3 } } + { \frac { \varepsilon } { 3 } } = \varepsilon .$ ✷

Let $d ( \{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } , \{ y _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 } ) =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } \big ( \frac { | x _ { j } - y _ { j } | } { 1 + | x _ { j } - y _ { j } | } \big ) \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { j } } } \end{array}$ . Show that (S, d) is a Polish space. 

A.27 If $s _ { k } = \{ x _ { k n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ and $s = \{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ , are elements of $\mathbb { S } = \mathbb { R } ^ { \infty }$ as in Problem A.26, verify that as $k \to \infty , s _ { k } \to s \mathrm { i f f } x _ { k n } \to x _ { n }$ for all $n \geq 1$ 

A.28 Establish Theorem A.4.1. 

A.29 Let $\mathbb { S } = C [ 0 , 1 ]$ and $\begin{array} { r } { d _ { p } ( f , g ) \equiv \left( \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } | f ( t ) - g ( t ) | ^ { p } d t \right) ^ { \frac { 1 } { p } } } \end{array}$ for $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $d _ { \infty } ( f , g ) = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ | f ( t ) - g ( t ) | : t \in [ 0 , 1 ] \}$ 

(a) Let $f ( x ) \equiv 1$ . Let $f _ { n } ( t ) \equiv 1$ for $0 \leq t \leq 1 - \frac { 1 } { n }$ , and $f _ { n } ( t ) = n ( 1 { - } t )$ for $1 - { \frac { 1 } { n } } \leq t \leq 1$ . Show that $d _ { p } ( f _ { n } , f ) \to ^ { \mathrm { ~ \ " ~ } } 0$ for $1 \leq p < \infty$ but $d _ { \infty } ( f _ { n } , \ddot { f } ) \not \to 0 .$ 

(b) $\operatorname { F i x } f \in C [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { g _ { n } ( t ) = f ( t ) , 0 \le t \le 1 - \frac { 1 } { n } } \end{array}$ , and $g _ { n } ( t ) =$ $\begin{array} { r } { f ( 1 - \frac { 1 } { n } ) + ( f ( 1 ) - f ( 1 - \frac { 1 } { n } ) ) n ( t + \frac { 1 } { n } - 1 ) , 1 - \frac { 1 } { n } \leq t \leq 1 } \end{array}$ 

Show that $d _ { p } ( g _ { n } , f ) \to 0$ for all $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ 

A.30 Show that if $\{ x _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ is a convergent sequence in a metric space $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ 2 then it is Cauchy. 

A.31 Verify (b) of Example A.4.2 from the axioms of real numbers (cf. Proposition A.2.3). Verify (c) of the same example from (b). 

A.32 Let $\mathbb { S } = C [ 0 , 1 ]$ and d be the supremum metric, i.e., 

$$
d (f, g) = \sup \{| f (x) - g (x) |: 0 \leq x \leq 1 \}.
$$

By approximating any continuous function with piecewise linear functions with rational end points and rational values, show that $( \mathbb { S } , d )$ is Polish, i.e., it is complete and separable. 

A.33 Show that the function $f ( x ) = x ^ { 2 }$ is continuous on R, uniformly so on any bounded set $B \subset \mathbb { R }$ but not uniformly on R. 

A.34 Show that unions of open sets are open and intersection of any two open sets is open. Give an example to show that the intersection of an infinite number of open sets need not be open. 

A.35 Prove Theorem A.4.3. 

A.36 Let $f _ { n } ( x ) = x ^ { n }$ and $g ( x ) \equiv 0$ on R. Then $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converges pointwise to g on $( - 1 , 1 )$ , uniformly on $[ a , b ]$ for $- 1 < a < b < 1$ , but not uniformly on (0, 1). 

A.37 Let $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \ge 1 } , \ f \in C [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Let $\{ f _ { n } \} _ { n \geq 1 }$ converge to f uniformly on [0, 1]. Show that lim $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } | f _ { n } ( x ) - f ( x ) | d x = 0 } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r l r } {  { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } f _ { n } ( x ) = } } \end{array}$ n→∞ $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } f ( x ) d x } \end{array}$
